High‐Performance 2D MXene‐Derived TiO
                    <sub>2</sub>
                    Integrated Optical Polarizers
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Polarization control is essential for modern optical systems. Recently, 2D materials featuring highly anisotropic absorption across broad wavelength regions have emerged as a promising solution for realizing optical polarizers with operation bandwidths far exceeding those achievable using bulk materials. Despite this, existing 2D‐material‐based optical polarizers face critical limitations in simultaneously delivering high polarizer figures of merit (FOMs), robust power endurance, and scalable fabrication, hindering their practical deployment beyond the laboratory. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by demonstrating optical polarizers through integrating 2D MXene films onto silicon photonic devices and subsequently converting them in situ into 2D titanium dioxide (TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ). The 2D TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    exhibits significantly improved anisotropic absorption and thermal/chemical stability compared with MXene, enabling the hybrid polarizers that achieve high polarizer FOMs of up to ∼19.3 (a record among 2D‐material‐coated devices) and excellent power tolerance (stable under > 2 W coupled average power), together with a broad operation bandwidth (> 140 nm) and a high fabrication yield (∼98%). We also demonstrate microring resonator polarizers achieving high polarization extinction ratios of up to ∼12 dB. With outstanding overall performance and strong potential for large‐scale manufacturing, these devices represent a solid step toward industrial implementation of 2D‐material‐based optical polarizers.
                  </jats:p>

title: Laser-Scattering-Image-Based Intelligent Sensing for Dust Concentration Prediction in Top-Blown Furnace Applications with ICPO-CKGPR
abstract: <jats:p>Top-blown furnaces are important equipment in non-ferrous metal smelting processes, where dust concentration variations provide useful information for process monitoring and environmental management. However, conventional dust measurement methods may suffer from limited measurement efficiency and insufficient adaptability under complex operating conditions. To address these challenges, this study proposes a laser-scattering-image-based intelligent sensing framework with an improved crested porcupine optimizer-based combined-kernel Gaussian process regression model, termed ICPO-CKGPR, for dust concentration prediction under simulated top-blown furnace conditions. First, a laboratory-scale laser scattering image acquisition platform was established to collect scattering images under different dust concentration conditions, and 5000 timestamp-matched image–concentration sample pairs were obtained using a particulate matter sensor as the reference measurement source. Subsequently, a multi-domain feature representation strategy integrating grayscale-domain, frequency-domain, and spatial-domain information was developed to enhance the characterization capability of dust scattering images under multi-scale variations and disturbances. Furthermore, a combined-kernel Gaussian process regression model consisting of radial basis function, Matérn, and rational quadratic kernels was constructed to improve the modeling capability for complex nonlinear dust concentration variations. Meanwhile, the crested porcupine optimizer was improved by incorporating good-point-set initialization and periodic oscillation mutation strategies for adaptive hyperparameter optimization. Experimental results on the independent test set demonstrate that the proposed ICPO-CKGPR model achieves an RMSE of 3.086 mg/m3, an MAE of 1.784 mg/m3, and an R2 of 0.992 against the sensor-derived reference measurements. Compared with the benchmark models, the proposed method shows closer agreement with the sensor-derived PM10 reference measurements, indicating its potential for laser-scattering-image-based PM10 estimation under the investigated laboratory conditions.</jats:p>

title: Effect of Laser Remelting on the Microstructure, Mechanical and Tribological Properties of Detonation-Sprayed NiCrFeBSiC Coatings for Mechanical Engineering Applications
journal: Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing
abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates the effect of laser remelting on the microstructure, phase composition, mechanical properties, tribological behavior, and corrosion resistance of self-fluxing NiCrFeBSiC coatings deposited onto AISI 321 stainless steel by detonation spraying. The coatings were characterized before and after laser treatment using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), instrumented indentation, adhesion testing, ball-on-disk tribometry, and potentiodynamic polarization measurements. SEM analysis revealed that laser remelting reduced coating porosity from 0.306 ± 0.014% to 0.15 ± 0.09%, accompanied by microstructural densification and a reduction in coating thickness. XRD analysis confirmed the preservation of the principal crystalline phases, including Ni3Fe, Cr7C3, CrB, and Ni3B, following laser treatment. The Vickers hardness increased from 1049.1 ± 43.4 to 1206.1 ± 63.1 HV, while the elastic modulus increased from 233.6 ± 6.2 to 258.4 ± 5.3 GPa. Furthermore, adhesion strength increased by 19.4%, whereas surface roughness decreased by 19.2%. Laser remelting significantly improved tribological performance, reducing the average coefficient of friction from 0.535 ± 0.048 to 0.409 ± 0.086 and the specific wear rate from 2.864 × 10−4 to 1.447 × 10−4 mm3/(N·m), corresponding to a 49.5% reduction in wear. Electrochemical measurements indicated a modest decrease in corrosion current density of approximately 3.0%, accompanied by changes in the morphology of corrosion-affected regions. The improvements are associated with laser-induced microstructural densification, redistribution of alloying elements, and preservation of hard reinforcing phases. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining detonation spraying with laser remelting to produce wear-resistant nickel-based protective coatings for mechanical and power engineering applications.</jats:p>

title: Plasma Immersion Ion Implantation of AISI 316L Stainless Steel Parts Manufactured by Laser Powder Bed Fusion
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Austenitic stainless steel (SS) AISI 316L is highly compatible with laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), an advanced additive manufacturing (AM) technique for producing high-quality near-net-shape parts with complex geometries, especially for aerospace and medical applications. To further enhance its surface properties, temperature-controlled nitrogen plasma immersion ion implantation (TC-NPIII) was applied to LPBF-manufactured AISI 316L to obtain an expanded austenite (
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    N) layer, thereby enhancing surface performance and expanding the applicability of this material in demanding environments. The present work investigates the influence of TC-NPIII treatment temperature and duration on the microstructural evolution and mechanical performance of LPBF-manufactured AISI 316L. Samples were produced by LPBF in a laser-adapted powder bed system and subsequently treated by TC-NPIII, varying treatment duration for 1 and 3 h at controlled temperatures (450-520 °C). Microstructural analysis after treatment revealed a modified layer with a thickness that ranged from approximately 18.30 to 28.40 µm, superimposed on the characteristic LPBF microstructure. Grazing Incidence x-ray Diffraction (GI-XRD) analysis confirmed the formation of the desired
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    N phase, while no diffraction peaks associated with chromium nitrides were detected within the investigated processing window. Cross-sectional nanoindentation measurements of the treated samples yielded hardness values of approximately 386-751 HV, representing a substantial increase compared with the untreated LPBF sample (238 HV). These results indicate that, among the treatment temperatures and durations investigated, 450 °C for 3 h represents the optimal processing condition, promoting
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    N formation while preventing chromium nitride precipitation. The present work demonstrates that TC-NPIII can effectively produce expanded austenite and achieve significant surface hardening within treatment durations as short as 1-3 h. Moreover, these findings confirm the effectiveness of the TC-NPIII treatment in modifying the surface of LPBF-produced AISI 316L stainless steel, thereby enhancing its mechanical performance while preserving the characteristic hierarchical microstructure generated during LPBF.
                  </jats:p>

title: ESCRT-III assembly restores membrane tension in micron-scale plasma membrane repair
abstract: <jats:p>Plasma membrane integrity is essential for cellular survival, yet how cells repair micron-scale plasma membrane ruptures remains poorly understood. Here, using the genetically tractable Caenorhabditis elegans epidermis, we combine live imaging, genetics, super-resolution microscopy, and biophysical approaches to define a size-dependent role for endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT)-III in large-scale membrane repair. Small wounds induce transient, focal VPS-32 accumulation, whereas large wounds trigger the formation of a persistent but dynamic, circumferential ESCRT-III assembly that remains associated with the wound during repair. Formation of this assembly requires conserved ESCRT regulators, including ALX-1, TSG-101, and VPS-4, together with VPS-32 polymerization. The wound-associated ESCRT-III assembly is required for membrane tension restoration and efficient membrane repair, while disrupting VPS-32 polymerization impairs tension recovery, reduces vesicle recruitment and wound closure, and consequently compromises axon regeneration and organismal survival following injury. Together, our findings suggest that large plasma membrane wounds induce a persistent, dynamic ESCRT-III assembly that restores membrane tension and facilitates vesicle-mediated membrane addition to promote wound repair.</jats:p>

title: Reliability and Agreement of Infrared Thermography and a Digital Laser Thermometer for Non-Invasive Body Temperature Assessment in Sows
abstract: <jats:p>Early detection of heat stress in intensive pig production is critical for maintaining animal welfare and production efficiency; however, routine rectal thermometry is labor-intensive and impractical under farm conditions. This study aimed to evaluate the reliability and agreement of non-contact temperature measurement methods—digital laser thermometry and infrared thermography (IRT)—against rectal core temperature on a commercial farm. Measurements were performed at multiple anatomical sites (ear, flank, labial, and rectal surface regions), and data were analyzed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Bland–Altman methods. Traditional handheld infrared measurements showed poor reliability (ICC: 0.09–0.27) and substantially underestimated core temperature (−1.16 to −2.27 °C), with wide limits of agreement. In contrast, IRT demonstrated higher but imprecisely estimated reliability (ICC: 0.56–0.67; labial region: 95% CI 0.19–0.76; rectal region: 95% CI 0.41–0.82), lower bias (−0.37 to −0.59 °C), and narrower agreement intervals. However, significant proportional bias (p < 0.001) indicated temperature-dependent deviations between methods. Closer agreement with rectal temperature was observed for infrared thermography than for handheld infrared thermometry, particularly at the labial and perianal measurement sites.</jats:p>

Explainable AI-based framework for 3D structural as-built modeling of aging buildings in Korea using laser scanning
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study proposes a framework for automatically generating 3D structural as-built models of aging buildings by predicting the structural dimensions of members concealed behind finishes using laser scanning and machine learning, particularly when original construction drawings are unavailable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Laser scanning captures building geometry but includes both structural components and non-structural finishes (e.g. plaster), making it unsuitable for directly extracting structural dimensions. To address this, the proposed framework extracts geometric features from point clouds and employs machine learning techniques to predict structural dimensions of columns, beams, walls and slabs. Six machine learning models – Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Linear Regression and Support Vector Regression (SVR) – were trained using data collected on 1,560 column elements, 2,875 beam elements, 870 wall elements and 148 slab elements across 50 buildings and validated through two real-world case studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The best-performing model achieved MAPE of 10.51% for column width (95%CI: 8.47–12.71), 12.98% for column depth (95% CI: 10.86–15.41), 14.91% for beam width (95% CI: 13.63–16.15), 18.91% for beam depth (95% CI: 17.94–19.90), 10.42% for walls (95% CI: 8.89–12.00) and 10.70% for slabs (95% CI: 7.11–14.50). The predicted dimensions enabled reconstruction of 3D structural as-built models without relying on original drawings; the estimates are intended for planning-stage use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework provides a non-destructive, full-coverage estimate of structural member dimensions that would otherwise require original drawings or local removal of finishes. In practice, it is intended to reduce reliance on destructive investigation and, through the SHAP analysis, indicates where confirmatory openings could be prioritized, thereby supporting planning-stage decisions for the maintenance and retrofitting of buildings whose drawings are missing or outdated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study is among the first to formulate the discrepancy between laser-scanned surface geometry and concealed structural dimensions as a prediction problem and to propose a framework that returns the predicted dimensions to a 3D structural as-built model. Machine learning provides the enabling component, and explainability is used to direct in situ verification rather than as a methodological contribution in itself.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

This study investigates the impact of laser processing on the microstructure and corrosion resistance of Ti-35Nb alloys containing 0, 2, and 4 wt.% Sn.                     <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>

title:
Monolithically
Integrated Laser Chip for Interrogation
of Large-Capacity Weak Fiber Bragg Grating (WFBG) Arrays
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We report a monolithically integrated distributed feedback multiwavelength laser array (DFB-MLA) photonic chip for large capacity interrogation of weak fiber Bragg grating (WFBG) arrays. The chip integrates multiwavelength generation, optical power combining, power equalization, and pulse gating on a single InP platform. Based on the reconstruction-equivalent-chirp (REC) technique, the 8 × 3 laser array exhibits an adjacent-channel wavelength spacing of approximately 2.5 nm and a total tuning range of 60 nm. In the photonic chip, the outputs of different channels are combined through an on-chip three-stage Y-branch combiner and subsequently pass through two functionally separated semiconductor optical amplifiers (SOAs). The power-equalization SOA (PE-SOA) compensates for wavelength-dependent power variations, reducing the interchannel power variation from approximately 10 to 0.3 dB. The pulse-gating SOA (PG-SOA) converts the continuous wavelength-swept output into optical pulses for time-domain addressing. Based on a time- and wavelength-division multiplexing (TWDM) scheme, the chip-based demodulation system successfully demodulated 100 WFBGs with a spatial interval of 0.2 m between adjacent gratings. These results demonstrate the potential of the integrated photonic source for compact, large-capacity optical fiber sensing systems.</jats:p>

title: Passive imaging with quantum advantage
abstract: <jats:p>Far-field optical imaging inevitably involves low-pass spatial filtering, limiting the resolution. Moreover, conventional imaging suppresses high spatial frequency components close to the cutoff, making them invisible under noise—particularly the shot noise arising from discrete and random nature of quantum light. Here, we propose and implement a method for reducing the effect of this noise by optically preprocessing the incoming light before detection, thereby optimizing the quantum measurement performed on it. Our scheme, termed Fourier domain division (FDD), partitions the Fourier plane into multiple regions for independent detection and subsequent post-processing for image reconstruction. By analyzing the quantum and classical Fisher information, we show that our method is advantageous with respect to direct imaging for high spatial-frequency components. As a result, the number of photons required to achieve a certain signal-to-noise ratio in the Fourier domain is reduced, thus enhancing the overall resolution in the photon-starved regime. We demonstrate our method in microscopy, achieving fivefold improvement of Fisher information on high spatial frequency components. Unlike active super-resolution methods, FDD is passive, making it broadly applicable in microscopy and other imaging scenarios, where active illumination is impractical, including astronomy and remote sensing, in the photon-starved regime. Our work establishes a general strategy for designing quantum optimized superresolution imaging systems, bridging fundamental quantum limits, practical image analysis, and computer vision applications.</jats:p>

title: Excimer Laser Coronary Atherectomy (ELCA) Utilization in Complex PCI: A Position Paper of the Italian Society of Interventional Cardiology (SICI‐GISE)
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Excimer laser coronary atherectomy (ELCA) has significantly influenced interventional cardiology, particularly in complex percutaneous coronary interventions (PCIs). This expert review by the Italian Society of Interventional Cardiology (SICI‐GISE) provides a comprehensive overview of ELCA's applications, mechanisms of action, and clinical significance. ELCA uses ultraviolet (UV) energy to modify atheromatous plaque while minimizing damage to surrounding tissue. Its photochemical, photothermal, and photokinetic mechanisms enable effective plaque removal and improved clinical outcomes. The review traces the evolution of ELCA technology, including advances in laser catheters and techniques for diverse clinical and anatomical scenarios. It also discusses ELCA's clinical applications for conditions such as in‐stent restenosis, underexpanded stents, thrombotic lesions, and calcified plaques. The review further examines the histopathological effects of ELCA on vascular tissues, emphasizing its precision and minimal collateral damage. Data from multiple studies demonstrate ELCA's effectiveness and safety in complex PCI, with high success rates and acceptable complication rates. The review emphasizes the importance of careful patient selection, appropriate laser settings, and adjunctive therapies to achieve optimal results. Overall, ELCA is a valuable tool for interventional cardiologists, offering a versatile and practical approach to managing challenging coronary lesions.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Laser-based visible-light communication (VLC) can exploit wavelength and polarization multiplexing, but amplifier, channel, and coherent-receiver impairments interact. This paper develops an impairment-aware simulation of an eight-wavelength, dual-circular-polarization link carrying a 380.16-MHz occupied orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) resource grid within a nominal 400-MHz fifth-generation New Radio (5G NR)-aligned channel. The model includes laser-diode/semiconductor-optical-amplifier (LD–SOA) saturation and amplified spontaneous emission, wavelength-dependent gain ripple, Lambertian line-of-sight loss, residual wavelength-division-multiplexing (WDM) crosstalk, polarization mixing, coherent-receiver noise, phase/frequency offsets, and quadrature imbalance. The receiver combines covariance whitening, pilot-estimated 2 × 2 regularized multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) separation, pilot-assisted phase correction, and damped decision-directed refinement. With quadrature phase-shift keying, the nominal net payload rate after applying a 7 % FEC-overhead factor for rate reporting is 8.527 Gb/s. In the controlled reference realization, the proposed receiver remains below the 3.8 × 10
                    <jats:sup>−3</jats:sup>
                    pre-FEC bit-error-rate screening level through 50 m. A receiver ablation shows that both Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization and symmetric covariance whitening remove most of the reference I/Q-imbalance penalty, while the decision-directed update provides a smaller incremental improvement near the reach boundary. A separate sweep gives 17.054 Gb/s with 16-level quadrature-amplitude modulation through 16 m. The results provide a traceable baseline for joint optical-front-end and coherent-receiver design.
                  </jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This
                    <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                    study evaluated whether non-thermal argon plasma could improve the wettability of Grade 5 titanium alloy (Ti–6Al–4V) surfaces without producing detectable changes in elemental composition. Ninety commercially sourced Ti–6Al–4V discs were allocated to one of three surface conditions: machined, nitric acid-treated, or hydrochloric acid-treated. For wettability analysis, each surface condition was evaluated either without plasma treatment or after 60 s of non-thermal argon plasma exposure at 22 °C, with 13 independent discs per subgroup. Water contact angle was measured using the sessile-drop method, and the mean of the left and right contact angles was used as the specimen-level outcome. Surface morphology and elemental composition were evaluated qualitatively by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDX) before plasma exposure and immediately and at 30 and 60 min after treatment. Argon plasma significantly reduced the water contact angle in all surface groups (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                    < 0.0001), indicating a marked increase in wettability. Mean contact angle decreased from 162.6° to 32.74° on machined surfaces, from 150.5° to 12.96° on nitric acid-treated surfaces, and from 110.0° to 21.87° on hydrochloric acid-treated surfaces. Plasma-treated acid-conditioned surfaces exhibited lower contact angles than plasma-treated machined surfaces. SEM indicated that plasma exposure made pre-existing topographic features more visually distinct, particularly on acid-treated surfaces, whereas EDX revealed no appreciable changes in elemental composition. These findings support non-thermal argon plasma as a short-term surface-activation strategy for Ti–6Al–4V biomaterials; however, the durability and biological relevance of this effect require further investigation.
                  </jats:p>

title: Atomic density optimization of quasi-one-dimensional diffuse laser cooling under a two-dimensional magnetic-field gradient
abstract: <jats:p>Diffuse laser cooling (DLC) provides a compact, robust, and scalable approach to generating cold-atom ensembles, offering significant potential for ground-based and spaceborne microwave atomic clocks. However, the performance of DLC systems remains limited by the weak atom-light interaction arising from their relatively low atomic density. This limitation is characterized by the optical density (OD), which quantifies the effective interaction strength between the atomic ensemble and the probe light and strongly influences the achievable signal-to-noise ratio. Although quasi-one-dimensional (quasi-1D) DLC extends the probe interaction length and improves atomic utilization, increasing the local atomic density within the interrogation region remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a magnetically enhanced quasi-1D DLC system that simultaneously maintains the extended interaction length and increases the atomic density through a two-dimensional magnetic-field gradient. By spatially compressing and accumulating atoms near the probe axis, we enhance the OD of a 70-cm-long cold rubidium ensemble from 2.49 to 3.94, representing a 58% enhancement and an equivalent increase in the local atomic density. The dependence of the OD on the magnetic-field gradient, probe intensity, beam size, and cooling-light polarization is systematically investigated. This work establishes a practical pathway for enhancing optical interrogation efficiency and could pave the way for the development of high-performance DLC-based cold-atom clocks and quantum sensing systems.</jats:p>

title: Platelet-rich plasma in tendinopathies: Current evidence and limits of indication
abstract: <jats:p>Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been proposed as a biologic treatment for symptomatic tendinopathy, yet its clinical use has expanded faster than evidence of an additional benefit over adequately controlled care. This critical narrative review examines the comparative effectiveness of PRP, identifies sources of disagreement between trials, and defines defensible limits to its indication across major tendon sites. Relevant randomized studies, systematic reviews, and clinical practice guidelines were examined through PubMed-indexed literature, Cochrane publications, and professional society sources available up to 2026. For chronic midportion Achilles tendinopathy, larger sham-controlled studies and an updated meta-analysis do not demonstrate clinically important improvements. Similarly, placebo-controlled findings for lateral elbow and patellar tendinopathy do not justify routine use. Rotator cuff recommendations discourage PRP as a first-line strategy or routine injection, despite some positive small trials. A potentially favorable signal in gluteal tendinopathy derives largely from comparisons with corticosteroid, not sham treatment, and must be interpreted alongside evidence supporting education and exercise. Preparation variability, co-interventions, limited long-term safety reporting, and weak identification of responders restrict generalizability. PRP remains a selective, preference-sensitive option in narrowly defined circumstances, not a substitute for progressive loading or a validated method of tendon regeneration.</jats:p>

title: A simple model for evaporation-driven migration of liquid metal between plasma pulses in a fusion reactor with liquid metal plasma-facing components
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Liquid metal plasma-facing components (PFCs) are being considered for a variety of fusion power plant designs, and careful control of the liquid metal inventory will be essential in these systems to mitigate challenges with liquid metal corrosion and hydrogen fuel retention. Since many power plant designs and existing test facilities rely on pulsed plasma sources, it is critical to understand how liquid metal evaporation leads to material migration within a reactor over the periods of time when no plasma is present. This work addresses this question by developing a simple particle balance model to efficiently calculate liquid metal vapor transport patterns over indefinitely long time periods, using a particle redistribution matrix to capture the vapor transport details. After developing the mathematical model, characteristics of a future Liquid Metal Core-Edge (LMCE) research facility with liquid lithium divertors are used as a reference to demonstrate how the particle balance model can be used. Examples of lithium migration during the cooldown period between plasma pulses show that the pattern of lithium deposition depends primarily on the system geometry. An important secondary effect in these scenarios is the relative cooldown rate of the lithium divertor with respect to other PFCs in the device. Examples are also provided to demonstrate how the particle balance model can be used to optimize the design of a cold finger to collect liquid metal condensation for extraction and reprocessing, with the results showing that a future LMCE facility may be capable of collecting all of the lithium evaporated between plasma pulses if the main chamber walls can be maintained above 350 C during operation.</jats:p>

Saha ionization equation in its new perspective: An astrochemical equilibrium and plasma chemistry framework
journal: International Journal of Modern Physics D
abstract: <jats:p>The Saha ionization equation, originally formulated within the framework of stellar astrophysics, is reinterpreted in this work as a high-temperature extension of classical chemical equilibrium theory. Ionization is treated as a reversible chemical reaction whose equilibrium state is governed by temperature, electron pressure, and the thermodynamic properties of the participating species. By employing the formalism of Gibbs free energy, equilibrium constants, and molecular partition functions, we demonstrate that the Saha relation is mathematically equivalent to the canonical expression [Formula: see text] used in physical chemistry. Building on this equivalence, we introduce a quantitative Van’t Hoff-style analysis of the Saha equilibrium, showing that the characteristic curvature of [Formula: see text] versus [Formula: see text] is a direct, measurable signature of the translational entropy carried by the liberated electron. Worked numerical examples for hydrogen and calcium connect this thermodynamic treatment directly to the Balmer-line maximum in A-type stars and the Ca II H&K lines of solar-type stars. The electron number density is identified as a chemical control parameter analogous to pressure in Le Chatelier’s principle. The implications of this framework are discussed in the context of astrochemistry: ionization balance governs spectral classification across the Harvard O–M sequence, structures the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram as a plasma-chemical phase space, and determines astrochemical reaction pathways in diffuse interstellar clouds and cold molecular cloud environments. This work establishes a quantitative, chemistry-first conceptual bridge between laboratory plasma chemistry and astrophysical stellar behavior.</jats:p>

title: PLASMA RICO EN PLAQUETAS ACTIVADO COMO ADYUVANTE A LA DILATACIÓN ENDOSCÓPICA EN ESTENOSIS ESOFÁGICAS BENIGNAS
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Introducción:</jats:bold>
                    Las estenosis esofágicas benignas pueden recurrir tras la dilatación endoscópica por inflamación y remodelación fibrótica, condicionando nuevas sesiones. El plasma rico en plaquetas (PRP) aporta mediadores de reparación tisular y podría modular la cicatrización esofágica.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Objetivos:</jats:bold>
                    Describir factibilidad técnica, eventos adversos y evolución clínica y endoscópica tras dilatación con Savary-Gilliard sobre guía Savary e infiltración submucosa de PRP autólogo activado con gluconato de calcio al 10%.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Métodos:</jats:bold>
                    Estudio observacional retrospectivo, descriptivo y unicéntrico de cinco adultos con estenosis benignas: tres pépticas, una cáustica y una postquirúrgica por ascenso gástrico secundario a estenosis cáustica. La dilatación se realizó con Savary-Gilliard sobre guía Savary. El PRP se obtuvo de 20 mL de sangre citratada mediante doble centrifugación (1500 rpm/8 min y 2500 rpm/5 min); se recuperaron 8 mL, activados con 0,20 mL de gluconato de calcio al 10% e infiltrados submucosamente en cuatro cuadrantes post dialtacion. Se evaluaron disfagia (Mellow-Pinkas), número de dilataciones, cicatrización endoscópica a 8 semanas despues de la última sesión, recurrencia y eventos adversos mediante análisis descriptivo.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Resultados:</jats:bold>
                    Tres mujeres y dos hombres; edad media 43 años (22–63). El diámetro inicial fue 8–10 mm en cuatro pacientes y 2 mm en uno. La mediana de disfagia disminuyó de 3 (2–4) a 0; todos alcanzaron Mellow-Pinkas 0. Tres pacientes requirieron dos sesiones, uno tres y el caso de 2 mm, ocho. A las 8 semanas hubo cicatrización mucosa adecuada en 5/5 y no se observaron perforación, sangrado significativo ni otros eventos adversos relacionados. El seguimiento mediano fue 70 semanas (35–144); dos pacientes presentaron recurrencia tardía de disfagia a las 70 y 72 semanas.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Conclusión:</jats:bold>
                    La dilatación con Savary-Gilliard sobre guía Savary seguida de PRP activado fue factible y no presentó eventos adversos relacionados. La mejoría clínica, la cicatrización endoscópica y las recurrencias tardías respaldan estudios prospectivos controlados para determinar eficacia.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Palabras clave:</jats:bold>
                    Estenosis Esofágica; Endoscopía Gastrointestinal; Plasma Rico en Plaquetas; Trastornos de Deglución.
                  </jats:p>

title: Study of Microstructure and Fatigue Behavior of Laser Melting Forging Repair Layers for Surface Cracks in X80 High-Strength Pipelines
abstract: <jats:p>This study adopted laser melting forging (LMF) technology to repair surface cracks on X80 high-strength steel pipes. LMF technology combines laser cladding (LC) with in situ laser shock peening (LSP), achieving strengthening and material forming simultaneously. This study innovatively utilized a galvanometer to adjust the size of laser shock spots and the high-frequency scanning path, achieving high-efficiency strengthening along the specific isothermal zone around the molten pool. By adjusting technological parameters, a high-density microstructure can be achieved. When the edge of the molten pool is impacted, microdefects (such as pores) can be noticeably reduced, and the grain size can also be significantly refined. This is mainly attributed to the fact that the high-frequency forging induces flow in the molten pool, promoting the escape of bubbles and causing the breakup of dendritic crystals. Compared with LC repair layers, the microhardness of the LMF repair layer increased by 10%, and its residual compressive stress increased by 62.6%. These improvements enhanced the resistance to crack propagation, and the average fatigue life was extended by more than 100% under a stress of 700 MPa ultimately. Meanwhile, fracture morphologies indicate that LMF significantly reduced fatigue sources such as microdefects. A finer-grained microstructure increases resistance to crack propagation. The research provides a systematic explanation of the mechanism and technical support for the application of LMF technology in remanufacturing engineering.</jats:p>

title: Analyses of plasma protein levels in relation to body composition in the UK Biobank
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Excess fat mass is causally linked to multiple diseases, but the use of existing therapies, such as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, is limited by varying effects and common side effects, including loss of fat-free mass. We aimed to identify proteins associated with fat mass, but ideally not also associated with fat-free mass, as potential drug targets for alternative therapeutic strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We used UK Biobank data on plasma levels of 3K proteins (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 35K) and fat and fat-free mass (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 368K). We applied a machine learning procedure to select proteins for downstream
                      <jats:italic>cis</jats:italic>
                      Mendelian randomisation analyses, which estimated associations of genetically predicted protein levels with fat mass. These were followed by colocalisation analyses to assess shared causal genetic variants and further
                      <jats:italic>cis</jats:italic>
                      Mendelian randomisation analyses to assess associations with fat-free mass.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Here we present evidence on the associations of genetically predicted levels of 21 proteins with fat mass, including five which also colocalise with the trait (AGER, CRIM1, DNER, NEFL, and PRRT3). Seven of the 21 proteins have no clear association with fat-free mass, and ADM has an association with fat-free mass opposite in direction to its association with fat mass, suggesting that modulating these proteins may be less likely to also lower fat-free mass. Two proteins, AGER and ADM, have been investigated in advanced-stage clinical trials for indications unrelated to adiposity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings support prioritising several proteins for further research as potential drug targets for fat mass reduction. They highlight proteins that may help diversify therapy options beyond glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and suggest possible repurposing opportunities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Coaxial Monitoring of Meltpool for Laser Powder Bed Fusion Process Control
journal: Strojniški vestnik - Journal of Mechanical Engineering
abstract: <jats:p>Reliable process monitoring is critical for advancing laser powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), as it provides the process information required for corrective control actions to prevent defects such as lack-of-fusion and keyhole porosity. A promising approach for PBF-LB/M process monitoring is coaxial measurement of light emitted from the meltpool area. More than two hundred research studies on coaxial monitoring of the meltpool have been performed, but there is still no validated and reliable method for measuring a suitable variable that could be directly used as an input for high-resolution control of the PBF-LB/M process, enabling process parameters such as laser power and scan speed to be dynamically adjusted not only at the part level, but locally for individual micrometer-scale segments along the scan track. This work reviews existing research studies on coaxial meltpool monitoring and identifies potential future research and development directions toward a standard and reliable meltpool monitoring method. Meltpool depth is identified as a particularly promising control-relevant variable. With the ability to monitor and control meltpool depth, it is possible to avoid undesirable process conditions due to too high or too low energy input, which would result in defects like keyhole porosity or lack-of-fusion. However, only five studies have attempted to estimate the melt pool depth coaxially during the PBF-LB/M process. Despite these attempts, there is no sufficiently validated method for high-resolution coaxial monitoring of meltpool depth in PBF-LB/M. The potential solution seems to be in combining concepts and recent discoveries from two-color coaxial camera- and photodiode-based meltpool area monitoring approaches. Based on the existing literature and hands-on experiences with establishing and working with coaxial monitoring systems, this work also provides guidelines and lists the most common challenges for implementing coaxial monitoring of the meltpool in the PBF-LB/M process.</jats:p>

title: Neighborhood Exposome at Birth and Trajectories of Epigenetic Age Acceleration Across Childhood
abstract:
<jats:sec id="ab-zoi261190-4">
                    <jats:title>Importance</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) has been linked to increased disease risk in adults, yet its developmental trajectories and early-life neighborhood determinants remain poorly understood.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="ab-zoi261190-5">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To examine whether there are associations between the neighborhood exposome at birth and EAA trajectories from early childhood through adolescence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="ab-zoi261190-6">
                    <jats:title>Design, Setting, and Participants</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This longitudinal cohort study used data from Project Viva, a prebirth cohort that enrolled pregnant women in eastern Massachusetts from April 22, 1999, to July 31, 2002. Participants included 570 children with available peripheral blood DNA methylation data, complete neighborhood characteristics, and complete covariates. Data were analyzed from August 19, 2024, to August 21, 2026.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="ab-zoi261190-7">
                    <jats:title>Exposures</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Neighborhood exposome profiles at birth derived from 22 census tract–level characteristics across 4 domains (area deprivation, social fragmentation, population density, and environmental quality) using self-organizing maps.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="ab-zoi261190-8">
                    <jats:title>Main Outcomes and Measures</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>EAA was calculated at 3, 8, and 13 years of age using the Horvath, Skin &amp;amp; Blood, and Wu epigenetic clocks. Trajectories were identified using latent class linear mixed models. Associations between neighborhood profiles and EAA trajectories were estimated using multinomial mixed models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="ab-zoi261190-9">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 570 children (mean [SD] age at early childhood, 3.2 [0.4] years; 305 [53.5%] male), 3 EAA trajectory groups (stable, increasing, and decreasing for the Horvath and Skin &amp;amp; Blood clocks or low-baseline for the Wu clock) and 3 neighborhood profiles were identified. Compared with profile 1 (suburban, lowest adverse exposures [n = 278]), children born into profile 2 (urban, high residential instability and single-person households, and highway proximity [n = 168]) had greater odds of increasing EAA for the Wu clock (adjusted odds ratio, 1.67 [95% CI, 1.03-2.69]). Profile 3 (urban, high socioeconomic deprivation and pollution [n = 124]) showed no associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="ab-zoi261190-10">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions and Relevance</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this longitudinal cohort study, birth into neighborhoods characterized by high residential instability and single-person households and highway proximity was associated with increasing Wu EAA trajectories across childhood. These findings suggest that early-life neighborhood conditions, encompassing both social and physical environmental factors, may represent targets for interventions aimed at reducing long-term disease risk. Further research is needed to clarify the implications of these findings for later health and prevention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A gray-distribution-based adaptive laser stripe center extraction algorithm
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate laser stripe center extraction is critical for high-precision line-structured laser 3D reconstruction. Many existing methods assume that the cross-sectional grayscale distribution of a laser stripe follows a fixed pattern. However, in practical scanning, variations in working distance, object geometry, and surface material lead to significant changes in grayscale distributions across the same stripe, which introduce center localization errors and degrade reconstruction accuracy and robustness. To address this issue, this paper proposes an adaptive laser stripe center extraction method with the core idea of adaptively selecting the most suitable center extraction algorithm for each stripe cross-section based on its estimated grayscale distribution model. Specifically, a real laser stripe dataset covering various typical scanning scenarios is first constructed. Based on statistical analysis of this dataset, a cross-sectional grayscale distribution estimation framework integrating four descriptors, namely Gaussianity, Symmetry, Peak Number, and Brightness Uniformity, is established. The optimal extraction algorithm for each grayscale distribution model is then determined through theoretical derivation and simulation analysis. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method maintains high extraction completeness while producing more continuous laser stripe center across different grayscale distributions. Under diverse camera exposure configurations, the average 3D reconstruction error is reduced by 0.13 mm, 0.33 mm, and 0.09 mm compared with the Gray Centroid Method, Gaussian Fitting Method, and Steger Method, respectively. Moreover, the proposed algorithm runs 2.02 times faster than the Steger Method, demonstrating superior robustness to stripe profile variations while maintaining high reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency.</jats:p>

Maternal plasma cell-free RNAs and sonographic parameters for predicting spontaneous preterm birth in twin pregnancies: A prospective cohort study
abstract:
<jats:p>Objective: To evaluate whether cervical length (CL), uterocervical angle (UCA), and five maternal plasma cell-free RNA (cfRNAs) markers can predict spontaneous preterm birth (sPTB) before 37 and 34 weeks in twin pregnancies.
Methods: This prospective study included 80 twin pregnancies examined at 14 - 24 weeks’ gestation at Hai Phong Medical University Hospital, from February 2023 to February 2025. CL and UCA were measured by transvaginal ultrasonography, and plasma cfRNA concentrations of PSME2, NAMPT, APOA1, APOA4, and Hsa-let-7g were quantified using droplet digital PCR. Participants were followed until delivery. Associations with sPTB were assessed using multivariable binary logistic regression, and predictive performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis.
Results: Women who delivered preterm had a significantly larger UCA and shorter CL than those delivering at term. Among the five RNA markers, only Hsa-let-7g differed significantly between women with sPTB before 34 weeks and those delivering at or after 34 weeks (1.89 ± 0.51 vs. 1.03 ± 0.54, p = 0.024). After adjusting, UCA was independently associated with sPTB before 37 weeks (OR 1.042, 95% CI 1.005 - 1.081) and before 34 weeks (OR 1.056, 95% CI 1.004 - 1.111). Hsa-let-7g was associated with sPTB before 34 weeks (OR 3.391, 95% CI 1.089 - 10.556). Area under the curve for predicting sPTB before 34 weeks was 0.799 for UCA, 0.712 for Hsa-let-7g, and 0.829 for their combination.
Conclusion: Second-trimester UCA and plasma Hsa-let-7g showed potential as non-invasive markers for predicting sPTB in twin pregnancies. Their combined use may improve the prediction of sPTB before 34 weeks.</jats:p>

title: Feasibility and safety of dual-wavelength 980/1470 nm laser for laparoscopic fenestration of hepatic cysts: a preliminary clinical study
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Laparoscopic fenestration and drainage is the standard treatment for symptomatic hepatic cysts. Conventional high-frequency electrocautery and ultrasonic scalpels have inherent limitations in simultaneously achieving efficient cutting and hemostasis, complete epithelial ablation, and preservation of intrahepatic vascular structures, leading to thermal injury, incomplete cyst wall treatment, and recurrence. The 980/1470 nm dual-wavelength laser leverages differential photothermal absorption by hemoglobin and water to enable layered, targeted therapy, offering a novel approach to optimizing minimally invasive hepatic cyst treatment, though clinical evidence remains limited. This study explores the feasibility, safety, and early efficacy of 980/1470 nm dual-wavelength laser in laparoscopic hepatic cyst fenestration, summarizes its technical essentials, and reports a preliminary single-port laparoscopic application of this laser system as an illustrative case.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A retrospective analysis was conducted of 10 patients who underwent laparoscopic hepatic cyst fenestration and drainage using 980/1470 nm dual-wavelength laser between May 2024 and September 2026. Intraoperatively, the 980/1470 nm dual-wavelength laser was used for cyst fenestration, combined with 1470 nm laser for precise superficial epithelial ablation of the cyst wall. Preoperative demographics, laser parameters, operative time, intraoperative blood loss, postoperative hospital stay, and complications were analyzed. Short-term imaging follow-up was performed to assess cyst recurrence and cavity healing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ten patients were enrolled, all of whom underwent successful laparoscopic surgery, including one case performed with a flexible single-port laparoscope. Postoperative pathology confirmed biliary hepatic cysts in all patients. Intraoperative blood loss was minimal, surgical trauma and stress were low, and no severe complications such as bile leakage, intra-abdominal hemorrhage, or infection occurred. All patients recovered uneventfully. Short-term imaging at a mean follow-up of 3 months demonstrated cyst cavity reduction or closure in all patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this small pilot cohort, 980/1470 nm dual-wavelength laser laparoscopic fenestration and drainage appeared feasible and safe, with no severe perioperative complications and favorable short-term imaging outcomes; the single-port application described here represents a single illustrative case. Given the small sample size, absence of a comparator group, and short follow-up, these findings are preliminary and require confirmation in larger controlled studies with longer-term surveillance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Discrete-EDFA-Free Amplification: EDF-Assisted Random DFB Raman Laser
abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a simulation-based study of an erbium-doped-fibre-assisted random distributed-feedback (rDFB) Raman amplifier for long-haul wavelength-division multiplexed transmission. The proposed architecture combines distributed Raman amplification over a 50 km standard single-mode-fibre span with a 25 cm terminal erbium-doped fibre (EDF) section pumped only by the residual 1460 nm rDFB field. The terminal EDF is intended to compensate span-end connection losses without a dedicated 980 nm or 1480 nm pump source. The model is calibrated against an experimentally measured optical-time-domain-reflectometer (OTDR) power profile, and an additional 2 dB EDF-gain margin is introduced to represent inter-span losses. The study considers a single 2 dB net-gain operating point, selected by minimizing signal-power variation along the span. The optimized configuration is applied to a 50-channel C-band WDM system over an equivalent 150-span, 7500 km link with idealized per-span power reset. The simulated central-channel OSNR reaches approximately 18.9 dB after 7500 km, while the channel OSNRs remain between about 17.5 and 19 dB. However, central-channel optimization produces a strongly nonuniform gain profile, increasing from approximately 2 dB near the band centre to 6.5 dB at the long-wavelength edge. The Kerr nonlinear-product power also increases by about 30 dB between one span and 7500 km. These results demonstrate the potential of the proposed architecture for span-end loss compensation, while showing that gain flattening, multi-channel optimization, system-level nonlinear analysis, and experimental validation are required before practical deployment.</jats:p>

title: Prediction of oxide coating thickness on moving polymer films using quantum cascade laser spectroscopy and machine learning
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nanometer-accurate inline monitoring of oxide coating thickness on polymer films is&#xD;essential for quality control in roll-to-roll production. However, measuring coatings in the&#xD;nanometer range on moving polymer films remains challenging because the measurement&#xD;samples spatially varying polymer thickness and reflective background conditions along the&#xD;measurement path, in addition to the low optical contrast between oxide and polymer in&#xD;the mid-infrared. We present a transflection measurement approach that combines&#xD;quantum cascade laser (QCL) spectroscopy with data-driven spectral analysis. We apply it&#xD;to moving oriented polypropylene (OPP) and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) films&#xD;coated with silicon oxide under laboratory conditions to assess its feasibility for future&#xD;inline monitoring. In transflection mode, reflected intensity is captured across a spectral&#xD;range covering the Si–O absorption band, enabling measurements on both transparent and&#xD;opaque films. Two spectral analysis approaches are proposed and compared. The first&#xD;combines spectral averaging with linear regression, achieving a mean root mean square&#xD;error (RMSE) of 7.6 nm for OPP and 15.9 nm for PET. The second combines linear&#xD;regression and Gaussian process regression (LR-GPR) on blockwise-aggregated spectra.&#xD;For thickness levels represented in the training data, this approach reduces the RMSE to&#xD;approximately 4nm for both OPP and PET, corresponding to improvements of&#xD;approximately 50% for OPP and 75% for PET. While the former approach offers&#xD;simplicity and interpretability, the latter captures nonlinear spectral relationships.&#xD;However, generalization of LR-GPR to unseen thickness levels remains the central&#xD;limitation, with RMSE values of approximately 10 nm to 11 nm. The results show&#xD;potential for oxide coating thickness estimation, while improved generalization and further&#xD;validation are needed to establish broader applicability.</jats:p>

title: Quantum Higgs Echo in Superconductors: A Novel Form of Quantum Memory
journal: International Journal of Pure Science Research Studies (IJPSRS)
abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical investigation of quantum information storage via the Higgs amplitude mode in superconductors. We propose a novel quantum memory mechanism based on coherent excitation and echo retrieval of the Higgs mode, exploiting the collective nature of the superconducting condensate. Through rigorous theoretical analysis combining time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory with quantum master equations, we demonstrate that Higgs mode excitations can store quantum information with coherence times exceeding 100 ns. We derive analytical expressions for storage fidelity as a function of temperature, gap anisotropy, and disorder, achieving theoretical fidelities above 95% for storage times up to 100 ns in clean s-wave superconductors below. Numerical simulations validate our theoretical predictions and reveal optimal parameter regimes for NbN thin films. Our findings establish fundamental bounds on Higgs-based quantum memory and propose experimental protocols compatible with current THz spectroscopy capabilities. This work opens new directions for exploiting collective modes in quantum technologies.</jats:p>

title: Giant-atom-enabled quantum optics with valley-polarized photons
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Valleytronics and valley photonics exploit the valley degree of freedom to encode and manipulate information. Here we show that photonic valleys can be selectively addressed in quantum optics using a simple two-level emitter, provided it is coupled nonlocally to the field, thereby realizing a so-called giant atom. Specifically, we consider a qubit coupled at multiple points to an engineered honeycomb lattice of resonators with detuned sublattice frequencies. By tailoring the geometry and phases of the coupling points, the giant atom can be made to emit selectively into a single valley. The emitted photons thereby acquire a well-defined valley character and effectively nonzero Berry curvature. By placing the qubit near a domain wall between regions of opposite sublattice detuning, whose interface supports valley-polarized edge modes, emission becomes chiral along the domain wall. This provides a promising route toward implementation of single-photon disorder-robust chiral emission without breaking time-reversal symmetry of the electromagnetic medium in platforms such as circuit QED.</jats:p>

title: A comprehensive benchmark and dual-encoder baseline for terraced field extraction in complex mountainous regions
abstract: <jats:p>Terraces play a vital role in mitigating runoff and intercepting sediment. Large-scale, high-precision extraction of terraces from remote sensing imagery is essential for environmental monitoring and soil erosion control. However, accurate spatial identification of terraces still presents significant challenges, including scale variability, shadow interference, and complex geometric configurations. To address these issues, we propose DETS-Net, a dual-encoder network that integrates CNN and Transformer architectures. The network employs ResNet-34 as the CNN encoder for local feature detail extraction, utilizes a Transformer encoder to strengthen long-range dependency modeling, and incorporates an adaptive feature fusion (AFF) module for the dynamic integration of the two feature branches. We develop the THDIR dataset, which covers four typical terrain types, namely, plateau mountains, hills, and mountain-basin transition zones, and contains 9,336 standardized 256 × 256 pixel images. We conduct systematic comparisons with eight representative deep learning models. Experimental results demonstrate that DETS-Net achieves an overall accuracy (OA) of 89.91%, a mean intersection over union (MIoU) of 81.28%, and an F1-score of 87.99% on the THDIR dataset, outperforming current mainstream methods in segmentation precision. We apply the optimized model to 2023 remote sensing imagery of Luotian County in the Dabie Mountains, Hubei Province, and generate a high-precision county-level terrace spatial distribution map. This framework supports the assessment of soil and water conservation benefits through area statistics, slope distribution data, and high-precision boundary extraction and provides a reproducible technical pathway for automated terrace mapping using high-resolution remote sensing imagery in complex mountainous regions.</jats:p>

title: Temporal Complexity Hierarchies in Solvable Quantum Many-Body Dynamics
abstract: <jats:p>The influence matrix (IM) provides a powerful framework for characterizing nonequilibrium quantum many-body dynamics by encoding multitime correlations into tensor-network states. Understanding how its computational complexity relates to underlying dynamics is crucial for both theoretical insight and practical utility yet remains largely unexplored despite a few case studies. Here, we address this question for a family of brickwork quantum circuits ranging from integrable to chaotic regimes. Using tools from geometric group theory, we identify three qualitatively distinct scalings of temporal entanglement entropy, establishing a hierarchy of computational resources required for accurate tensor-network representations of the IM for these models. We further analyze the memory structure of the IM and distinguish between classical and quantum temporal correlations. In particular, for certain examples, we identify effectively classical IMs that admit an efficient Monte Carlo algorithm for computing multitime correlations. In more generic settings without an explicit classical description of the IM, we introduce an operational measure of quantum memory with an experimental protocol and discuss examples exhibiting long-time genuinely quantum correlations. Our results establish a new connection between quantum many-body dynamics and group theory, providing fresh insights into the complexity of the IM and its intricate connection to the physical characteristics of the dynamics.</jats:p>

title: Inverse energy transfer in three-dimensional quantum vortex flows
abstract: <jats:p>Vortex reconnections play a fundamental role in fluids. They increase the complexity of flow and develop small-scale motions. In this work we report that in superfluids they can also excite large scales. We numerically illustrate that during a superfluid vortex reconnection energy is injected into the thermal (normal) component of helium II at small length scales, but is transferred nonlinearly to larger length scales, increasing the integral length scale of the normal fluid. This inverse energy transfer constrasts with the reconnection-triggered energy transfer to smaller scales observed along the superfluid vortices and in classical fluids, underlining that similarities and differences between quantum and classical vortex dynamics may depend on the fluid component investigated. In addition, by studying about 50 different reconnections, we show that the reconnection event injects a nonzero net helicity in the normal fluid as a result of the chiral character of the mutual friction force coupling the superfluid vortices and the normal component, contributing to the understanding of the impact of topology-changing events on the helical balance of superfluid flows.</jats:p>

title: Topological Optimization and Robust Active Disturbance Rejection Control of an ACLD Cylindrical Shell with Breathing Cracks Under Multi-Field Coupling Degradation
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>To address the issues of time-varying stiffness softening and multi-field nonlinear degradation in a cylindrical laminated shell containing breathing cracks and covered with a locally segmented active constrained layer damping (ACLD), this study establishes a multi-field coupled dynamic theoretical framework that integrates “degradation modeling, topological optimization, and anti-saturation robust control.” This framework is constructed using a three-dimensional fully coupled dynamic flexibility matrix based on the extended Layerwise-Sanders kinematics and the bilinear cohesive zone model(CZM), and employs a spatial domain decomposition differential-quadrature method (DD-DQM) to solve for discrete solutions at discontinuous boundaries; The Crested Porcupine Optimization (CPO) algorithm, driven by a damage strain energy distortion field, is introduced to perform the spatial topological configuration of ACLD patches, and a closed-loop linear active disturbance rejection control (LADRC) strategy with a state-corrected anti-saturation mechanism is established. The results show that the CPO optimization captures the energy accumulation characteristics caused by localized damage, precisely and universally locking the optimal initial patch coordinates for different matrix materials at the upper boundary limit xacld1 = 10.00 cm; When faced with high-order nonlinear harmonic perturbations triggered by a 50 N transient impact, the designed anti-saturation LADRC strategy can effectively suppress the system’s asymmetric oscillations within approximately 0.05 s, while keeping the control voltage confined within the hardware safety boundary of ±150 V throughout the entire time domain. This study provides a reference for robust control and topological optimization of damaged intelligent flexible structures under multidimensional perturbation environments.</jats:p>

title: Organic Photodetectors With Surpassing 50% External Quantum Efficiency at 1100 nm Using a Narrow Bandgap Donor Polymer
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Organic photodetectors (OPDs) have garnered significant attention for their low‐cost fabrication, mechanical flexibility, and tunable spectral response. However, low external quantum efficiency (EQE) in short‐wave infrared (SWIR), especially above silicon's cutoff (≈1100 nm), limits their application. Herein, we report SWIR‐OPDs using a narrow‐bandgap donor polymer, PDCBT‐DP2O, blended with the acceptor BTPCN. The devices achieve an EQE of 51.1% at 1100 nm under −3 V bias. The incorporation of 5,6‐dicyano‐2,1,3‐benzothiadiazole and 3,3′‐dimethoxy‐2,2′‐bithiophene units significantly narrows the polymer bandgap, pushing absorption past silicon's limit. Moreover, the finely tuned alkyl side chains improve the skeleton coplanarity and solid‐state packing, resulting in a longer exciton diffusion length, higher carrier mobility, and reduced trap density. These combined effects facilitate the conversion of absorbed photons into collected charge carriers. As a result, the OPD achieves detectivity (
                    <jats:italic>D</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>sh</jats:sub>
                    <jats:sup>*</jats:sup>
                    ) over 10
                    <jats:sup>11</jats:sup>
                    Jones across 320–1250 nm at −0.5 V, which ranks among the highest reported for SWIR‐OPDs. We also demonstrate sensitive SWIR sensing in representative application prototypes including optical communication, noncontact photoplethysmography, broadband spectroscopy and SWIR imaging. This work proves narrow bandgap donor polymers as a distinct material pathway for high‐performance SWIR photodetection.

title: Loop Quantum Gravity Black Holes Surrounded by Quintessence
journal: International Journal of Geometric Methods in Modern Physics
abstract: <jats:p>Quantum gravity corrections act on the near-horizon geometry of a black hole (BH), while dark energy acts on its asymptotic region, and how the two imprints combine is still poorly understood. We study a static, spherically symmetric BH of Loop Quantum Gravity (LQG) surrounded by a quintessence field. The metric function carries the LQG parameters [Formula: see text] and the quintessence parameters [Formula: see text], and for suitable values it has three horizons, a structure found neither in pure LQG BHs nor in classical quintessence BHs. We analyze null and timelike geodesics, photon spheres and the shadow seen by a static observer placed between the event and the cosmological horizons. Sixth-order WKB quasinormal modes (QNMs) of scalar and electromagnetic fields confirm stability over the ranges examined. The quantum term behaves as a short-range repulsive correction: it shrinks the photon sphere and the shadow, raises the QNM oscillation frequency and lowers the light deflection. Quintessence works the other way on the photon sphere, the ringing frequency and the bending. With the Gauss-Bonnet method we obtain a weak deflection angle valid for [Formula: see text], which we check against direct numerical integration, and in which quintessence dominates at large impact parameters and the LQG terms at small ones.</jats:p>

title: LQ-HybridNet: A Parameter-Compact Classical Architecture with Quantum-Inspired Feature Transformations for Skin Lesion Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: This study evaluates LQ-HybridNet, a parameter-compact classical architecture for skin-lesion classification. Methods: MobileNetV2 is augmented with amplitude–phase channel gating and a four-qubit variational circuit feature transformation. Crucially, all evaluations enforce a rigorous, leakage-resistant stratified lesion-level split to prevent data contamination. Here, quantum-inspired denotes a classical mathematical inductive bias, not quantum hardware execution or computational advantage. Results: On HAM10000, LQ-HybridNet achieved 90.80±0.25% accuracy, 0.7714 macro precision, 0.7257 macro recall, and 0.7428 macro F1-score, compared with 88.50±0.30% accuracy for MobileNetV2. The 2.30 percentage-point gain required 45.9K additional parameters. Across the evaluated backbones, accuracy gains ranged from 1.10 to 2.40 percentage points on HAM10000 and 1.77 to 4.00 points on ISIC 2018. Latency increased from 12.4 to 48.7 ms per batch of 32 images. Conclusions: The structured classical transformations yielded incremental benchmark improvements with small parameter overhead but approximately 3.9-fold higher latency. These results concern the evaluated architectures and benchmark distributions; parameter compactness does not imply inference efficiency.</jats:p>

title: A Loss-Limited Optimum for Fixed Uniform Multi-Pass Quantum Sensing per Absorbed Photon
abstract: <jats:p>Multi-pass schemes send a photon through a sample several times to learn more about it. When the sample rather than the light is scarce, the natural figure of merit is the information gained per photon the object absorbs. We show that three properties fix the loss-limited optimum of every fixed scheme in which a single photon passes repeatedly and uniformly through the sample and is detected once at the end: a payoff that grows as the square of the pass number, the same survival probability on every pass, and no dose from a photon already lost. They force a single trade-off function h(x)=x2/(ex−1), where x is the number of passes times the loss per pass. Its maximum, 0.648, sits at xopt=1.594. The multi-pass optima of Koppell and Kasevich and of Yu et al. are two instances, and the loss-limited ceiling of interaction-free interrogation is a third when its payoff is counted as conclusive detections. Phase sensing of a weakly absorbing object is optimal at mopt=xopt/(ϵ+α) passes; the absorption α and the parasitic loss ϵ enter the optimum only through their sum, but the damage counts only α. N00N states and their loss-robust generalisations do worse per absorbed photon, and optimising over photon number and pass number together returns a single recycled photon; Gaussian probes and chains tailored pass by pass lie outside this class and can exceed its ceiling by a bounded factor. Two further problems are priced in the same measure. Absorption estimation gains nothing, for any scheme. Above the crosstalk crossover of the mode sorter, detecting a faint companion below the Rayleigh limit costs the companion a dose that does not depend on its faintness; below it, and in direct imaging at any separation, the dose grows without bound as the companion fades. Among single photons and path-entangled number states, the gentlest measurement of a fragile sample is also the simplest one: a single photon, recycled.</jats:p>

title: Pulsed Electromagnetic Field-Stimulated Alginate–Chitosan/Hydroxyapatite Nanocomposite Scaffolds for Accelerated Repair of Critical-Size Femoral Bone Defects
abstract: <jats:p>Critical-size bone defects remain a major clinical challenge, as impaired endogenous healing and an unfavorable local microenvironment prevent spontaneous bridging of the defect. Here, we report a bio-physical regenerative strategy that combines a three-dimensional, porous alginate–chitosan/hydroxyapatite (Alg-CS/HA) nanocomposite scaffold with targeted pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) stimulation. Rod-like hydroxyapatite (HA) nanoparticles (~12 × 86 nm, Ca/P = 1.64) were synthesized and incorporated at 30 wt% into an ionically crosslinked Alg-CS polyelectrolyte matrix. HA incorporation significantly increased the compressive strength (22.41 ± 1.35 vs. 14.53 ± 1.81 kPa) and modulus (156.51 ± 2.15 vs. 74.34 ± 1.43 kPa) of the scaffold, while preserving an interconnected porous architecture (75.97 ± 7.8% porosity) and slowing enzymatic biodegradation (76.70 ± 3.82% mass loss at 28 days). MTT assays on human skin fibroblasts confirmed that both formulations were highly cytocompatible, with viability exceeding 85% at concentrations up to 50 mg/mL. In vivo, bilateral critical-size femoral defects (6 mm diameter) were created in New Zealand rabbits to evaluate bone regeneration under two PEMF regimes (5 and 50 Hz; 0.22 and 0.5 mT) applied for 3 weeks. Untreated defects showed essentially no repair (1.0 ± 2.4%), whereas scaffold implantation alone yielded 20.0 ± 4.3% new bone formation. PEMF stimulation produced a clear frequency- and intensity-dependent enhancement of osteogenesis, culminating in 90.0 ± 5.2% defect bridging in the low-frequency, high-intensity group (5 Hz, 0.5 mT), a 4.5-fold increase over the scaffold-only control. Histological analysis showed dense, mature trabecular bone with abundant osteocytes, active osteoid deposition, and histological features consistent with vascularization in this group. These preliminary results were obtained with n = 3 defect sites per group. Together, they suggest that coupling an Alg-CS/HA nanocomposite scaffold with low-frequency, high-intensity PEMF stimulation is a promising, non-invasive strategy for enhancing the repair of critical-size bone defects, warranting confirmation in larger studies.</jats:p>

title: Image-Decomposition-Based Encryption Using Triple-Gated Feedback Field-Effect Transistors
abstract: <jats:p>Image-decomposition-based encryption is an effective approach for enhancing security, as it requires both decryption of the decomposed images and subsequent image processing to reconstruct the original image. In this study, we demonstrate image-decomposition-based encryption using a reconfigurable logic-in-memory (R-LIM) cell and a true random number generator (TRNG), both based on triple-gated feedback field-effect transistors (TG FBFETs). The R-LIM cell, composed of eight TG FBFETs, outputs symmetric voltages of ±0.7 V with clearly distinguishable logic levels and performs reconfigurable logic operations without modifying the circuit configuration or input bias. The TRNG, composed of one TG FBFET and one resistor, generates random bits without requiring initial seeds and enables control of the probability of bit ‘1’ by adjusting the input voltage. For image processing and encryption, virtual R-LIM cell arrays are constructed using Python, and encryption keys are generated by the TRNG. Image encryption is performed using a sum operation within a single R-LIM cell, enabling key splitting through two independent random keys that are both required for decryption. As a result, the TG FBFET-based system enables image-decomposition-based encryption with approximately 71% fewer transistors than a conventional complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor-based implementation.</jats:p>

title: Fully integrated entangled photon-pair source on a photonic chip for a wavelength-multiplexed multiparty quantum key distribution network
abstract: <jats:p>The development of QKD networks as a possible answer to the threat to encrypted communication posed by quantum computers has given rise to a variety of concepts and implementations in recent years. In terms of the scalability of such systems, photonic integrated circuits (photonic chips) are a promising approach. This makes the systems not only much more miniaturized and robust, but also more attractive for industrial production. Here we present the concept and characterization of a photonic chip that can act as a source in an entanglement-based QKD network employing spontaneous four-wave mixing in microring resonators. In addition to photon-pair production, the chip also directly performs essential filtering tasks. Moreover, the photon-pair rate can be maintained constant over an extended period using a Pound-Drever-Hall locking method.</jats:p>
