title: Interface Engineering of Magnetic Ni x Co3– x O4 Cathodes by Field Polarity for Li-O2 Batteries
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Lithium-oxygen (Li-O2) batteries offer ultrahigh theoretical energy density, but sluggish cathodic oxygen reduction reaction (ORR)/oxygen evolution reaction (OER) kinetics restrict practical application. Here, magnetically tunable NixCo3–xO4 (NCOx) spinel cathode catalysts were prepared by regulating the Ni:Co ratio to clarify the relationship among catalyst magnetization, magnetic-field polarity, and Li-O2 battery performance. Increasing Ni content raises the fraction of high-spin octahedral Ni2+, enhancing saturation magnetization; NCO3 (Ni:Co = 2:1) exhibits the highest Ms (28 emu/g) and strongest response under 300 mT. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy reveals a polarity-dependent effect: an N-pole field decreases Rct from 27.42 to 19.74 Ω, whereas an S-pole field increases Rct, likely because it aggravates the spin mismatch between catalyst electrons and triplet-state O2, thereby increasing the interfacial charge-transfer barrier. Density functional theory (DFT) descriptor calculations show that the high-spin (HS)-initialized reference configuration strengthens O2 adsorption (–2.95 eV) and exhibits more favorable calculated ORR/OER energetics than the low-spin (LS)-initialized reference configuration; these calculations do not explicitly simulate the external magnetic field. Under optimal NCO3/N-pole/300 mT conditions, the discharge voltage increases by 107 mV and cycling life exceeds 990 h at 0.2 mA cm–2. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observations show that the N-pole-facing magnetic-field condition changes the discharge-product morphology from irregular agglomerates to more uniformly distributed platelet-like structures. Ex situ Li 1s X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) is consistent with more extensive removal of Li2O2 containing products during recharge, although it does not by itself prove complete Li2O2 decomposition or suppression of Li2CO3 formation. This work establishes a cooperative strategy combining catalyst magnetic design and magnetic field regulation, providing insights into the rational design of magnetic field-assisted Li-O2 batteries.</jats:p>

title: A road-field population model with climate change: forced wave patterns and stability
abstract: <jats:p>Recently, increasing attention is being devoted to spatial invasion and wave propagation phenomena in high-dimensional heterogeneous media (such as road-field interchange network), due to their significance in applications to population models. The combined effects of road diffusion and climate change in an unbounded high-dimensional domain introduce further complexity and challenges. In this paper, we study the propagation dynamics of a road-field system in a shifting environment. Our results indicates that forced traveling waves exist as long as the shifting speed is less than a critical value. For each such speed, the forced wave profile is unique, and exponentially stable. While the shifting speed is greater than that critical value, we further establish propagation dynamics in connection to extinction and persistence. We found that the propagation of persistence cannot be faster than the critical speed. Numerical simulations are also presented to not only illustrate the theoretical results, but also provide deep insight for further study.</jats:p>

title: Quantum singularity theorem for the evaporating black hole
IoT-Based Technological Retrofitting of Urban Collective Public Transport in Intermediate Cities of the Global South: Edge–Cloud Architecture, Field Validation and a Digital Twin in Tunja, Colombia
abstract: <jats:p>Intermediate cities of the Global South concentrate a growing share of the urban population but lack the financial and institutional capacity to renew their urban collective public transport (UCPT) systems according to smart-city references conceived in the Global North. This article presents the design, implementation and validation of an intelligent system for UCPT based on the technological retrofitting of existing elements (seats, buses, bus-stops and pedestrian crossings), developed within a research macro-project with a case study in Tunja, Colombia. The system derives its requirements from a citizen-centred multidimensional evaluation model of sustainable and smart mobility and is structured in the three layers of an IoT architecture: four low-cost perception modules (i-Seat, i-Bus, i-Bus-Stop and i-Crossing/Traffic-Light), a hybrid Edge–Cloud telematic system with LoRaWAN as the main technology and LTE/4G as backup, and the MueveT platform, which integrates telemetry, estimated time of arrival, detection of presumed infringements, device monitoring and service quality indicators. Validation was carried out with prototypes installed in a private vehicle that emulated UCPT journeys and with a usability evaluation completed by project researchers as a proof of concept. On a 3.72 km route, the mobile node recorded packet error rates of 38.7% with DR1 and 40.4% with DR2, the latter with half the time on air; on a 6.53 km route with four gateways, the fixed bus-stop node recorded no LoRaWAN losses, and the LTE link delivered the samples with a median latency of 272 ms to the platform. A digital twin fed with these records projected deliveries above 85% for 25 buses per gateway, and the platform achieved user experience ratings between 4.25 and 5.00. A comparative analysis with similar developments shows that the main contribution lies in the explicit traceability between the evaluation model, the captured data and the functions, providing a basis for daily operation and evidence for the maturity level of urban mobility.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>
                    III‐V group colloidal quantum dots (CQDs) are promising semiconductors for short‐wavelength infrared optoelectronic devices because of their narrow bandgaps and size tunability. Furthermore, their composition complies with the ‘Restriction of Hazardous Substances’ directive of the European Union, making them attractive for consumer electronics, including photodetectors and light‐emitting diodes. title: LIGO detector characterization in the second and third parts of the fourth observing run
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO) detector characterization efforts enabled the confident detection of gravitational waves (GWs) from hundreds of compact binary coalescences (CBC) during the fourth observing run. Reliable production of high quality detector data and rapid noise mitigation efforts allow the extraction of the most in-depth knowledge of GW sources and their progenitors. In this paper we describe LIGO detector characterization activities during the second and third parts of O4—O4b and O4c. We summarize changes in detector configuration and performance at the LIGO Hanford and LIGO Livingston Observatories between the end of the first part of O4a and the end of O4c, including upgrades made during the commissioning break preceding O4b and during repairs performed in O4c. We describe instrumental investigations carried out at both sites designed to understand and subsequently mitigate the effect on detector sensitivity of transient glitches, narrowband spectral lines, and vibration-driven noise, among other data quality (DQ) concerns. We then review the tools and procedures used to validate GW candidates and the DQ products thus supplied to searches for GWs from CBC and unmodeled transients, continuous GWs, and the stochastic GW background. The efforts of the detector characterization group are essential for maintaining and improving the sensitivity and reliability of the LIGO detectors especially as observing runs lengthen and more events are detected. We conclude with prospects for LIGO detector characterization activities in future observing runs.</jats:p>

title: Fracture anisotropy in additively manufactured SS 316L: A phase-field approach
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Additively manufactured (AM) metallic components often exhibit pronounced anisotropy due to deposition-induced microstructural features, which strongly influence their deformation and fracture behavior. In this work, a coupled anisotropic phase-field fracture framework incorporating rate-independent elastoplasticity is developed to model fracture in directed energy deposited AISI 316L stainless steel, with explicit sensitivity to deposition direction. The formulation combines isotropic linear elasticity with stress-based spectral decomposition to ensure tension–compression asymmetry. Fracture anisotropy is introduced through a structural tensor embedded in the crack surface density function, while plastic deformation is described using classical
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:msub>
                          <mml:mi>J</mml:mi>
                          <mml:mn>2</mml:mn>
                        </mml:msub>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    plasticity with isotropic hardening. The model preserves the variational structure of the phase-field approach, with plasticity influencing fracture indirectly through the evolution of elastic strains and a crack-driving history variable. An extensive experimental campaign, including quasi-static tensile testing of specimens extracted along multiple build orientations, digital image correlation, and microstructural and fractographic analyses, is conducted to characterize anisotropic mechanical response and failure mechanisms. Numerical simulations successfully reproduce the experimentally observed orientation-dependent stress–strain behavior, crack paths, and fracture modes, demonstrating the capability of the proposed framework to capture the interplay between plasticity, anisotropy, and fracture in AM metals. The results highlight the critical role of deposition direction in governing fracture resistance and provide a robust predictive tool for failure analysis of AM structures.
                  </jats:p>

title:
Surface Polarity-Dependent Cellular Uptake and Apoptotic
Response of Liposomal Carbon Quantum Dots in MCF-7 Cells
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Carbon quantum dots have emerged as promising nanomaterials for cancer theranostics owing to their tunable fluorescence properties, biocompatibility, and potential therapeutic activity. In this study, the anticancer effects of hydrophobic CQDs (Hb-CQD) and 3-APTMS functionalized hydrophilic CQDs (Hp-CQD) derived from a single precursor curcumin and their liposomal formulations (L-Hb-CQD and L-Hp-CQD) were investigated in MCF-7 breast cancer cells. Cellular uptake and cell-associated fluorescence were evaluated by fluorescence microscopy, while cytotoxicity and apoptosis induction were assessed using MTT and Annexin V-FITC/propidium iodide assays, respectively. All CQD formulations exhibited concentration-dependent cytotoxicity toward MCF-7 cells. L-Hp-CQD showed the greatest antiproliferative activity with the lowest IC50 value (119.7 μg mL–1), followed by Hb-CQD (124.5 μg mL–1), L-Hb-CQD (125.4 μg mL–1), and Hp-CQD (156.2 μg mL–1). Fluorescence imaging revealed that liposomal encapsulation significantly enhances cell-associated fluorescence, particularly in the case of L-Hp-CQD. Flow cytometric analysis demonstrated a pronounced shift from viable to apoptotic cell populations following treatment. Hb-CQD induced the highest total apoptotic population (73.43%), followed by Hp-CQD (72.01%), L-Hp-CQD (68.20%), and L-Hb-CQD (51.47%). Importantly, necrotic cell populations remained low across all treatment groups, indicating that cell death occurred predominantly through apoptosis rather than nonspecific cytotoxic damage. These findings demonstrate that CQD surface polarity and liposomal delivery significantly influence cellular uptake and anticancer efficacy. The ability of these fluorescent nanomaterials to combine efficient cellular imaging with apoptosis-mediated cancer cell killing highlights their potential as multifunctional platforms for future cancer theranostic applications.</jats:p>

title: Understanding How Coronal Heating and Magnetic Field Scaling Affect Global Properties of the Low and Middle Corona
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The magnetic field of the Sun is a key driver of coronal heating and solar wind acceleration. In tandem, these influence the observable morphology of the corona, along with defining the magnetic connectivity and magnitude of open magnetic flux. Here, we investigate how coronal heating affects the magnetothermal state of the 3D global corona by analyzing a series of data-constrained, thermodynamic magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations for solar minimum conditions. We vary the overall heat deposited in the corona via modifying the input Poynting flux of a wave-turbulence-driven (WTD) model for coronal heating and by scaling the inner boundary magnetic field. We quantify the magnetic, thermodynamic, and combined magnetothermal effects on our simulations. We find that increasing the overall amount of heat leads to a higher magnitude of open flux and a more visibly open white-light morphology in the K-Corona between 1.5 and 6
                    <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>⊙</jats:sub>
                    . We quantify how plasma
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                    evolves and drives morphological differences between simulations. We also compare these runs to an extremely high-resolution reference solution that includes small-scale magnetic information in the surface boundary condition. This latter comparison provides insight into the further development of “subgrid” corrections for low(er) resolution models to best represent the structure and observables of the corona and inner heliosphere.
                  </jats:p>

title: Beyond Energy Nationalism: Contractual Lock-In, Gas Export Diversion, LNG Trading Hubs, and Asymmetric Energy Security in Indonesia Singapore Natural Gas Relations
journal: Journal on Political Sciences & International Relations
abstract: <jats:p>This qualitative literature review examines the economic, contractual, infrastructural, and environmental consequences of diverting Indonesian natural gas exports from Singapore toward domestic users. It distinguishes Indonesian pipeline gas from shipborne liquefied natural gas (LNG), Singapore-based LNG trading and transshipment, and final Singaporean gas consumption. Using recent peer-reviewed literature and contemporaneous official information, the study critically assesses claims that a small temporary supply reduction implies negligible bilateral dependence or that export interruption necessarily triggers  financial  default  and  gas  flaring.  The  synthesis  identifies  asymmetric  but  conditional  vulnerabilities:  Singapore  may  replace  a  limited  pipeline  shortfall through diversified procurement, while Indonesian producers can face revenue and financing risks if domestic offtake or contractual settlement is inadequate. Conversely, a connected and creditworthy domestic customer may create significant economic value through greater electricity reliability and industrial activity. A conceptual framework links physical flows, gas sales agreements, project-finance covenants, infrastructure absorption, political credibility, and methane outcomes. The study concludes that sound resource nationalism requires reconciled gas-flow accounting, scenario-based netback and welfare analysis, contract-specific impact assessments, infrastructure readiness, and credible environmental safeguards. It offers a practical decision framework  for  balancing  Indonesian  domestic  energy  needs,  producer  bankability,  and  bilateral  commercial  relationships  without  treating  an  isolated  percentage as decisive evidence</jats:p>

title: High Concordance of Clinical and Pathological Staging Supports Core Needle Biopsy-Based MammaPrint Testing in Early Breast Cancer
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Background Accurate characterization of early breast cancer (EBC) at diagnosis is essential for timely treatment selection. Genomic profiling assays such as MammaPrint® are increasingly performed on Core Needle Biopsy (CNB) specimens to enable earlier risk stratification and optimized treatment planning. Here we investigated whether clinical staging at diagnosis remains sufficiently consistent with final pathology to support MammaPrint testing on the CNB specimen without awaiting surgical resection. Methods Using prospectively collected real-world data from the FLEX Study (NCT03053193), we identified patients with invasive ductal carcinoma and hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative (HR+/HER2−) disease who had MammaPrint performed on CNB specimens and available clinical and pathologic T and N staging data. Patients who received neoadjuvant therapy or had missing staging information were excluded. We assessed whether tumors remained within the clinically defined MammaPrint-valid population (cT1-cT2 and cN0-cN1) following surgical pathology, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) calculated using the Wilson score method. Results A total of 4,399 FLEX patients were evaluated for tumor staging and 4,238 for nodal staging. Overall, 98.4% of clinical T stage assessments remained within validated T stage ranges at pathologic assessment (pT1-pT2; 4,330/4,399, 95% CI 97.9%-98.8%). The T stage concordance among patients with HR+, HER2- breast cancer was 98.3% (4,003/4,071; 95% CI 97.9%-98.6%). Similarly, 98.0% of clinical N stage assessments remained with validated nodal ranges at pathologic assessment (pN0-pN1; 4,155/4,238, 95% CI 97.5%-98.4%). Among patients with HR+/HER2− breast cancer, clinical N stage concordance within validated testing criteria was 98.0% (3,842/3,921; 95% CI 97.5%–98.3%) at surgical pathology. Conclusion In this large real-world cohort, clinical staging at diagnosis reliably identified patients whose disease remained within validated MammaPrint tumor and nodal staging criteria following surgery in 98% of cases. These findings support the reliability of clinical staging to enable genomic testing on CNB specimens at diagnosis, without waiting for definitive surgical pathology.</jats:p>

title: Multi-scale simulations of wind farm impacts on nighttime near-surface temperature in complex terrain
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Various studies have shown that wind turbine wakes can induce temperature variations. Investigating these effects near the ground is particularly important for assessing their potential impact on vegetation and human activities. In this study, the multi-scale Meso-NH/SURFEX/EOL modeling framework, which includes coupled atmosphere, land-surface and actuator models, is used to evaluate the impact of the
                    <jats:italic>Ensemble Éolien Catalan</jats:italic>
                    wind farm on ground and near-surface temperatures, as well as terrain-specific flow dynamics during a stable nocturnal radiative cooling event associated with frost risk in nearby vineyards. The simulations are performed using nested domains to dynamically downscale the atmospheric conditions from the operational weather forecast AROME-1.3km to a horizontal resolution of 5 m, allowing explicit representation of turbine wakes through rotative actuator disk representation. Turbine-induced meteorological variations are quantified by comparing simulations performed with and without the actuator model. The results reveal that near-surface meteorological responses arise from the combined influence of individual turbine wakes and the large-scale impact of the wind farm, which modifies the flow dynamics and temperature field. In the wind farm, a mean near-surface warming of approximately 0.4 °C is found, with localized temperature increases reaching up to 1.6 °C in the near wake of individual turbines. The strongest perturbations occur for turbines located within valleys, where strong temperature inversions enhance turbine-induced temperature changes. In addition, the wind farm shifts the position of a convergence zone associated with a katabatic flow by about 100–400 m, producing warming anomalies of up to 2 °C along the displaced meteorological front.
                  </jats:p>

Metformin Attenuates Cardiac Developmental Toxicity in High-Glucose-Exposed Zebrafish Larvae: Oxidative Stress, Hif-1α-Associated Metabolic Gene Alterations, and Wnt Signaling Changes
abstract: <jats:p>Background: Maternal hyperglycemia is associated with embryonic developmental abnormalities and congenital heart defects, yet the mechanisms and effective interventions remain unclear. We examined high-glucose-induced cardiac developmental injury in zebrafish and whether metformin co-administered with high glucose is associated with protection. Methods: Wild-type AB and Tg(myl7:EGFP) zebrafish (Danio rerio) embryos were exposed to control medium, high glucose (150 mM), or high glucose plus metformin (0.75, 3.0, or 6.0 mM); metformin alone was not tested. Hatching and survival rates, cardiac morphology and function, larval locomotor activity, oxidative-stress markers, and cardiac developmental and pathway transcripts/proteins were assessed. Results: Under high-glucose exposure conditions (150 mM), hatching and survival were reduced, cardiac morphology/function and locomotor activity were altered, hand2, gata4, tbx1, and tbx5 were downregulated, Gata4 was decreased, oxidative stress was increased, and Hif-1α expression and downstream metabolic targets were increased. Wnt-related readouts were heterogeneous: Gsk3β Ser9 phosphorylation, β-catenin and Daam1 decreased, whereas Dvl2 increased. Metformin was associated with improved survival, cardiac phenotypes, and locomotor outcomes, together with partial molecular restoration. As an osmolarity-matched control was not included, these phenotypes cannot be attributed exclusively to glucose-specific effects. Conclusions: High-glucose exposure conditions are associated with cardiac developmental injury and pathway dysregulation, and metformin shows protective associations. These findings are not causal, do not distinguish glucose-specific effects from hyperosmotic stress, and require osmolarity-matched controls, functional metabolic assays, and Hif-1α/Wnt perturbation studies.</jats:p>

title:
High‐Performance 2D MXene‐Derived TiO
                    <sub>2</sub>
                    Integrated Optical Polarizers
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Polarization control is essential for modern optical systems. Recently, 2D materials featuring highly anisotropic absorption across broad wavelength regions have emerged as a promising solution for realizing optical polarizers with operation bandwidths far exceeding those achievable using bulk materials. Despite this, existing 2D‐material‐based optical polarizers face critical limitations in simultaneously delivering high polarizer figures of merit (FOMs), robust power endurance, and scalable fabrication, hindering their practical deployment beyond the laboratory. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by demonstrating optical polarizers through integrating 2D MXene films onto silicon photonic devices and subsequently converting them in situ into 2D titanium dioxide (TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ). The 2D TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    exhibits significantly improved anisotropic absorption and thermal/chemical stability compared with MXene, enabling the hybrid polarizers that achieve high polarizer FOMs of up to ∼19.3 (a record among 2D‐material‐coated devices) and excellent power tolerance (stable under > 2 W coupled average power), together with a broad operation bandwidth (> 140 nm) and a high fabrication yield (∼98%). We also demonstrate microring resonator polarizers achieving high polarization extinction ratios of up to ∼12 dB. With outstanding overall performance and strong potential for large‐scale manufacturing, these devices represent a solid step toward industrial implementation of 2D‐material‐based optical polarizers.
                  </jats:p>

title: Optimal Power Flow for Sustainable Operation of Transmission Systems with High Renewable Penetration
abstract: <jats:p>The paper presents an integrated approach to Optimal Power Flow (OPF) in transmission systems with a high share of renewable energy sources (RESs) supported by energy storage systems (ESSs). Unlike conventional approaches, the proposed integrated evaluation framework minimizes operating cost subject to technical (network and ESS) constraints, while separately reporting RES utilization/curtailment and CO2 outcomes as post-solve indicators. The model was implemented as a browser-based JavaScript application using a custom Big-M Simplex linear programming solver and tested on a 24 h horizon under multiple scenarios representing conditions informed by Baltic/Latvian load, generation, and price profiles, applied to a modified IEEE 9-bus test network, including standard operation, high price volatility, high RES penetration, and a transmission line outage (N-1 criterion). The results demonstrate that ESS integration together with RES usage maximization reduces total operating costs by up to 10.2% compared to the baseline strategy without ESS and optimization (about 4.7 percentage points of this saving come from the lower minimum output of the conventional unit alone), increases RES share by about 5 percentage points, and decreases RES curtailment to 0%, under a terminal state of charge condition that prevents the ESS from ending the horizon more depleted than it started (imposed in HiGHS runs of the same linear program). Under high RES scenarios, ESSs become essential for balancing variability, while in volatile markets they support stable dispatching within the model. A sensitivity analysis highlights the dominant influence of market price fluctuations, with smaller effects of ESS capacity and RES share on total operating cost. The findings indicate that, within the transportation-type network model used, the proposed approach improves economic efficiency and environmental performance, offering a practical decision-support tool for transmission system operators and energy planners.</jats:p>

title: Effect of By-Product-Derived Low-Melting-Point Additive on Mineralogical and Metallurgical Properties of Iron Ore Sinter
abstract: <jats:p>Reducing solid fuel consumption in iron ore sintering is an important strategy for lowering fossil fuel use and associated CO2 emissions. However, insufficient heat input can limit liquid-phase formation and compromise sinter quality. In this study, a by-product-derived low-melting-point additive (LMA) was used under reduced-fuel sintering condition, and the resulting mineralogical characteristics, pore structural, and metallurgical properties were evaluated. Preformed Ca–Fe–O phases accounted for 46.2 wt.% of the quantified crystalline phase assemblage in the LMA. Differential scanning calorimetry revealed a thermal event near 1200 °C, interpreted as being associated with the onset of liquid-phase formation. In sinter pot tests, the LMA-containing reduced-fuel condition (RFL) exhibited a lower maximum bed temperature than the conventional reference condition (STD), decreasing from 1375 to 1339 °C. With the mean STD values normalized to 100%, the relative mean reducibility index, tumble index, and reduction disintegration index of RFL were 104.7%, 101.8%, and 100.3%, respectively, indicating that these quality indices remained broadly comparable despite the reduced fuel input. Rietveld refinement indicated a higher magnetite fraction and a lower SFCA-I fraction in RFL, suggesting that the higher mean reducibility could not be explained by bulk mineralogy alone. Optical microscopy of entire specimen cross-sections revealed a lower pore area fraction and a more consolidated structure in RFL, whereas mercury intrusion porosimetry indicated that mercury-accessible pore volume associated with pore-entry sized below 50 μm was largely maintained. Overall, these findings suggest that the combined use of LMA and reduced fuel input can maintain sinter quality at a lower maximum bed temperature. The pore-structure results provide a possible explanation for the higher mean reducibility despite the mineralogical changes, although a causal relationship has not been established.</jats:p>

The Influence of Students' Perceptions of the Method Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) Towards English Language Achievement With Motivation to Study as a Mediator in Junior High School X
journal: Enrichment: Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Development
abstract: <jats:p>English language achievement is associated with instructional experiences and students’ learning motivation; however, the mediating role of motivation in the relationship between perceptions of Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) and academic achievement requires further investigation. This study examined the direct and indirect relationships between students’ perceptions of CLT and English language achievement, with learning motivation serving as a mediating variable. A quantitative, nonexperimental research design employing path analysis was conducted at a private junior high school in Pantai Indah Kapuk, Indonesia. The participants included 120 eighth-grade students, while an additional 30 students participated in instrument testing. Data were collected using a 40-item CLT perception questionnaire, a 30-item learning motivation questionnaire, and second-semester English report card grades. Content validity was evaluated using Aiken’s V coefficient, while internal consistency reliability was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha. Data were analyzed using JASP statistical software. The results revealed positive associations between students’ perceptions of CLT and learning motivation (? = 0.978) and between CLT perceptions and English language achievement (? = 0.550). Learning motivation was also positively associated with English language achievement (? = 0.407), with a statistically significant indirect association (? = 0.398), indicating partial mediation. These findings suggest that favorable perceptions of communicative language instruction are associated with improved English language achievement, partly through learning motivation. Nevertheless, the exceptionally strong association between CLT perceptions and motivation suggests potential construct overlap, warranting cautious interpretation. The findings highlight the importance of communicative instructional practices and motivational support, while further longitudinal research is recommended to establish temporal relationships and examine the generalizability of these findings across diverse educational settings.</jats:p>

title:
An N-Heterocyclic
Imine-Supported Two-Coordinate
1,2-Bis(borinium) Dication
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Two-coordinate diboron(II) dications represent highly electron-deficient species that deviate substantially from the classical octet rule. Their extreme electrophilicity, significant Coulombic repulsion, and inherent instability render their isolation particularly challenging, leaving them hitherto elusive. Herein, we report an N-heterocyclic imine (NHI)-supported formal 1,2-bis(borinium) dication, an isoelectronic analogue of the diberyllocene, featuring a unique B(sp)–B(sp) bonding motif devoid of σ-donor stabilization and free from counterion and solvent interactions. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis reveals that the resulting two-coordinate diboron(II) dication adopts a nearly linear −C–N–B–B–N–C– arrangement. DFT calculations suggest that it is best described as an N≡B–B≡N core, with two B≡N-type units linked by a B–B single bond and capped by imidazolium-type rings, with two vacant π*(B–N) orbitals localized at the boron atoms. Reactivity studies further establish that this species behaves as a Lewis superacid, capable of small molecule activation and functions as an efficient precatalyst to promote diverse catalytic transformations under mild conditions.</jats:p>

EXTREPSO: An Energy Estimator Based on Machine Learning with PSO Optimization for UASNs
abstract: <jats:p>Underwater acoustic sensor networks (UASNs) are severely affected by propagation delay, limited bandwidth, and constrained node energy. This work presents EXTREPSO, a machine learning framework that combines an Extra Trees Regressor with Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) for offline hyperparameter tuning of a hop-level energy-efficiency predictor. The target is derived from Aqua-Sim NG trace fields using the payload size, the simulator Tx_power field, and observed hop delay. Aqua-Sim NG defines PT as transmitted signal power in watts, so the target has dimensional units of bit/J; however, because the observed hop delay includes propagation and protocol-related waiting, it is treated as an operational trace-derived metric rather than a state-resolved modem-energy measurement. In the original 80:20 benchmark, Extra Trees was the strongest baseline among seven classical ML and three DL models. A leakage-resistant sender-grouped outer five-fold evaluation with inner grouped validation was subsequently used to compare baseline Extra Trees, PSO-tuned Extra Trees, and an interpretable inverse-power baseline on untouched test folds. PSO tuning produced a modest average improvement over baseline Extra Trees (mean RMSE 2107.31 versus 2230.58), but the improvement was not consistent across folds; the inverse-power baseline achieved the lowest mean RMSE (1765.88). A separate five-run equal-budget PSO/GWO sensitivity check also found no meaningful superiority of PSO over GWO. These results support the trace-driven prediction and hyperparameter-tuning workflow while limiting claims of universal optimizer benefit or direct network-energy improvement.</jats:p>

title: Sustainable Procurement Optimization Using Predictive Compliance Dashboards in ESG-Critical Energy Infrastructure Projects
journal: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
abstract:
<jats:p>The growing emphasis on Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) criteria has intensified
the need for sustainability-oriented procurement strategies within energy infrastructure projects.
This review explores the integration of predictive compliance dashboards to enhance procurement
optimization in ESG-critical contexts. These dashboards leverage real-time analytics, historical
compliance data, and AI-driven insights to forecast risks, enforce regulatory alignment, and
support proactive decision-making across procurement lifecycles. By embedding sustainability
metrics into procurement processes, energy firms can ensure supplier transparency, reduce
environmental footprints, and strengthen social responsibility and governance standards. The
study examines existing frameworks, case applications in energy infrastructure projects, and the
technological architecture underlying predictive dashboards. It further highlights challenges
related to interoperability, data governance, and regulatory fragmentation, proposing a roadmap
for the scalable adoption of dashboard-driven procurement systems. This paper contributes to
sustainable infrastructure development by underscoring the strategic importance of data-centric
tools in managing ESG performance across complex supply networks.</jats:p>

title: Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Solid-State Sintered SiC Brazed with a Novel Si-Ti-Al/Mo Composite Filler
abstract: <jats:p>In this study, to advance the research on near-homogeneous welding technology for silicon carbide ceramics required for service in nuclear environments and to meet the high-performance welding and reliable service requirements of silicon carbide ceramic fuel elements, a novel Si-Ti-Al/Mo composite filler was employed to achieve the joining of solid-state sintered silicon carbide (SiC) via vacuum brazing, thereby providing an innovative technical solution for the integration of high-performance SiC components. The research systematically elucidated the interfacial metallurgical mechanism governed by this novel alloy, and comprehensively investigated the effects of brazing temperature on joint microstructure, room-temperature and high-temperature mechanical properties, as well as fracture morphology. In the filler metal design, the pre-added Mo served as a heterogeneous nucleating agent, preferentially reacting with Si, which effectively suppressed the extensive formation of the TiSi2 phase. Concurrently, the introduction of Mo significantly refined the grain structure within the joint region. Brazing at 1360 °C yielded a peak room-temperature shear strength of 144 MPa. Moreover, the joints exhibited excellent high-temperature service reliability, retaining a shear strength of 64 MPa at a test temperature of 1000 °C. This novel joining technology is expected to promote the widespread engineering application of high-performance SiC components in extremely harsh environments.</jats:p>

title: Geomechanics of Refracturing and Infill Well Development in Unconventional Reservoirs: A Review on Stress Evolution and Fracture Propagation
abstract: <jats:p>Secondary stimulation introduces fractures into reservoirs whose pressure, stress and fracture condition have been altered by earlier development. Refracturing and infill-well treatments can consequently reactivate old pathways, create new orientations or produce unequal fracture wings. This review links these responses through an evolved geomechanical state that retains primary-fracturing, closure and production history. Published analytical, numerical, laboratory and field studies are compared using two coupled controls: path selection and pathway activation or propagation resistance. Principal-stress orientation, gradients and interfaces influence direction, while resolved normal traction, contact, toughness and hydraulic access determine whether a candidate pathway opens and continues to grow. The distinction explains why a favorable reorientation zone may still feed an old fracture, and why parent-directed steering can coexist with local resistance near inherited fractures. Refracturing evidence emphasizes the sequence of access modification, new initiation and subsequent competition; parent-child studies emphasize heterogeneous depletion, asymmetric growth and the difference between mechanical accessibility and remaining resource. Modeling methods are assessed by their ability to reconstruct the produced state and transfer it consistently into a propagation calculation. Monitoring studies show how pressure, seismicity, deformation, distributed strain and temperature constrain different parts of that calculation. Agreement should be tested in the observation domain and against withheld treatments. The synthesis identifies contact history, three-dimensional connectivity, proppant placement and verified state transfer as priorities for predicting useful reservoir contact after secondary stimulation.</jats:p>

title: Modeling individual nearby radio galaxies as ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray accelerators
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Nearby radio galaxies are among the most promising candidates for the acceleration of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs). In this work, we develop a physically motivated, source-resolved framework to quantify the contribution of the three nearest Fanaroff–Riley Class I (FR-I) radio galaxies – Centaurus A, Virgo A, and Fornax A – to the UHECR flux measured by the Pierre Auger Observatory. By fitting our simulation exclusively to the measured UHECR energy spectrum, we determine the relative contribution of each source and constrain the fraction of jet power converted into UHECR luminosity. title: Dietary Energy Density Functions as a Transferable Decision Principle in Children: Evidence from Structured Errors, Generalization, and Time-Constrained Decisions
abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objective: Dietary energy density (ED; kcal/g) influences energy intake and is central to obesity prevention. Little is known about how children understand energy density and apply the knowledge in decision-making contexts. This study examines classification accuracy, structured error patterns, and decision-making during a serious game intervention: a cognitive decision-process analysis of how children apply the concept of dietary ED, using serious gameplay data as behavioral readout. Methods: Gameplay data from a cluster-randomized controlled trial were analyzed. Children aged 9–11 years (n = 82) participated in a serious game intervention targeting energy density of foods (tasks with and without time pressure), beverage sugar content, and overall meal composition. Analyses focused on first-attempt responses to assess spontaneous application of the dietary ED concept. In-game decision patterns were used to assess children’s ability to classify foods by ED, estimate sugar content in beverages, and adapt food choices across repeated gameplay sessions. Results: Children understand ED. Misclassifications occurred predominantly between adjacent ED categories, with medium-ED (1.5–2.5 kcal/g) foods posing the greatest challenge. Classification accuracy was highest for fruits, vegetables, and high-energy sweets, while cereals and dairy products showed greater variability. Under time pressure, accuracy remained largely stable, with modestly longer decision times for nutritionally similar item pairs. Sugar content in fruit-based beverages was underestimated. Over repeated gameplay sessions, children increasingly selected lower-energy-density foods, reflecting a shift toward more energy-density-appropriate choices. Conclusions: The findings suggest that children acquire a transferable decision principle rather than memorizing isolated food properties. Teaching transferable nutritional concepts rather than isolated food facts may promote lasting improvements in nutritional literacy and support early obesity prevention.</jats:p>

journal: Balkan Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering
abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">The objective of this study was to predict the onset of high demand, the highest half-hourly average power, and the total duration of high demand over the next two hours using historical electricity consumption data from residential households. Half-hourly measurements from 2013 for 200 standard-tariff residential households selected from the Low Carbon London dataset were used. High demand was defined as exceeding the 90th percentile of each household’s average power values during the January–February period. The models were developed using data from 160 households; transfer performance was evaluated on the 40 households not included in model training. The process was divided into a training period (March–June), model selection in July, calibration of prediction intervals in August, and a testing period (September–December). The selected models were retrained using March–July data. Separate models were built for the three targets; Random Forest, histogram-based gradient boosting (HistGB), XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost were compared against a weekly seasonal reference. Model selection was initially based on average precision (AP) for the target and mean absolute error (MAE) for power and duration. For the residential units used in the training, the HistGB model selected during the testing period produced an AP of 0.4183; the CatBoost models produced an MAE of 0.2704 kW for power and 9.2361 minutes for duration. The contributions of historical consumption and calendar features to the model predictions were examined using the SHAP method. In the early warning evaluation, 78.81% of relevant events in known residential units were detected in advance; 60.93% of early warnings were identified as false alarms. The improvement in duration prediction relative to a reference that yields a duration of zero in every window remained limited. The findings indicate that the approach could contribute to monitoring residential demand; however, the burden of false alarms and the limited success in duration prediction must be taken into account from a practical standpoint.</jats:p>

title: An Augmented Lagrangian Lyrebird Optimization for UPQC-based optimal power flow in wind-integrated power systems
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part A: Journal of Power and Energy
abstract: <jats:p>The large-scale integration of wind energy into modern power systems introduces operational uncertainties, voltage instability, and power quality degradation due to the intermittent nature of wind speed variations. This paper proposes a Power Quality-Constrained Optimal Power Flow (PQ-OPF) framework for wind-integrated power systems using the Augmented Lagrangian Lyrebird Optimization Algorithm (AL-LOA). A probabilistic wind generation model based on the Weibull distribution is employed to capture stochastic wind behavior, and the wind turbine output is modeled using a piecewise nonlinear power curve. The formulated PQ-OPF problem incorporates voltage deviation, reactive power limits, line flow constraints, and total harmonic distortion (THD) as power quality constraints. The Augmented Lagrangian method effectively handles equality and inequality constraints, while the Lyrebird Optimization algorithm enhances global search capability and convergence robustness in nonlinear and non-convex solution spaces. To further improve system performance, a Unified Power Quality Conditioner (UPQC) is optimally installed at a critical bus identified based on voltage and harmonic analysis. The proposed method is validated on the IEEE 57-bus test system under varying wind penetration levels (20%–50%). Simulation results show that the proposed AL-LOA-based PQ-OPF achieves up to 14.6% reduction in real power losses, 6.8% improvement in minimum bus voltage, and 30% reduction in THD compared to conventional OPF and existing metaheuristic techniques. In addition, improved convergence characteristics and constraint satisfaction demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for reliable, efficient, and high-quality operation of wind-integrated power systems.</jats:p>

Classification Evaluation Parameters and Criteria for Coal Reservoirs in the Shuixigou Group, Taibei Sag, Turpan-Hami Basin, China
abstract: <jats:p>Deep coalbed methane (CBM) has increasingly become a critical alternative resource in unconventional natural gas exploration. However, the classification and evaluation of deep coal reservoirs in the Turpan-Hami Basin remain insufficient, considerably hindering CBM exploration and development. This study investigates the Shuixigou Group coal reservoirs in the Taibei Sag, by analyzing their thermal evolution, physical properties, microscopic pore-throat structures, and peat-accumulation paleoenvironment, integrated with measured gas content data. Furthermore, key parameters and criteria for reservoir classification are proposed. The results indicated the following: (1) the coal rank was primarily low to medium, with well-developed pores and fractures. The Pore geometry is predominantly slit like, with mesopores constituting the main reservoir space. (2) the paleoenvironments ranged from strongly waterlogged to very humid-waterlogged conditions, with relatively high vitrinite contents. The coal assemblages can be categorized into three types: “mudstone interbedded with thick coal seams,” “tight sandstone interbedded with thin coal seams,” and “tight sandstone interbedded with thin coal seams.” (3) Very humid-waterlogged forest swamp environments, reducing conditions, and lower delta plain settings were favorable for the development of high-rank coal reservoirs. With increasing burial depth and coal rank, the proportion of mesopores and micropores increased, pore size distribution became more uniform, and both porosity and fracture density improved. (4) Based on gas content as the primary indicator, along with 11 key parameters, the coal reservoirs are classified into three categories. This study provides practical guidance for the exploration and development of deep CBM in the Taibei Sag of the Turpan-Hami Basin.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>A estrutura curricular do atual Ensino Médio brasileiro foi marcada, nos últimos dez anos, por profundas mudanças. Este estudo, por meio de uma pesquisa bibliográfica-documental, tem como objetivo situar a Educação Física (EF) no currículo do Ensino Médio ofertado pelas escolas da rede pública do Espírito Santo. title: Interfacial Integration of Cross-Kingdom Membranes Establishes a Rechargeable Energy Cascade
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Engineering modular adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-mediated energy transduction pathways from the bottom up faces two key bottlenecks: first, detergent-dependent reconstitution typically impairs protein activity and energetic coupling efficiency due to disrupted native lipid environments and randomized protein orientation; second, physically separated ATP production and consumption modules suffer from severe diffusional ATP losses and inefficient intermodule cascade coupling. To address both limitations, we report a programmable, nondestructive strategy to construct a high-performance artificial organelle—the “chrometabosome”—through orthogonal peptide-driven fusion of photosynthetic chromatophores and energy-consuming erythrosomes. Bypassing detergent solubilization and reconstitution, this strategy not only preserves membrane proteins in their native lipid environment and functional state but also colocalizes ATP-producing and ATP-consuming modules within a single nanoscale compartment. This colocalization reduces the dependence of ATP utilization on intervesicle transport, producing a 3- to 4-fold kinetic enhancement at lower vesicle concentrations relative to nonintegrated controls. This light-rechargeable system offers a modular framework for versatile biohybrid energy nanosystems.</jats:p>

title: Inverse energy transfer in three-dimensional quantum vortex flows
abstract: <jats:p>Vortex reconnections play a fundamental role in fluids. They increase the complexity of flow and develop small-scale motions. In this work we report that in superfluids they can also excite large scales. We numerically illustrate that during a superfluid vortex reconnection energy is injected into the thermal (normal) component of helium II at small length scales, but is transferred nonlinearly to larger length scales, increasing the integral length scale of the normal fluid. This inverse energy transfer constrasts with the reconnection-triggered energy transfer to smaller scales observed along the superfluid vortices and in classical fluids, underlining that similarities and differences between quantum and classical vortex dynamics may depend on the fluid component investigated. In addition, by studying about 50 different reconnections, we show that the reconnection event injects a nonzero net helicity in the normal fluid as a result of the chiral character of the mutual friction force coupling the superfluid vortices and the normal component, contributing to the understanding of the impact of topology-changing events on the helical balance of superfluid flows.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Gravitational boundary constructions as diverse as Israel junction conditions, the black-hole membrane paradigm, stochastic inflation, and vacuum bubble dynamics all require boundary compensating stress-energy where a localized stress-energy source transitions to zero. This paper identifies the common structure behind them: a Bianchi-required compensator, forced when smooth finite-domain localization makes the stress-energy divergence, by the Leibniz rule of covariant differentiation, pick up a boundary term. The need for a completion is therefore not an added ingredient or model choice, but a structural consequence of restricting matter to a finite spacetime domain. A Vanishing Lemma shows that, for phase-incoherent boundary layers with integrable renormalized connected stress correlations, bounded local stress, and the minimal-retarded prescription, the compensator disappears under coarse-graining far beyond the boundary thickness, recovering general relativity (GR). A macroscopic remnant survives only when localization density invalidates independent-event suppression, the boundary remains causally inaccessible throughout the decoherence interval, and the aggregate boundary source has nonzero connected content. These requirements form a Compensator Remnant Formation Theorem. Inflationary Hubble crossing provides the cosmological realization: the horizon window generates the boundary source. Human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes alleviate experimental colitis by maintaining the intestinal barrier and remodeling macrophage polarization
abstract:
<jats:p>BACKGROUND</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, nonspecific inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract for which there are currently no safe and effective therapeutic options. Human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes (hucMSC-Ex) have emerged as a new treatment strategy for IBD owing to their tissue repair and immunoregulatory functions. However, the mechanisms by which hucMSC-Ex exerts their effects on IBD are not yet fully understood.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>AIM</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>To investigate the therapeutic effects of intraperitoneal injection of hucMSC-Ex on intestinal inflammation, intestinal barrier function, and macrophage phenotype in a mouse model of IBD induced with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS).</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>METHODS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>A mouse colitis model was constructed using 2.5% DSS. Three groups were established: Normal control group (NC), DSS model group (DSS), and DSS + hucMSC-Ex group (hucMSC-Ex) (n  = 8/group). General indicators such as body weight change, disease activity index score, colon length, and spleen index were measured. Histopathological damage was evaluated by hematoxylin and eosin staining. The expression of inflammatory factors was detected by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR), Western blot, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Antioxidant stress indicators, including glutathione, superoxide dismutase, and the Nrf2/HO-1/GPX4 axis, were assessed using commercial kits, RT-qPCR, and Western blot. The intestinal mucus barrier and mechanical barrier were examined by immunofluorescence, RT-qPCR, and Western blot. Macrophage polarization was detected by immunofluorescence, flow cytometry, and RT-qPCR. The RAW264.7 cell line was used in vitro  to verify the above findings. A signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) inhibitor was employed to demonstrate that hucMSC-Ex functions via  the Janus kinase (JAK) 1/STAT1 signaling pathway.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>RESULTS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>We found that hucMSC-Ex ameliorated the clinical symptoms of DSS-induced colitis, which mimics human IBD, by reducing colonic inflammation, colonic goblet cell loss, and intestinal mucosal permeability, while promoting the transformation of immature pro-inflammatory macrophages into mature anti-inflammatory macrophages. In vitro , hucMSC-Ex also modulated phenotypic changes in macrophages after RAW264.7 cells were induced toward M1 or M2 phenotypes. Furthermore, hucMSC-Ex altered macrophage phenotypic transformation, thereby ameliorating experimental colitis through modulation of the JAK/STAT signaling pathway both in vivo  and in vitro .</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>CONCLUSION</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>HucMSC-Ex partially alleviates experimental colitis by restoring the intestinal barrier and intestinal immune homeostasis. This finding provides new insights into the therapy of IBD.</jats:p>

Case Report: Running through transplant: preserved aerobic capacity in an elite endurance athlete after allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) imposes profound hematologic, inflammatory, and immunologic stress, and survivors typically show reduced cardiorespiratory fitness that may be further compromised by chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGvHD) and corticosteroid therapy. Competitive, performance-oriented endurance training through these phases has not been described. We report the longitudinal clinical and training course of a 54-year-old elite endurance runner with previously treated Hodgkin lymphoma who resumed structured treadmill exercise on Day +1 after matched-sibling allogeneic peripheral blood stem cell transplantation for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma transformed from follicular lymphoma. Daily physiologic training data were aligned with transplant milestones, donor chimerism, donor lymphocyte infusions (DLI), and immunosuppression, and serial cardiopulmonary exercise testing was performed before and after HCT. The patient exercised through marrow aplasia and progressed to timed running within 100 days; he recorded a 5K of 17:55 (Day +314) and a 10K of 41:00 (Day +340), both during active cGvHD on prednisone plus cyclosporine. Directly measured peak oxygen uptake (VO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    peak) was 75.8 mL/kg/min before HCT and 71.5 mL/kg/min at 7 months post-HCT. Oxygen uptake (VO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ) at the first ventilatory threshold (VT1) was 53.0, 48.0, and 42.4 mL/kg/min before HCT and at 7 and 20 months post-HCT, respectively. VO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    at the second ventilatory threshold (VT2) was 66.0 and 59.9 mL/kg/min before HCT and at 7 months post-HCT, respectively. The 20-month assessment was submaximal; therefore, VO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    peak was not determined. This case illustrates that exceptional aerobic capacity and high-level endurance performance can be maintained during recovery from allogeneic HCT, including during corticosteroid-treated cGvHD, with continued structured training.
                  </jats:p>

Microbial-origin and microbiota-mimic tumor antigens in cancer immunotherapy: from tumor-resident peptides to cross-reactive T-cell targets
abstract: <jats:p>Microbial peptides and microbial mimics of host antigens expand the targets and immunogens available for cancer immunotherapy. Their therapeutic roles depend on which cells present the antigen and how the resulting T-cell response reaches the tumor. Building on reviews of antigen discovery, molecular mimicry, and vaccination, this review compares the cellular mechanisms connecting recognition to tumor injury. Microbial ligands have been recovered from human tumor HLA peptidomes, and individual receptors can recognize both microbial and host peptides. Selected human cell systems connect microbial-peptide stimulation to responses against unpulsed tumor cells. Mouse experiments reveal additional routes through antigen presentation by nonmalignant host cells, local cytotoxic effects, and follicular helper T-cell-supported immune organization. Together, these findings identify different uses for microbial antigens: a ligand displayed by cancer cells can provide a direct target, a mimic can recruit tumor-reactive clones, and a locally presented microbial antigen can sustain cooperating immune populations. These routes place different demands on antigen processing, clone selection, and tissue distribution. Host antigen transfer provides a further source of immune responses, while the antigenic consequences of microbial mutagenesis remain uncharacterized. We examine how these differences affect immunogen design, receptor engineering, tumor selectivity, and interpretation of human immune monitoring. The resulting synthesis identifies testable development options without assigning a single mechanism to all microbial antigens. Human immunological findings support continued investigation; their relationship to sustained clinical benefit remains to be established.</jats:p>

Paneth Cell Metaplasia in Pediatric Distal Colon Biopsies: Incidental Finding or a Predictor of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)?
abstract: <jats:p>Paneth cells are normally found in the small intestine and its presence in the distal colon is referred to as Paneth cell metaplasia (PCM). PCM in children is commonly seen in patients with newly diagnosed inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and in unremarkable rectal mucosa in patients with chronic constipation. However, the significance of PCM in children in a consecutive clinical cohort remains unknown. All distal colon biopsies obtained from pediatric patients during a 6-month period were reviewed for PCM. PCM was identified in 32 of 188 cases (17%), median age of 14 years (range: 3-17), and 75% were male. The most common location for PCM was the descending colon, and abdominal pain was the most common indication for colonoscopy. Nineteen cases (59%) had at least 1 additional feature of chronic mucosal injury and 4 patients (12%) had non-necrotizing mucosal granulomas. At the time of the biopsy, only 9 patients (28.1%) had a clinical diagnosis of IBD (4 Crohn disease [CD] and 5 ulcerative colitis [UC]) but at the end of the follow-up period, most patients (87.5%) had a diagnosis of IBD (15 CD and 13 UC). Six patients with PCM had a normal colonoscopy and an otherwise normal histology and of these 3 developed IBD. Our findings suggest a strong association with PCM in the distal colon in pediatric patients and the subsequent development of IBD. This highlights the importance of identifying PCM in distal colon biopsies.</jats:p>

title: Combined Saussurea costus and doxorubicin suppresses breast cancer cell migration and proliferation through MMP2/MMP9 downregulation: in vitro and molecular docking evidence
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Breast cancer (BC) is still a major cause of cancer-related death in women and requires new strategies for treatment.
                    <jats:italic>Saussurea costus</jats:italic>
                    (COS) has been reported to exhibit anticancer activity, and doxorubicin (DOX) is a commonly used chemotherapeutic agent. The relationship between their roles and BC cell behavior and regulation remains unclear. 28 compounds were identified in the COS ethanolic extract by LC–ESI–MS/MS. The docking and dynamics study of major compounds with MMP2 and MMP9 was performed. The effects of COS, DOX, and their combination on MCF7 and MDA-MB-231 cells were assessed for cytotoxicity, proliferation, migration (wound healing and transwell), colony formation, apoptosis (annexin-V), cell cycle, and MMP2/MMP9 mRNA expression. The main compounds found were apigenin (12.99%), medioresinol (8.32%), and luteolin (8.12%). Luteolin had the most negative value for protein binding (MMP2: − 8.90 kcal/mol; MMP9: − 9.50 kcal/mol) and medioresinol for mRNA binding. COS demonstrated dose-dependent cytotoxicity (IC
                    <jats:sub>50</jats:sub>
                    : 106.8 ± 1.43 μg/mL for MCF7; 116.8 ± 5.66 μg/mL for MDA-MB-231). The COS + DOX combination significantly reduced proliferation, migration, and colony formation, and increased apoptosis (MCF7: 34.85 ± 1.84%, MDA-MB-231: 45.56 ± 7.74%), and induced G2/M arrest in MDA-MB-231 cells. The expression of MMP2 and MMP9 mRNA was significantly downregulated. The COS + DOX treatment had a combinatorial effect in suppressing BC cell growth and migration, which was associated with downregulation of MMP2/MMP9 and induction of apoptosis. While these findings suggest a potential mechanistic role for MMP2/MMP9 downregulation, future studies measuring protein expression and enzymatic activity are required to confirm functional inhibition. Given its potential therapeutic significance, further in vivo studies are warranted.
                  </jats:p>

title:
Preparation of Ether-free Polycarbazole-Based Anion
Exchange Membranes and Regulation of Cations on Membrane Properties
and Fuel Cell Performance
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quaternized ether-free aromatic polymers from superacid-catalyzed polycondensation are excellent candidates for high-performance anion exchange membranes (AEMs). Most current studies mainly focus on cation-modified carbon-aromatic AEMs. However, the structure–property relationship of cation-functionalized heteroaromatic polyarylene systems is still insufficiently understood. This work develops a series of carbazole-based ether-free AEMs with different side-chain quaternary ammonium (QA) cations, including conventional trimethylammonium, charge-delocalized imidazolium, and N-cyclic piperidinium and quinuclidinium. All membranes share the same polycarbazole backbone. Thus, the side-chain cation structure primarily determines membrane comprehensive performance. QPC-TMA with trimethylammonium groups exhibits the highest hydroxide conductivity at 80 °C, owing to its high ion exchange capacity and well-developed microphase separation. In comparison, QPC-QUI with bulky quinuclidinium groups shows outstanding alkaline and oxidative stability under harsh aging conditions. It shows least conductivity loss (2.65% loss for 1080 h) and weight loss (0.81% loss for 72 h).In fuel cell tests, the QPC-QUI-based AEM achieves a peak power density of 998 mW cm–2, which is higher than QPC-TMA (928 mW cm–2). This work proves that rational cation structural design of ether-free heteroaromatic polymers is a reliable strategy to prepare high-conductivity and durable AEMs for electrochemical energy applications.</jats:p>

Creating a palliative care skills training for health care professionals in allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation recipients: symptom management to end-of-life care
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) presents a complex procedure with curative intent in haematological disorders, but is associated with high toxicity. Acute graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) and infections are early complications with high mortality, while fatigue and chronic GvHD contribute to significant late morbidity. Our preceding study revealed substantial palliative care needs, including patients’ uncertainty and existential fears, alongside Health Care Professionals (HCP) reported uncertainty and call for further training in addressing these challenges.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To address these needs, we developed and piloted a one-day training for HCPs, based on Brown’s Design Thinking principles, covering symptom management, end-of-life care, patients’ and family caregivers’ perceived life threat, and goals-of-care discussions. The training, led by a palliative care specialist, was held in three 6-8 h sessions with a total of 28 participants. It was delivered through various learning modules, interactive components, and group discussions. The programme was evaluated at three time points (pre-training, post-training, one-month follow-up) using self-confidence and practice transfer surveys, complemented by open feedback, and analysed descriptively.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At one month post-training, participants reported increased self-confidence across all domains on a 10-point scale (Δmdn = + 1 to + 2), with the most substantial gains in goals-of-care discussions and end-of-life care. Training content was positively evaluated across all HCP groups, and practice transfer was rated as moderate. Feedback highlighted the value of case-based discussions, with calls for more interactive and interdisciplinary elements.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite a small sample, single-centre design, and short-term follow-up, this study provides a scalable model for integrating palliative care education into haematology settings. The findings suggest that structured, interdisciplinary training can strengthen HCPs’ confidence and competence in addressing palliative care needs in the allo-HSCT context. Future studies should evaluate the intervention across multiple centres to assess its broader applicability and impact.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>It was registered in the German Registry of Clinical Trials (DRKS00027290) on January 10, 2022.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Prognostic and clinicopathological significance of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene amplification in oral squamous cell carcinoma: systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the current evidence in relation to the clinicopathological and prognostic significance of
                      <jats:italic>EGFR</jats:italic>
                      gene amplification in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A comprehensive search was undertaken in MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Web of Science and Scopus for studies published before June-2026. We evaluated the quality of primary-level studies using QUIPS tool, conducted meta-analyses, examined inter-study heterogeneity via subgroup analyses and meta-regressions, and performed small-study effects analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In total, fifteen primary-level studies (1,561 patients) met inclusion criteria.
                      <jats:italic>EGFR</jats:italic>
                      amplification was significantly associated with poor overall survival (HR = 1.98, 95% CI = 1.32–2.98,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.001), disease-free survival (HR = 1.66, 95% CI = 1.03–2.67,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.04),
                      <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                       + status (OR = 1.73, 95% CI = 1.08–2.77,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.02) and advanced clinical stage (OR = 1.78, 95% CI = 1.08–2.94,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.02). Subgroup meta-analyses also revealed significant associations among Asian subpopulations, patients with tongue tumors, and studies with a lower risk of bias.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Our systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrated, based on the available evidence, that
                      <jats:italic>EGFR</jats:italic>
                      gene amplification may be useful as a prognostic biomarker for OSCC.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Systematic Review Registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:ext-link>https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO</jats:ext-link>

                    </jats:p>

title: Low-dose curcumin inhibits ferroptosis in human periodontal ligament stem cells via ROCK1 downregulation
journal: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Periodontitis is pathologically characterized by impaired function of human periodontal ligament stem cells (hPDLSCs). Curcumin has attracted considerable attention due to its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties; however, its effects on ferroptosis in hPDLSCs and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the role of curcumin in hPDLSC ferroptosis and its potential regulatory mechanisms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Following curcumin treatment at various concentrations, cell proliferation was assessed by CCK-8 assay, ROCK1 expression was detected by real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) and Western blotting, ferrous iron (Fe
                      <jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>
                      ) and glutathione (GSH) levels were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay kits, and mitochondrial membrane potential was evaluated by JC-1 staining.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Low-dose curcumin (0.001–0.01 μM) significantly promoted hPDLSC proliferation, reduced intracellular Fe
                      <jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>
                      levels, elevated GSH content, suppressed the aberrant expression of ferroptosis-related proteins, and restored mitochondrial membrane potential. Notably, ROCK1 overexpression effectively reversed these protective effects, indicating that the action of curcumin is ROCK1-dependent. Furthermore, under Erastin-induced ferroptotic stress, low-dose curcumin reversed the Erastin-induced increases in Fe
                      <jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>
                      , ACSL4, and lipid peroxidation, restored GSH, Ferritin, and GPX4 levels, and rescued hPDLSC proliferation, with effects comparable to those of Ferrostatin-1.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Low-dose curcumin exerts cytoprotective effects on hPDLSCs by simultaneously promoting proliferation and suppressing ferroptosis via downregulation of ROCK1 expression. These findings unveil a novel mechanism by which curcumin modulates hPDLSC fate, provide a theoretical basis for hPDLSC-based protective strategies in periodontitis therapy, and highlight ROCK1 as a potential molecular target for periodontal regenerative intervention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: An Integrated Explainable Machine Learning Framework for Cell-to-Pack Imbalance Prediction in Electric Vehicle Battery Systems
journal: International Journal of Electrical and Electronics Engineering
abstract: <jats:p>This study presents a machine learning framework for predicting cell-to-pack imbalance in electric vehicle batteries. A set of battery attributes that affect battery performance, including State of Charge (SOC), State of Health (SOH), temperature (including ambient temperature and humidity), and cabin temperature, were used to make this prediction. The collected battery data were pre-processed to improve prediction performance. Three preprocessing methods were used: (i) Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD); (ii) deep denoising autoencoders, and (iii) feature selection using minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance (mRMR) mutual information. This preprocessing step removes noise from the dataset and identifies useful information for prediction. Cell-to-pack imbalance prediction was performed using three interpretable machine learning models: (i) an Explainable Boosting Machine (EBM); (ii) fuzzy regression; and (iii) RuleFit. These models provide transparent predictions and help in understanding the factors responsible for battery imbalance. Models were evaluated on an independent 20-sample test set held out from the 100-record dataset. Among the three interpretable models, Fuzzy Regression achieved the strongest predictive performance (R² = 0.998), followed by RuleFit (R² = 0.976), while EBM achieved a lower R² of 0.201 on this independent test set despite providing detailed feature-level explanations. These results indicate that combining signal preprocessing, feature selection, and interpretable regression can provide useful and explainable information for cell-to-pack imbalance prediction, while also showing that performance can vary substantially between interpretable models on a small, two-pack dataset; validation on larger and more varied battery datasets is needed to confirm generalizability.</jats:p>

Multiscale Drug–Cell
Interaction Modeling via
Hybrid Graph Architectures and Knowledge-Aware Fusion for Drug Synergy
Prediction
journal:
Journal of Chemical Information
and Modeling
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate prediction of drug combination synergy remains challenging due to the vast combinatorial space and strong cellular context dependency of drug responses. To address these limitations, we present MILSyn, a multimodal interaction learning framework designed to capture multiscale drug–cell interactions through three integrated components: (1) relational modeling of heterogeneous graph structures using a hybrid RGCN-GATv2 architecture, (2) cross-modal fusion of biochemical features spanning SMILES, substructures, 3D conformations, and multiomic profiles, and (3) knowledge-aware reasoning via LLM-derived semantic embeddings. Evaluated on DrugComb and four benchmark data sets, MILSyn consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models, demonstrating robust generalization in cold-start scenarios and notable performance gains under few-shot fine-tuning for rare tumors. Attention-based analyses provide exploratory summaries of gene-, pathway-, and substructure-level features associated with the model’s predictions, generating hypotheses for further investigation. By combining scalability with interpretability, MILSyn provides a practical framework for prioritizing candidate drug combinations in precision oncology.</jats:p>
