title: Optimizing psychiatric hospitalization decisions: staff perspectives on a machine learning clinical decision support tool for suicidal veterans in the emergency department
journal: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although hospitalization is the standard of care for emergency department (ED) patients judged to have high risk of suicide, experimental and non-experimental studies have failed to find evidence that hospitalization of suicidal ED patients is associated with reduced prevalence of subsequent suicides. However, a recent machine learning analysis of Veterans Health Administration (VHA) data found evidence that this failure might be due to hospitalization helping some suicidal veterans (i.e., reducing their risk of subsequent suicide) but hurting others (i.e., increasing risk). If made readily available to ED staff, this information creates an opportunity to optimize hospitalization decisions, thereby improving clinical outcomes and decreasing costs associated with low-value hospitalization. Similar to other acute issues seen in the ED (e.g., concern for heart attack), this can be accomplished through use of a clinical decision support (CDS) tool available through the medical record that uses VHA data to provide real-time risk classification and hospitalization recommendations. In this qualitative study, we sought to conduct an initial implementation assessment to understand ED suicide prevention-related workflows and ED-based staff perspectives on barriers and facilitators to using a prototype CDS tool.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Two phases of individual interviews (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 18) were conducted with VHA ED-based staff (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 14) using an interview guide informed by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, a framework which seeks to explain implementation barriers and facilitators across domains such as where the implementation is occurring (e.g., inner setting, outer setting), who is implementing (e.g., characteristics of individuals), what is being implemented (e.g., innovation), and how the implementation is happening (e.g., implementation process). The interviews focused on the best way to present CDS recommendations to clinicians. Interview data were analyzed using rapid qualitative analysis and themes were identified through use of templated summaries, matrices, and discussion to reach consensus.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Interviewees are generally open to integrating a simple, easy to access CDS tool to assist with hospitalization decisions. Most interviewees found the refined CDS tool prototype to be user-friendly, with some caveats. Namely, (1) workflow integration would need to be individualized to maximize uptake, (2) comprehensive staff training on use of the tool would be necessary, (3) strong evidence that the tool is effective would be needed to support use in clinical practice. Interviewees maintained that the tool would be most useful in situations where clinicians are undecided about whether to hospitalize a veteran expressing suicidal ideation and other behaviors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Feedback from ED staff facilitated the refinement of a user-friendly CDS tool to be used in a future pilot implementation study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Modelling Loan Default Data of German Customers: Predictive Machine Learning Studies
abstract: <jats:p>This study considered logistic regression and random forest models in modelling the loan default data of German Customers. The data were randomly partitioned into an 80% training set and a 20% test set. The train set was used to fit the data, while the test set served as the out-of-sample data used to evaluate the performance of the model. On the train set, the random forest performs better than the logistic regression model across all the evaluation metrics. On the test dataset, the random forest has superior specificity, precision, accuracy, and F1-score, but the logistic regression model produced a better sensitivity. This means that the model was better at identifying a bad loan; this is, in fact, the desire and priority of every financial institution – a model that is capable of detecting the risk of loan default. In terms of efficiency, the logistic regression model produced lower variance than the random forest, which had high variance.</jats:p>

title: HESS J1832-085: Evidence of a new gamma-ray binary candidate
abstract:
<jats:p>The Galactic plane survey conducted by the High Energy Stereoscopic System (H.E.S.S.) has revealed numerous teraelectronvolt (TeV) sources, many of which remain unidentified. HESS J1832-085 is a point-like TeV source lacking a confirmed multiwavelength (MWL) counterpart. In this paper, we present evidence supporting a gamma-ray binary interpretation of HESS J1832-085 .
We aim to investigate the nature of HESS J1832-085 using the available X-ray and Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) data, complemented by a near-infrared (NIR) identification of a possible stellar companion and broadband radiative modeling, to assess its classification as a potential gamma-ray binary.
Archival X-ray observations were examined to search for a counterpart and to characterize its spectrum and potential variability. We further analyzed ∼17.3 yrs of Fermi LAT data between 1 and 300 GeV to establish a possible gigaelectronvolt (GeV) counterpart of HESS J1832-085. We also examined archival NIR images from the UKIRT Infrared Deep Sky Survey (UKIDSS) and the Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS), together with 2MASS catalog photometry. The broadband emission was interpreted using models commonly applied to gamma-ray binaries.
A potential X-ray counterpart was identified in archival X-ray data, exhibiting a hard, absorbed spectrum and moderate variability. We also identified a tentative GeV gamma-ray excess that is spatially consistent with HESS J1832-085 and the proposed X-ray counterpart. We further identified a candidate stellar counterpart in both the UKIDSS and 2MASS images, located in close spatial proximity to the X-ray counterpart. The adopted illustrative binary radiative model broadly reproduces the X-ray and TeV emission, but fails to explain the emission from the tentative GeV excess.
Our results support HESS J1832-085 as a promising gamma-ray binary candidate , motivating dedicated MWL follow-up observations to confirm the source nature.</jats:p>

title: Model Predictive Control for a Multiport 4L NPC DAB Converter Under Unbalanced and No-Load Conditions
abstract: <jats:p>Multilevel (ML) neutral-point-clamped (NPC) dual-active-bridge (DAB) topologies have emerged as a promising solution for multiport dc-dc power conversion systems. In particular, the 4L NPC DAB is a promising solution for the auxiliary power module (APM) in electric vehicles (EVs) featuring a multiple-voltage architecture in their auxiliary system (AS). By connecting three low-voltage (LV) battery modules between the 4L dc-link nodes, multiple dc ports with different operating voltages are obtained. Then, EV auxiliary loads can be grouped according to their optimum voltage ratings and supplied from three distinct-voltage dc ports. In this configuration, the main challenge is to regulate the state of charge (SoC) of the LV-battery modules. For this purpose, this paper proposes a moving-discretized-control-set model predictive control (MDCS-MPC) for a 2L–4L NPC DAB in the EV APM application. The proposed control strategy combines the adjustment of modulation angles with the use of redundant switching patterns to regulate the LV-battery modules SoC in a wide operating range, including no-load conditions in the partial-voltage dc ports. Hardware-in-the-loop experiments verify the real-time performance of the proposed control.</jats:p>

title: Image–Morphometric Learning for ZooScan Object Size Classification: Source-Verified Target Auditing and Fusion Reanalysis
abstract: <jats:p>High classification scores are meaningful only if the prediction target is physically consistent. We audited image-only, tabular-only and fusion experiments on 9000 ZooScan objects drawn from the 1,153,507-object PELGAS collection. The archived three-class labels were tertiles of the stored equivalent spherical diameter (ESD), not biomass classes. All 893,542 records exported with version v7.26 followed the documented ESD formula, whereas all 259,965 v7.24 records equalled twice the integer part of projected area divided by π. All 2017 v7.24 objects in the subset fell in the highest archived class. Recomputing ESD consistently from area and pixel calibration changed 3430 of the 9000 labels. The subset spans 13 cruises and 697 cruise–station groups and includes 2639 objects annotated as non-living. On the corrected target, tree-based controls using all descriptors reached a macro-F1 of about 0.998 under both object-stratified and station-grouped evaluation. In preliminary single-seed neural runs without area- or length-based descriptors, tabular networks reached a macro-F1 of 0.89, a Swin-T image model 0.946 and gated fusion 0.944; the image-based runs covered three folds and retained scale cues, so they do not isolate the contribution of each modality. Target provenance should be verified before multimodal performance rankings are used in ecological monitoring.</jats:p>

title: Excursion Depth and the Limits of Boosted Trees on a Drifting Target: The S&P 500 Level as a Stress Test Asset
abstract: <jats:p>Gradient-boosted tree ensembles are widely fitted to economic and financial series that trend, yet a regression tree predicts an average of its training targets and cannot follow a target that rises above its training range. This study measures how much of the forecast error of such ensembles that restriction accounts for, and what the available correction costs. It is a diagnostic study rather than a forecasting one: the log level of the S&P 500 is used as a stress test asset because it drifts steadily beyond any training window. The log index is forecast from five United States macroeconomic indicators lagged one month, over January 2003 to January 2026, at seven rolling origins under two training window rules. We define excursion depth, the distance of a test target beyond the training target range, computed in a backtest from the targets alone. Four boosting implementations are compared with a ridge regression, linear leaf boosting, a linear trend, a random walk with drift, and anchored residual boosting (ARB), which fits the ensemble to the residual of a ridge anchor. The error gap between unanchored and anchored boosting widens with excursion depth, from 0.0065 to 0.1498 in root mean squared error between the shallowest and deepest thirds of beyond-range months, and it tracks depth and not forecast horizon when both are controlled. Diebold–Mariano tests reject equal accuracy for one of the four families and not for their average. Ridge alone is ahead of three of the four anchored ensembles under the expanding origin, while linear leaf boosting leaves the range without the same gain, so a linear term fitted to the whole window is what matters. Inside the training range, unanchored boosting remains more accurate for three of the four families. The random walk with drift is the most accurate forecast of the level, and on monthly log returns no model improves on the historical mean. The results identify the conditions under which boosted trees are an unsuitable estimator for a level target, and excursion depth locates those conditions in a backtest before any model is fitted.</jats:p>

title: Exploring the Role of DDIT3 in Tumorigenesis and Its Potential as a Target for Novel Cancer Therapies
abstract: <jats:p>Cancer continues to be the leading cause of death globally, with mounting evidence associating cellular stress with tumor initiation, progression, and therapeutic resistance. DNA damage-inducible transcript 3 (DDIT3), a key stress-responsive transcription factor, plays a central role in cellular stress responses by regulating apoptosis, cell survival, and the tumor microenvironment. Although DDIT3 has been extensively studied in neurodegenerative and metabolic diseases, its dual role in cancer has only recently begun to emerge. This review systematically explores the intricate functions of DDIT3 in cancer biology, emphasizing its involvement in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, apoptosis regulation, and modulation of the tumor microenvironment. We investigate how DDIT3 interacts with key signaling pathways and its impact on cellular stress responses, such as autophagy and macrophage recruitment within the tumor microenvironment. Furthermore, we evaluate the therapeutic potential of targeting DDIT3 through clinical and preclinical drug studies, concentrating on compounds that enhance its pro-apoptotic functions or inhibit its cancer-promoting activities. This review seeks to provide a comprehensive understanding of DDIT3′s role in tumors, offering insights into future therapeutic strategies targeting this stress-related protein in oncology.</jats:p>

title: Total gamma coloring in graphs
abstract: <jats:p>A coloring of a graph [Formula: see text] is the assignment of colors to the vertices of [Formula: see text] such that no two adjacent vertices receive the same color. The minimum number of colors required to color [Formula: see text] is said to be the chromatic number of [Formula: see text], and is denoted by [Formula: see text]. A subset [Formula: see text] of [Formula: see text] is said to be a dominating set of [Formula: see text] if every vertex in [Formula: see text] is adjacent to some vertex in [Formula: see text]. If the graph induced on [Formula: see text] has no isolates, the [Formula: see text] is said to be a total dominating set of [Formula: see text]. The minimum cardinality of a dominating (total dominating) set of [Formula: see text] is said to be the domination (total domination) number of [Formula: see text], and is denoted by [Formula: see text] ([Formula: see text]). For a graph [Formula: see text] without isolated vertices, a total gamma coloring is a coloring of [Formula: see text], if there is a total dominating set [Formula: see text] of [Formula: see text] such that all vertices in [Formula: see text] receive distinct colors. The minimum number of colors required for a total gamma coloring of [Formula: see text] is called the total gamma chromatic number, and is denoted by [Formula: see text]. In this paper, we investigate [Formula: see text] number of graphs, bounds in terms of chromatic number and total domination number, and characterization of extremal graphs attaining a given [Formula: see text] number.</jats:p>

title: HER2 as a treatment target in desmoplastic small round cell tumors (DSRCT): a retrospective study in a certified sarcoma center
journal: Journal of Cancer Research and Clinical Oncology
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Desmoplastic small round cell tumors (DSRCT) are exceptionally rare and aggressive sarcomas with limited therapeutic options and scarce clinical evidence. We aimed to characterize the clinical course and treatment of patients with molecularly confirmed DSRCT and to investigate HER2 expression as a potential therapeutic target, including real-world experience with trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We retrospectively analyzed patients with DSRCT treated at our specialized and certified sarcoma center. Diagnosis was confirmed by detection of the pathognomonic EWSR1::WT1 fusion. Clinical characteristics, treatment strategies, surgical outcomes, HER2 immunohistochemistry (IHC), and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) results were assessed. Clinical outcomes of patients receiving T-DXd were reviewed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Eleven patients were identified (median age 22 years, range 5–63; 81.8% male). HER2 IHC was 0 in three patients (27.3%), 1 + in three (27.3%), and 2 + in five (45.5%); none showed 3 + expression, and all tumors were FISH-negative. Two extensively pretreated patients with HER2 IHC 2+/FISH-negative tumors received off-label treatment with T-DXd and demonstrated initial radiological responses. One patient experienced subsequent progression and died, whereas the second maintained disease control after more than 10 cycles despite chronic dialysis and without substantial additional toxicity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This molecularly confirmed cohort highlights the aggressive clinical course and substantial unmet therapeutic need in DSRCT. HER2 protein expression was observed in a considerable proportion of tumors despite the absence of HER2 amplification. Responses to T-DXd in two HER2 IHC 2+/FISH-negative patients provide a hypothesis-generating clinical signal supporting further investigation of HER2-directed antibody–drug conjugates in DSRCT.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A novel target capture probe set reveals widespread unknown hybridization in North American pondweeds (Potamogetonaceae)
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Premise</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Advancements in phylogenomics and bioinformatics provide opportunities to more robustly characterize hybrid lineages and incorporate them into phylogenetic hypotheses. Target capture remains the most cost‐effective molecular method of hybrid determination at scale. The pondweed family is an ecologically important but taxonomically difficult freshwater plant family due to high rates of hybridization. Historically, hybrid pondweeds have been challenging to characterize with limited molecular data, and hybridization is thought to be underdescribed as a result.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We designed a novel target capture probe set for Potamogetonaceae targeting 350 loci (Pondweeds350), combining 132 custom Potamogetonaceae targets, 205 Angiosperms353 loci, and 13 functional genes for aquatic adaptation. The probe set was tested on 285 samples of North American Potamogetonaceae. HybPhaser was used to identify and phase hybrid accessions for phylogenetic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Target enrichment was successful for 280 of 285 samples with an average of 336 genes producing contigs per sample. HybPhaser provided evidence for 16 novel hybrid combinations in
                      <jats:italic>Potamogeton</jats:italic>
                      .
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We demonstrate the effectiveness of the Pondweeds350 probe set as well as the utility of HybPhaser in detecting hybrids at a large scale. We provide evidence for undetected
                      <jats:italic>Potamogeton</jats:italic>
                      hybrids in addition to the most densely sampled and well‐resolved phylogeny of North American Potamogetonaceae to date.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A Reproducible Multi-Target Computational Framework for Prioritizing Plant-Derived Natural Products in Alzheimer’s Disease
abstract: <jats:p>Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is biologically heterogeneous, and plant-derived natural products provide chemically diverse starting points for multi-target discovery. Reproducible prioritization is needed to distinguish literature-supported evidence from candidate-specific predictions not yet generated. Our objective was to develop a reproducible, evidence-informed framework for prioritizing plant-derived natural products in AD and define a transparent candidate library and prespecified screening set for subsequent computational and experimental evaluation. Completed work included selection of an AD target panel (AChE/BChE, BACE1, GSK-3β and MAO-B), synthesis of a published target-specific machine-learning (ML) benchmark, curation of a 20-compound candidate library with traceable chemical identities and literature support, and selection of a 13-compound prespecified screening set. Published performance metrics were treated solely as external benchmark evidence. Study-specific model training, prospective ML screening, molecular docking, BBB/drug-likeness and ADMET evaluation, multi-objective ranking, and experimental validation were prespecified as future work and were not performed. The framework links mechanistically justified targets, published ML benchmarks, a chemically diverse 20-compound library, and a 13-compound set for future screening. The library includes evidence-rich reference compounds and comparatively underexplored scaffolds; no candidate-specific computational ranking or selection outcome is reported. This study presents an evidence-informed, multi-target computational framework for prioritizing plant-derived natural products in Alzheimer’s disease. Its methodological contribution lies in integrating a mechanistically defined target panel, published machine-learning benchmarks, a traceable 20-compound candidate library, and a prespecified 13-compound screening set within a transparent prospective evaluation strategy. By distinguishing completed framework-development activities from future computational and experimental analyses, the study establishes a structured foundation for subsequent model validation, multi-objective prioritization, and experimental investigation.</jats:p>

Memory-window engineering: target specifications for duration, retention through division, and amplitude in immune epigenome editing
abstract: <jats:p>Immune activation, tolerance, exhaustion, trained immunity and regulatory stability are held in place by chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, histone modification, and enhancer-promoter wiring. CRISPR-based epigenome editors rewrite these layers without cutting DNA, but most reports address editing efficiency and leave time unanswered. Target duration is a design input to be specified before an editor is chosen; the duration achieved remains an experimental outcome. Memory-window engineering defines a candidate immune edit by three parameters: duration after editor clearance, retention through cell division, and amplitude at single-cell resolution, with target-compartment division rate as an explicit modifier. For passively diluted marks, division rate constrains post-clearance duration; transcriptional and phenotypic persistence may follow different trajectories. Published results from methylation editing at IL1RN, FOXP3 enhancer demethylation, PD-1 enhancer tuning, exhaustion circuits and CRISPRoff programming of primary human T cells are interpreted using their readouts and observation windows; some persistence endpoints remain censored by study duration. Three testable predictions concern CpG density, transcript-versus-mark recovery and division-dependent loss, with competing mechanisms and measurement artefacts considered. Specificity, the nuclease-knockout comparison, and the ethics of durable edits are treated as parts of the same specification. Two design consequences follow. TET-dependent erasure requires oxygen and 2-oxoglutarate; reduced erasure in hypoxic or metabolically inhibitory tumour regions is therefore a hypothesis for edited immune cells. Sustained programming of circulating monocyte output requires an upstream progenitor strategy, whereas long-lived resident myeloid cells are a separate case. A worked CAR T example and five-item reporting minimum distinguish development-stage characterisation from lot-release testing.</jats:p>

title: Precise and Intelligent Registration of Multi-Station Point Clouds for Segmental Girders Based on Automatic Spherical Target Extraction and Two-Stage Radius Refinement
abstract: <jats:p>To address the issues of reliance on manual operation for spherical target extraction and limited sphere center positioning accuracy caused by the absence of radius priors in multi-station laser scanning point cloud registration for precast segmental girders, this paper proposes an intelligent multi-station point cloud registration method based on automatic spherical target extraction and two-stage radius refinement. Spherical targets are automatically extracted via surround-view projection and image cross-correlation, and point cloud backtracking is realized through pixel-to-3D point index mapping. Two-stage radius fitting is then conducted by integrating a prior radius knowledge base with robust statistical filtering: RANSAC and probabilistic filtering are first used to obtain the prior radius and feasible interval, which is subsequently treated as a hard constraint, and TRF and L-BFGS-B are then adopted for two-level optimization to refine the sphere centers. Finally, correspondences are established according to the spherical target distance matrix, and SVD is employed to solve the rigid transformation, thereby completing multi-station registration and fusion. Using a segmental girder for extraction, fitting, and comparative ablation experiments, the experimental results show that the proposed method is highly automated, with a 100% spherical target detection rate and an average matching degree higher than 0.80; the fitted radius differences range from 0 to 1.34 mm; the mean of the average consistency residuals of homologous sphere centers after registration is 1.26 mm; and the fitted radius difference and the corresponding segmental girder length difference are 0.52 mm and 3.5 mm, respectively, outperforming commonly used international fitting methods in accuracy. Three segmental girders were used for dimensional inspection validation, and the results show that the dimensional measurement errors of all three segmental girders meet the engineering tolerance requirements, verifying the generalization ability and stability of the proposed registration method.</jats:p>

Epicardial Adipose Tissue as a Modifiable Cardiometabolic Target: The Role of Nutrition and Physical Exercise—A Narrative Review
abstract: <jats:p>Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) is an active endocrine and paracrine organ involved in coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation (AF), and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Beyond its role as a risk marker, EAT is increasingly investigated as a potentially modifiable target, and exploratory, low-certainty evidence suggests that its response to intervention is only partly explained by weight loss. This narrative review addresses two core themes: the pathophysiology of EAT as a distinct, regionally heterogeneous adipose organ; and the effects of nutrition and physical exercise—particularly the Mediterranean diet, caloric restriction, structured training, and bariatric surgery—on EAT quantity and inflammatory quality. Pharmacological data are summarized only as a complementary comparator. Multimodality imaging—echocardiography, cardiac computed tomography (cCT), and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR)—is discussed as the means by which EAT is measured, and minimum standards for its assessment are proposed. Finally, we outline a hypothesis-generating framework for incorporating EAT assessment into lifestyle-based cardiovascular prevention. This framework has not been validated, and whether reducing EAT improves cardiovascular outcomes independently of weight loss and other risk factors remains unknown; EAT should currently be regarded as a modifiable biomarker rather than an established therapeutic target.</jats:p>

title: Design and Experimental Validation of a Three-Port Unidirectional Isolated DC–DC Converter with Dual Outputs
abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a three-port unidirectional isolated DC–DC converter for high-power applications, featuring two isolated output ports supplied by a single input source. The proposed topology integrates a full-bridge switching stage, a high-frequency transformer with two secondary windings, and independent rectification stages to provide two output voltages. The converter operating principle is analyzed through its main switching stages, and closed-form expressions are derived for the DC voltage gains, inductor design, capacitor design, and voltage and current stresses of the main semiconductor and passive components. In addition, a parameterized expression for the input inductor current ripple is obtained, showing complete ripple cancellation at a duty cycle of 0.5 and identifying the operating points associated with the maximum ripple. A 7.5 kW laboratory prototype with a 260 V input voltage and 800 V and 400 V output ports was developed to experimentally validate the proposed analysis. The experimental results show good agreement with the theoretical prediction. The converter achieves a maximum measured efficiency of 96.81% at approximately 4.5 kW and maintains an efficiency above 96.5% from approximately 3.5 to 7 kW. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed three-port isolated converter for high-power applications.</jats:p>

title: Multi-target effect-directed high-performance thin-layer chromatography profiling of cholinesterase and tyrosinase inhibitors in cosmopolitan weed species
journal: JPC – Journal of Planar Chromatography – Modern TLC
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Effect-directed analysis in high-performance thin-layer chromatography (HPTLC–EDA) was applied as a rapid screening platform for the localization of enzyme inhibitory constituents with potential relevance to neurodegenerative disorders. An HPTLC–EDA workflow enabling simultaneous localization of acetylcholinesterase, butyrylcholinesterase and tyrosinase inhibitors was established and demonstrated using extracts of three cosmopolitan weed species. Distinct and spatially resolved inhibition profiles were observed, revealing multiple bioactive zones particularly in methanolic extracts of
                      <jats:italic>Stellaria media</jats:italic>
                      (L.) Vill. and
                      <jats:italic>Chenopodium album</jats:italic>
                      L., indicating a high diversity of cholinesterase inhibitors. In contrast, tyrosinase inhibition was more pronounced in dichloromethane extracts, suggesting the presence of less polar inhibitory constituents. Spectrophotometric assays confirmed higher phenolic content and antioxidant activity in methanolic–aqueous extracts, supporting a complementary role of redox-active compounds. The integration of multi-target enzyme profiling with effect-directed analysis highlights these widely distributed plant species as underexplored sources of bioactive constituents with potential neuroprotective properties. The applied approach enables rapid prioritization of complex extracts and supports the identification of candidate fractions for further phytochemical and pharmacological characterization.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Target trial emulation of randomised controlled trials: lessons from benchmarking and risk of bias assessment
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Target trial emulations (TTE) offer a framework for assessing comparative effectiveness to complement randomised controlled trials (RCT). However, little attention has been given to challenges that arise in emulating a published RCT from routine data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We aimed to evaluate the validity of a TTE by benchmarking it against the published RCT and assessing potential biases arising from limitations in the emulation. We followed methodological guidance in emulating the FIRST-ABC step-up RCT from PICANet data. This TTE compared two modes of non-invasive respiratory support in children admitted to paediatric intensive care according to the primary outcome, the time to liberation from respiratory support. The complete-case analysis included 5,405 children. To reduce the risk of confounding we applied doubly robust methods. A structured risk of bias assessment using the ROBINS-I framework was conducted to evaluate potential biases arising from departures of the TTE from the benchmark RCT, with the ROBINS-I domains applied across each component of the target trial framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The estimated risk ratio for liberation from respiratory support at the median follow-up was 1.33 (95% CI 1.27–1.40) from the TTE versus 1.03 (95% CI 0.90–1.18) from the RCT. The risk of bias assessment identified important limitations in the emulation, including inability to fully replicate the RCT eligibility criteria and outcome measurement, and the potential for residual unmeasured confounding.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings highlight key challenges in replicating an ideal trial from routine data and offer practical insights to improve the conduct and interpretation of TTEs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Detection of TeV emission during early afterglow from poorly localized gamma-ray bursts with ground-based IACTs
abstract: <jats:p>Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most luminous and rapidly evolving transients in the Universe. While space-based instruments have extended GRB observations up to energies of ∼100 GeV, the detection of very high-energy (VHE; E>100 GeV) emission from ground-based telescopes, especially during prompt and/or the early afterglow phases, remains challenging. These difficulties arise from the rapid temporal decay of GRB afterglows, strong attenuation by the extragalactic background light, observational latency, and the typical poor sky localization provided by MeV detectors such as Fermi/GBM. In this work, we investigated the prospects for detecting TeV (∼100 GeV--1 TeV) emission from poorly localized GRBs by adopting optimized follow-up strategies based on rapid tiling of large localization regions. We simulated a realistic population of GRBs informed by more than 15 years of Fermi/GBM and Swift/XRT detections and recent progress in the afterglow emission modeling. Using these simulations, we evaluated the detectability of GRB early afterglows by the next-generation imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes, which are equipped with larger fields of view, as a function of latency, exposure time, and observational strategy. Our strategy can significantly enhance the detection rate; for instruments such as ASTRI and LACT, it increases by up to a factor of two compared to strategies limited to well-localized (Swift-like) events. For CTAO, our proposed approach provides up to four VHE detections per year.</jats:p>

title: Mechanical Properties Evolution and Aging Mechanism of NBR Sealing Materials Under Multiple Environmental Factors in Ultra-High Voltage Converter Station
abstract: <jats:p>Nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) is commonly served as a sealing element for oil-tight seals in ultra-high voltage converter stations. Due to the harsh environmental conditions in these stations, NBR is frequently exposed to thermal oxidation, ultraviolet radiation, and low temperatures, as well as the effects of the sealed medium. This work focuses on evaluating the impacts of various environmental conditions on the mechanical characteristics of NBR and analyzes the underlying mechanisms. Stress distribution under the combined action of force, heat and hypothetical electric field is analyzed with the aid of ABAQUS simulation; the aging test only investigates single factors without verifying the multi-field coupling mechanism, and the conclusions are only for qualitative reference of the simulation. The service life of NBR is effectively predicted based on the compression set decay curve. Analysis of TGA measurements reveals the gradual loss of incorporated additives upon aging, accompanied by a reduction in the thermal stability of aged NBR. Results from crosslinking density tests, FTIR, and XPS analyses demonstrate that oxidation crosslinking progressively increases as thermal-oxidative aging proceeds, the rise in C–C and C–H content is associated with the degradation of C=C bonds, oxygen-containing functional groups (carboxyl, hydroxyl, and carbonyl) are generated during the thermal-oxidative aging of NBR, and the cleavage of C–S bonds leads to the formation of S=O species.</jats:p>

title: Propofol-remifentanil target-controlled infusion for emergency craniotomy following multiple trauma in a resource-limited setting
abstract:
<jats:sec id="st1">
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Target-controlled infusion (TCI) allows intravenous anesthetics to be titrated to model-predicted plasma or effect-site concentrations. In emergency neuroanesthesia, however, its clinical value depends not only on the selected target concentration but also on how these targets are adjusted in response to changing surgical stimulation while maintaining cerebral and systemic physiologic stability. We report the use of propofol TCI with the Schnider model and remifentanil TCI with the Minto model during emergency craniotomy in a patient with severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) and major thoracic trauma in Eastern Indonesia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="st2">
                    <jats:title>Case Description:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 32-year-old male weighing approximately 80 kg presented with severe TBI after a 5-m fall, accompanied by right hemopneumothorax, multiple rib fractures, and a clavicular fracture. A chest tube was inserted before anesthetic induction. Propofol was administered using the Schnider model with an effect-site target concentration (Ce) of 3–5 µg/mL during induction and 2.5–4 µg/mL during maintenance. Remifentanil was administered using the Minto model at target concentrations of 4–5 ng/mL during induction and 2–3 ng/mL during maintenance, although the anesthesia record did not consistently specify whether plasma or effect-site targeting was used for remifentanil during maintenance. After induction, the targets were reduced and subsequently adjusted according to the stage and intensity of surgical stimulation, hemodynamic response, ventilation, and surgical conditions. During the 4-h procedure, systolic blood pressure remained between 102 and 125 mmHg, oxygen saturation was maintained at 99–100%, and end-tidal carbon dioxide remained between 30 and 35 mmHg. The brain remained relaxed without clinically apparent swelling. This case illustrates how separate hypnotic and opioid targets can be used to guide stepwise titration of propofol and remifentanil during emergency craniotomy when advanced depth-of-anesthesia and intracranial monitoring are not available.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="st3">
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Propofol TCI using the Schnider model and remifentanil TCI using the Minto model provided a practical framework for independently titrating the hypnotic and opioid components of anesthesia during emergency craniotomy. In a resource-limited setting, model-predicted concentrations should not be regarded as fixed doses but rather as adjustable targets interpreted in conjunction with surgical stimulation, hemodynamic tolerance, ventilation, brain relaxation, and the limitations of available monitoring.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

From inactivity to initiation: moderate-to-vigorous physical activity and subsequent functional outcomes in older adults—a sequential target trial emulation
journal: European Review of Aging and Physical Activity
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Most studies of physical activity and functional ageing examine static activity levels or long-term trajectories, leaving the implications of an episode-specific transition to moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Health and Retirement Study data (2004–2018) were used to emulate four sequential trials among adults aged 60 years or older who were below the MVPA threshold at the preceding wave. MVPA initiation was defined from self-reported HRS frequency items as moderate- or vigorous-intensity activity at least once per week at the trial baseline among participants below that threshold at the preceding wave; the items assessed frequency rather than session duration or weekly minutes. The sample included 7,463 participants and 12,421 person-trial records. Multiple imputation, inverse probability weighting, and weighted generalized estimating equations assessed functional limitation scores among survivors and the composite outcome of incident ADL limitation or death over 2–6 years.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>MVPA initiation was associated with lower functional limitation scores at 2 years (mean difference, − 0.408 points; 95% CI, − 0.509 to − 0.307), 4 years (− 0.396 points; 95% CI, − 0.513 to − 0.278), and 6 years (− 0.352 points; 95% CI, − 0.493 to − 0.211). Risk ratios for incident ADL limitation or death were 0.844 (95% CI, 0.776 to 0.919), 0.869 (95% CI, 0.809 to 0.933), and 0.908 (95% CI, 0.854 to 0.965), respectively. Findings were directionally consistent under a stricter definition of more than once-weekly moderate or vigorous activity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Episode-specific MVPA initiation was associated with subsequent functional outcomes in older adults. These estimates may represent a potentially relevant behavioral transition, although residual confounding and selection related to survival cannot be excluded.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

A Pythia8 tune for open charm and beauty production in fixed-target collisions
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    We present
                    <jats:sc>FTFT</jats:sc>
                    (Fixed-Target Fragmentation Tune), a set of
                    <jats:sc>Pythia8</jats:sc>
                    parameters optimised for the production of charm and beauty hadrons in fixed-target collisions at centre-of-mass energies
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$\sqrt{s} \simeq 20$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:msqrt>
                              <mml:mi>s</mml:mi>
                            </mml:msqrt>
                            <mml:mo>≃</mml:mo>
                            <mml:mn>20</mml:mn>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    –
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$42\,\text {GeV} $$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mn>42</mml:mn>
                            <mml:mspace/>
                            <mml:mtext>GeV</mml:mtext>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    . Accurate heavy-flavour production in this regime is needed to predict neutrino fluxes and hidden-particle yields at beam-dump experiments such as SHiP. The tune is derived in two stages. First, differential distributions in Feynman-
                    <jats:italic>x</jats:italic>
                    (
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$x_F$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:msub>
                            <mml:mi>x</mml:mi>
                            <mml:mi>F</mml:mi>
                          </mml:msub>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ), transverse momentum squared (
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$p_T^2$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:msubsup>
                            <mml:mi>p</mml:mi>
                            <mml:mi>T</mml:mi>
                            <mml:mn>2</mml:mn>
                          </mml:msubsup>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ), and charge or leading-particle production asymmetry of
                    <jats:italic>D</jats:italic>
                    mesons are fitted to data from pion- and proton-beam fixed-target experiments. Second,
                    <jats:italic>K</jats:italic>
                    -factors for each beam are extracted from inclusive charm cross-section measurements to scale the simulated cross section to the measured data. The fitted charm-fragmentation and multiparton-interaction parameters depart from standard LHC-tuned defaults, in line with earlier fixed-target studies.
                  </jats:p>

title: NOD1 priming by IFN-gamma regulates inflammatory responses and perturbs differentiation of skeletal muscle
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nod-like receptors (NLRs) are intracellular sensors acting as major regulators of cytokine secretion, gene expression and various signaling pathways, modulating immune responses, metabolism and cell fate. Beyond leukocytes, NLRs are also expressed in various non-immune competent cells, however, their expression and function in skeletal muscle, the largest tissue in the human body, are largely unknown.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We studied NLR expression in response to IFN-γ treatment in
                      <jats:italic>ex vivo Tibialis anterior</jats:italic>
                      , and
                      <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                      C2C12 myoblast (MB) and myotube (MT) with RT-qPCR and Western blot. We focused on the assessment of gene expression changes and cytokine production in MT following IFN-γ priming and activation of NOD1, a key NLR identified, using RNA-seq, RT-qPCR and ELISA, followed by functional studies to understand its immunomodulatory roles. NOD1 function in the context of differentiation of MT was studied with scratch assay, while lipid droplet accumulation was determined with Oil Red O staining.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We found that the expression of regulatory NLRs (NOD1, NOD2, NLRX1, NLRC3) dynamically changed during MB to MT differentiation, and identified NOD1, as a key immunomodulatory NLR in skeletal muscle. IFN-γ treatment in MT highly induced NOD1 expression, and NOD1 activation following IFN-γ priming resulted in global gene expression changes. We found that most myokines are induced in a NOD1-dependent manner, while a cluster of genes related to migration and differentiation were strongly downregulated. In particular, upon IFN-γ priming NOD1 regulates IL-6 production via NF-kB. In addition, IFN-γ-induced NOD1 strongly reduces the differentiation of MT, while enhances lipid accumulation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our results show that while NLRs are expressed in MB and dynamically change during MT differentiation, NOD1 has important, so far uncharacterized function in skeletal muscle. Our results suggest that NOD1 and tentatively other NLRs in the skeletal muscle are connected to diverse physiological and pathological processes, implying their potential roles in myopathies or as therapeutic targets in other disease states.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Statin–Ezetimibe Therapy and Incident Myocardial Infarction Across Modified Cardiovascular–Kidney–Metabolic Risk Groups: A Nationwide Target Trial Emulation
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome integrates metabolic risk, kidney dysfunction, and cardiovascular disease. Whether statin-ezetimibe combination therapy is associated with lower subsequent myocardial infarction risk than statin monotherapy among patients across modified cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk groups remains uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using the Korean National Health Insurance Service database, we emulated separate two-arm landmark target trials within modified early and late cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk groups. Adults aged 30-74 years with dyslipidemia who received prescriptions covering a total of 180 days with statin monotherapy or a fixed-dose statin-ezetimibe combination were eligible. Treatment was assigned at the 180-day landmark. Stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting and cause-specific Cox regression were used to calculate hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence interval (CI), with death treated as a competing event for cumulative incidence estimation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 309,371 treated participants, 239,954 had modified early risk and 69,417 had modified late risk. Compared with statin monotherapy, statin-ezetimibe therapy was associated with lower myocardial infarction risk after weighting in both early-risk participants (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.81-0.95) and late-risk participants (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.79-0.98). 10-year weighted cumulative incidence was 1.97% versus 2.23% in the early-risk group and 3.52% versus 3.94% in the late-risk group. In same-intensity comparisons, the association was most evident with moderate-intensity therapy, particularly in the early CKM group (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.79-0.95).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among adults with dyslipidemia who received prescriptions covering a total of 180 days, statin-ezetimibe combination therapy was associated with a lower subsequent risk of myocardial infarction than statin monotherapy across modified CKM risk groups. The association was most evident in moderate-intensity comparisons.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Neural architecture of the jhānas: a gamma-infraslow duet with quantum overtones
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Building on previous electrophysiological investigations that posited meditative absorption (jhāna) as a radical disruption of sensory default consciousness (DCs), this study explores the underlying non-linear neural architectures and state transitions. Re-analysis of long-duration (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 18) DC-stabilized records reveals that alpha spindles index three distinct developmental stages of the first jhāna, reflecting attentional mastery through
                    <jats:italic>vitakka</jats:italic>
                    (directed attention) and
                    <jats:italic>vicāra</jats:italic>
                    (sustained attention). A broadband (0.005–150 Hz) 3D eLoreta source analysis of a major 4,000 µV relaxation-oscillation (R-O) transition into the second jhāna, confirms the active silencing of fronto-temporal linguistic networks, leading to the profound mental stillness characteristic of higher absorption states. This macro state transition is driven by a near-absolute variance concentration of infraslow rhythms localized to the midline vertex (
                    <jats:italic>z</jats:italic>
                     = 70) supplementary motor area (SMA), supported by a lateralized left-hemisphere temporal and visual-gating gamma network. As the jhāna hierarchy deepens, the brain recruits an unprecedented electrophysiological dynamic range. Spanning four orders of magnitude in time (10
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    –10
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    s) bridging the absolute physical boundaries of human neurobiology, this architecture couples high-amplitude infraslow carriers (2,000–4,000 µV) to ultra-fast gamma microbursts (100–200 µV). This coordinated gamma–infraslow duet constructs an impenetrable, low-entropy Markov blanket, actively insulating the internal cognitive field from sensory perturbation while maintaining waking alertness. Concurrently, the 600-fold deceleration of cortical rhythms at the vertex facilitates heightened synchrony with visceral neurovascular systems. At critical R-O inflection thresholds, brief (1–2 s) global high-gamma microbursts function as inhibitory sweeps across left-lateralized hubs (BA 47, BA 21/22/38), dismantling emerging inner speech to protect absorptive stability. The study further demonstrates that the jhāna hierarchy follows a scale-free trajectory distinct from the θ, α, β frequency bands of default sensory consciousness (DCs), bypassing the 1 Hz deep-sleep transition, replacing nested sensory Markov blankets with a singular global boundary at the fourth-jhāna limit—a system with intriguing similarities to noise-shielded quantum “superposition.” We conclude that jhāna consciousness (JCs) constitutes an autonomous and previously unrecognized, highly structured second-tier of human consciousness, rather than an altered state of (sensory) consciousness (ASC).
                  </jats:p>

title: Oxidized LDL pathophysiology and potential as a therapeutic target in atherosclerosis
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Uptake of oxidized and other forms of modified low-density lipoprotein (LDL) drives formation of foam cells, a hallmark of atherosclerotic plaques. Experimental studies demonstrating the proinflammatory and cytotoxic properties of oxidized LDL have led to the concept of LDL oxidation as one key factor in both development and destabilization of atherosclerotic plaques. Such data positioned oxidized LDL as a promising target for prevention or mitigation of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Yet the failure of multiple antioxidants to reduce cardiovascular risk in large randomized clinical trials has hampered this prospect. Such null studies have stimulated interest in an alternative approach: the therapeutic potential of antibodies against oxidized LDL. High levels of IgM against oxidized LDL phospholipids are associated with lower cardiovascular risk and these antibodies function primarily through neutralization and stimulation of clearance of modified LDL. IgG antibodies against aldehyde-modified peptide sequences in apolipoprotein B-100, the signature protein component of LDL, are also associated with lower risk of cardiovascular disease but experimental studies have shown that these antibodies function by locally forming immune complexes with oxidized LDL that limit the inflammatory activity of certain plaque macrophages. A phase 2 pilot study showed that one such antibody, orticumab, reduces an imaging index of local coronary arterial inflammation in patients with psoriasis. Thus, emerging evidence supports the possibility of using oxidized LDL antibodies to limit atherothrombotic disease.</jats:p>

title: Associations between different peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha genotypes and falls in community-dwelling older adults
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Falls are a significant health concern for older adults, often leading to injury, disability, and increased healthcare burden. Given the multifactorial nature of falls, genetic predispositions may contribute to individual susceptibility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This study aimed to examine the association between different peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">PPARGC1A)</jats:italic>
                      genotypes and fall history in community-dwelling older adults.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Fall history was assessed using a self-reported question regarding falls in the past year.
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">PPARGC1A</jats:italic>
                      genotypes (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Gly/Gly, Gly/Ser</jats:italic>
                      , and
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Ser/Ser</jats:italic>
                      ) were identified using polymerase chain reaction analysis. A total of 271 Japanese older adults (mean age: 74.0 ± 5.8 years) were included in the analysis. Of these, 75 (27.7%) had the
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Gly/Gly</jats:italic>
                      genotype, 144 (53.1%) had
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Gly/Ser</jats:italic>
                      , and 52 (19.2%) had
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Ser/Ser</jats:italic>
                      . Multiple logistic regression analysis was conducted with fall history as the dependent variable and
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">PPARGC1A</jats:italic>
                      genotype as the independent variable.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Participants with the
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Ser/Ser</jats:italic>
                      genotype had significantly higher odds of reporting falls than those with the
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Gly/Gly</jats:italic>
                      genotype (odds ratio [OR]: 3.58; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.28–10.07;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.015). No significant association was observed between
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Gly/Ser</jats:italic>
                      and
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Gly/Gly</jats:italic>
                      genotypes (OR: 1.87; 95% CI: 0.76–4.60;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.171).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The Ser/Ser genotype of
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">PPARGC1A</jats:italic>
                      may be linked to greater fall susceptibility among community-dwelling older adults. These findings may contribute to the identification of genetic risk profiles and the development of personalized fall prevention strategies in aging populations.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Occurrence and radiological risk assessment of 11 target γ-emitting radionuclides in seafood from the Ningbo coastal area, China during 2022–2025
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dietary ingestion is a major exposure pathway for environmental radionuclides, and the radiological safety of seafood, an important component of the global diet, has attracted increasing public concern. As a Chinese coastal city where seafood is a traditional part of local residents’ daily diet, Ningbo lacks systematic baseline data on radionuclide levels in locally common edible seafood and associated dietary radiological risks for local residents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five categories of locally common edible seafood (fish, shrimp, crabs, mollusks and algae) were collected from the southern coastal area of Ningbo during 2022–2025. Specific activities of 11 target γ-emitting radionuclides were quantified via high-purity germanium γ spectrometry in accordance with GB/T 16145–2022, and annual effective ingestion dose (AED) was estimated using local per capita seafood consumption data and ingestion dose conversion coefficients recommended in ICRP Publication 119.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Natural radionuclides dominated across all five seafood categories, with
                      <jats:sup>40</jats:sup>
                      K detected in 100% of samples. Algae had the highest detection rates of
                      <jats:sup>238</jats:sup>
                      U (77.8%) and
                      <jats:sup>210</jats:sup>
                      Pb (55.6%), crabs had the highest
                      <jats:sup>228</jats:sup>
                      Ra detection rate (100%), and
                      <jats:sup>226</jats:sup>
                      Ra was detected at the highest rate in both crabs and algae (77.8%). For specific activities, algae exhibited the highest specific activities of
                      <jats:sup>238</jats:sup>
                      U (median 0.78, maximum 12.80 Bq/kg),
                      <jats:sup>40</jats:sup>
                      K (284.10, 931.00 Bq/kg) and
                      <jats:sup>210</jats:sup>
                      Pb (0.41, 7.96 Bq/kg); crabs had the highest
                      <jats:sup>226</jats:sup>
                      Ra (0.54, 13.09 Bq/kg); shrimp had the highest median
                      <jats:sup>228</jats:sup>
                      Ra activity (1.26 Bq/kg) while algae had the highest maximum activity (7.90 Bq/kg). Mollusks had the lowest median specific activities overall, but a higher
                      <jats:sup>238</jats:sup>
                      U detection rate than fish, shrimp and crabs. Only trace
                      <jats:sup>137</jats:sup>
                      Cs was detected in one fish (0.05 Bq/kg) and one mollusk (0.02 Bq/kg) sample from 2025. The median total AED was 30.43 μSv/y, with a conservative constructed upper-bound maximum of 133.64 μSv/y.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For the measured γ-emitting radionuclides only, natural radionuclides dominate in seafood from the study area, and all regulated radionuclides meeting China’s food radiological safety requirements. Artificial radionuclides were negligible with no significant anthropogenic perturbation, and the dietary dose for local adults in the study area remains below the ICRP-recommended public dose limit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Reduced entorhinal and dentate theta-gamma coupling associated with adult Reelin loss in Alzheimer’s disease relevant mice
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Early Alzheimer’s disease (AD) affects entorhinal-hippocampal circuits, motivating functional measures of altered network coordination. We examined local field potentials and multiunit activity in head-fixed mice in a virtual-reality (VR) environment, comparing WT, App
                    <jats:sup>NL-F</jats:sup>
                    , and App
                    <jats:sup>NL-F</jats:sup>
                    -Reln-cKO groups (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 3 male mice per genotype). Reelin deletion was induced in adulthood using a ubiquitous tamoxifen-inducible Cre driver and was not restricted to entorhinal cortex (EC). Recordings sampled EC, dentate gyrus (DG), and CA1. Theta–gamma phase–amplitude coupling was quantified using modulation index (MI) and phase-locking value (PLV) between theta phase and the phase of the gamma-amplitude envelope. Nominal genotype effects were detected for DG-theta/DG-gamma coupling (MI,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.034; PLV,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.035) and EC-theta/DG-gamma coupling (MI,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.0043; PLV,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.0079), with descriptively lower means in App
                    <jats:sup>NL-F</jats:sup>
                    -Reln-cKO mice. Regional power spectra appeared broadly similar; a nominal genotype effect was reported for DG theta power (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.029), rather than a selective DG gamma-power reduction. Exploratory analyses suggested stronger coupling attenuation in the 35–55-Hz range and lower DG-associated coupling in both high and low theta/delta states. These findings identify DG-associated theta–gamma coupling as a candidate functional readout of adult Reelin loss in an AD-relevant background. The small cohort, uncorrected comparisons, widespread deletion, and absence of coupling–behavior analyses limit anatomical and functional inference.
                  </jats:p>

title: From the brain to the liver: A pharmacokinetic dilemma and safety barriers in levodopa-based antifibrotic therapy
abstract: <jats:p>Levodopa, a cornerstone therapy for Parkinson’s disease, has recently been reported to suppress hepatic stellate cell activation through the dopamine receptor D1 (DRD1)-Hippo/yes-associated protein (YAP) signaling axis, providing a novel mechanistic rationale for antifibrotic therapy in liver disease. However, its direct repurposing for peripheral organ indications faces a fundamental pharmacokinetic contradiction. Standard levodopa formulations are coadministered with peripheral aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase inhibitors to minimize peripheral dopamine production, a strategy that may markedly limit the hepatic dopamine generation required for this antifibrotic effect. Moreover, nonselective dopamine receptor activation, potential impairment of liver regeneration via  YAP inhibition, and possible adverse effects on portal hemodynamics represent critical translational challenges that warrant systematic evaluation. Future studies should prioritize the development of liver-targeted delivery systems or highly selective DRD1 agonist-based strategies to enable the safe and effective clinical translation of this mechanism.</jats:p>

title: Aurantii Fructus Immaturus Flavonoid tablets for functional dyspepsia: A multicenter, double-blind, dose-exploring IIb randomized controlled trial
abstract:
<jats:p>BACKGROUND</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Functional dyspepsia (FD) is a prevalent chronic upper gastrointestinal disorder with limited safe long-term treatment options, highlighting the need to explore novel therapies such as Aurantii Fructus Immaturus Flavonoid (AFIF).</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>AIM</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>To evaluate the efficacy and safety of AFIF tablets as a potential long-term treatment option for patients with FD in this multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase IIb trial.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>METHODS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This double-blind randomized controlled trial used central stratified block randomization and was designed to enroll 400 eligible participants aged 18-65 years who met the Rome III criteria. Participants were allocated in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to receive high-dose AFIF (4 tablets/tid), medium-dose AFIF (3 tablets/tid), low-dose AFIF (2 tablets/tid), or placebo for 4 weeks. The primary efficacy endpoints were the resolution rates for all 4 FD symptoms (postprandial fullness, early satiety, epigastric burning sensation, and abdominal pain) and the individual symptom resolution rates after 4 weeks of medication. Secondary endpoints included the resolution rates of all four FD symptoms and individual symptoms at other visit time points, the postprandial 2-hour gastric emptying rate, and gastric half-emptying time. Safety was assessed through adverse events (AEs) and laboratory tests.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>RESULTS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Of the 399 enrolled participants, 267 were included in the Full Analysis Set. In the Full Analysis Set, the 4-week resolution rates of all four symptoms differed significantly across groups [22.39% (high), 27.27% (medium), 2.99% (low), and 5.97% (placebo); P  < 0.0001]. The high- and medium-dose AFIF groups showed higher rates than the low-dose and placebo groups, with no significant differences between the high- and medium-dose groups or between the low-dose and placebo groups. Individual symptom resolution rates showed similar patterns. AFIF improved gastric emptying, although the improvement was not significant compared with placebo. AE incidence was comparable across groups [5.97% (high), 6.06% (medium), 0.00% (low), and 7.46% (placebo); P  = 0.112], with no serious AEs reported in the AFIF groups.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>CONCLUSION</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Medium- and high-dose AFIF significantly improved FD symptoms with good safety. The medium dose (3 tablets/tid) is recommended for phase III trials and may be a safer alternative to proton pump inhibitors or prokinetics. Limitations include small follow-up samples and restricted gastric emptying testing; therefore, larger long-term studies are needed.</jats:p>

title: Nivolumab/Cabozantinib
Comparative Effectiveness of Hormonal Replacement Therapy Versus Integrative Non-Pharmacological Interventions in the Management of Menopausal Syndrome: A 24-Month Longitudinal Analysis
journal: Journal of Health Science and Reports
abstract: <jats:p>Background:  Menopausal  syndrome  substantially  diminishes  health-related  quality  of  life  in  midlife  women  globally.  Hormone  replacement  therapy (HRT) has long been the standard of care for symptom management; however, long-term safety concerns—including elevated risks of breast malignancy, cardiovascular events, and venous thromboembolism—have prompted growing interest in holistic, non-pharmacological alternatives. Direct longitudinal comparative data across Southeast Asian populations remain scarce.Objective: To evaluate and contrast the efficacy of HRT versus a structured integrative intervention programme on symptom severity and quality of life over a 24-month follow-up period.Methods: This prospective, comparative longitudinal study enrolled 500 women aged 45–60 years presenting with moderate-to-severe menopausal syndrome across six Type B hospitals in Indonesia between January 2023 and December 2025. Participants were allocated to either HRT (conjugated equine oestrogen plus progestin; n = 250) or integrative care (individualised lifestyle modification, cognitive behavioural therapy, mindfulness-based stress reduction, and standardised phytoestrogen supplementation; n = 250). Primary outcomes were change in Menopause Rating Scale (MRS) total score and WHO Quality of Life–BREF (WHOQOL-BREF) domain scores at baseline, 6, 12, and 24 months. Mixed-effects regression models were used to estimate group differences over time.Results: Both groups demonstrated statistically significant reductions in MRS scores over the study period (p < 0.001 for each). HRT produced more rapid symptomatic improvement at 6 months (adjusted mean difference −6.4; 95% confidence interval −7.8 to −5.0; p < 0.001). By 24 months, the between-group difference was no longer statistically significant (−0.4; −1.1 to 0.3; p = 0.08). Integrative-care participants recorded significantly higher WHOQOL-BREF domain scores at 24 months, particularly in the psychological (difference 8.2; p < 0.001) and social (difference 8.3; p < 0.001) domains.Conclusion: HRT confers rapid, short-term relief of menopausal symptoms, whereas integrative non-pharmacological interventions yield equivalent long-term symptomatic control and superior sustained quality-of-life outcomes. A stratified, shared-decision approach—aligning treatment selection with patient priorities, risk profiles, and cultural context—is recommended.</jats:p>

title: High Concordance of Clinical and Pathological Staging Supports Core Needle Biopsy-Based MammaPrint Testing in Early Breast Cancer
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Background Accurate characterization of early breast cancer (EBC) at diagnosis is essential for timely treatment selection. Genomic profiling assays such as MammaPrint® are increasingly performed on Core Needle Biopsy (CNB) specimens to enable earlier risk stratification and optimized treatment planning. Here we investigated whether clinical staging at diagnosis remains sufficiently consistent with final pathology to support MammaPrint testing on the CNB specimen without awaiting surgical resection. Methods Using prospectively collected real-world data from the FLEX Study (NCT03053193), we identified patients with invasive ductal carcinoma and hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative (HR+/HER2−) disease who had MammaPrint performed on CNB specimens and available clinical and pathologic T and N staging data. Patients who received neoadjuvant therapy or had missing staging information were excluded. We assessed whether tumors remained within the clinically defined MammaPrint-valid population (cT1-cT2 and cN0-cN1) following surgical pathology, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) calculated using the Wilson score method. Results A total of 4,399 FLEX patients were evaluated for tumor staging and 4,238 for nodal staging. Overall, 98.4% of clinical T stage assessments remained within validated T stage ranges at pathologic assessment (pT1-pT2; 4,330/4,399, 95% CI 97.9%-98.8%). The T stage concordance among patients with HR+, HER2- breast cancer was 98.3% (4,003/4,071; 95% CI 97.9%-98.6%). Similarly, 98.0% of clinical N stage assessments remained with validated nodal ranges at pathologic assessment (pN0-pN1; 4,155/4,238, 95% CI 97.5%-98.4%). Among patients with HR+/HER2− breast cancer, clinical N stage concordance within validated testing criteria was 98.0% (3,842/3,921; 95% CI 97.5%–98.3%) at surgical pathology. Conclusion In this large real-world cohort, clinical staging at diagnosis reliably identified patients whose disease remained within validated MammaPrint tumor and nodal staging criteria following surgery in 98% of cases. These findings support the reliability of clinical staging to enable genomic testing on CNB specimens at diagnosis, without waiting for definitive surgical pathology.</jats:p>
