title: Bridging disciplines for quantum futures: homologation and professional skills in an interdisciplinary MSc in quantum information science & technology (QIST)
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantum technologies increasingly require professionals who can work fluently across physics, computer science, electrical engineering and mathematics. A persistent challenge for quantum master’s programmes is the heterogeneity of incoming students’ preparation, which can slow early progress and impede collaboration. Building on prior calls for dedicated quantum engineering education, we describe two curricular pillars implemented in the MSc in Quantum Information Science & Technology (QIST), jointly offered by Delft University of Technology and Leiden University: (i) a structured 10 ECTS homologation module that aligns foundational competencies via tailored submodules spanning quantum physics, mathematics, computer science, information theory, electronics, and computer engineering; and (ii) a credit-bearing professional skills module that integrates career orientation, ethics and reflection early on in the curriculum. Together with multi-stage team projects and diverse thesis pathways, these elements provide a practical model for interdisciplinary quantum education aimed at inclusive participation, shared vocabulary and workforce readiness. Presented as an educational innovation report, we propose homologation and early professional formation as transferable curricular design patterns, adaptable to other quantum graduate programmes facing similar challenges of cohort heterogeneity and interdisciplinary breadth.</jats:p>

title: Dynamics of photoluminescence quenching in GaAs induced by a strong THz field
abstract: <jats:p>A photoluminescence (PL) quenching under strong-field (up to 150 kV/cm) picosecond terahertz pulses in a semi-insulating GaAs crystal illuminated by femtosecond laser radiation was studied. We showed that the optical-terahertz time-delay dependence of the PL quenching significantly depends on the optical pump fluence. For high fluences (&gt;200 μJ/cm2), the quenching interval is governed by the terahertz pulse duration (1–2 ps), in agreement with previous studies, whereas for fluences ≲100 μJ/cm2, it is determined by the recombination time (∼80 ps) of photoexcited carriers. This difference is mainly attributed to terahertz field screening by photoexcited electrons in GaAs. A simple model of hot electron density dynamics accounting for nonradiative recombination and the carrier-density-dependent terahertz field strength was found to successfully describe the time-delay quenching at moderate optical fluence (50–120 μJ/cm2). For high fluences, the terahertz pulse dynamics under screening by photoexcited carriers was calculated to qualitatively explain the observed time-delay quenching dependence.</jats:p>

title: Cyclic universe and uniform rate inflation from polymerized scalar field in loop quantum cosmology
journal: International Journal of Modern Physics D
abstract: <jats:p>We investigate the uniform rate inflationary universe in the framework of Loop Quantum Cosmology (LQC) and find that this seemingly simple inflationary model is interlinked with various concepts such as cyclic evolution, HNI inflation, and polymer-quantized scalar fields when the background spacetime is loop-quantized. The potential for an exactly uniform rate inflation in a loop-quantized FRW spacetime turns out to be a polymerized version of the corresponding potential in general relativity, which mimics the potentials for a polymerized scalar field and Hybrid Natural Inflation (HNI). There is also a radical modification of the background spacetime, leading to a cyclic universe with identical epochs separated by quantum bounces that replace the classical singularity. The energy density and Hubble rate are bounded. Polymerization of the scalar field is found to be intimately tied to the polymerization of the background geometry in LQC. Remarkably, a single polymerized scalar field simultaneously governs the cyclic evolution of the universe and drives the inflationary phase. Preliminary predictions for cosmological perturbations are worked out and are found to depend on the value of the field at the end of inflation. The parameter space is explored to compare the results for the spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio with observational constraints.</jats:p>

title: Estimation of systematic error from bulk deformation of end test mass induced by photon calibrator for LIGO post-O5 gravitational wave projects
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We studied bulk deformation of the end test masses (ETMs) of gravitational wave detectors caused by calibration devices named Photon calibrator (Pcal). This bulk deformation is one of the source of calibration error since it induces non-linear displacement from the ideal pendulum motion of the ETM. Particularly, it is the dominant error source above 1500 Hz which is crucial to the studies of neutron star mergers. The displacement also depends on beam offsets of the main interferometer (IFO) beam and Pcal beams. We conceptually described frequency dependent effect of bulk deformation and evaluated it in several cases of the beam offset with finite-element analysis software, for ETM models of Advanced Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO), KAGRA, Advanced Virgo , and LIGO A#.</jats:p>

title: Quantifying quantum coherence via the interpolated Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability
A Century of the Schrödinger Equation (1926–2026): Recovering the Wave Picture and Its Physical Intuition
abstract: <jats:p>One century after Schrödinger’s 1926 papers, the optical–mechanical analogy remains a useful guide to wave mechanics. This pedagogical perspective connects action and phase, stationary states, superposition, field modes, and electromagnetic gauge coupling. Its contribution is a unified account that explicitly separates exact identities, controlled approximations, and heuristic analogies. We distinguish Fourier representations from independently evolving momentum modes, exhibit the assumptions required to recover Hamilton–Jacobi dynamics, and separate classical mode selection from canonical field quantization. Electromagnetic phase factors are presented with their domains of validity, while operational measurement rules are distinguished from interpretative claims. The article proposes neither new dynamics nor a resolution of the measurement problem; it offers a physically motivated route through established results while identifying where classical wave intuition ceases to be sufficient.</jats:p>

                    , where
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>

The bound is geometric: although the ergotropy is defined by an optimisation over unitaries, it reduces to a fixed function of the angle swept by the collective spin on the Bloch sphere, and the drive bounds the rate at which that angle can grow, so the charging time is at least the required arc divided by the maximum angular velocity. The reduction rests on an exact statement about work extraction: only the coherent component of the drive delivers extractable work, while its vacuum fluctuations deposit energy that remains locked in the passive state. This makes the short-time coefficient independent of the charger occupation, and it is what separates a bound on extractable work from a bound on stored energy, which no instantaneous-power argument can supply. The familiar square-root estimate is the chord to this arc, recovered in the small-angle limit and weaker whenever a large fraction of the maximum work is required.

title: Giant-atom-enabled quantum optics with valley-polarized photons
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Valleytronics and valley photonics exploit the valley degree of freedom to encode and manipulate information. Here we show that photonic valleys can be selectively addressed in quantum optics using a simple two-level emitter, provided it is coupled nonlocally to the field, thereby realizing a so-called giant atom. Specifically, we consider a qubit coupled at multiple points to an engineered honeycomb lattice of resonators with detuned sublattice frequencies. By tailoring the geometry and phases of the coupling points, the giant atom can be made to emit selectively into a single valley. The emitted photons thereby acquire a well-defined valley character and effectively nonzero Berry curvature. By placing the qubit near a domain wall between regions of opposite sublattice detuning, whose interface supports valley-polarized edge modes, emission becomes chiral along the domain wall. This provides a promising route toward implementation of single-photon disorder-robust chiral emission without breaking time-reversal symmetry of the electromagnetic medium in platforms such as circuit QED.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A robust pulse is traditionally obtained by optimizing the fidelity of one target gate at a time, each gate on its own landscape, so a robust gate family appears only as a sequence of separately optimized pulses. Here we define a target-independent quantum control robustness landscape (QCRL) from the Magnus expansion of the noise propagator in the toggling frame. Robust controls of every gate in a parametric family lie on the same zero set of this landscape, at regular points a smooth local branch of dimension p − r for p control parameters and r independent constraints, and traversing it produces the family: robustness-invariant pulse variation (RIPV), the predictor–corrector continuation we use, varies one optimized seed pulse along the branch at a constraint residual of 10−10. For Rx(θ) under quasistatic dephasing one branch spans the full family at first and at first-plus-second order, with exact-propagation fidelity above 0.999 for every pulse up to relative detunings of 4.7% and 10.5%; the same construction yields a dual-control family robust to three-axis noise. By shifting from optimizing target-dependent fidelity to maintaining target-independent robustness, we unify the synthesis of robust gate families into a single geometric traversal.</jats:p>

Quantum Higgs Echo in Superconductors: A Novel Form of Quantum Memory
journal: International Journal of Pure Science Research Studies (IJPSRS)
abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical investigation of quantum information storage via the Higgs amplitude mode in superconductors. We propose a novel quantum memory mechanism based on coherent excitation and echo retrieval of the Higgs mode, exploiting the collective nature of the superconducting condensate. Through rigorous theoretical analysis combining time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory with quantum master equations, we demonstrate that Higgs mode excitations can store quantum information with coherence times exceeding 100 ns. We derive analytical expressions for storage fidelity as a function of temperature, gap anisotropy, and disorder, achieving theoretical fidelities above 95% for storage times up to 100 ns in clean s-wave superconductors below. Numerical simulations validate our theoretical predictions and reveal optimal parameter regimes for NbN thin films. Our findings establish fundamental bounds on Higgs-based quantum memory and propose experimental protocols compatible with current THz spectroscopy capabilities. This work opens new directions for exploiting collective modes in quantum technologies.</jats:p>

title: Toward chemically accurate quantum simulations on quantum hardware: A quantum-HPC hybrid approach
abstract: <jats:p>We report one of the most comprehensive experimental demonstrations to date of quantum-computing-based molecular simulation on IQM’s Sirius 24-qubit superconducting quantum processor, using up to 16 operational qubits. We employ Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) with the Local Unitary Cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) Ansatz to compute ground-state energies of benchmark molecular systems, including H2, LiH, BeH2, H2O, and NH3. We further introduce the linear-CNOT unitary coupled-cluster singles and doubles Ansatz within the SQD framework, reducing the classical pre-computation overhead at the cost of increased quantum circuit depth and demonstrate its effectiveness by accurately recovering the ground-state energies of H2, LiH, and BeH2. A comparative analysis of the two Ansätze is presented, highlighting their respective merits, demerits, and practical use cases in near-term quantum simulations. In addition, we perform one-dimensional potential energy surface (1D-PES) scans for H2 and HeH+ using STO-3G and 6-31G basis sets and for LiH and BeH2 using STO-3G. We also report the first experimental generation of a full two-dimensional potential energy surface (2D-PES) map, consisting of a 32 × 32 grid in bond length and bond angle, for the water molecule in the STO-3G basis on IQM quantum hardware. Beyond small-molecule benchmarks, we integrate Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET) with SQD(LUCJ) to obtain chemically accurate 4-electron-in-4-orbital active-space energies for eight ligand-like molecules, as well as for the pharmacologically relevant amantadine molecular system, representing the first of such experimental demonstrations. Across all studies, the majority of quantum-computed energies agree with reference full configuration interaction results and with DMET-complete active space CI energies for embedded systems, to within chemical accuracy for the chosen basis sets. These results demonstrate the robustness of quantum sampling-based classical diagonalization approaches while highlighting the promise of hybrid embedding strategies combined with near-term Ansätze for advancing quantum chemistry toward classically intractable molecular systems and establishing their practicality on current quantum hardware.</jats:p>

title: Making sense of quantum teleportation: an intervention study on students’ conceptions using a diagrammatic approach
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Quantum physics education at the upper-secondary level traditionally follows a historical approach, rarely extending beyond early 20th-century ideas, leaving students unprepared for comprehending modern quantum technologies central to everyday life and many facets of modern industry. To address this gap, we investigated how upper-secondary students and pre-service teachers understand quantum teleportation when taught with a simplified diagrammatic formalism based on the ZX-calculus, which represents quantum processes as diagrams of wires and boxes. Through phenomenographic analysis of video-recorded group work sessions, written responses to exercises, and a group interview, with a total of
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$n=21$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mi>n</mml:mi>
                          <mml:mo>=</mml:mo>
                          <mml:mn>21</mml:mn>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    participants, we identified an outcome space consisting of four qualitatively different, hierarchically ordered categories of description encapsulating the different ways of experiencing quantum teleportation. The categories revealed that a conceptual progression depends on how one understands the temporality in quantum processes, the role of entanglement in quantum teleportation, the active nature of quantum measurements, and interpretations of mathematical operations in the diagrams. Our findings indicate that while a simplified diagrammatic formalism for teaching quantum physics can provide an accessible entry point at the upper-secondary level, it does not automatically resolve fundamental conceptual challenges, and requires careful consideration in terms of developing teaching and learning sequences. Finally, these results provide educators with a deeper understanding of conceptual affordances and challenges for designing and improving instruction, while also highlighting the need for further exploring how students and teachers alike understand quantum phenomena.
                  </jats:p>

title: Electron-phonon coupling and electronic transport at the moiré scale in twisted bilayer graphene
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    First-principles calculations can accurately describe electron-phonon (e-ph) interactions and electronic transport in a wide range of materials, but are currently limited to unit cells with up to ~100 atoms due to computational cost. Here, we develop an atomistic electronic potential with Holstein- and Peierls-like terms for modeling e-ph interactions and phonon-limited electronic transport that enables the study of moiré systems with thousands of atoms per unit cell. This method can accurately reproduce first-principles e-ph coupling and resistivity in graphene and large-angle twisted bilayer graphene (TBG). Using this approach, we study TBG over a range of twist angles down to 1.6
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    (5044-atom unit cell), and report the evolution of e-ph interactions and phonon-limited resistivity with twist angle. The predicted resistivity increases by two orders of magnitude between 13.2
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    and 1.6
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    , driven by the progressive reduction of the electronic energy scale. Our calculations can predict key experimental trends in 2.0
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    and 1.6
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    TBG, including the resistivity and its dependence on temperature and band filling. Our work establishes a scalable approach for quantitative studies of e-ph interactions and transport in moiré materials and other systems with previously inaccessible length scales.
                  </jats:p>

title: Extracting Information from a Superradiant Burst Using Simple Measurements
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    It is well known that superradiant decay of an ensemble of
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <a:mi>N</a:mi>
                    </a:math>
                    spins generates a complex non-classical state of light. Here, we consider the estimation of a phase encoded in the initial spin state from a superradiant burst of photons: how is information about this phase distributed among the emitted photons and can the phase be estimated using simple measurements? Despite the complexity of the photonic burst state, we show that a simple homodyne measurement combined with an optimized filter and linear estimator recovers the
                    <c:math xmlns:c="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <c:mi>N</c:mi>
                    </c:math>
                    -scaling of the quantum Fisher information of the initial spin state (including cases exhibiting
                    <e:math xmlns:e="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <e:msup>
                        <e:mi>N</e:mi>
                        <e:mn>2</e:mn>
                      </e:msup>
                    </e:math>
                    Heisenberg scaling). Even more surprising, the temporal mode with optimal information content contains a vanishing fraction of the total emitted photons in the large-
                    <g:math xmlns:g="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <g:mi>N</g:mi>
                    </g:math>
                    limit, suggesting an effective compression of phase information. Our results and setup represent a new approach to quantum metrology for spin systems, in that they enable cavity-based readout of solid-state spin ensembles that utilizes resonant spin-photon interactions.

title: Rotational motion and axial strain near a strong lateral discontinuity
abstract:
<jats:title>SUMMARY</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ground-shaking site effects, which are anomalous earthquake ground motions at the Earth’s surface, are caused by the generation of specific wavefields in specific near-surface structures. The best known are effects in surface sedimentary layers, sedimentary basins and valleys, which are related to wave trapping in softer materials. To a lesser degree, topographic effects, associated with irregular surface geometry and often also with collocated softer or cracked material, have also received much attention and gave rise to specific provisions in some building codes (e.g., EC8). By contrast, site effects related to sharp lateral boundaries between media with very different stiffness have been much less investigated, despite consistent macroseismic observations of a significant increase in damage intensity on “stripes” located along strong lateral discontinuities. In this study we consider a semi-infinite layer as a canonical model for many real situations with sediments relatively sharply laterally bounded or with abrupt change of sediment thickness. We investigate numerically simulated particle velocity, rate of rotational motion and rate of axial strain for the vertically incident SH, SV and P waves. We use a novel type of characterization of transfer properties – time-frequency transfer functions for the particle velocity and rates of rotational motion and axial strain. We found that the rates of rotational motion and axial strain display sharp peaks at the lateral discontinuity mainly in the case of the incident SV and P waves. Particle-velocity components exhibit a maximum close to the discontinuity, but at variable distances depending on central frequency and incident wave type (“basin-edge” effect). At larger distances from the discontinuity, the decay of rotational motion and axial strain is controlled by the attenuation in sediments. The sharp peaks of the rates of rotational motion and axial strain across the lateral discontinuity, together with the well-known basin-edge effects for translational motion, are found to be the key site effects of the laterally bounded sedimentary layer.</jats:p>

title: Hardware-tailored logical Clifford circuits for stabilizer codes
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantum error correction is the art of protecting fragile quantum information through suitable encoding and active interventions. However, it is notoriously difficult to manipulate encoded quantum data without causing uncorrectable errors. Here, we introduce a mathematical framework for constructing hardware-tailored circuits that implement any desired Clifford unitary on the logical level of any given stabilizer code. We formulate this task as a discrete optimization problem that minimizes the number of CZ gates while naturally incorporating a parameterization of all Clifford stabilizers. Despite the intrinsic difficulty of the circuit compilation problem, our methods scale to at least 16 physical qubits. Because our circuits require very few CZ gates, they provide excellent starting points for constructing fault-tolerant implementations using flag gadgets. Using a brute-force search, we develop several such flag gadgets, including weakly fault-tolerant logical Hadamard circuits for the [[8, 3, 2]] code that require an unprecedentedly small number of physical two-qubit gates. Our work introduces both the mathematics and software for compiling hardware-tailored logical Clifford circuits. From a broader perspective, we turn away from the standard generator decomposition and instead focus on the holistic compilation of entire logical circuits, leading to significant savings in practice.</jats:p>

title: Flat band excitons and quantum metric
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We discuss the excitons in flat band systems. Quantum metric plays a central role in determining the properties of single exciton excitations as well as the exciton condensate. While the electrons and holes are supposed to be extremely heavy in flat bands, the excitons (the bound state of an electron-hole pair) could be light and mobile. In particular, we show that the inverse of the effective mass tensor of excitons is proportional to the quantum metric tensor. Meanwhile, the flat band excitons have a finite size, lower bounded by the trace of the quantum metric tensor. Given the properties of single exciton excitation, one can argue for the formation of exciton condensate. Because of the quantum metric, the exciton condensate can support dissipationless counterflow supercurrent, implying the stability of exciton condensate.</jats:p>

title: High-Current Accelerator-Driven Neutron Sources (HiCANSs): Current Projects and Perspectives in Europe
abstract: <jats:p>To provide neutrons for science and industry, various processes are applied, such as nuclear fission, spallation, fusion or low-energy nuclear reactions. With the availability of high-current proton accelerators, the latter process has gained growing interest in recent years. The prospect of access to versatile neutron sources with affordable cost and efficient and strong neutron flux has inspired many projects worldwide to establish high-current accelerator-driven neutron sources (HiCANSs). While compact accelerator-driven neutron sources (CANSs) using low-energy nuclear reactions have been used for decades, this novel class of sources, HiCANSs, would open new opportunities to access and exploit neutrons in science and industry. The most ambitious projects in this field have been developed in Europe, including the ARGITU project in Spain, the ICONE project in France and the HBS project in Germany. In the present paper, the basic physical and technological properties of HiCANSs will be outlined briefly, and the European HiCANS projects will be described. A short outlook on the future opportunities for HiCANSs in the landscape of the neutron facilities in Europe will be given.</jats:p>

Confinement-Driven Selectivity for Alkanol Dehydration in Ti-BEA Zeolites
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Zeolite catalysts offer unique opportunities for tuning catalytic behaviors through modifications to both the active site and the surrounding pore environment. Although confinement effects in zeolites have been investigated, their specific contributions—particularly in Lewis acid catalysts—remain difficult to isolate from active-site chemistry and diffusive limitations. Here, we use density functional theory combined with microkinetic modeling to demonstrate confinement effects on the dehydration of ethanol, n-propanol, and n-butanol to alkene and dialkyl ether products catalyzed by Ti-BEA zeolites. Dehydration mechanisms are proposed over “closed” heteroatom-substituted sites, partially hydrolyzed “hydroxy-open” sites, and “alkoxy-open” sites formed through the dissociative adsorption of an alkanol. Closed-site dehydration dominates both alkene and ether formation at low alkanol partial pressures in the absence of co-fed water. Dispersion stabilization increases with alkanol size, decreasing the ratio of alkene-forming reactant-state coverages relative to ether-forming states. For alkanols that are smaller than the surrounding zeolite framework, dispersion stabilizes the closed-site alkene transition state, resulting in similar alkene selectivities for EtOH and n-PrOH. Repulsive interactions between the n-BuOH backbone and the framework raise the closed-site alkene formation energy barrier, yielding an order-of-magnitude lower alkene selectivity compared to EtOH and n-PrOH. With increasing alkanol pressure, site saturation suppresses closed-site alkene formation, causing alkene selectivity to decrease and eventually plateau.</jats:p>

title: Crowding types in high-density tourist cities: Based on a physical and-perceived density clustering analysis
abstract: <jats:p>Driven by global urbanization and the rise of mass tourism, crowding in high-density tourist cities has become a significant concern in the academic community. However, existing studies often lack a systematic categorization of crowding types, resulting in insufficiently targeted governance strategies. In this study, a two‑dimensional framework of physical and perceived crowding is employed to construct a comprehensive indicator system comprising eight physical crowding indicators and six perceived crowding indicators. Furthermore, twenty‑eight high‑density urban areas worldwide are selected, and cluster analysis is applied to identify crowding types and examine the key influencing factors of each type. The results present four crowding types: closely spaced narrow alley, high building quantity, high‑rise low‑greenery, and high vehicle interference. Additionally, correlation analysis reveals the interaction mechanisms that exist among factors. Building coverage is positively correlated with road network density. Moreover, building spacing is positively correlated with both the building height and the building height‑to‑width ratio. Façade color is positively correlated with the road network density. Finally, the number of vehicles within an area is positively correlated with both the road width and site area. Conversely, building coverage is negatively correlated with the building spacing, depth‑to‑height ratio (D/H), and green space ratio. In addition, building spacing is negatively correlated with the number of buildings within an area, and façade color is negatively correlated with the green space ratio. This research enriches the evaluation indices considered in both the physical and perceived dimensions. The four identified types of crowded spaces derived from empirical analysis can provide a scientific basis for developing future differentiated planning strategies.</jats:p>

title: Collisional energy loss distribution of a fast parton in a hot or dense QCD medium
abstract:
<jats:title>
                    A
                    <jats:sc>bstract</jats:sc>
                  </jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    We compute the probability distribution for collisional energy loss of an ultrarelativistic parton crossing a quark-gluon plasma. This
                    <jats:italic>collisional quenching weight</jats:italic>
                    has not been determined previously, unlike the average collisional loss per unit distance, although it should be a more accurate quantity to use in jet-quenching phenomenology. The quenching weight is obtained from a well-known kinetic equation which resums an arbitrary number of elastic scatterings of the energetic parton with the medium, providing a complete description of the stochastic energy exchange, including the possibility of energy gain from thermal fluctuations. The formulation also naturally extends the standard treatment of collisional energy loss to finite path lengths, which could be relevant not only for heavy-ion collisions, but also for light-ion, and possibly proton-nucleus and proton-proton collisions. We predict the quenching weight in a setup where individual elastic scatterings are described using the hard thermal loop approximation for soft exchanges, with a smooth matching to the hard domain.
                  </jats:p>

title: Ductile Polycrystalline AgCuSe With Preferred Orientation for High Power Density Flexible Thermoelectric Device
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The recently discovered ductile inorganic thermoelectric (TE) materials provide a promising solution for developing flexible TE devices with high output power density used in wearable electronics. However, the current ductile polycrystalline TE materials are still very rare. In this work, we show that engineering a polycrystal with a strong preferred orientation along the crystal plane with a high ratio of cleavage energy to slip barrier energy can convert it from brittle into ductile. Taking AgCuSe as a case study, via controlling the rolling temperature and speed during the hot‐rolling process, the polycrystalline AgCuSe with (0
                    <jats:italic>k</jats:italic>
                    0) preferred orientation is successfully obtained, which exhibits excellent ductility at room temperature. Likewise, the ductile AgCuSe retains the good TE performance of brittle AgCuSe, with the room‐temperature power factor (∼21.7 µW cm
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                     K
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    ) much higher than the best flexible AgCuSe‐based materials reported before. By using the ductile polycrystalline AgCuSe, an ultrathin flexible cross‐plane π‐shaped TE device is developed to show a maximum normalized power density up to 46 µW cm
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                     K
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    , a record‐high value in flexible thermoelectrics. This work not only provides a novel ductile TE material for flexible thermoelectrics, but also offers an alternative route to discover more ductile inorganic materials by using the anisotropic mechanical properties.
                  </jats:p>

title: Asymptotic freedom for holographic energy correlators
abstract:
<jats:title>
                    A
                    <jats:sc>bstract</jats:sc>
                  </jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We calculate energy correlators in a holographic model incorporating elements of asymptotic freedom and confinement. We model a running coupling by considering a geometry with a warp factor that deviates logarithmically from anti-de Sitter (AdS). A novel aspect of our bulk metric is that it smoothly interpolates between a Randall-Sundrum solution with a hard wall and a geometry corresponding to a logarithmic running typical of gauge theories. By studying shockwave deformations of this metric, we compute a two-point energy correlator assuming a high-energy scalar source. This extends techniques recently developed for correlators in asymptotically AdS geometries. We use numerical methods to find the profile of shockwaves along the extra dimension, as it does not admit an analytical form. The running coupling leads to a decay of the two-point correlator at small angular separation, unlike the flat correlator one finds in AdS. In the back-to-back limit we observe an exponential falloff similar to other hard-wall models.</jats:p>

title: Minimal Majoron dark matter
abstract:

Remaining agnostic about the origin and value of the Majoron mass, we evaluate the DM abundance from both the freeze-in and misalignment mechanisms, and identify the viable parameter space consistent with observational constraints. title: Spectral spacetime entropy for quasifree theories
abstract:
<jats:title>
                    A
                    <jats:sc>bstract</jats:sc>
                  </jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Motivated by the necessity to UV-regularise entanglement entropy, we present a spectral method for calculating the entropy of quasifree states, for both bosonic and fermionic field theories. This construction is defined in spacetime rather than on a hypersurface, enabling the covariant regularisation of entropies, and its calculation in generic spacetime regions. We derive these formulae, which have previously appeared in the literature, in a new manner and highlight certain aspects of them, such as their connection to the density matrix and its eigenvalues. The spacetime nature of the formulation makes it particularly apt in the context of semiclassical and quantum gravity and in connection to black hole entropy. Another useful property of the formulation is its application to settings where no notion of a Cauchy surface exists, such as in the causal set theory approach to quantum gravity. We show example applications of the formulae which demonstrate their ability to reproduce known results. We also show a calculation in a causal set in 1 + 1 dimensions which makes use of several of the unique and useful features of the formalism. In this last example, we obtain a novel result of a slightly modified entanglement entropy scaling coefficient, giving a possible signature of spacetime discreteness.</jats:p>

title: A quark-diquark model for parity doublet structure of baryons
abstract:
<jats:title>
                    A
                    <jats:sc>bstract</jats:sc>
                  </jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The chiral invariant mass of baryons is a phenomenological input of parity doublet models, and its microscopic origin remains an open question. We propose that the chiral invariant mass and the parity doublet structure originate from the diquarks: the scalar (0
                    <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                    ) and pseudoscalar (0
                    <jats:sup>
                      <jats:italic>−</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sup>
                    ) diquarks form a parity doublet whose invariant mass is generated by gluon dynamics rather than by the quark condensate. We construct a three-flavor chiral quark-diquark model in which a quark and a diquark are bounded into a baryon through a chiral-invariant four-body interaction whose structure is reduced from one-gluon exchange. It is shown that the quark-diquark structure automatically yields the two chiral representations and the mirror assignment of the parity doublet model, and the composite baryons acquire chiral invariant masses even for massless quarks. We find that the octet baryon spectrum and the nucleon sigma terms are reproduced very well with a minimal set of parameters. Furthermore, after chiral symmetry restoration, the model predicts a distinctive inverted mass hierarchy: the nucleon remains relatively heavy, whereas the Σ and Ξ baryon become lighter than the nucleon. This inverse mass ordering may therefore provide a novel, experimentally testable signature towards chiral symmetry restoration.
                  </jats:p>

title: Candidate gaugings of categorical continuous symmetry
abstract:

                    <jats:sc>bstract</jats:sc>

                  <jats:p>
                    Different gaugings of the global symmetry of a quantum field theory are closely related to its various phases. In this work, we study candidate gaugeable sub-symmetries by analyzing candidate Lagrangian algebra data in the Drinfeld center of a symmetry category
                    <jats:inline-formula>

                    <jats:italic>G</jats:italic>
                    -symmetry and possible ’t Hooft anomaly labeled by an integer
                    <jats:italic>k</jats:italic>
                    . We use the combination of the
                    <jats:italic>BF</jats:italic>
                    theory and the level-
                    <jats:italic>k</jats:italic>
                    Chern-Simons theory with gauge group
                    <jats:italic>G</jats:italic>
                    as a semiclassical kernel-theoretic working model for the corresponding SymTFT. Under two explicit working assumptions, namely that this
                    <jats:italic>BF</jats:italic>
                    +
                    <jats:italic>k</jats:italic>
                    CS theory provides the relevant SymTFT model and that the common +1 eigenspaces of the resulting modular kernels detect candidate Lagrangian algebra data in the continuous setting, we derive candidate modular

title: Thermal evolution and hydrodynamic filtering of pseudoscalar dark matter
abstract:
<jats:title>
                    A
                    <jats:sc>bstract</jats:sc>
                  </jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Filtered dark matter provides a mechanism for producing massive dark matter particles during a first order phase transition. The resulting abundance can be modified by plasma hydrodynamics. We investigate this effect in a complex singlet extension of the Standard Model, focusing on the deflagration regime. The entropy normalized dark matter abundance
                    <jats:italic>Y</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>
                      <jats:italic>χ</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sub>
                    is calculated using both analytic and numerical methods. As the dark matter mass increases, we identify three patterns of abundance evolution before nucleation, ranging from thermal equilibrium to thermal suppression and freeze-out. For
                    <jats:italic>ξ</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>
                      <jats:italic>w</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sub>
                    = 0.01, the numerical results show that hydrodynamic effects increase the final
                    <jats:italic>Y</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>
                      <jats:italic>χ</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sub>
                    by factors of approximately 4.1, 5.7, and 31.6 for
                    <jats:italic>m</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>
                      <jats:italic>χ</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sub>
                    = 1.78, 2.30, and 5.03 TeV, respectively. For the two lighter masses, the numerical and analytic results agree within 5%, and the difference is reduced to about 1% or less when hydrodynamic effects are included. The heaviest case requires a numerical treatment because dark matter freeze-out before nucleation. Our results show that hydrodynamic reheating can enhance
                    <jats:italic>Y</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>
                      <jats:italic>χ</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sub>
                    even when dark matter has already frozen out before the phase transition. In this regime,
                    <jats:italic>Y</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>
                      <jats:italic>χ</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sub>
                    is determined by the dark matter abundance established before nucleation and hydrodynamic filtering at the bubble wall.
                  </jats:p>

title: Magnetic field-induced enhancement and quenching of Urca emission in quark matter
abstract:
<jats:title>
                    A
                    <jats:sc>bstract</jats:sc>
                  </jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Using first-principles field-theoretic methods, we investigate neutrino emission from strongly magnetized dense quark matter under conditions relevant to compact stars. We account for Landau-level quantization of both electron and quark states and show that it strongly modifies the kinematics of Urca processes. In particular, quark quantization restricts the available phase space in which both quark and electron energies can simultaneously lie near their respective Fermi surfaces. At moderately strong magnetic fields, before pronounced quark quantization sets in, the emission rate tends to increase on average with increasing field strength. In the regime of very strong fields, however, the increasingly restricted phase space first gives rise to Shubnikov-de Haas-type oscillations and then to resonance-like spikes near a discrete sequence of Urca-resonant magnetic field values, separated by regions of strong suppression. Finally, the emission rate becomes nearly completely quenched once |
                    <jats:italic>eB</jats:italic>
                    | ≳ 6

                    <jats:sub>

title: Which functions admit a positive geometry? from branch cuts to string amplitudes
abstract:
<jats:title>
                    A
                    <jats:sc>bstract</jats:sc>
                  </jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Positive geometry provides a geometric framework where physical observables are encoded as canonical forms associated to regions of kinematic space. In this paper we consider a generalisation to an infinite union of line segments, which allows us to capture canonical forms beyond rational functions. In the continuum limit of positive geometries, we show that we can generalise even further and describe positive geometries whose canonical forms contain branch cuts. We will constrain which functions can be obtained as the canonical form of one-dimensional positive geometries. We introduce the notion of the
                    <jats:italic>pseudogenus</jats:italic>
                    to classify meromorphic function, and show that canonical forms can be written as the d log of a function with pseudogenus zero. Furthermore, we argue that the spectrum encoded by a union of line segments is consistent with the presence of a stringy tower of states or a Kaluza–Klein tower with four or more compact directions only if nearly all such states do not contribute to the scattering amplitude. In addition, we show how the d log of both open and closed string amplitudes admit a positive geometry. This allows us to give a fully geometric interpretation for the KLT double copy at four points.
                  </jats:p>

Effects of early Universe inhomogeneity on bubble formation: primordial black holes as an extreme case
abstract:
<jats:title>
                    A
                    <jats:sc>bstract</jats:sc>
                  </jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Our early Universe is not perfectly homogeneous and it may contain some inhomogeneous sources, which might distort the local spacetime and modify the bubble nucleation rate. Taking the primordial black hole as an extreme example, we investigate the bubble nucleation rate of a first-order phase transition in the vicinity of primordial black holes or other primordial gravitational sources. Our analysis reveals that the presence of primordial black holes can reduce the effective action and might modify the nucleation rate due to their gravitational effects, potentially altering the dynamics of the phase transition in the early Universe. As a byproduct, new gravitational wave signals could be produced since the gravitational effects of primordial black holes or other possible inhomogeneous sources could lead to nucleation of nonspherical bubbles.</jats:p>

title: Fermion mass relations in one-parameter modular models
abstract:
<jats:title>
                    A
                    <jats:sc>bstract</jats:sc>
                  </jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Modular flavour symmetries provide a possible organizing principle for the Standard Model Yukawa sector, by replacing generic couplings with a potentially small number of modular forms controlled by a single complex modulus. We study the extreme limit of this idea: one-parameter modular models (OPMs), in which each charged-fermion mass matrix is fixed by a single modular invariant contraction. We develop a systematic method to construct such models, showing that the one-parameter modular model (OPM) requirement is already highly constraining at the level of possible fermion hierarchies. In a concrete realization, the charged-lepton and down-quark sectors are controlled by the common modulus, leading to exact mass relations at the flavour scale,
                    <jats:disp-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$ {m}_s^5=2\sqrt{2}{m}_d^3{m}_b^2,\kern0.5em {m}_{\mu}^3=\sqrt{2}{m}_e{m}_{\tau}^2,\kern0.5em {m}_s^2{m}_{\tau }=\sqrt{2}{m}_e{m}_b^2. $$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">

                            <mml:mi>m</mml:mi>

                          </mml:msubsup>
                          <mml:mo>=</mml:mo>

                            <mml:mi>m</mml:mi>

                            <mml:mn>3</mml:mn>
                          </mml:msubsup>

                            <mml:mi>m</mml:mi>

                          </mml:msubsup>
                          <mml:msub>
                            <mml:mi>m</mml:mi>
                            <mml:mi>τ</mml:mi>
                          </mml:msub>
                          <mml:mo>=</mml:mo>
                          <mml:msqrt>
                            <mml:mn>2</mml:mn>
                          </mml:msqrt>
                          <mml:msub>
                            <mml:mi>m</mml:mi>

                          </mml:msub>

                            <mml:mi>m</mml:mi>

                  <jats:p>We show that, once renormalization-group evolution and selective supersymmetric threshold effects are included, these high-scale relations can be made compatible with low-energy charged-fermion data. title: Revisiting relativistic corrections to inclusive J/ψ production at B factories: complete expansion for three-body quarkonium production
abstract:

title: Association of the Cholesterol–High-Density Lipoprotein–Glucose Index with Large-Artery Atherosclerotic Versus Cardioembolic Stroke: A Single-Center Retrospective Study
abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: We aimed to assess the association of the cholesterol–high-density lipoprotein–glucose index (CHG) with large-artery atherosclerotic stroke (LAA) versus cardioembolic stroke (CE), and to compare its discrimination and incremental value beyond a clinical model with those of the triglyceride–glucose index (TyG). Methods: This single-center retrospective study consecutively screened patients hospitalized with ischemic stroke at Beijing Anzhen Hospital, Capital Medical University, from September 2024 to August 2025 and included eligible patients with acute LAA or CE. CHG and TyG were calculated from the first examination results after admission. Missing BMI values were handled using 20 multiple imputations. Logistic regression, restricted cubic splines, and exploratory subgroup analyses were used to evaluate associations, with further adjustment for lipid-lowering and glucose-lowering medication use before the current stroke onset. Firth-penalized regression was also used to assess the robustness of the association estimates. Model performance was evaluated using 1000 paired outcome-stratified bootstrap resamples, comparing CHG, TyG, and joint modeling of the three component indicators and estimating differences in corrected AUC and their 95% confidence intervals. Results: The study included 921 patients, comprising 790 with LAA and 131 with CE. After multivariable adjustment, each 1-standard-deviation increase in CHG was associated with an odds ratio of 2.83 for LAA versus CE (95% confidence interval: 2.20–3.65, p < 0.001), with a nonlinear association (p for nonlinearity = 0.003). The OR in the Firth sensitivity analysis was 2.77 (95% confidence interval: 2.17–3.59). The single-index AUCs of CHG and TyG were 0.725 and 0.662, respectively (paired DeLong p < 0.001). Adding CHG increased the bootstrap-corrected AUC of the clinical model from 0.647 to 0.743 and reduced the corrected Brier score from 0.119 to 0.105. The difference in corrected AUC between the CHG-enhanced model and the TyG-enhanced model was 0.051 (95% confidence interval: 0.025–0.079), whereas its difference from the model jointly including the three component indicators remained uncertain. The direction of the main associations was consistent in sensitivity analyses, and no clear subgroup interactions were identified. Conclusions: In this cohort, higher CHG was positively associated with LAA versus CE after adjustment for measured covariates. Its enhanced model had higher discrimination than the TyG-enhanced model in internal validation, but its advantage over joint modeling of the component indicators remained uncertain. This was a single-center retrospective study with a substantial imbalance in group sizes, and residual confounding may remain. All performance estimates were derived from internal validation. The clinical utility of CHG and its applicability across centers have not been established and require independent external validation.</jats:p>

title: Multi-Feature Fusion for Dual-Energy X-Ray Transmission Sorting of Copper and Lead–Zinc Ores
abstract: <jats:p>Dual-energy X-ray transmission sorting of copper ores is often constrained by strong coupling between conventional features and particle thickness. To address this, we propose two decoupled features: R3, an improved R-value feature, and Zeff from basis material decomposition, which are designed to mitigate thickness interference and improve high-Z mineral identification. Copper and lead–zinc ore particles from the Yinshan Mine (Dexing, China), with particle thickness ranges of 8–60 mm for the copper ore and 8–25 mm for the lead–zinc ore, were tested on a laboratory DE-XRT sorter. A support vector machine regression model was trained on 314 phyllite copper ore particles (8–60 mm) to predict a weighted comprehensive grade (Cu+Fe+S), using R-value, R3, Zeff, and w3–w2 as inputs. The method showed favorable performance for porphyry copper ores (particle thickness: 8–60 mm): feed grades of 0.068%–0.109% Cu were upgraded to concentrates of 0.127%–0.244% Cu, with waste grades of 0.030%–0.051% and recoveries of 61.69%–79.67%. For phyllite copper ores (particle thickness: 8–60 mm), enrichment was observed through yield adjustment, with recoveries of 33.38%–71.69%. A plausible reason for the poor performance of the intermediate-grade Cu phyllite ore (Cu: 0.098%) is a combination of two factors: the chalcopyrite grain size (~0.1 mm) being below the detector resolution (0.8 mm), which causes mineral signals to be swamped by gangue, and the fundamental limitation of dual-energy XRT in distinguishing Cu from Fe. For lead–zinc ore (4.744% Pb+Zn feed), the sorter rejected 21.99% as waste while achieving 98.87% Pb+Zn recovery, with only 0.245% Pb+Zn in the waste. These results indicate that the proposed multi-feature fusion and SVM regression strategy provides a feasible approach for the preconcentration of low-grade copper ores and waste rejection for lead–zinc ores.</jats:p>

title: An Adaptive Double-Inertial Algorithm for Variational Inequality and Split Common Fixed Point Problems with Applications to Image Restoration
abstract: <jats:p>In this paper, we introduce a new adaptive double-inertial viscosity algorithm to solve a variational inequality and split common fixed point problem in Hilbert spaces. In our proposed method, we combine two inertial terms with a projected variational inequalities with a self-adaptive step size, an averaged demicontractive mapping and a viscosity approximation. This combination allows the algorithm to use information from previous iterates in each step. Under suitable assumptions on mappings used and sequences of the parameters, we prove the proposed sequence converges strongly to a solution of the considered problem. Several numerical examples are presented to study the convergence behavior of the proposed method. The numerical results show that the proposed algorithm converges faster for different initial points and performs better than the comparable existing algorithm in the tested cases. As an application, the proposed method is used for image restoration. The restoration quality is evaluated using PSNR, SSIM, and MSE, together with CPU time and the number of iterations. The proposed method gives the highest PSNR and SSIM values and the lowest MSE for all considered images. The visual results also show that the proposed method can remove degradation while preserving important image structures. The proposed algorithm is also assessed through a numerical example, and its performance is compared graphically with several existing methods from the literature. These results show that the proposed algorithm is effective both for the theoretical problem and for the considered image-restoration application.</jats:p>

title: Skin‐Interfaced Wearable Device for Synchronically Harvesting High‐Entropy Body Energy and Monitoring Deep Tissue Temperature
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Efficiently harvesting thermal energy from human skin poses formidable challenges owing to its high‐entropy characteristics. While Seebeck‐effect wearable thermoelectric devices can convert skin heat flux into electrical voltage, prevailing generators remain constrained in delivering sustainable energy and multifunctionality. This limitation stems from a fundamental trade‐off where the output voltage falls below the effective charging threshold, leaving the ultra‐low skin heat flux underexplored for physiological sensing. In this study, we report a skin‐interfaced wearable thermoelectric sensor and generator that synchronously harvests body high‐entropy energy and monitors deep tissue temperature (< 0.2°C). This dual functionality is enabled by a thermal meta‐design that guides inherently dispersed cutaneous heat flux into a vertical, one‐dimensional path through geometric confinement, ensuring signal fidelity for both sensing and energy conversion. To overcome the limited skin‐ambient temperature gradient, we introduce a reusable cooling hydrogel patch based on a dual‐mode evaporation mechanism, boosting the electrical output to 120 mV and power density to 45.7 μW cm
                    <jats:sup>–2</jats:sup>
                    . Furthermore, during daily wear under an approximate 10 K skin‐environment temperature differential, the system achieved a sustained output of up to 34 mV. The integrated voltage boost‐storage circuit maintained the capacitor voltage at around 1.044 V, facilitating a sustainable power supply to electronic loads, and stabilized at approximately 5.2 V near full charge. The integrated system demonstrates continuous, multi‐parameter health monitoring powered solely by body heat. This research establishes a co‐design paradigm for concurrent deep body temperature monitoring and high‐entropy energy recovery, paving the way for self‐powered, multimodal integrated wearable devices.
                  </jats:p>

title: THE INFLUENCE OF HIGH-FREQUENCY RADIATION ON THE PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF PRODUCTS (RAW MATERIALS: STRAWBERRIES, APPLES, PEARS)
abstract: <jats:p>The purpose of the article is to substantiate approaches to the controlled influence of high-frequency electromagnetic radiation on the physicochemical and structural-mechanical properties of fruit and berry raw materials, taking into account their further integration into drying and vibration-based technological processes. Particular attention is paid to identifying relationships between energy input parameters and changes in the internal structure of the material, which determine its behavior under industrial conditions. The research methodology is based on a combination of computational modeling and a factorial experiment with variation of frequency, power, and exposure time of electromagnetic treatment. Strawberries, apples, and pears were selected as research objects due to their differences in tissue density and moisture content. The evaluation was carried out using a set of indicators, including changes in density, firmness, electrical conductivity, moisture content, and color parameters. The obtained results demonstrate a pronounced relationship between high-frequency processing regimes and the degree of transformation of the physical properties of raw materials. It has been established that increasing power and frequency leads to intensification of heat and mass transfer processes, accompanied by a decrease in density and mechanical strength of the material. Different levels of sensitivity of the studied objects to elect-omagnetic influence have been identified, which necessitates a differentiated approach to the selection of processing regimes. The practical significance of the results lies in the development of technological recommendations for integrating high-frequency radiation into combined drying systems and vibration transport lines. The proposed solutions allow reducing product losses, improving the stability of physical characteristics, and increasing the efficiency of production processes. The scientific novelty of the study consists in a comprehensive approach to assessing the impact of electromagnetic fields on the structure of fruit and berry raw materials, considering their subsequent operation under mechanical loading conditions, which expands the possibilities of applying high-frequency technologies in the food industry.</jats:p>

title: Fully Conjugated Chiral Covalent Organic Frameworks Enabling High‐Density Polaron Hopping Conduction via Spin‐Frustration Relief
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Organic semiconductors are key materials for high‐performance organic electronics, where both high carrier density and fast carrier mobility are required to achieve high conductivity. However, increasing carrier concentrations inevitably introduces scattering effect that severely impair charge transport. Here we report a strategy to synthesize highly polarized covalent organic frameworks (COFs) through chirality‐induced crystallization and a subsequent COF‐to‐COF transformation, yielding benzothiazole‐linked fully conjugated frameworks. The resulting porous organic crystals feature an enhanced polarization arising from the parallel stacking of benzothiazole moieties, which enables precise N‐over‐N and S‐over‐S atomic alignment across neighboring layers. Benefiting from anisotropic polarization, the chiral COF film exhibits an excellent intrinsic conductivity of 1.9 × 10
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    S cm
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    , along with a high carrier concentration of 1.1 × 10
                    <jats:sup>17</jats:sup>
                    cm
                    <jats:sup>−3</jats:sup>
                    and a fast carrier mobility of 1.1 cm
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    V
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    s
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>

Upon iodine doping, the optimal conductivity of the chiral COFs is enhanced by more than one order of magnitude compared to that of the achiral analog with antiparallel stacking. We provide insights into the polaron‐mediated conduction mechanism through electron‐phonon coupling in the axisymmetric polarized frameworks, which addresses the carrier‐scattering issue even at high carrier densities. title: Cellulase-mediated surface engineering of cellulose fibers for high-performance cellulose fibers/polyaniline composites flexible electrodes
abstract: <jats:p>Cellulose-based flexible supercapacitor electrodes, exemplified by cellulose fibers/polyaniline (CFs/PANI) composite electrodes, have emerged as promising candidates for sustainable energy storage. However, their practical application is severely impeded by inherent interfacial incompatibility between CFs and PANI, which restricts PANI mass loading and compromises electrochemical performance. Herein, we propose a novel bio-etching strategy as a targeted pretreatment concept for cellulose surface engineering. The bio-etching process selectively modulates the surface morphology and chemical functionality of CFs, especially increasing the surface roughness and titratable carboxyl group content of CFs while preserving the continuous fiber framework at the optimized treatment time. These changes are consistent with improved PANI deposition during in situ  polymerization, potentially aided by electrostatic and hydrogen bonding interactions. The optimized bio-etching (10 min) yields a high PANI:sulfosalicylic acid (SSA) active-phase loading of 2.93 mg/cm2. Benefiting from the bio-etched fiber architecture and increased active-phase loading, the as-fabricated paper-based electrode delivers an areal capacitance of 2,098 mF/cm2 at 1 mA/cm2. In addition, the assembled symmetric supercapacitor exhibits an areal energy density of 111.6 μWh/cm2 at 1 mA/cm2. This work identifies controlled bio-etching as a promising surface engineering strategy for cellulose-based flexible energy-storage electrodes.</jats:p>

title: Strategic Consistency and Structural Fairness in Dynamic Efficiency Evaluation: The Inertial Cross-Efficiency Malmquist Productivity Index
abstract: <jats:p>Cross-efficiency-based Malmquist productivity measurement involves both the selection of DEA-optimal weights across Malmquist states and the aggregation of heterogeneous peer assessments. This study develops the Inertial Cross-Efficiency Malmquist Productivity Index (I-CEMPI). The method retains the state-specific primary-optimal weighting sets and coordinates the four Malmquist states through minimum intertemporal adjustment, yielding a unique and reproducible weight representation while preserving primary DEA optimality. Peer Cross-Malmquist assessments are subsequently combined through strategic-perspective-balanced geometric aggregation, which preserves the multiplicative decomposition into efficiency change and technical change. Applying I-CEMPI to 440 listed Chinese SRDI “Little Giant” enterprises over 2019–2024 shows substantial scope for intertemporal selection within the empirical optimal sets. Perspective balancing produces larger changes in aggregate productivity assessments than intertemporal coordination, while comparisons with the standard MPI and a published Cross-GMPI show high overall agreement together with differences in a subset of firm-level classifications. Innovation productivity contracts over most horizons, with technical change accounting for the larger share of cumulative contraction. Strategic perspectives differ more clearly in their efficiency-change and technical-change compositions than in persistent aggregate productivity rankings.</jats:p>

title: Enhanced shock pressure via Teflon tape confinement: a soft conformable tamper for laser-driven shock applications
abstract: <jats:p>Soft, pliable tampers, particularly commercially available fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP), commonly known as Teflon tape, have been shown to substantially increase laser-driven shock pressure and impulse relative to unconfined ablation. These materials provide an inexpensive, readily deployable alternative to rigid or liquid confinement systems. However, previous characterizations of tape tampers have focused on idealized, single-strip configurations, leaving unresolved how practical deployment considerations, including increased thickness for durability and the joining of adjacent strips, affect shock performance. Here, we present a systematic experimental study of Teflon tape in three practically motivated configurations: multilayer stacking, partial coverage, and stitched strips separated by a controlled gap. Consistent with previous reports, a single continuous layer confines the ablation plasma effectively, increasing the peak pressure and impulse by factors of 12.0 ± 2.3 and 16.8 ± 0.8, respectively, relative to the untamped condition. Adding multiple layers does not measurably change this enhancement since the optical transmission remained nearly the same. Under partial tamper coverage, the compression response transitions over a band of roughly ±2 mm about the tamper edge, from nearly full confinement on the tamped side to essentially unconfined ablation on the untamped side. Stitched strips exhibit a strong, nonlinear dependence on gap size, with an approximately 1 mm gap reducing both peak pressure and impulse by roughly 70%. A model is developed to relate the pressure to the gap width. Our study can provide guidance for extending tape-based confinement to large scale targets.</jats:p>

title:
Voltage-Gated
Ionic Conductivity in Ultranarrow Confinement
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Voltage-controlled ion transport in subnanometer pores underpins the operation of emerging filtration, energy-storage, and iontronic technologies, yet its microscopic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Using classical molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate ionic transport in ultranarrow (≤1 nm) quasi-two-dimensional nanopores in MXene electrodes filled with an ionic liquid. We reveal a nonmonotonic dependence of linear-response conductivity on electrode potential, with a pronounced asymmetry between positive and negative electrode polarizations. These behaviors originate from a competition between confinement-induced ionic ordering and charging-induced ion crowding within the pore. The resulting transition from a structure-limited to an ion-crowding-limited transport regime provides a general framework for understanding voltage-gated ionic conduction under extreme confinement, which facilitates the formulation of design principles for MXene-based nanofluidic, electrochemical, and iontronic devices.</jats:p>

title: The Gravitational Constant G and the Confinement of the Strong Force: Proton Quantum Dynamics Within the Baryonic Expansion Framework
journal: PHYSICS Journal: Theoretical and Experimental Studies
abstract:
<jats:p>Newton’s gravitational constant G is measured but has never been derived from more fundamental quantities. Within the
baryonic expansion framework developed by the author since 1990, we examine how G is related to the proton’s mass,
radius and internal pressure. The principal findings are three. (i) Applying the author’s 1993 expansion equation to the
proton and comparing the result with the acceleration its internal pressure (≈1035 Pa) would produce in the absence of
confi nement defines a confinement leakage factor k ≈ 3 × 10-40.
(ii) G is then bound to proton quantities by the exact relation G = 4π k Pp rp

leakage factor equals the proton’s gravitational coupling αG ≈ 6 × 10-39 divided by a geometric factor of about 20. As

title: Development of a Wing Mass Estimation Method for a High-Aspect-Ratio Box-Wing Regional Aircraft
abstract: <jats:p>Computationally efficient and sufficiently accurate mass estimation methods are required for the design exploration of aircraft with nonconventional configurations at the conceptual design stage. This paper investigates a box-wing regional aircraft developed within the LuFo project DOXWING, characterized by high-aspect-ratio wings and small stagger, for which traditional semi-empirical equations are insufficient to accurately estimate the wing mass due to the high aspect ratio and closed-wing configuration. To successfully perform the sizing of the box-wing configuration while accounting for aeroelastic effects, an aero-structural analysis framework was used and refined by taking all six sectional force and moment resultants into account in the sizing methodology, and using a more comprehensive definition of load cases based on the top-level aircraft requirements to ensure a wider coverage of the flight envelope. Following the framework’s validation through a comparison of its analysis results with corresponding reference values for both conventional and unconventional aircraft configurations, a parametric study was carried out for the DOXWING aircraft, which is comparable in size to the ATR72-class aircraft, by varying the wingspan, wing area, and wing loading. A better understanding of how these design parameters affect the wing mass and aerodynamic performance will enable more meaningful analyses in the subsequent conceptual aircraft design processes. Finally, a weight-estimation-relationship (WER) equation for wing-mass estimation is derived from the results of the parametric study, while a surrogate model is introduced to further enhance the prediction accuracy in regions where the nonlinear interactions between design variables cannot be fully represented by the WER equation. The proposed framework achieves a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 2.71% against reference wing masses from the literature, while the derived WER equation approximates sizing results for the DOXWING aircraft with 0.98% MAPE, supporting rapid conceptual design studies and showing that wing mass increases progressively with aspect ratio at fixed wing area and wing loading within the investigated design space.</jats:p>

title: Control Strategies and Stability Enhancement in Smart Grids with High Renewable Energy Penetration: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: <jats:p>The high penetration of renewable energy sources (RES), particularly power-electronic-interfaced wind and solar generation, is transforming conventional power systems into converter-dominated smart grids. While this transition supports decarbonization goals, it introduces major control and stability challenges due to reduced inertia, weakened grid strength, and complex interactions among converters and network dynamics. This paper presents a comprehensive review of control strategies and stability enhancement techniques for smart grids with high renewable energy penetration. Grid-forming and grid-following control strategies, including virtual inertia and damping emulation, droop-based, adaptive, and distributed control schemes, are reviewed, with emphasis on their operating principles, advantages, limitations, and suitable applications. Stability issues under weak grid conditions, high converter density, and hybrid AC/DC configurations are discussed, including frequency and voltage instability, converter interactions, synchronization challenges, and system response to disturbances. The roles of energy storage systems, flexible AC transmission system (FACTS) devices, and high-voltage direct current (HVDC) technologies in enhancing power system stability are also examined. Finally, the paper identifies key research gaps, practical implementation challenges, and emerging trends, supported by a comparative assessment of representative existing review studies, highlighting future directions toward resilient, flexible, and stable smart grids capable of accommodating very high shares of renewable energy.</jats:p>

title: Deep B and Plasma Cell Depletion in Pemphigus  and Other Autoantibody-Mediated Diseases
Beads, Springs, and Fields: Particle-Based Versus Continuum Models in Cell Biophysics
journal: Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics
abstract: <jats:p>Quantitative modeling has become an essential tool in modern biology, driven by advances in both experimental techniques and theoretical frameworks. Powerful high-resolution techniques now provide detailed datasets spanning molecular to tissue scales, allowing visualization of cellular structures with unprecedented detail. In parallel, developments in soft and active matter physics have established a robust theoretical basis for describing biological systems. In this context, two main modeling paradigms have emerged: particle-based models, which explicitly represent discrete components and their interactions, and continuum models, which describe systems through spatially varying fields. We compare these approaches across biological scales, highlighting their respective strengths, limitations, and domains of applicability. To keep our discussion biologically relevant, we focus on five systems of fundamental importance: the cytoskeleton, membranes, chromatin, biomolecular condensates and tissues. With this review, we aim to provide a framework for both theorists and experimentalists to select appropriate modeling strategies, and highlight future directions in biophysical modeling.</jats:p>

title: Exact Solution of the Direct and Inverse Quasi‐Stationary Dynamo Problem in the Expanding Plasma Ball
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>It is shown that differential equation of the quasi‐stationary dynamo effect (i.e., generation of the electric fields and currents) in a uniformly‐expanding plasma ball with strongly anisotropic conductivity possesses the unique mathematical property: namely, the spectrum of its eigenvalues is universal and independent of physical parameters of the medium. As a result, it becomes possible to introduce a special set of eigenfunctions—which we called the generalized spherical functions—that can be used to solve the dynamo problem in exactly the same way as ordinary spherical functions are used to solve the Laplace equation. The corresponding exact solutions should be especially valuable for treating the inverse dynamo problem, that is, determination of the plasma parameters from the experimentally measured electric fields and currents.</jats:p>
