title: Associations between different peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha genotypes and falls in community-dwelling older adults
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Falls are a significant health concern for older adults, often leading to injury, disability, and increased healthcare burden. Given the multifactorial nature of falls, genetic predispositions may contribute to individual susceptibility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This study aimed to examine the association between different peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">PPARGC1A)</jats:italic>
                      genotypes and fall history in community-dwelling older adults.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Fall history was assessed using a self-reported question regarding falls in the past year.
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">PPARGC1A</jats:italic>
                      genotypes (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Gly/Gly, Gly/Ser</jats:italic>
                      , and
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Ser/Ser</jats:italic>
                      ) were identified using polymerase chain reaction analysis. A total of 271 Japanese older adults (mean age: 74.0 ± 5.8 years) were included in the analysis. Of these, 75 (27.7%) had the
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Gly/Gly</jats:italic>
                      genotype, 144 (53.1%) had
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Gly/Ser</jats:italic>
                      , and 52 (19.2%) had
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Ser/Ser</jats:italic>
                      . Multiple logistic regression analysis was conducted with fall history as the dependent variable and
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">PPARGC1A</jats:italic>
                      genotype as the independent variable.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Participants with the
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Ser/Ser</jats:italic>
                      genotype had significantly higher odds of reporting falls than those with the
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Gly/Gly</jats:italic>
                      genotype (odds ratio [OR]: 3.58; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.28–10.07;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.015). No significant association was observed between
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Gly/Ser</jats:italic>
                      and
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Gly/Gly</jats:italic>
                      genotypes (OR: 1.87; 95% CI: 0.76–4.60;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.171).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The Ser/Ser genotype of
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">PPARGC1A</jats:italic>
                      may be linked to greater fall susceptibility among community-dwelling older adults. These findings may contribute to the identification of genetic risk profiles and the development of personalized fall prevention strategies in aging populations.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Reduced entorhinal and dentate theta-gamma coupling associated with adult Reelin loss in Alzheimer’s disease relevant mice
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Early Alzheimer’s disease (AD) affects entorhinal-hippocampal circuits, motivating functional measures of altered network coordination. We examined local field potentials and multiunit activity in head-fixed mice in a virtual-reality (VR) environment, comparing WT, App
                    <jats:sup>NL-F</jats:sup>
                    , and App
                    <jats:sup>NL-F</jats:sup>
                    -Reln-cKO groups (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 3 male mice per genotype). Reelin deletion was induced in adulthood using a ubiquitous tamoxifen-inducible Cre driver and was not restricted to entorhinal cortex (EC). Recordings sampled EC, dentate gyrus (DG), and CA1. Theta–gamma phase–amplitude coupling was quantified using modulation index (MI) and phase-locking value (PLV) between theta phase and the phase of the gamma-amplitude envelope. Nominal genotype effects were detected for DG-theta/DG-gamma coupling (MI,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.034; PLV,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.035) and EC-theta/DG-gamma coupling (MI,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.0043; PLV,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.0079), with descriptively lower means in App
                    <jats:sup>NL-F</jats:sup>
                    -Reln-cKO mice. Regional power spectra appeared broadly similar; a nominal genotype effect was reported for DG theta power (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.029), rather than a selective DG gamma-power reduction. Exploratory analyses suggested stronger coupling attenuation in the 35–55-Hz range and lower DG-associated coupling in both high and low theta/delta states. These findings identify DG-associated theta–gamma coupling as a candidate functional readout of adult Reelin loss in an AD-relevant background. The small cohort, uncorrected comparisons, widespread deletion, and absence of coupling–behavior analyses limit anatomical and functional inference.

title: Memory-window engineering: target specifications for duration, retention through division, and amplitude in immune epigenome editing
abstract: <jats:p>Immune activation, tolerance, exhaustion, trained immunity and regulatory stability are held in place by chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, histone modification, and enhancer-promoter wiring. CRISPR-based epigenome editors rewrite these layers without cutting DNA, but most reports address editing efficiency and leave time unanswered. Target duration is a design input to be specified before an editor is chosen; the duration achieved remains an experimental outcome. Memory-window engineering defines a candidate immune edit by three parameters: duration after editor clearance, retention through cell division, and amplitude at single-cell resolution, with target-compartment division rate as an explicit modifier. For passively diluted marks, division rate constrains post-clearance duration; transcriptional and phenotypic persistence may follow different trajectories. Published results from methylation editing at IL1RN, FOXP3 enhancer demethylation, PD-1 enhancer tuning, exhaustion circuits and CRISPRoff programming of primary human T cells are interpreted using their readouts and observation windows; some persistence endpoints remain censored by study duration. Three testable predictions concern CpG density, transcript-versus-mark recovery and division-dependent loss, with competing mechanisms and measurement artefacts considered. Specificity, the nuclease-knockout comparison, and the ethics of durable edits are treated as parts of the same specification. Two design consequences follow. TET-dependent erasure requires oxygen and 2-oxoglutarate; reduced erasure in hypoxic or metabolically inhibitory tumour regions is therefore a hypothesis for edited immune cells. Sustained programming of circulating monocyte output requires an upstream progenitor strategy, whereas long-lived resident myeloid cells are a separate case. A worked CAR T example and five-item reporting minimum distinguish development-stage characterisation from lot-release testing.</jats:p>

title: NOD1 priming by IFN-gamma regulates inflammatory responses and perturbs differentiation of skeletal muscle
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nod-like receptors (NLRs) are intracellular sensors acting as major regulators of cytokine secretion, gene expression and various signaling pathways, modulating immune responses, metabolism and cell fate. Beyond leukocytes, NLRs are also expressed in various non-immune competent cells, however, their expression and function in skeletal muscle, the largest tissue in the human body, are largely unknown.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We studied NLR expression in response to IFN-γ treatment in
                      <jats:italic>ex vivo Tibialis anterior</jats:italic>
                      , and
                      <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                      C2C12 myoblast (MB) and myotube (MT) with RT-qPCR and Western blot. We focused on the assessment of gene expression changes and cytokine production in MT following IFN-γ priming and activation of NOD1, a key NLR identified, using RNA-seq, RT-qPCR and ELISA, followed by functional studies to understand its immunomodulatory roles. NOD1 function in the context of differentiation of MT was studied with scratch assay, while lipid droplet accumulation was determined with Oil Red O staining.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We found that the expression of regulatory NLRs (NOD1, NOD2, NLRX1, NLRC3) dynamically changed during MB to MT differentiation, and identified NOD1, as a key immunomodulatory NLR in skeletal muscle. IFN-γ treatment in MT highly induced NOD1 expression, and NOD1 activation following IFN-γ priming resulted in global gene expression changes. We found that most myokines are induced in a NOD1-dependent manner, while a cluster of genes related to migration and differentiation were strongly downregulated. In particular, upon IFN-γ priming NOD1 regulates IL-6 production via NF-kB. In addition, IFN-γ-induced NOD1 strongly reduces the differentiation of MT, while enhances lipid accumulation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our results show that while NLRs are expressed in MB and dynamically change during MT differentiation, NOD1 has important, so far uncharacterized function in skeletal muscle. Our results suggest that NOD1 and tentatively other NLRs in the skeletal muscle are connected to diverse physiological and pathological processes, implying their potential roles in myopathies or as therapeutic targets in other disease states.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Impact of Target Costing on New Product Development Strategy for  SMES in Nigeria's Manufacturing Sector
journal: JOURNAL OF ACCOUNTING AND FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT
abstract:
<jats:p>Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) constitute over 96% of businesses and 84% of employment 
in Nigeria’s manufacturing sector and are critical to economic diversification and industrial 
growth (National Bureau of Statistics [NBS], 2024). Central to the survival and competitiveness 
of manufacturing SMEs is their ability to continuously develop new products that meet customer 
needs at profitable prices. However, Nigerian manufacturing SMEs operate in a challenging 
environment characterized by high production costs, unstable exchange rates, poor infrastructure, 
limited access to finance, and intense competition from imports (Ariyo, 2022). These conditions 
often lead to cost overruns, product failures, and low profitability during New Product 
Development (NPD). Traditional cost management approaches such as cost-plus pricing is 
ineffective in this context because they determine price after costs have been incurred (Horngren, 
Datar, & Rajan, 2022). Target Costing, a proactive, market-driven cost management technique 
that determines allowable cost as `Market Price to Desired Profit` and works backward during 
the design phase, offers a viable alternative (Cooper & Slagmulder, 1997). Despite its documented 
benefits in developed economies, there is limited empirical evidence on the adoption and impact 
of target costing on NPD strategy among manufacturing SMEs in Nigeria. Anchored on 
Contingency Theory (Fisher, 1998) and Resource-Based View (Barney, 1991), this study examined 
the impact of target costing on NPD strategy and performance outcomes of manufacturing SMEs 
in Nigeria. Specifically, the study assessed the level of awareness and adoption of target costing, examined its impact on NPD strategy, identified implementation challenges, evaluated its effect on performance outcomes, and determined the future outlook for adoption. A descriptive survey 
research design was adopted. The population comprised 18,500 registered manufacturing SMEs 
in five major industrial hubs: Lagos, Ogun, Anambra, Kano, and Rivers States. Using the Taro 
Yamane (1967) formula, a sample size of 470 was determined and 412 usable questionnaires were 
retrieved, representing an 87.7% response rate. A multi-stage sampling technique was used. 
Primary data were collected using a structured 50-item questionnaire divided into six sections: 
Bio-Data, Awareness and Adoption, Impact on NPD, Implementation Challenges, Performance 
Outcomes, and Future Outlook. Sections B–F used a 5-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed 
using SPSS v26 through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple and hierarchical 
regression. The findings revealed that the level of target costing adoption among Nigerian 
manufacturing SMEs is moderate, with only 39.6% of firms confirming current use. Regression 
analysis showed that Target Costing Adoption has a positive and significant effect on NPD 
Strategy (β = 0.667, p < 0.001, R² = 0.539). This implies that SMEs that adopt target costing are 
better able to align product features with customer willingness to pay, reduce cost overruns, 
encourage cross-functional teamwork, and achieve faster time-to-market. Similarly, Target 
Costing Adoption has a positive and significant effect on Performance Outcomes (β = 0.518, p < 
0.001, R² = 0.315), leading to improved profitability, cost control, product quality, market share, 
and return on investment. Furthermore, Implementation Challenges significantly moderate the 
relationship between target costing and NPD strategy (β = -0.118, p = 0.005). Key challenges 
identified include unstable raw material costs, foreign exchange volatility, poor access to market 
information, inadequate accounting software, and limited technical expertise. This finding 
supports Contingency Theory, which posits that the effectiveness of management practices 
depends on contextual fit. The study concludes that target costing is an effective tool for improving 
NPD strategy and performance of Nigerian manufacturing SMEs. However, its benefits are 
constrained by the prevailing business environment. Therefore, for target costing to deliver 
optimal results, SMEs must institutionalize it as part of NPD, while government and professional 
bodies must address structural and capacity challenges. The study contributes to theory by 
extending Contingency Theory and RBV to the Nigerian SME context and by providing empirical 
evidence on target costing in a developing economy. Practically, it recommends that SMEDAN 
and ICAN should develop simplified target costing toolkits and training programs for SMEs, while 
government should stabilize macroeconomic variables and improve market data availability. The 
study is limited by its cross-sectional design and focus on five states. Future research should adopt 
longitudinal designs and explore the role of technology in target costing adoption.</jats:p>

title: A Core-Shared Inductor for Magnetic-Component Volume Reduction in a Two-Stage Low-Voltage DC–DC Converter
abstract: <jats:p>This paper proposes a core-shared inductor for a two-stage low-voltage DC–DC converter (LDC) system to improve power density while satisfying a wide input and output voltage range. In the proposed structure, the 4-switch buck–boost and LLC resonant inductors are integrated into a shared magnetic core assembly to reduce their combined volume. To verify the feasibility of the proposed approach, a 2-kW LDC prototype was experimentally evaluated using both the conventional separate inductors and the proposed core-shared inductor. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed system maintains conversion efficiency comparable to that of the conventional system, with no appreciable efficiency improvement, while reducing the combined volume and mass of the 4-switch buck–boost and LLC resonant inductors by approximately 9% and 10%, respectively, compared with the conventional design. Therefore, the proposed magnetic integration method provides an effective approach to reducing the volume of magnetic components in wide-range two-stage LDC systems.</jats:p>

title: Propofol-remifentanil target-controlled infusion for emergency craniotomy following multiple trauma in a resource-limited setting
abstract:
<jats:sec id="st1">
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Target-controlled infusion (TCI) allows intravenous anesthetics to be titrated to model-predicted plasma or effect-site concentrations. In emergency neuroanesthesia, however, its clinical value depends not only on the selected target concentration but also on how these targets are adjusted in response to changing surgical stimulation while maintaining cerebral and systemic physiologic stability. We report the use of propofol TCI with the Schnider model and remifentanil TCI with the Minto model during emergency craniotomy in a patient with severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) and major thoracic trauma in Eastern Indonesia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="st2">
                    <jats:title>Case Description:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 32-year-old male weighing approximately 80 kg presented with severe TBI after a 5-m fall, accompanied by right hemopneumothorax, multiple rib fractures, and a clavicular fracture. A chest tube was inserted before anesthetic induction. Propofol was administered using the Schnider model with an effect-site target concentration (Ce) of 3–5 µg/mL during induction and 2.5–4 µg/mL during maintenance. Remifentanil was administered using the Minto model at target concentrations of 4–5 ng/mL during induction and 2–3 ng/mL during maintenance, although the anesthesia record did not consistently specify whether plasma or effect-site targeting was used for remifentanil during maintenance. After induction, the targets were reduced and subsequently adjusted according to the stage and intensity of surgical stimulation, hemodynamic response, ventilation, and surgical conditions. During the 4-h procedure, systolic blood pressure remained between 102 and 125 mmHg, oxygen saturation was maintained at 99–100%, and end-tidal carbon dioxide remained between 30 and 35 mmHg. The brain remained relaxed without clinically apparent swelling. This case illustrates how separate hypnotic and opioid targets can be used to guide stepwise titration of propofol and remifentanil during emergency craniotomy when advanced depth-of-anesthesia and intracranial monitoring are not available.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="st3">
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Propofol TCI using the Schnider model and remifentanil TCI using the Minto model provided a practical framework for independently titrating the hypnotic and opioid components of anesthesia during emergency craniotomy. In a resource-limited setting, model-predicted concentrations should not be regarded as fixed doses but rather as adjustable targets interpreted in conjunction with surgical stimulation, hemodynamic tolerance, ventilation, brain relaxation, and the limitations of available monitoring.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Statin–Ezetimibe Therapy and Incident Myocardial Infarction Across Modified Cardiovascular–Kidney–Metabolic Risk Groups: A Nationwide Target Trial Emulation
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome integrates metabolic risk, kidney dysfunction, and cardiovascular disease. Whether statin-ezetimibe combination therapy is associated with lower subsequent myocardial infarction risk than statin monotherapy among patients across modified cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk groups remains uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using the Korean National Health Insurance Service database, we emulated separate two-arm landmark target trials within modified early and late cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk groups. Adults aged 30-74 years with dyslipidemia who received prescriptions covering a total of 180 days with statin monotherapy or a fixed-dose statin-ezetimibe combination were eligible. Treatment was assigned at the 180-day landmark. Stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting and cause-specific Cox regression were used to calculate hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence interval (CI), with death treated as a competing event for cumulative incidence estimation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 309,371 treated participants, 239,954 had modified early risk and 69,417 had modified late risk. Compared with statin monotherapy, statin-ezetimibe therapy was associated with lower myocardial infarction risk after weighting in both early-risk participants (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.81-0.95) and late-risk participants (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.79-0.98). 10-year weighted cumulative incidence was 1.97% versus 2.23% in the early-risk group and 3.52% versus 3.94% in the late-risk group. In same-intensity comparisons, the association was most evident with moderate-intensity therapy, particularly in the early CKM group (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.79-0.95).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among adults with dyslipidemia who received prescriptions covering a total of 180 days, statin-ezetimibe combination therapy was associated with a lower subsequent risk of myocardial infarction than statin monotherapy across modified CKM risk groups. The association was most evident in moderate-intensity comparisons.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Correctly Parsed, Wrong Lesion: Where Target Mix-Ups Arise When AI Binds Measurement Requests to Lung CT Nodules—A Staged, Hypothesis-Generating Evaluation
abstract: <jats:p>AI systems that measure lesions on request can compute correctly on the wrong lesion, an outcome no benchmark I found scores. I located where such mix-ups arise, in three stages on public lung CTs. A stratified audit of 1785 DICOM segmentation series found identical coded semantics for all 5192 pairs of different nodules on one scan; nodule numbers existed but needed linking to the request. A gate trusting structural checks authorized all 200 constructed requests, 89 for a mismatched and 41 for an ambiguous target. An expert wrote 60 requests in three sets, with each design frozen first. A rule parser carried a misread rank (“longest diameter” read as “largest”) in every resolution; removing it post hoc kept 13 of 26 correct resolutions, and agreement with a choice-constrained model parser removed all 25 rank-dependent wrong ones. A whole-lung definition of “lateral” excluded an intended nodule. In the confirmatory set, both pre-specified consensus gates authorized the nearest unintended nodule in two of 20 requests. Adjudication found three requests naming a lobe the images contradicted and two unassignable lobes; no map error was demonstrated. Parser agreement did not catch a request–image discordance. Clinical safety and workflow benefit were not evaluated.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Temporomandibular Joint Imaging: Diagnostic Performance Across Input Modality–Target Pairings—A Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-Analysis
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To estimate standalone artificial intelligence (AI) diagnostic performance in temporomandibular joint (TMJ) imaging across input modality–target pairings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four databases were searched through 18 June 2026. Eligible studies assessed standalone imaging AI and supplied an exact test-set 2 × 2 table in the report or after author contact. Four pairings were analysed by bivariate meta-regression. Two reviewers applied QUADAS-3 at estimate level.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sixteen studies contributed 17 estimates. For disc displacement, magnetic resonance imaging input yielded pooled sensitivity 0.924 (95% CI, 0.859–0.960) and specificity 0.812 (0.709–0.885), compared with 0.765 (0.618–0.867) and 0.741 (0.592–0.850) for panoramic or cone-beam computed tomography input. The sensitivity difference was 0.159 and remained 0.152–0.198 in leave-one-out and replicate analyses; the omnibus pairing test was not significant (χ²(6) = 10.38, P = .110). Reference-standard relation and pairing partitioned the disc-displacement evidence identically. No estimate had low overall risk of bias, and several otherwise eligible estimates lacked exact published 2 × 2 data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sensitivity was higher when disc displacement was depicted directly on magnetic resonance imaging than when inferred from imaging that does not depict the disc. However, the cross-domain group contained only three estimates, the omnibus pairing test was not significant, and design factors were entangled. Performance should therefore be interpreted by pairing, while direct depiction versus proxy inference requires prospective testing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Advances in knowledge</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>TMJ imaging AI performance should be interpreted in the context of the input modality–target pairing rather than as a property of the algorithm alone; exact test-set confusion matrices are essential for verification.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Image–Morphometric Learning for ZooScan Object Size Classification: Source-Verified Target Auditing and Fusion Reanalysis
abstract: <jats:p>High classification scores are meaningful only if the prediction target is physically consistent. We audited image-only, tabular-only and fusion experiments on 9000 ZooScan objects drawn from the 1,153,507-object PELGAS collection. The archived three-class labels were tertiles of the stored equivalent spherical diameter (ESD), not biomass classes. All 893,542 records exported with version v7.26 followed the documented ESD formula, whereas all 259,965 v7.24 records equalled twice the integer part of projected area divided by π. All 2017 v7.24 objects in the subset fell in the highest archived class. Recomputing ESD consistently from area and pixel calibration changed 3430 of the 9000 labels. The subset spans 13 cruises and 697 cruise–station groups and includes 2639 objects annotated as non-living. On the corrected target, tree-based controls using all descriptors reached a macro-F1 of about 0.998 under both object-stratified and station-grouped evaluation. In preliminary single-seed neural runs without area- or length-based descriptors, tabular networks reached a macro-F1 of 0.89, a Swin-T image model 0.946 and gated fusion 0.944; the image-based runs covered three folds and retained scale cues, so they do not isolate the contribution of each modality. Target provenance should be verified before multimodal performance rankings are used in ecological monitoring.</jats:p>

title: Analysis Of the Implementation of Target Costing as An Effort To Save Operational Costs in Lingga Salon
abstract: <jats:p>This study analyzes the application of target costing as an effort to improve operating cost efficiency at Lingga Salon. It identifies actual operating costs, calculates target cost based on revenue and desired profit, measures the cost gap, and evaluates savings alternatives through value engineering. The study uses a descriptive method with a quantitative approach supported by qualitative information. Data were collected through interviews with the owner and three employees, observation, business documentation, and literature review. The data show revenue of IDR 398,820,000 and actual operating costs of IDR 308,414,000, resulting in actual profit of IDR 90,406,000 or a 22.67% margin. With a target profit of 25% of revenue, the target profit is IDR 99,705,000 and the target cost is IDR 299,115,000. The resulting cost gap is IDR 9,299,000, equivalent to a minimum efficiency requirement of approximately 3.02%. A value engineering scenario covering salon supplies, electricity and water, maintenance, cleaning, administration/promotion, and internet produces potential savings of IDR 9,850,840. Operating costs would decrease to IDR 298,563,160, profit would increase to IDR 100,256,840, and the profit margin would reach 25.14%. These findings suggest that target costing supported by value engineering can serve as a planning and cost-control tool for salon service businesses, provided service quality is maintained</jats:p>

title: A novel target capture probe set reveals widespread unknown hybridization in North American pondweeds (Potamogetonaceae)
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Premise</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Advancements in phylogenomics and bioinformatics provide opportunities to more robustly characterize hybrid lineages and incorporate them into phylogenetic hypotheses. Target capture remains the most cost‐effective molecular method of hybrid determination at scale. The pondweed family is an ecologically important but taxonomically difficult freshwater plant family due to high rates of hybridization. Historically, hybrid pondweeds have been challenging to characterize with limited molecular data, and hybridization is thought to be underdescribed as a result.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We designed a novel target capture probe set for Potamogetonaceae targeting 350 loci (Pondweeds350), combining 132 custom Potamogetonaceae targets, 205 Angiosperms353 loci, and 13 functional genes for aquatic adaptation. The probe set was tested on 285 samples of North American Potamogetonaceae. HybPhaser was used to identify and phase hybrid accessions for phylogenetic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Target enrichment was successful for 280 of 285 samples with an average of 336 genes producing contigs per sample. HybPhaser provided evidence for 16 novel hybrid combinations in
                      <jats:italic>Potamogeton</jats:italic>
                      .
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We demonstrate the effectiveness of the Pondweeds350 probe set as well as the utility of HybPhaser in detecting hybrids at a large scale. We provide evidence for undetected
                      <jats:italic>Potamogeton</jats:italic>
                      hybrids in addition to the most densely sampled and well‐resolved phylogeny of North American Potamogetonaceae to date.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

IMPACT OF MOSQUITO CONTROL ON NON-TARGET ENTOMOFAUNA IN URBAN ECOSYSTEMS
journal: ANNALS OF THE UNIVERSITY OF CRAIOVA, Biology, Horticulture, Food products processing technology, Environmental engineering
abstract: <jats:p>Urban mosquito management is an important public-health intervention, but mosquito suppression occurs within complex urban food webs. Adulticides may expose non-target terrestrial arthropods, whereas larvicides are applied directly to aquatic habitats where mosquito larvae develop. This review summarizes evidence on the ecological effects of pyrethroids, organophosphates, methoprene, Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti) and spinosad, with emphasis on pollinators, aquatic Diptera, Odonata and trophic interactions. Available evidence indicates that effects are context dependent and are determined by toxicity together with actual exposure. Recent operational-scale evidence suggests low acute risk for non-target arthropods under properly conducted ultra-low-volume applications, while experimental studies have detected effects under some exposure scenarios. Bti treatment can reduce chironomid abundance and emergence and may alter prey-mediated interactions in aquatic and terrestrial food webs. Integrated vector management, source reduction, surveillance and targeted interventions are therefore preferable to indiscriminate insecticide use.</jats:p>

Machine Learning-Assisted Electrical Impedance Spectroscopy for Evaluating Bioelectrical Response in Low-Dose Gamma-Irradiated Mice Treated with Mitragyna speciosa Extract
journal: Journal of Multidisciplinary Applied Natural Science
abstract: <jats:p>This exploratory study integrated electrical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), Cole-Cole modeling, multivariate analysis, and machine learning to characterize liver and blood bioelectrical profiles in mice subjected to low-dose irradiation using a mixed-radionuclide source assembly and treated with Mitragyna speciosa extract. Thirty-five male BALB/c mice were assigned to seven groups : control, irradiation only, and irradiation with extract doses of 50–150 mg kg-1 body weight. Irradiated mice received daily 40 min exposures for 7 days, corresponding to an estimated cumulative dose of 11.33 mGy. Ex vivo impedance spectra measured from 100 Hz to 100 kHz were summarized using , , , and . Distinct tissue-specific and non-monotonic patterns were observed. AO-100 had the smallest Euclidean distance from the control centroid in liver (1.42) and blood (2.66). Repeated nested cross-validation identified SVM as the highest-performing liver classifier (  balanced accuracy), whereas random forest and kNN achieved identical highest performance in blood . Nested LOOCV and 500-permutation testing supported non-random internal discrimination . SHAP indicated greater contributions from  and  in liver and from  and  in blood. Cole-Cole-based EIS provides a promising exploratory framework, although these findings do not independently establish radioprotective efficacy or external generalizability.</jats:p>

title: Exploring the Role of DDIT3 in Tumorigenesis and Its Potential as a Target for Novel Cancer Therapies
abstract: <jats:p>Cancer continues to be the leading cause of death globally, with mounting evidence associating cellular stress with tumor initiation, progression, and therapeutic resistance. DNA damage-inducible transcript 3 (DDIT3), a key stress-responsive transcription factor, plays a central role in cellular stress responses by regulating apoptosis, cell survival, and the tumor microenvironment. Although DDIT3 has been extensively studied in neurodegenerative and metabolic diseases, its dual role in cancer has only recently begun to emerge. This review systematically explores the intricate functions of DDIT3 in cancer biology, emphasizing its involvement in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, apoptosis regulation, and modulation of the tumor microenvironment. We investigate how DDIT3 interacts with key signaling pathways and its impact on cellular stress responses, such as autophagy and macrophage recruitment within the tumor microenvironment. Furthermore, we evaluate the therapeutic potential of targeting DDIT3 through clinical and preclinical drug studies, concentrating on compounds that enhance its pro-apoptotic functions or inhibit its cancer-promoting activities. This review seeks to provide a comprehensive understanding of DDIT3′s role in tumors, offering insights into future therapeutic strategies targeting this stress-related protein in oncology.</jats:p>

title: Mechanical Properties Evolution and Aging Mechanism of NBR Sealing Materials Under Multiple Environmental Factors in Ultra-High Voltage Converter Station
abstract: <jats:p>Nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) is commonly served as a sealing element for oil-tight seals in ultra-high voltage converter stations. Due to the harsh environmental conditions in these stations, NBR is frequently exposed to thermal oxidation, ultraviolet radiation, and low temperatures, as well as the effects of the sealed medium. This work focuses on evaluating the impacts of various environmental conditions on the mechanical characteristics of NBR and analyzes the underlying mechanisms. Stress distribution under the combined action of force, heat and hypothetical electric field is analyzed with the aid of ABAQUS simulation; the aging test only investigates single factors without verifying the multi-field coupling mechanism, and the conclusions are only for qualitative reference of the simulation. The service life of NBR is effectively predicted based on the compression set decay curve. Analysis of TGA measurements reveals the gradual loss of incorporated additives upon aging, accompanied by a reduction in the thermal stability of aged NBR. Results from crosslinking density tests, FTIR, and XPS analyses demonstrate that oxidation crosslinking progressively increases as thermal-oxidative aging proceeds, the rise in C–C and C–H content is associated with the degradation of C=C bonds, oxygen-containing functional groups (carboxyl, hydroxyl, and carbonyl) are generated during the thermal-oxidative aging of NBR, and the cleavage of C–S bonds leads to the formation of S=O species.</jats:p>

title: Ultra-high dose rate and high-LET effects on DNA damage distribution in 3D genome: a predictive mechanistic model for cell survival in FLASH irradiation
A cascade deep learning network for simultaneous prediction of dose and linear energy transfer in proton therapy of prostate cancer
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Objective.</jats:italic>
                    Prediction of dose-averaged linear energy transfer (LETd) may facilitate LET-aware evaluation of proton therapy plans. This study developed a cascade deep learning framework for simultaneous three-dimensional prediction of dose and LETd distributions for conventional dose-based optimization (DoseOpt) and LETd-incorporated optimization (LETOpt) in prostate intensity-modulated proton therapy.
                    <jats:italic>Approach.</jats:italic>
                    A total of 150 patients with prostate cancer were included, each with DoseOpt and LETOpt plans. Planning CT images and anatomical structure masks were used as inputs. The cascade network transferred an intermediate latent representation from the dose prediction pathway to the LETd prediction pathway. Stepwise, multitask, and anatomy-only LETd (only-LET) networks served as comparators. Model performance was evaluated using five-fold cross-validation.
                    <jats:italic>Main results.</jats:italic>
                    All dose-predicting models showed high spatial agreement, with cascade Dice similarity coefficients of approximately 0.93, 0.96, and 0.95 for the 50%, 75%, and 95% prescription isodose volumes. No significant differences in structure-specific dose errors remained after false discovery rate correction. The cascade model achieved the lowest global LETd mean absolute error (MAE) for DoseOpt and LETOpt, 0.108 ± 0.025 and 0.111 ± 0.025 keV
                    <jats:italic>μ</jats:italic>
                    m
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    , respectively, significantly lower than those of the multitask, stepwise, and only-LET models. Structure-specific LETd performance was endpoint dependent, with favorable cascade performance for several clinical target volume and organ-at-risk endpoints. LETOpt primarily redistributed LETd while largely preserving dose, and the cascade model reproduced the principal plan-specific changes, including reductions in rectal and rectal-wall LETd. Mean inference time was 0.505 ± 0.020 s per patient.
                    <jats:italic>Significance.</jats:italic>
                    The proposed framework enables rapid simultaneous prediction of dose and LETd for predefined planning strategies from patient anatomy without requiring a precomputed dose distribution, supporting LET-aware plan comparison and providing a basis for future LETd-guided biological optimization.
                  </jats:p>

title: Incidental Findings in Asymptomatic Healthy Individuals Screened with Total-Body Ultra-Low-Dose 18F-FDG-PET/Low-Dose CT
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate the prevalence and clinical significance of incidental findings (IF) detected by Total-body 18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography/Computed Tomography (FDG-PET/CT) in a genuinely asymptomatic cohort of blood donors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>117 healthy, asymptomatic blood donors underwent ultra-low-dose FDG-PET/low-dose CT. The primary objective was to create an atlas of glucose metabolism in healthy individuals. A secondary objective was to assess the frequency and nature of IF, informing future considerations of the clinical value of potential screening programs. Here we report on IF.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>IF were detected in 64 participants (55%), with 51 (44%) presenting clinically insignificant IF and 13 (11%) clinically significant IF. Common insignificant IF included benign or inflammatory metabolic activity in the esophagus or lung parenchyma (n = 19), metabolically active reactive lymph nodes (n = 14), and degenerative skeletal changes (n = 13). Clinically significant IF comprised pathologically metabolically active cysts and polyps (n = 8), significantly enlarged vessels (n = 1), suspected malignant tumors (n = 1), large lipomas (n = 1), sarcoidosis (n = 1), and liver steatosis (n = 1).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This is the first study to systematically investigate incidental findings in an asymptomatic cohort using ultra-low-dose total-body FDG-PET/CT. Even in this highly selected population, numerous IFs were revealed, underscoring the need for risk-stratified, data-driven screening strategies integrating genetic biomarkers identifying individuals who will truly benefit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Advances in knowledge</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This first study of ultra-low-dose total-body FDG-PET/CT in asymptomatic donors found frequent incidental findings (55%, 11% clinically significant), establishing lower-bound estimates and supporting risk-stratified screening approaches.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Fixed-Dose Combination Versus Add-On Therapy: Clarifying the Role of Cilostazol–Rosuvastatin in Peripheral Artery Disease

Competition between
Proton Transfer and Electron-Transfer-Mediated
Decay in a Microsolvated Environment
journal:
The Journal of Physical
Chemistry A
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We investigate the relaxation dynamics of the 1s-ionized state of the Li+ ion in microsolvated Li+(H2O)n (n = 1, 2) cluster, which decays via an intermolecular electron-transfer-mediated decay (ETMD) process. For Li+H2O, the ETMD decay rates are evaluated as a function of Li–O separation. The results reveal a pronounced distance dependence of the ETMD lifetime, reflecting the nonlocal nature of the decay. To probe solvent effects, ETMD is also examined in Li+H2S. The ETMD decay rate is computed using a highly correlated Fano equation-of-motion coupled-cluster singles and doubles (Fano-EOMCCSD) method. In Li+(H2O)2, we identify proton transfer as a highly competing relaxation pathway. By evaluating ETMD decay widths at frozen nuclear geometries sampled along the nuclear dynamics trajectories, we elucidate how changes in cluster geometry and hydrogen-bond rearrangements modulate the instantaneous propensity of the ETMD process during proton transfer.</jats:p>

title: An Ultra-High-Throughput MultiCore QDI Asynchronous Hardware Architecture for AES Encryption
abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a multi-core asynchronous AES-128 encryption architecture designed for ultra-high-throughput applications. The proposed design uses quasi-delay-insensitive (QDI) dual-rail logic and a four-phase return-to-zero handshake protocol, eliminating the need for a global clock. Several AES cores share a common pipelined key-expansion unit to reduce the overall area and power overhead. Within each core, throughput is improved using a deeply pipelined 31-stage architecture. The architecture is described at the register-transfer level using Verilog and synthesized in a 15 nm CMOS technology. The results show that a single core can achieve a throughput of up to 107 Gbit/s, while ten cores operating in parallel can provide a throughput of up to 1.07 Tbit/s. The proposed architecture is therefore well suited for high-speed communication standards such as IEEE 802.3bs-2017, which supports data rates of up to 400 Gbit/s.</jats:p>

title: High-Performance SPR-Based Biosensor for Non-invasive Urinalysis: Achieving Ultra-High Sensitivity and Detection Precision
Ultra-High Data Rate, Terahertz, and Femtosecond Concurrent Up- and Down-Conversion Based on an Electro-Optical SOA-MZI Differential Modulation
abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a comprehensive investigation of a concurrent electro-optical up- and down-conversion architecture based on a semiconductor optical amplifier Mach–Zehnder interferometer (SOA-MZI) operating under a differential modulation configuration. The proposed system employs a high-repetition-rate optical pulse clock (OPC) to generate the sampling control signal required for concurrent frequency conversion. A 4096-QAM data signal modulated at 100 GHz is simultaneously up- and down-converted at the SOA-MZI output through the interaction between the optical sampling signal and the electrically driven SOA branches. The influence of the OPC repetition rate and pulse width on the conversion performance is experimentally analyzed. By increasing the sampling repetition rate to 150 GHz with a pulse width of 0.5 ps, concurrent frequency conversion is achieved over a wide frequency range extending up to 1.6 THz. The performance of the converted signals is evaluated using error vector magnitude (EVM) measurements and temporal characterization. For the up-converted replicas, an EVM of 5.5% is obtained at 1.6 THz for a 1 Tbit/s 4096-QAM transmission. For the down-converted replica at 50 GHz, the EVM reaches 4% at a data rate of 10 Tbit/s. In addition, pulse compression based on a parallel grating pair connected by a 3 km optical fiber is investigated for temporal characterization of the concurrent signal. A compressed pulse width of 45 fs is achieved at full width at half maximum (FWHM). Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed electro-optical SOA-MZI differential modulation architecture provides improved conversion efficiency, reduced noise floor, ultra-wide frequency operation, and high-capacity data transmission capability, making it suitable for terahertz communications, microwave photonics, and ultra-high-speed optical transmission systems.</jats:p>

title: A unified quenching model in Geant4 simulation for $$\alpha $$, proton and electron particles in liquid scintillator detectors
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The liquid scintillator (LS) detectors are widely used in reactor neutrino experiments. To precisely measure the oscillated neutrino spectrum, it is crucial to understand the LS energy response, especially the quenching effect. Numerous bench-top measurements have been conducted on quenching effects for
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$\alpha $$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mi>α</mml:mi>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    particles, protons, and electrons. These results have typically been described by Birks’ law, but with different Birks’ coefficients required for different particle species. In this study, we find that if more secondary electrons are allowed to be generated in Geant4 simulations, the bench-top results for all particles can be well fitted using a single Birks’ coefficient of about
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$0.013~\mathrm{g\,cm^{-2}\,MeV^{-1}}$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mn>0.013</mml:mn>
                            <mml:mspace/>
                            <mml:mrow>
                              <mml:mi>g</mml:mi>
                              <mml:mspace/>
                              <mml:msup>
                                <mml:mi>cm</mml:mi>
                                <mml:mrow>
                                  <mml:mo>-</mml:mo>
                                  <mml:mn>2</mml:mn>
                                </mml:mrow>
                              </mml:msup>
                              <mml:mspace/>
                              <mml:msup>
                                <mml:mi>MeV</mml:mi>
                                <mml:mrow>
                                  <mml:mo>-</mml:mo>
                                  <mml:mn>1</mml:mn>
                                </mml:mrow>
                              </mml:msup>
                            </mml:mrow>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    . The underlying reason is that a large fraction of the primary energy is deposited through the generation of
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$\delta $$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mi>δ</mml:mi>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    -electrons with energies below 4 keV, which should be tracked separately due to their different quenching behavior compared to primary particles. This study provides a unified framework for comparing Birks’ coefficients from different bench-top measurements and helps experiments like JUNO and SNO+ better tune their simulations for precision energy measurements.
                  </jats:p>

title: Short-course, high-dose beta-lactam therapy versus conventional dose and duration in critically ill patients: the HIT-HARD trial protocol for a phase III multicenter, cluster randomized, cross-over, non-inferiority trial
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In critically ill patients with severe infections, beta-lactam antibiotics are frequently underdosed, while studies indicate that shorter treatment durations may be sufficient when adequately dosed. The HIT-HARD trial aims to evaluate whether short-course, high-dose beta-lactam therapy is non-inferior to conventional dosing and duration in critically ill patients with severe infections. A shorter course may reduce the development of antimicrobial resistance and serve a public health benefit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The HIT-HARD trial (EU ref. 2024-514730-21-00) is a prospective, multicenter, cluster-randomized, cross-over, non-inferiority trial conducted in 14 hospitals (7 in Belgium and 7 in the Netherlands). The study aims to enroll 1,282 patients with organ dysfunction due to common infections (community-acquired pneumonia, hospital-acquired pneumonia, ventilator-associated pneumonia, intra-abdominal infection, or bloodstream infection). Patients treated with ceftriaxone, cefuroxime, cefotaxime, piperacillin–tazobactam, or meropenem can be included in the study. Exclusion criteria include prior study-antimicrobial therapy > 12 h for the current infection, absence of adequate source control, and infections requiring prolonged or specific dosing regimens. Participants are allocated to either the HIT-HARD strategy, a high-dose regimen (around 150–200% of standard dosing) for a short course of 3–5 days (72–120 h), or the CONTROL strategy, a conventional dosing regimen for 6–9 days (144–216 h). The primary endpoint is all-cause 90-day mortality. Secondary endpoints include mortality, recurrence of infection, antimicrobial resistance development, toxicity, antimicrobial exposure, clinical cure, resource utilization, health-related quality of life, and cost-effectiveness. Non-inferiority will be assessed using a pre-specified 7% margin by estimating the risk difference between the HIT-HARD and CONTROL groups with an unweighted cluster-level summary regression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By determining whether this short-course, high-dose approach is non-inferior to conventional regimens, the trial has the potential to directly inform antibiotic policy and guide an evidence-based approach to safely shorten antimicrobial therapy as part of an ICU stewardship program.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>20245147302100 (EUCT), prospective trial registration date 05DEC2024. Protocol version 3.0, protocol date 01JUN2026.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Ultra-high voltage transmission and corporate ESG performance: evidence from Chinese A-share listed firms
abstract: <jats:p>Whether large-scale clean-energy infrastructure can alleviate the trade-off between economic growth and environmental degradation is central to environmental regulation under China's dual-carbon goals. This study examines the relationship between ultra-high voltage (UHV) transmission access and corporate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance using firm-year observations of Chinese A-share listed companies with valid Sino-Securities ESG ratings from 2009 to 2022. We estimate a two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences model with firm and year fixed effects, complemented by the Callaway–Sant’Anna staggered DID estimator. Firms gaining UHV access exhibit higher ESG scores, with the largest point estimate observed for the environmental dimension and smaller positive estimates for the social and governance dimensions. The positive UHV-ESG association persists after accounting for local carbon-market exposure and is also observed under alternative ESG specifications and propensity-score-matched DID estimation. Mechanism estimates are consistent with production resilience, including liquidity buffers, and reduced transition risk as two potential channels. Subgroup estimates are larger for smaller firms and firms in other classified industries, with formal coefficient-difference tests indicating cross-group variation, while positive relationships are observed in both ownership groups. These findings suggest that clean-energy infrastructure may be relevant to corporate sustainability outcomes.</jats:p>

title: Low‐Dose Versus High‐Dose Drug‐Coated Balloon After Jetstream Atherectomy for Severely Calcified Femoropopliteal Lesions: The JUPITER Multicenter Study
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Second‐generation low‐dose drug‐coated balloons (LD‐DCBs) have shown clinical efficacy comparable to high‐dose DCBs (HD‐DCBs) for femoropopliteal artery (FPA) lesions. Whether paclitaxel dose density remains clinically relevant after aggressive vessel preparation with atherectomy in severely calcified FPA lesions remains uncertain. This study aimed to compare 1‐year clinical outcomes of second‐generation LD‐DCB and HD‐DCB following Jetstream atherectomy in patients with severely calcified FPA lesions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aims</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to compare 1‐year clinical outcomes of second‐generation LD‐DCB and HD‐DCB following Jetstream atherectomy in patients with severely calcified FPA lesions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This multicenter retrospective study included 262 patients with severely calcified FPA lesions who underwent endovascular therapy with Jetstream atherectomy followed by second‐generation LD‐DCB (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 175) or HD‐DCB (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 87). Propensity‐score matching yielded 79 well‐balanced pairs. The primary outcome was 1‐year primary patency; secondary outcomes included freedom from clinically driven target‐lesion revascularization (TLR), limb salvage, and overall survival.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In the overall cohort before matching, 1‐year primary patency was similar between second‐generation LD‐DCB and HD‐DCB (86.8% vs. 83.1%, log‐rank
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.578), with comparable freedom from TLR, limb salvage, and overall survival. After propensity score matching, primary patency remained similar between groups (88.5% vs. 84.9%, log‐rank
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.588), as did freedom from TLR, limb salvage, and overall survival. Findings were consistent across calcification‐related subgroups. In an exploratory Cox analysis, second‐generation LD‐DCB was not associated with an increased risk of restenosis compared with HD‐DCB.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>After Jetstream atherectomy for severely calcified FPA lesions, second‐generation LD‐DCB and HD‐DCB were associated with comparable 1‐year clinical outcomes, suggesting that either strategy may be a reasonable treatment option.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Nebulised
                      <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NAC</jats:styled-content>
                      with saline was associated with large improvements across symptom, laryngoscopic and quality‐of‐life domains in adults with
                      <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">LPS</jats:styled-content>
                      persisting despite
                      <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">PPI</jats:styled-content>
                      therapy and was well tolerated. As the study was uncontrolled and the saline vehicle may itself relieve symptoms, efficacy requires confirmation in a randomised trial against nebulised saline.

title: Structural Insights into Proton Exchange Membrane Water Electrolyzers after Long-Term Operation Using Advanced 3D Focused Ion Beam–Scanning Electron Microscopy Tomography
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs) are key to sustainable hydrogen production, but their long-term performance is limited by degradation, particularly in the membrane electrode assembly (MEA), which remains a barrier to commercial viability. Moreover, the need for corrosion-resistant materials and the intricate fabrication of bipolar plates and porous transport layers (PTLs) further impede large-scale deployment and account for a major share of the stack cost. Because lifetime and replacement costs are strongly influenced by the local microstructure and contact conditions, especially at the anode/PTL interface, a multiscale characterization approach combining 3D focused ion beam–scanning electron microscopy (FIB–SEM) with time-of-flight mass spectrometry is used to investigate degradation in an MEA after several thousand hours of operation under industrially relevant conditions. The 3D reconstruction and ppm-level chemical mapping show that local contact heterogeneities at welds in an expanded-metal mesh PTL act as degradation hotspots. At these sites, intensified catalyst utilization accelerates iridium dissolution, driving iridium migration and deposition as extended filaments into the membrane. Concurrently, membrane voids are formed beneath these sites, accompanied by iron contamination detected at both contact types. In contrast, general contact regions mainly show a thin redeposition layer without voids or filaments. These findings provide a mechanistic framework that links local contact conditions and microstructural heterogeneities to coupled catalyst and membrane degradation, supporting design rules for improved PEMWE durability.</jats:p>

title: Theoretical investigation of ferrocene dimer molecular junction for high thermoelectric performance
Pulsed Field Ablation of the Cavotricuspid Isthmus Using a Focal Catheter Combined with an Ultra-Minimal Analgosedation Protocol in High-Risk Patients: A Case Series
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Catheter ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) is the guideline-recommended curative treatment for typical right atrial flutter. In patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or morbid obesity—conditions that frequently underlie isolated typical atrial flutter—the risk of prolonged analgosedation often introduces clinical hesitation regarding ablation referral, frequently resulting in repeated electrical cardioversion rather than definitive arrhythmia control. We report a tailored procedural workflow that leverages the rapid energy delivery of focal pulsed field ablation (PFA) to enable an ultra-minimal, rapidly reversible analgosedation protocol—restricting systemic sedation strictly to the brief period of energy delivery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Case Summary</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four male patients with isolated typical right atrial flutter and high sedation risk—due to COPD GOLD III–IV, morbid obesity (BMI up to 40.2 kg/m2), or both—underwent CTI ablation using the FARAPOINT™ focal PFA catheter (Boston Scientific) integrated with the OPAL HDx mapping system. All procedures were initiated under local anaesthesia only. Midazolam (0.5 mg/10 kg body weight), fentanyl (50 µg), and glyceryl trinitrate (2 mg i.v.) were administered immediately prior to the first energy delivery. Bidirectional CTI block was achieved in all patients. Analgosedation was immediately reversed with flumazenil (0.5–1.0 mg) and naloxone (0.4 mg) upon completion of ablation. Mean total analgosedation duration was 7.7 ± 2.9 minutes (range 4:38–11:22 min:sec). Mean procedure duration was 36.5 ± 7.9 minutes; mean fluoroscopy time was 2.8 ± 0.3 minutes. No sedation-related or procedural complications occurred. All patients maintained sinus rhythm through hospital discharge and at follow-up (range 5–12 weeks).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Integrating focal PFA with an ultra-minimal analgosedation protocol demonstrated procedural feasibility and acute CTI block in high-sedation-risk patients. While initial freedom from flutter recurrence during short-term follow-up is encouraging, larger controlled trials with long-term follow-up are required to evaluate durable efficacy and directly compare this strategy with conventional radiofrequency ablation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Strain-engineering of SiNx layers for threshold voltage modulation of AlGaN/GaN high electron mobility transistors
abstract: <jats:p>This work investigates strain-engineering of silicon nitride passivation layers to modulate the threshold voltage of AlGaN/GaN high electron mobility transistors. Thermally stable compressive silicon nitride layers with stress up to −2.1 GPa were deposited using plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition with low-frequency plasma excitation at 100 kHz and 600 °C. Modification of the stress allows for controlled manipulation of the two-dimensional electron gas density at the AlGaN/GaN interface in the gate vicinity. A protection layer was introduced to prevent the AlGaN layer stack from damage caused by ion bombardment generated by the low-frequency excited plasma. Devices with the strained passivation show a positive threshold voltage shift from −1.7 to −0.4 V, confirming the feasibility of the method. In addition, the new passivation improves the extrinsic transconductance from 476 to 588 mS/mm. Current collapse measurements show no additional degradation. Both the strain-engineered and standard devices deliver 3.8 W/mm maximum output power at 10 GHz and 3.2 W/mm at 20 GHz. Power-added efficiencies of 34% at 20 GHz and 46% at 10 GHz for the strain-engineered devices, compared with 35% at 20 GHz and 48% at 10 GHz, respectively, for the reference transistors demonstrate stable high-frequency large-signal performance. Moreover, the maximum oscillation frequency increases from 145 to 171 GHz for the strained devices. This method offers an effective way of modulating the threshold voltage toward enhancement-mode operation of AlGaN/GaN high electron mobility transistors without causing degradation in electrical performance or high-frequency characteristics.</jats:p>

title: CryoET-DDM: restoring high-fidelity signals in cryo-electron tomography via a data-driven diffusion model
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Motivation</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is an essential technique for resolving high-resolution structures of macromolecular complexes in situ. However, the extremely low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in tilt series, caused by strict electron dose limitations, remains a major bottleneck for subtomogram averaging (STA). Although existing denoising methods can enhance tomogram contrast, they may compromise the high-frequency structural information required for downstream STA refinement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We introduce CryoET-DDM, a diffusion framework for high-fidelity restoration of cryo-ET tilt series that integrates data-driven noise modeling and fidelity-guided structural preservation. CryoET-DDM incorporates background noise patches extracted from the same experimental tilt series into the diffusion process to model the noise characteristics of low-dose imaging. A fidelity-guided learning objective promotes structural consistency during denoising, helping preserve high-frequency information needed for STA. Experiments on three public datasets (EMPIAR-10499, EMPIAR-10164, and EMPIAR-10651) show that CryoET-DDM improves particle quality, preserves structural fidelity, and yields downstream gains in STA resolution. These results support tilt series denoising as a promising strategy for cryo-ET data processing and improve the reliability of in situ structural biology analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Availability and implementation</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Code and models for our experiments are available at https://github.com/xinsheng44/CryoET-DDM. The real datasets used in this study are publicly available from EMPIAR.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Clinical advances in proton spatially fractionated radiation therapy
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Spatially fractionated radiation therapy (SFRT) intentionally creates a heterogeneous dose distribution within a tumor, with alternating high-dose peaks and low-dose valleys. This approach offers a different route to dose escalation for bulky, locally advanced tumors and lesions near organs at risk. Proton SFRT (pSFRT) combines this spatial heterogeneity with the finite range of protons, rapid distal dose fall-off, and pencil beam scanning. It may therefore reduce dose outside the target while preserving intratumoral peak-valley patterns. Current pSFRT platforms include proton GRID, proton LATTICE, and proton minibeam radiation therapy, but their clinical maturity differs markedly. Available studies support the technical feasibility and short-term tolerability of pSFRT and suggest potential benefits in tumor control and symptom relief across several cancer types. However, the evidence base is limited by cohort sizes, substantial disease heterogeneity, variability in treatment approaches, frequent use of subsequent radiation therapy or systemic therapy, and relatively short follow-up periods. No included comparative clinical study demonstrated an advantage over photon SFRT or conventional proton therapy. Additional barriers include range and motion uncertainty, inconsistent characterization of peak and valley doses, patient-specific quality assurance, limited radiobiological modeling, and uncertain patient selection. This review examines the evolution of SFRT, the physical rationale for proton delivery, the main pSFRT techniques, published human evidence, and current translational challenges. It also outlines priorities for dose-reporting standards, multicenter prospective studies, and rational integration with systemic therapies, and highlights major unresolved questions that must be addressed before broader clinical application.</jats:p>

title: Mechanical Properties Evolution and Aging Mechanism of NBR Sealing Materials Under Multiple Environmental Factors in Ultra-High Voltage Converter Station
abstract: <jats:p>Nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) is commonly served as a sealing element for oil-tight seals in ultra-high voltage converter stations. Due to the harsh environmental conditions in these stations, NBR is frequently exposed to thermal oxidation, ultraviolet radiation, and low temperatures, as well as the effects of the sealed medium. This work focuses on evaluating the impacts of various environmental conditions on the mechanical characteristics of NBR and analyzes the underlying mechanisms. Stress distribution under the combined action of force, heat and hypothetical electric field is analyzed with the aid of ABAQUS simulation; the aging test only investigates single factors without verifying the multi-field coupling mechanism, and the conclusions are only for qualitative reference of the simulation. The service life of NBR is effectively predicted based on the compression set decay curve. Analysis of TGA measurements reveals the gradual loss of incorporated additives upon aging, accompanied by a reduction in the thermal stability of aged NBR. Results from crosslinking density tests, FTIR, and XPS analyses demonstrate that oxidation crosslinking progressively increases as thermal-oxidative aging proceeds, the rise in C–C and C–H content is associated with the degradation of C=C bonds, oxygen-containing functional groups (carboxyl, hydroxyl, and carbonyl) are generated during the thermal-oxidative aging of NBR, and the cleavage of C–S bonds leads to the formation of S=O species.</jats:p>

title: Perioperative Therapy Versus Surgery-First Strategy for Resectable Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Current Evidence, High-Risk Stratification, and Future Directions
abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Long-term survival in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains poor. Although neoadjuvant therapy (NAT) has been increasingly investigated in resectable disease, its benefit compared with upfront surgery remains uncertain. This review evaluates evidence from randomized and prospective trials and explores clinical and molecular factors that may refine patient selection. Methods: We reviewed key randomized and prospective clinical trials evaluating NAT in resectable PDAC, including NORPACT-1, PANACHE01/PRODIGE-48, PREP-02/JSAP05, NEONAX, PREOPANC-1, PREOPANC-2, and CASSANDRA (PACT-21), the last two of which directly compared different NAT regimens head-to-head in the neoadjuvant setting, whereas PREOPANC-1 compared neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy with upfront surgery. Outcomes of interest included overall survival (OS), resection rates, and treatment-related differences across resectable and borderline resectable populations. We also examined emerging clinical and biomarker-driven stratification strategies. Results: Trials in strictly resectable PDAC have demonstrated mixed results. NORPACT-1 reported inferior OS with neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX compared to upfront surgery (median OS 25.1 vs. 38.5 months; HR 1.52). PANACHE01/PRODIGE-48 showed comparable OS despite higher R0 resection rates with NAT. In contrast, PREP-02/JSAP05 demonstrated improved OS with neoadjuvant gemcitabine plus S-1 (37.0 vs. 26.6 months; HR 0.73). PREOPANC-1 showed a survival advantage with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, although pooled analyses suggest this benefit is primarily driven by borderline resectable disease, with no statistically significant OS improvement in strictly resectable cohorts. PREOPANC-2 demonstrated no OS difference between neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX and gemcitabine-based chemoradiation. Conclusions: The benefit of NAT in resectable PDAC is not uniform and appears to depend on underlying tumor biology and risk features. High-risk characteristics, including elevated CA19-9, large tumor size, and nodal involvement, may identify patients most likely to benefit from upfront systemic therapy. Integration of molecular biomarkers such as SMAD4, GATA6, and homologous recombination deficiency into prospective trial design is critical. Ongoing phase III trials will further define optimal treatment strategies in this population.</jats:p>
