title: Exploring Variability in Infliximab Target Attainment and Implications for Concentration-Guided Dosing (CGD) in Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)
abstract: <jats:p>Background: Substantial interindividual variability in infliximab pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics (PKPD) complicates dose optimization in patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Infliximab concentration-guided dosing (CGD) mostly relies on the Therapeutic Window Approach (TWA). Although this approach is widely used in clinical practice, its implications in the setting of substantial variability remain insufficiently characterized. Methods: Model-based simulations evaluated the probability of target (non)-attainment across standard and intensified dosing strategies for intravenous and subcutaneous infliximab. Target attainment was predefined using a therapeutic window (3–7 mg/L) for intravenous infliximab and a threshold (≥12 mg/L) for subcutaneous infliximab. Results: Across dosing strategies, substantial exposure variability resulted in a proportion of patients remaining below the predefined targets. For intravenous infliximab, interval shortening achieved a greater probability of target attainment than dose escalation alone; for example, among patients receiving 5 mg/kg, 50.5% achieved concentrations ≥3 mg/L with Q6W versus 24.5% with Q8W. For subcutaneous infliximab, simulated 180 and 240 mg doses increased the probability of target attainment (≥12 mg/L) versus the approved 120 mg dose, in higher body weight cohorts (72.0% and 86.5%, respectively, vs. 35.5%), potentially highlighting limitations of the current “one-size-fits-all” dosing paradigm. Conclusions: In the presence of substantial infliximab PKPD variability and IBD dynamics, the predefined therapeutic window and fixed threshold may not adequately account for individual variability, potentially contributing to clinical discordance between drug exposure, predefined target attainment, and clinical outcomes. These considerations support evaluating the Target Concentration Approach (TCA) in clinical trials and routine IBD management, given its potential to dynamically adapt dosing to achieve patient-specific target concentration.</jats:p>

title: Memory-window engineering: target specifications for duration, retention through division, and amplitude in immune epigenome editing
abstract: <jats:p>Immune activation, tolerance, exhaustion, trained immunity and regulatory stability are held in place by chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, histone modification, and enhancer-promoter wiring. CRISPR-based epigenome editors rewrite these layers without cutting DNA, but most reports address editing efficiency and leave time unanswered. Target duration is a design input to be specified before an editor is chosen; the duration achieved remains an experimental outcome. Memory-window engineering defines a candidate immune edit by three parameters: duration after editor clearance, retention through cell division, and amplitude at single-cell resolution, with target-compartment division rate as an explicit modifier. For passively diluted marks, division rate constrains post-clearance duration; transcriptional and phenotypic persistence may follow different trajectories. Published results from methylation editing at IL1RN, FOXP3 enhancer demethylation, PD-1 enhancer tuning, exhaustion circuits and CRISPRoff programming of primary human T cells are interpreted using their readouts and observation windows; some persistence endpoints remain censored by study duration. Three testable predictions concern CpG density, transcript-versus-mark recovery and division-dependent loss, with competing mechanisms and measurement artefacts considered. Specificity, the nuclease-knockout comparison, and the ethics of durable edits are treated as parts of the same specification. Two design consequences follow. TET-dependent erasure requires oxygen and 2-oxoglutarate; reduced erasure in hypoxic or metabolically inhibitory tumour regions is therefore a hypothesis for edited immune cells. Sustained programming of circulating monocyte output requires an upstream progenitor strategy, whereas long-lived resident myeloid cells are a separate case. A worked CAR T example and five-item reporting minimum distinguish development-stage characterisation from lot-release testing.</jats:p>

title: Effective Concurrent Attack Detection Framework through Laser Fault Informed Balanced Optical Neural Network Observation
journal: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Silicon Photonics-based AI Accelerators (SPAAs) have been considered as promising AI accelerators achieving high energy efficiency and low latency. While many researchers focus on improving SPAAs’ energy efficiency and latency, their physical security has only recently received attention. While it is essential to deliver strong optical neural network inferencing approaches, their success and adoption are predicated on their ability to deliver a secure execution environment. Towards this end, this article extends
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">PrometheusFree</jats:italic>
                    to
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">PrometheusFreev2</jats:italic>
                    , an optical neural network framework that is capable of concurrent detection of laser fault injection attacks. This article first presents an illustrative threat of laser fault injection attacks on SPAAs, capable of subjecting the optical neural network to misclassifications.
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">PrometheusFreev2</jats:italic>
                    then addresses this threat by developing techniques for concurrent detection of the laser fault injection attacks. Furthermore,
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">PrometheusFreev2</jats:italic>
                    introduces an application of the Wavelength Division Perturbation (WDP) technique where wavelength-dependent Vector Matrix Multiplication (VMM) results are utilized to boost fault attack detection accuracy. This article goes on to introduce a novel optical vulnerability that overpowers the
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">PrometheusFree</jats:italic>
                    detection capability, the
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">swapping attack</jats:italic>
                    that exploits an architectural vulnerability of SPAAs. To address this practical and critical attack,
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">PrometheusFreev2</jats:italic>
                    features a dummy padding technique which injects random values to weight matrices to improve attack detectability. Simulation results show that
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">PrometheusFreev2</jats:italic>
                    achieves over 92% attack-caused misprediction recall as the use of the WDP technique squashes the attack success rate by 31–47% on average by using three wavelengths. Compared with prior art,
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">PrometheusFreev2</jats:italic>
                    constricts the average attack success ratio to 0.030, yielding a 92.8–95.0% reduction. The experimental results confirm the superiority of the concurrent detection and the boost in attack detection abilities imparted by the WDP and the dummy padding approaches.
                  </jats:p>

Impact of Target Costing on New Product Development Strategy for  SMES in Nigeria's Manufacturing Sector
journal: JOURNAL OF ACCOUNTING AND FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT
abstract:
<jats:p>Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) constitute over 96% of businesses and 84% of employment 
in Nigeria’s manufacturing sector and are critical to economic diversification and industrial 
growth (National Bureau of Statistics [NBS], 2024). Central to the survival and competitiveness 
of manufacturing SMEs is their ability to continuously develop new products that meet customer 
needs at profitable prices. However, Nigerian manufacturing SMEs operate in a challenging 
environment characterized by high production costs, unstable exchange rates, poor infrastructure, 
limited access to finance, and intense competition from imports (Ariyo, 2022). These conditions 
often lead to cost overruns, product failures, and low profitability during New Product 
Development (NPD). Traditional cost management approaches such as cost-plus pricing is 
ineffective in this context because they determine price after costs have been incurred (Horngren, 
Datar, & Rajan, 2022). Target Costing, a proactive, market-driven cost management technique 
that determines allowable cost as `Market Price to Desired Profit` and works backward during 
the design phase, offers a viable alternative (Cooper & Slagmulder, 1997). Despite its documented 
benefits in developed economies, there is limited empirical evidence on the adoption and impact 
of target costing on NPD strategy among manufacturing SMEs in Nigeria. Anchored on 
Contingency Theory (Fisher, 1998) and Resource-Based View (Barney, 1991), this study examined 
the impact of target costing on NPD strategy and performance outcomes of manufacturing SMEs 
in Nigeria. Specifically, the study assessed the level of awareness and adoption of target costing, examined its impact on NPD strategy, identified implementation challenges, evaluated its effect on performance outcomes, and determined the future outlook for adoption. A descriptive survey 
research design was adopted. The population comprised 18,500 registered manufacturing SMEs 
in five major industrial hubs: Lagos, Ogun, Anambra, Kano, and Rivers States. Using the Taro 
Yamane (1967) formula, a sample size of 470 was determined and 412 usable questionnaires were 
retrieved, representing an 87.7% response rate. A multi-stage sampling technique was used. 
Primary data were collected using a structured 50-item questionnaire divided into six sections: 
Bio-Data, Awareness and Adoption, Impact on NPD, Implementation Challenges, Performance 
Outcomes, and Future Outlook. Sections B–F used a 5-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed 
using SPSS v26 through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple and hierarchical 
regression. The findings revealed that the level of target costing adoption among Nigerian 
manufacturing SMEs is moderate, with only 39.6% of firms confirming current use. Regression 
analysis showed that Target Costing Adoption has a positive and significant effect on NPD 
Strategy (β = 0.667, p < 0.001, R² = 0.539). This implies that SMEs that adopt target costing are 
better able to align product features with customer willingness to pay, reduce cost overruns, 
encourage cross-functional teamwork, and achieve faster time-to-market. Similarly, Target 
Costing Adoption has a positive and significant effect on Performance Outcomes (β = 0.518, p < 
0.001, R² = 0.315), leading to improved profitability, cost control, product quality, market share, 
and return on investment. Furthermore, Implementation Challenges significantly moderate the 
relationship between target costing and NPD strategy (β = -0.118, p = 0.005). Key challenges 
identified include unstable raw material costs, foreign exchange volatility, poor access to market 
information, inadequate accounting software, and limited technical expertise. This finding 
supports Contingency Theory, which posits that the effectiveness of management practices 
depends on contextual fit. The study concludes that target costing is an effective tool for improving 
NPD strategy and performance of Nigerian manufacturing SMEs. However, its benefits are 
constrained by the prevailing business environment. Therefore, for target costing to deliver 
optimal results, SMEs must institutionalize it as part of NPD, while government and professional 
bodies must address structural and capacity challenges. The study contributes to theory by 
extending Contingency Theory and RBV to the Nigerian SME context and by providing empirical 
evidence on target costing in a developing economy. Practically, it recommends that SMEDAN 
and ICAN should develop simplified target costing toolkits and training programs for SMEs, while 
government should stabilize macroeconomic variables and improve market data availability. The 
study is limited by its cross-sectional design and focus on five states. Future research should adopt 
longitudinal designs and explore the role of technology in target costing adoption.</jats:p>

title: Guidelines development for design reviews with advanced collaboration tools
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Design Reviews (DRs) function as formal governance checkpoints within the product development process where cross-functional stakeholders evaluate design proposals against product requirements to determine their readiness for progression. As design teams become increasingly global, they rely heavily on remote and digital workflows to conduct DRs. While research explores the implementation of new tools to enhance collaboration in DRs, studies often focus on technical feasibility or interaction effects in isolated settings rather than on how these technologies can be embedded in actual industrial processes. In this study, we examine the use of advanced collaboration tools, defined here as digital systems that provide shared spatial environments, in-scene deictic referencing, and independent navigation. Currently, organizations lack actionable guidance on integrating these tools into their DR processes. Thus, this paper develops an evidence-informed set of procedural guidelines for planning, conducting, and documenting DRs using advanced collaboration tools. Working with two automotive companies, we conducted a multi-phase study where two real industrial cases (one per company) were reconstructed to facilitate collaborative workshops aimed at mapping technological capabilities to procedural rules. The analysis draws on established accounts of grounding, workspace awareness, distributed cognition, and organizational routines to interpret the coordination breakdowns observed and the routines that address them. By analyzing verbal data and interaction logs, we developed a set of guidelines grounded in the specific coordination problems identified by practitioners and the technological capabilities required to resolve them. The resulting guidelines identify five domains, including pre-read and preparation, attention management, documentation and traceability, integration and handoff, and modality and role distribution. The guidelines provide a transferable structure for organizations to transform advanced collaboration tools from isolated visualizers into reliable, managed elements of the DRs workflow.</jats:p>

title: Propofol-remifentanil target-controlled infusion for emergency craniotomy following multiple trauma in a resource-limited setting
abstract:
<jats:sec id="st1">
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Target-controlled infusion (TCI) allows intravenous anesthetics to be titrated to model-predicted plasma or effect-site concentrations. In emergency neuroanesthesia, however, its clinical value depends not only on the selected target concentration but also on how these targets are adjusted in response to changing surgical stimulation while maintaining cerebral and systemic physiologic stability. We report the use of propofol TCI with the Schnider model and remifentanil TCI with the Minto model during emergency craniotomy in a patient with severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) and major thoracic trauma in Eastern Indonesia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="st2">
                    <jats:title>Case Description:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 32-year-old male weighing approximately 80 kg presented with severe TBI after a 5-m fall, accompanied by right hemopneumothorax, multiple rib fractures, and a clavicular fracture. A chest tube was inserted before anesthetic induction. Propofol was administered using the Schnider model with an effect-site target concentration (Ce) of 3–5 µg/mL during induction and 2.5–4 µg/mL during maintenance. Remifentanil was administered using the Minto model at target concentrations of 4–5 ng/mL during induction and 2–3 ng/mL during maintenance, although the anesthesia record did not consistently specify whether plasma or effect-site targeting was used for remifentanil during maintenance. After induction, the targets were reduced and subsequently adjusted according to the stage and intensity of surgical stimulation, hemodynamic response, ventilation, and surgical conditions. During the 4-h procedure, systolic blood pressure remained between 102 and 125 mmHg, oxygen saturation was maintained at 99–100%, and end-tidal carbon dioxide remained between 30 and 35 mmHg. The brain remained relaxed without clinically apparent swelling. This case illustrates how separate hypnotic and opioid targets can be used to guide stepwise titration of propofol and remifentanil during emergency craniotomy when advanced depth-of-anesthesia and intracranial monitoring are not available.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="st3">
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Propofol TCI using the Schnider model and remifentanil TCI using the Minto model provided a practical framework for independently titrating the hypnotic and opioid components of anesthesia during emergency craniotomy. In a resource-limited setting, model-predicted concentrations should not be regarded as fixed doses but rather as adjustable targets interpreted in conjunction with surgical stimulation, hemodynamic tolerance, ventilation, brain relaxation, and the limitations of available monitoring.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Statin–Ezetimibe Therapy and Incident Myocardial Infarction Across Modified Cardiovascular–Kidney–Metabolic Risk Groups: A Nationwide Target Trial Emulation
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome integrates metabolic risk, kidney dysfunction, and cardiovascular disease. Whether statin-ezetimibe combination therapy is associated with lower subsequent myocardial infarction risk than statin monotherapy among patients across modified cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk groups remains uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using the Korean National Health Insurance Service database, we emulated separate two-arm landmark target trials within modified early and late cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk groups. Adults aged 30-74 years with dyslipidemia who received prescriptions covering a total of 180 days with statin monotherapy or a fixed-dose statin-ezetimibe combination were eligible. Treatment was assigned at the 180-day landmark. Stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting and cause-specific Cox regression were used to calculate hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence interval (CI), with death treated as a competing event for cumulative incidence estimation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 309,371 treated participants, 239,954 had modified early risk and 69,417 had modified late risk. Compared with statin monotherapy, statin-ezetimibe therapy was associated with lower myocardial infarction risk after weighting in both early-risk participants (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.81-0.95) and late-risk participants (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.79-0.98). 10-year weighted cumulative incidence was 1.97% versus 2.23% in the early-risk group and 3.52% versus 3.94% in the late-risk group. In same-intensity comparisons, the association was most evident with moderate-intensity therapy, particularly in the early CKM group (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.79-0.95).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among adults with dyslipidemia who received prescriptions covering a total of 180 days, statin-ezetimibe combination therapy was associated with a lower subsequent risk of myocardial infarction than statin monotherapy across modified CKM risk groups. The association was most evident in moderate-intensity comparisons.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Correctly Parsed, Wrong Lesion: Where Target Mix-Ups Arise When AI Binds Measurement Requests to Lung CT Nodules—A Staged, Hypothesis-Generating Evaluation
abstract: <jats:p>AI systems that measure lesions on request can compute correctly on the wrong lesion, an outcome no benchmark I found scores. I located where such mix-ups arise, in three stages on public lung CTs. A stratified audit of 1785 DICOM segmentation series found identical coded semantics for all 5192 pairs of different nodules on one scan; nodule numbers existed but needed linking to the request. A gate trusting structural checks authorized all 200 constructed requests, 89 for a mismatched and 41 for an ambiguous target. An expert wrote 60 requests in three sets, with each design frozen first. A rule parser carried a misread rank (“longest diameter” read as “largest”) in every resolution; removing it post hoc kept 13 of 26 correct resolutions, and agreement with a choice-constrained model parser removed all 25 rank-dependent wrong ones. A whole-lung definition of “lateral” excluded an intended nodule. In the confirmatory set, both pre-specified consensus gates authorized the nearest unintended nodule in two of 20 requests. Adjudication found three requests naming a lobe the images contradicted and two unassignable lobes; no map error was demonstrated. Parser agreement did not catch a request–image discordance. Clinical safety and workflow benefit were not evaluated.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Temporomandibular Joint Imaging: Diagnostic Performance Across Input Modality–Target Pairings—A Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-Analysis
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To estimate standalone artificial intelligence (AI) diagnostic performance in temporomandibular joint (TMJ) imaging across input modality–target pairings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four databases were searched through 18 June 2026. Eligible studies assessed standalone imaging AI and supplied an exact test-set 2 × 2 table in the report or after author contact. Four pairings were analysed by bivariate meta-regression. Two reviewers applied QUADAS-3 at estimate level.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sixteen studies contributed 17 estimates. For disc displacement, magnetic resonance imaging input yielded pooled sensitivity 0.924 (95% CI, 0.859–0.960) and specificity 0.812 (0.709–0.885), compared with 0.765 (0.618–0.867) and 0.741 (0.592–0.850) for panoramic or cone-beam computed tomography input. The sensitivity difference was 0.159 and remained 0.152–0.198 in leave-one-out and replicate analyses; the omnibus pairing test was not significant (χ²(6) = 10.38, P = .110). Reference-standard relation and pairing partitioned the disc-displacement evidence identically. No estimate had low overall risk of bias, and several otherwise eligible estimates lacked exact published 2 × 2 data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sensitivity was higher when disc displacement was depicted directly on magnetic resonance imaging than when inferred from imaging that does not depict the disc. However, the cross-domain group contained only three estimates, the omnibus pairing test was not significant, and design factors were entangled. Performance should therefore be interpreted by pairing, while direct depiction versus proxy inference requires prospective testing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Advances in knowledge</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>TMJ imaging AI performance should be interpreted in the context of the input modality–target pairing rather than as a property of the algorithm alone; exact test-set confusion matrices are essential for verification.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Long-term stone recurrence following ureteroscopic holmium laser lithotripsy: Association with perioperative nursing interventions in a retrospective cohort study
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>
                      This study aimed to examine the association between an enhanced systematic nursing program and postoperative stone recurrence following ureteroscopic holmium laser lithotripsy and to identify factors associated with recurrence in a retrospective cohort. In this single-center retrospective cohort study, medical records and follow-up documentation were reviewed for 185 adults treated between January 2024 and January 2025. The routine-care group comprised 123 patients treated from January to June 2024, and the enhanced-nursing group comprised 62 patients treated from July 2024 to January 2025. Outcomes included recorded stone recurrence at 6 and 12 months, time to first recurrence, recurrence-free status, adherence, and postoperative complications. The original analyses included Cox proportional hazards regression and exploratory subgroup interaction tests. Groups were defined by calendar period rather than randomized allocation. The 12-month recurrence rate was 9.7% (6/62) with enhanced nursing versus 22.8% (28/123) with routine care (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                       = .031); the corresponding reported 12-month recurrence-free proportions were 90.3% and 77.2% (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                       = .031). Reported time to first recurrence was 10.12 ± 2.51 versus 8.46 ± 2.83 months (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                       = .018). Water intake, dietary, and follow-up adherence were higher in the enhanced-nursing group (all
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                       < .01). Overall complication rates did not significantly differ (21.0% vs 30.9%,
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                       = .155). The reported multivariable model identified associations with stone diameter ≥ 1.5 cm (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.68, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.01–2.81), metabolic abnormalities (HR = 2.08, 95% CI 1.23–3.52), and enhanced nursing (HR = 0.44, 95% CI 0.20–0.96). In this retrospective, calendar-period cohort, enhanced nursing was associated with lower documented 12-month recurrence and improved adherence. Given the nonrandomized design, potential secular confounding, and differences in clinical surveillance and co-interventions, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than proof of causal benefit. Larger prospective studies are needed.
                    </jats:p>

title:
High‐Performance 2D MXene‐Derived TiO
                    <sub>2</sub>
                    Integrated Optical Polarizers
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Polarization control is essential for modern optical systems. Recently, 2D materials featuring highly anisotropic absorption across broad wavelength regions have emerged as a promising solution for realizing optical polarizers with operation bandwidths far exceeding those achievable using bulk materials. Despite this, existing 2D‐material‐based optical polarizers face critical limitations in simultaneously delivering high polarizer figures of merit (FOMs), robust power endurance, and scalable fabrication, hindering their practical deployment beyond the laboratory. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by demonstrating optical polarizers through integrating 2D MXene films onto silicon photonic devices and subsequently converting them in situ into 2D titanium dioxide (TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ). The 2D TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    exhibits significantly improved anisotropic absorption and thermal/chemical stability compared with MXene, enabling the hybrid polarizers that achieve high polarizer FOMs of up to ∼19.3 (a record among 2D‐material‐coated devices) and excellent power tolerance (stable under > 2 W coupled average power), together with a broad operation bandwidth (> 140 nm) and a high fabrication yield (∼98%). We also demonstrate microring resonator polarizers achieving high polarization extinction ratios of up to ∼12 dB. With outstanding overall performance and strong potential for large‐scale manufacturing, these devices represent a solid step toward industrial implementation of 2D‐material‐based optical polarizers.
                  </jats:p>

title: Analysis Of the Implementation of Target Costing as An Effort To Save Operational Costs in Lingga Salon
abstract: <jats:p>This study analyzes the application of target costing as an effort to improve operating cost efficiency at Lingga Salon. It identifies actual operating costs, calculates target cost based on revenue and desired profit, measures the cost gap, and evaluates savings alternatives through value engineering. The study uses a descriptive method with a quantitative approach supported by qualitative information. Data were collected through interviews with the owner and three employees, observation, business documentation, and literature review. The data show revenue of IDR 398,820,000 and actual operating costs of IDR 308,414,000, resulting in actual profit of IDR 90,406,000 or a 22.67% margin. With a target profit of 25% of revenue, the target profit is IDR 99,705,000 and the target cost is IDR 299,115,000. The resulting cost gap is IDR 9,299,000, equivalent to a minimum efficiency requirement of approximately 3.02%. A value engineering scenario covering salon supplies, electricity and water, maintenance, cleaning, administration/promotion, and internet produces potential savings of IDR 9,850,840. Operating costs would decrease to IDR 298,563,160, profit would increase to IDR 100,256,840, and the profit margin would reach 25.14%. These findings suggest that target costing supported by value engineering can serve as a planning and cost-control tool for salon service businesses, provided service quality is maintained</jats:p>

title: Laser-Scattering-Image-Based Intelligent Sensing for Dust Concentration Prediction in Top-Blown Furnace Applications with ICPO-CKGPR
abstract: <jats:p>Top-blown furnaces are important equipment in non-ferrous metal smelting processes, where dust concentration variations provide useful information for process monitoring and environmental management. However, conventional dust measurement methods may suffer from limited measurement efficiency and insufficient adaptability under complex operating conditions. To address these challenges, this study proposes a laser-scattering-image-based intelligent sensing framework with an improved crested porcupine optimizer-based combined-kernel Gaussian process regression model, termed ICPO-CKGPR, for dust concentration prediction under simulated top-blown furnace conditions. First, a laboratory-scale laser scattering image acquisition platform was established to collect scattering images under different dust concentration conditions, and 5000 timestamp-matched image–concentration sample pairs were obtained using a particulate matter sensor as the reference measurement source. Subsequently, a multi-domain feature representation strategy integrating grayscale-domain, frequency-domain, and spatial-domain information was developed to enhance the characterization capability of dust scattering images under multi-scale variations and disturbances. Furthermore, a combined-kernel Gaussian process regression model consisting of radial basis function, Matérn, and rational quadratic kernels was constructed to improve the modeling capability for complex nonlinear dust concentration variations. Meanwhile, the crested porcupine optimizer was improved by incorporating good-point-set initialization and periodic oscillation mutation strategies for adaptive hyperparameter optimization. Experimental results on the independent test set demonstrate that the proposed ICPO-CKGPR model achieves an RMSE of 3.086 mg/m3, an MAE of 1.784 mg/m3, and an R2 of 0.992 against the sensor-derived reference measurements. Compared with the benchmark models, the proposed method shows closer agreement with the sensor-derived PM10 reference measurements, indicating its potential for laser-scattering-image-based PM10 estimation under the investigated laboratory conditions.</jats:p>

title: Effect of Laser Remelting on the Microstructure, Mechanical and Tribological Properties of Detonation-Sprayed NiCrFeBSiC Coatings for Mechanical Engineering Applications
journal: Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing
abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates the effect of laser remelting on the microstructure, phase composition, mechanical properties, tribological behavior, and corrosion resistance of self-fluxing NiCrFeBSiC coatings deposited onto AISI 321 stainless steel by detonation spraying. The coatings were characterized before and after laser treatment using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), instrumented indentation, adhesion testing, ball-on-disk tribometry, and potentiodynamic polarization measurements. SEM analysis revealed that laser remelting reduced coating porosity from 0.306 ± 0.014% to 0.15 ± 0.09%, accompanied by microstructural densification and a reduction in coating thickness. XRD analysis confirmed the preservation of the principal crystalline phases, including Ni3Fe, Cr7C3, CrB, and Ni3B, following laser treatment. The Vickers hardness increased from 1049.1 ± 43.4 to 1206.1 ± 63.1 HV, while the elastic modulus increased from 233.6 ± 6.2 to 258.4 ± 5.3 GPa. Furthermore, adhesion strength increased by 19.4%, whereas surface roughness decreased by 19.2%. Laser remelting significantly improved tribological performance, reducing the average coefficient of friction from 0.535 ± 0.048 to 0.409 ± 0.086 and the specific wear rate from 2.864 × 10−4 to 1.447 × 10−4 mm3/(N·m), corresponding to a 49.5% reduction in wear. Electrochemical measurements indicated a modest decrease in corrosion current density of approximately 3.0%, accompanied by changes in the morphology of corrosion-affected regions. The improvements are associated with laser-induced microstructural densification, redistribution of alloying elements, and preservation of hard reinforcing phases. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining detonation spraying with laser remelting to produce wear-resistant nickel-based protective coatings for mechanical and power engineering applications.</jats:p>

title: Plasma Immersion Ion Implantation of AISI 316L Stainless Steel Parts Manufactured by Laser Powder Bed Fusion
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Austenitic stainless steel (SS) AISI 316L is highly compatible with laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), an advanced additive manufacturing (AM) technique for producing high-quality near-net-shape parts with complex geometries, especially for aerospace and medical applications. To further enhance its surface properties, temperature-controlled nitrogen plasma immersion ion implantation (TC-NPIII) was applied to LPBF-manufactured AISI 316L to obtain an expanded austenite (
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    N) layer, thereby enhancing surface performance and expanding the applicability of this material in demanding environments. The present work investigates the influence of TC-NPIII treatment temperature and duration on the microstructural evolution and mechanical performance of LPBF-manufactured AISI 316L. Samples were produced by LPBF in a laser-adapted powder bed system and subsequently treated by TC-NPIII, varying treatment duration for 1 and 3 h at controlled temperatures (450-520 °C). Microstructural analysis after treatment revealed a modified layer with a thickness that ranged from approximately 18.30 to 28.40 µm, superimposed on the characteristic LPBF microstructure. Grazing Incidence x-ray Diffraction (GI-XRD) analysis confirmed the formation of the desired
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    N phase, while no diffraction peaks associated with chromium nitrides were detected within the investigated processing window. Cross-sectional nanoindentation measurements of the treated samples yielded hardness values of approximately 386-751 HV, representing a substantial increase compared with the untreated LPBF sample (238 HV). These results indicate that, among the treatment temperatures and durations investigated, 450 °C for 3 h represents the optimal processing condition, promoting
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    N formation while preventing chromium nitride precipitation. The present work demonstrates that TC-NPIII can effectively produce expanded austenite and achieve significant surface hardening within treatment durations as short as 1-3 h. Moreover, these findings confirm the effectiveness of the TC-NPIII treatment in modifying the surface of LPBF-produced AISI 316L stainless steel, thereby enhancing its mechanical performance while preserving the characteristic hierarchical microstructure generated during LPBF.
                  </jats:p>

title: Reliability and Agreement of Infrared Thermography and a Digital Laser Thermometer for Non-Invasive Body Temperature Assessment in Sows
abstract: <jats:p>Early detection of heat stress in intensive pig production is critical for maintaining animal welfare and production efficiency; however, routine rectal thermometry is labor-intensive and impractical under farm conditions. This study aimed to evaluate the reliability and agreement of non-contact temperature measurement methods—digital laser thermometry and infrared thermography (IRT)—against rectal core temperature on a commercial farm. Measurements were performed at multiple anatomical sites (ear, flank, labial, and rectal surface regions), and data were analyzed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Bland–Altman methods. Traditional handheld infrared measurements showed poor reliability (ICC: 0.09–0.27) and substantially underestimated core temperature (−1.16 to −2.27 °C), with wide limits of agreement. In contrast, IRT demonstrated higher but imprecisely estimated reliability (ICC: 0.56–0.67; labial region: 95% CI 0.19–0.76; rectal region: 95% CI 0.41–0.82), lower bias (−0.37 to −0.59 °C), and narrower agreement intervals. However, significant proportional bias (p < 0.001) indicated temperature-dependent deviations between methods. Closer agreement with rectal temperature was observed for infrared thermography than for handheld infrared thermometry, particularly at the labial and perianal measurement sites.</jats:p>

Explainable AI-based framework for 3D structural as-built modeling of aging buildings in Korea using laser scanning
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study proposes a framework for automatically generating 3D structural as-built models of aging buildings by predicting the structural dimensions of members concealed behind finishes using laser scanning and machine learning, particularly when original construction drawings are unavailable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Laser scanning captures building geometry but includes both structural components and non-structural finishes (e.g. plaster), making it unsuitable for directly extracting structural dimensions. To address this, the proposed framework extracts geometric features from point clouds and employs machine learning techniques to predict structural dimensions of columns, beams, walls and slabs. Six machine learning models – Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Linear Regression and Support Vector Regression (SVR) – were trained using data collected on 1,560 column elements, 2,875 beam elements, 870 wall elements and 148 slab elements across 50 buildings and validated through two real-world case studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The best-performing model achieved MAPE of 10.51% for column width (95%CI: 8.47–12.71), 12.98% for column depth (95% CI: 10.86–15.41), 14.91% for beam width (95% CI: 13.63–16.15), 18.91% for beam depth (95% CI: 17.94–19.90), 10.42% for walls (95% CI: 8.89–12.00) and 10.70% for slabs (95% CI: 7.11–14.50). The predicted dimensions enabled reconstruction of 3D structural as-built models without relying on original drawings; the estimates are intended for planning-stage use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework provides a non-destructive, full-coverage estimate of structural member dimensions that would otherwise require original drawings or local removal of finishes. In practice, it is intended to reduce reliance on destructive investigation and, through the SHAP analysis, indicates where confirmatory openings could be prioritized, thereby supporting planning-stage decisions for the maintenance and retrofitting of buildings whose drawings are missing or outdated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study is among the first to formulate the discrepancy between laser-scanned surface geometry and concealed structural dimensions as a prediction problem and to propose a framework that returns the predicted dimensions to a 3D structural as-built model. Machine learning provides the enabling component, and explainability is used to direct in situ verification rather than as a methodological contribution in itself.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:sub>38</jats:sub>

                    Cu

abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Coral lead (Pb) isotope records provide multi-decadal perspectives on marine Pb histories, but how individual records represent regional isotope histories remains an important interpretive question. We present a 1951–1998 Pb isotope record from a
                    <jats:italic>Porites</jats:italic>
                    coral at Lutao, southeast of Taiwan, and compare it with published records from Dongsha and Ogasawara in the Northwest Pacific. The three coral records exhibited substantial inter-site isotopic differences during 1953–1963, smaller differences in interval-mean
                    <jats:sup>208</jats:sup>
                    Pb/
                    <jats:sup>207</jats:sup>
                    Pb during 1964–1984, and persistent site-specific characteristics. In 1985–1998, Lutao had a statistically distinguishable lower
                    <jats:sup>208</jats:sup>
                    Pb/
                    <jats:sup>207</jats:sup>
                    Pb composition than Dongsha, whereas the middle-to-late change within Lutao itself was not statistically resolved. This contrast shows that inter-site isotopic differences need not imply an equivalent temporal shift at an individual site. Published Pb isotope reference fields are compatible with multiple possible source combinations but do not uniquely identify historical sources or marine transport mechanisms. Together, these results reveal spatial heterogeneity in coral Pb isotope histories, with smaller inter-site differences during 1964–1984, and highlight the need to evaluate the spatial representativeness of individual coral Pb isotope records before extrapolating site-specific signatures to regional historical interpretations.
                  </jats:p>

title: Microstructure and Corrosion Behavior of Laser-Remelted Ti-35Nb(-Sn) Alloys
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Ti-35Nb-Sn alloys are being investigated for biomedical applications as hard tissue replacements due to their reduced elastic modulus, which is closer to that of natural bone, and helping to minimize stress shielding and bone resorption. Laser remelting is a promising processing route for the manufacture of implants with a graded elastic modulus and optimized performance. This study investigates the impact of laser processing on the microstructure and corrosion resistance of Ti-35Nb alloys containing 0, 2, and 4 wt.% Sn. Microstructural morphology, chemical composition, and phase formation were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), and x-ray diffraction (XRD), respectively. Corrosion resistance of the alloys was assessed in the base metal, heat-affected zone (HAZ), and fusion zone (FZ) using linear polarization tests in a physiological saline solution, using a three-electrode setup and an in-house developed microcell with a mask to limit the exposed area. Laser processing increased the fraction of the
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>

Integrated Laser Chip for Interrogation
of Large-Capacity Weak Fiber Bragg Grating (WFBG) Arrays
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We report a monolithically integrated distributed feedback multiwavelength laser array (DFB-MLA) photonic chip for large capacity interrogation of weak fiber Bragg grating (WFBG) arrays. The chip integrates multiwavelength generation, optical power combining, power equalization, and pulse gating on a single InP platform. Based on the reconstruction-equivalent-chirp (REC) technique, the 8 × 3 laser array exhibits an adjacent-channel wavelength spacing of approximately 2.5 nm and a total tuning range of 60 nm. In the photonic chip, the outputs of different channels are combined through an on-chip three-stage Y-branch combiner and subsequently pass through two functionally separated semiconductor optical amplifiers (SOAs). The power-equalization SOA (PE-SOA) compensates for wavelength-dependent power variations, reducing the interchannel power variation from approximately 10 to 0.3 dB. The pulse-gating SOA (PG-SOA) converts the continuous wavelength-swept output into optical pulses for time-domain addressing. Based on a time- and wavelength-division multiplexing (TWDM) scheme, the chip-based demodulation system successfully demodulated 100 WFBGs with a spatial interval of 0.2 m between adjacent gratings. These results demonstrate the potential of the integrated photonic source for compact, large-capacity optical fiber sensing systems.</jats:p>

title: Investigation of the active laser pyrometer with reflection for platinum dynamic surface true temperature measurement
abstract: <jats:p>The dynamic temperature evolution in semiconductor manufacturing has been difficult to measure accurately by non‑contact means, largely due to the effect of emissivity variations—where unknown and changing emissivity is one of the primary reasons. To address this issue, active laser pyrometry with reflection (ALPR) offers an emissivity‑independent technical approach. However, existing studies have mainly focused on steady‑state temperature measurements, without in‑depth analysis of the measurement response when the target temperature changes dynamically, and no public reports have been made on dynamic true‑temperature measurements. Therefore, in this study, based on the ALPR principle, we propose a temperature measurement model that incorporates a time‑dependent term, and we build a reflective dynamic measurement system. Experimental investigations are conducted on the dynamic true temperature of a platinum surface in the range of 1020 K to 1140 K. Within the temperature interval covered in this paper, the spectral radiation exhibits good linearity. The measurement results are compared with the thermocouple-extrapolated temperatures at corresponding time points, yielding a relative deviation of 1.0%. This work provides robust technical support for traceability of dynamic surface temperatures.</jats:p>

title: Excimer Laser Coronary Atherectomy (ELCA) Utilization in Complex PCI: A Position Paper of the Italian Society of Interventional Cardiology (SICI‐GISE)
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Excimer laser coronary atherectomy (ELCA) has significantly influenced interventional cardiology, particularly in complex percutaneous coronary interventions (PCIs). This expert review by the Italian Society of Interventional Cardiology (SICI‐GISE) provides a comprehensive overview of ELCA's applications, mechanisms of action, and clinical significance. ELCA uses ultraviolet (UV) energy to modify atheromatous plaque while minimizing damage to surrounding tissue. Its photochemical, photothermal, and photokinetic mechanisms enable effective plaque removal and improved clinical outcomes. The review traces the evolution of ELCA technology, including advances in laser catheters and techniques for diverse clinical and anatomical scenarios. It also discusses ELCA's clinical applications for conditions such as in‐stent restenosis, underexpanded stents, thrombotic lesions, and calcified plaques. The review further examines the histopathological effects of ELCA on vascular tissues, emphasizing its precision and minimal collateral damage. Data from multiple studies demonstrate ELCA's effectiveness and safety in complex PCI, with high success rates and acceptable complication rates. The review emphasizes the importance of careful patient selection, appropriate laser settings, and adjunctive therapies to achieve optimal results. Overall, ELCA is a valuable tool for interventional cardiologists, offering a versatile and practical approach to managing challenging coronary lesions.</jats:p>

title: Integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning with isotope hydrology to support sustainable water management
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) with isotope-based approaches has demonstrated a strong potential for enhancing the analysis of hydrological processes, tracer dynamics, system responses, and strengthening water resource management under increasing environmental pressures. However, this integration has not been fully explored and formulated yet.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To fill this knowledge gap, this paper conceptualizes perspectives on the application of AI/ML tools in isotope hydrology to promote sustainable water management. Results were developed based on the expert consultations and group work following the modified Delphi and Nominal Group Technique method. Fourteen international experts with diverse background worked together during the technical meeting coordinated by International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) (Vienna, Austria, 2025).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Diverse applications of AI/ML methods to enhance interpretation of isotope data, improve isotope-enabled modeling accuracy, and support decision-making were conceptualized in this paper. The results showed the need for developing interoperable data platforms, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration and hybrid physical-AI modeling, ensuring ethical AI/ML practices and the advancement of IAEA Global Water Analysis Laboratory (GloWAL) Network. The approach presented here has broader applicability and could be implemented across other networks and related programmes to support resilient and sustainable water resource management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Laser-based visible-light communication (VLC) can exploit wavelength and polarization multiplexing, but amplifier, channel, and coherent-receiver impairments interact. This paper develops an impairment-aware simulation of an eight-wavelength, dual-circular-polarization link carrying a 380.16-MHz occupied orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) resource grid within a nominal 400-MHz fifth-generation New Radio (5G NR)-aligned channel. The model includes laser-diode/semiconductor-optical-amplifier (LD–SOA) saturation and amplified spontaneous emission, wavelength-dependent gain ripple, Lambertian line-of-sight loss, residual wavelength-division-multiplexing (WDM) crosstalk, polarization mixing, coherent-receiver noise, phase/frequency offsets, and quadrature imbalance. The receiver combines covariance whitening, pilot-estimated 2 × 2 regularized multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) separation, pilot-assisted phase correction, and damped decision-directed refinement. With quadrature phase-shift keying, the nominal net payload rate after applying a 7 % FEC-overhead factor for rate reporting is 8.527 Gb/s. In the controlled reference realization, the proposed receiver remains below the 3.8 × 10
                    <jats:sup>−3</jats:sup>
                    pre-FEC bit-error-rate screening level through 50 m. A receiver ablation shows that both Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization and symmetric covariance whitening remove most of the reference I/Q-imbalance penalty, while the decision-directed update provides a smaller incremental improvement near the reach boundary. A separate sweep gives 17.054 Gb/s with 16-level quadrature-amplitude modulation through 16 m. The results provide a traceable baseline for joint optical-front-end and coherent-receiver design.
                  </jats:p>

title: Gravitational pinning and commensurability constrain a rigid-sheet thermo-magnetic mechanism for laser-driven levitating graphite
Atomic density optimization of quasi-one-dimensional diffuse laser cooling under a two-dimensional magnetic-field gradient
abstract: <jats:p>Diffuse laser cooling (DLC) provides a compact, robust, and scalable approach to generating cold-atom ensembles, offering significant potential for ground-based and spaceborne microwave atomic clocks. However, the performance of DLC systems remains limited by the weak atom-light interaction arising from their relatively low atomic density. This limitation is characterized by the optical density (OD), which quantifies the effective interaction strength between the atomic ensemble and the probe light and strongly influences the achievable signal-to-noise ratio. Although quasi-one-dimensional (quasi-1D) DLC extends the probe interaction length and improves atomic utilization, increasing the local atomic density within the interrogation region remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a magnetically enhanced quasi-1D DLC system that simultaneously maintains the extended interaction length and increases the atomic density through a two-dimensional magnetic-field gradient. By spatially compressing and accumulating atoms near the probe axis, we enhance the OD of a 70-cm-long cold rubidium ensemble from 2.49 to 3.94, representing a 58% enhancement and an equivalent increase in the local atomic density. The dependence of the OD on the magnetic-field gradient, probe intensity, beam size, and cooling-light polarization is systematically investigated. This work establishes a practical pathway for enhancing optical interrogation efficiency and could pave the way for the development of high-performance DLC-based cold-atom clocks and quantum sensing systems.</jats:p>

title: Study of Microstructure and Fatigue Behavior of Laser Melting Forging Repair Layers for Surface Cracks in X80 High-Strength Pipelines
abstract: <jats:p>This study adopted laser melting forging (LMF) technology to repair surface cracks on X80 high-strength steel pipes. LMF technology combines laser cladding (LC) with in situ laser shock peening (LSP), achieving strengthening and material forming simultaneously. This study innovatively utilized a galvanometer to adjust the size of laser shock spots and the high-frequency scanning path, achieving high-efficiency strengthening along the specific isothermal zone around the molten pool. By adjusting technological parameters, a high-density microstructure can be achieved. When the edge of the molten pool is impacted, microdefects (such as pores) can be noticeably reduced, and the grain size can also be significantly refined. This is mainly attributed to the fact that the high-frequency forging induces flow in the molten pool, promoting the escape of bubbles and causing the breakup of dendritic crystals. Compared with LC repair layers, the microhardness of the LMF repair layer increased by 10%, and its residual compressive stress increased by 62.6%. These improvements enhanced the resistance to crack propagation, and the average fatigue life was extended by more than 100% under a stress of 700 MPa ultimately. Meanwhile, fracture morphologies indicate that LMF significantly reduced fatigue sources such as microdefects. A finer-grained microstructure increases resistance to crack propagation. The research provides a systematic explanation of the mechanism and technical support for the application of LMF technology in remanufacturing engineering.</jats:p>

title: Testing subsistence in the medieval lower Syr-Darya through an archaeobotanical and stable isotope approach: a pilot study
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    This study provides a preliminary assessment of the subsistence base and possible dietary patterns of communities along the lower Syr-Darya River (modern-day Kazakhstan) in Central Asia from the fourth century BCE to the eighteenth century CE, with a deep focus on the medieval period, particularly attention to the Antiquity and Mongol periods. Stable carbon and nitrogen isotope analyses of animal bone collagen (fourth-second centuries BCE and twelfth-fifteenth centuries CE) and human bone collagen (twelfth-fifteenth centuries CE) were combined with archaeobotanical evidence (fourth century BCE to eighteenth century CE) and published palaeoenvironmental data to examine subsistence strategies in these desert-oasis settings. This research challenges several hypotheses previously proposed by scholars, including Aral regressions in Antiquity due to intensive agriculture and irrigation (the second half of the first millennium BCE) and the shift to pastoralism after the Mongol Conquest (the thirteenth to fifteenth century CE). The isotope data further suggest that livestock diets were predominantly based on C
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    resources, while elevated herbivore
                    <jats:italic>δ</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                    N values may reflect aridity, soil salinization, or grazing and foddering in nitrogen-enriched environments. Human
                    <jats:italic>δ</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                    N values from Kyshkala are consistent with substantial animal-protein consumption, although the specific dietary sources of this enrichment remain uncertain. By providing some of the first isotope data for fish remains from the Syr Darya region, this study establishes a preliminary ecological baseline for future reconstructions of human diet in Mongol and post-Mongol Central Asia. Overall, this pilot study demonstrates the potential of integrating archaeobotanical and stable isotope evidence to critically evaluate existing models of subsistence change. Future research should apply this approach to larger, systematically sampled datasets to test these preliminary interpretations at a regional scale.
                  </jats:p>

abstract:

                    <jats:p>
                      This study aimed to examine the association between an enhanced systematic nursing program and postoperative stone recurrence following ureteroscopic holmium laser lithotripsy and to identify factors associated with recurrence in a retrospective cohort. In this single-center retrospective cohort study, medical records and follow-up documentation were reviewed for 185 adults treated between January 2024 and January 2025. The routine-care group comprised 123 patients treated from January to June 2024, and the enhanced-nursing group comprised 62 patients treated from July 2024 to January 2025. Outcomes included recorded stone recurrence at 6 and 12 months, time to first recurrence, recurrence-free status, adherence, and postoperative complications. The original analyses included Cox proportional hazards regression and exploratory subgroup interaction tests. Groups were defined by calendar period rather than randomized allocation. The 12-month recurrence rate was 9.7% (6/62) with enhanced nursing versus 22.8% (28/123) with routine care (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                       = .031); the corresponding reported 12-month recurrence-free proportions were 90.3% and 77.2% (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                       = .031). Reported time to first recurrence was 10.12 ± 2.51 versus 8.46 ± 2.83 months (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                       = .018). Water intake, dietary, and follow-up adherence were higher in the enhanced-nursing group (all
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                       < .01). Overall complication rates did not significantly differ (21.0% vs 30.9%,
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                       = .155). The reported multivariable model identified associations with stone diameter ≥ 1.5 cm (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.68, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.01–2.81), metabolic abnormalities (HR = 2.08, 95% CI 1.23–3.52), and enhanced nursing (HR = 0.44, 95% CI 0.20–0.96). In this retrospective, calendar-period cohort, enhanced nursing was associated with lower documented 12-month recurrence and improved adherence. Given the nonrandomized design, potential secular confounding, and differences in clinical surveillance and co-interventions, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than proof of causal benefit. title: Seeing the Invisible: A Hydrogen‐Centred View of Heterogeneous Catalysis Enabled by Neutron Spectroscopy
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hydrogen governs virtually every stage of heterogeneous catalytic reactions, yet its chemical identity, location, mobility, and mechanistic role are often difficult to establish by experiments. Recent advances in neutron spectroscopy have enabled direct observation of hydrogen species across increasingly complex catalytic systems, generating a rapidly growing body of mechanism insights. However, general principles of hydrogen behaviour have not been fully extracted. In this mini‐review, we present a hydrogen‐centred framework that reorganises recent neutron‐spectroscopic studies around four fundamental questions: what hydrogen species exist, where hydrogen resides, how it moves, and how it participates in catalytic reactions. This mini‐review integrates hydrogen species, spatial distribution, dynamics, and reactivity into understanding across diverse systems, and emphasises how neutron spectroscopy provides direct mechanism insights into the chemistry of hydrogen and enables discrimination between competing catalytic pathways. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future opportunities for combining neutron spectroscopy with complementary experimental and theoretical approaches to establish a more comprehensive understanding of hydrogen‐controlled catalysis.</jats:p>

title: Coaxial Monitoring of Meltpool for Laser Powder Bed Fusion Process Control
journal: Strojniški vestnik - Journal of Mechanical Engineering
abstract: <jats:p>Reliable process monitoring is critical for advancing laser powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), as it provides the process information required for corrective control actions to prevent defects such as lack-of-fusion and keyhole porosity. A promising approach for PBF-LB/M process monitoring is coaxial measurement of light emitted from the meltpool area. More than two hundred research studies on coaxial monitoring of the meltpool have been performed, but there is still no validated and reliable method for measuring a suitable variable that could be directly used as an input for high-resolution control of the PBF-LB/M process, enabling process parameters such as laser power and scan speed to be dynamically adjusted not only at the part level, but locally for individual micrometer-scale segments along the scan track. This work reviews existing research studies on coaxial meltpool monitoring and identifies potential future research and development directions toward a standard and reliable meltpool monitoring method. Meltpool depth is identified as a particularly promising control-relevant variable. With the ability to monitor and control meltpool depth, it is possible to avoid undesirable process conditions due to too high or too low energy input, which would result in defects like keyhole porosity or lack-of-fusion. However, only five studies have attempted to estimate the melt pool depth coaxially during the PBF-LB/M process. Despite these attempts, there is no sufficiently validated method for high-resolution coaxial monitoring of meltpool depth in PBF-LB/M. The potential solution seems to be in combining concepts and recent discoveries from two-color coaxial camera- and photodiode-based meltpool area monitoring approaches. Based on the existing literature and hands-on experiences with establishing and working with coaxial monitoring systems, this work also provides guidelines and lists the most common challenges for implementing coaxial monitoring of the meltpool in the PBF-LB/M process.</jats:p>

title: A gray-distribution-based adaptive laser stripe center extraction algorithm
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate laser stripe center extraction is critical for high-precision line-structured laser 3D reconstruction. Many existing methods assume that the cross-sectional grayscale distribution of a laser stripe follows a fixed pattern. However, in practical scanning, variations in working distance, object geometry, and surface material lead to significant changes in grayscale distributions across the same stripe, which introduce center localization errors and degrade reconstruction accuracy and robustness. To address this issue, this paper proposes an adaptive laser stripe center extraction method with the core idea of adaptively selecting the most suitable center extraction algorithm for each stripe cross-section based on its estimated grayscale distribution model. Specifically, a real laser stripe dataset covering various typical scanning scenarios is first constructed. Based on statistical analysis of this dataset, a cross-sectional grayscale distribution estimation framework integrating four descriptors, namely Gaussianity, Symmetry, Peak Number, and Brightness Uniformity, is established. The optimal extraction algorithm for each grayscale distribution model is then determined through theoretical derivation and simulation analysis. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method maintains high extraction completeness while producing more continuous laser stripe center across different grayscale distributions. Under diverse camera exposure configurations, the average 3D reconstruction error is reduced by 0.13 mm, 0.33 mm, and 0.09 mm compared with the Gray Centroid Method, Gaussian Fitting Method, and Steger Method, respectively. Moreover, the proposed algorithm runs 2.02 times faster than the Steger Method, demonstrating superior robustness to stripe profile variations while maintaining high reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency.</jats:p>

Feasibility and safety of dual-wavelength 980/1470 nm laser for laparoscopic fenestration of hepatic cysts: a preliminary clinical study
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Laparoscopic fenestration and drainage is the standard treatment for symptomatic hepatic cysts. Conventional high-frequency electrocautery and ultrasonic scalpels have inherent limitations in simultaneously achieving efficient cutting and hemostasis, complete epithelial ablation, and preservation of intrahepatic vascular structures, leading to thermal injury, incomplete cyst wall treatment, and recurrence. The 980/1470 nm dual-wavelength laser leverages differential photothermal absorption by hemoglobin and water to enable layered, targeted therapy, offering a novel approach to optimizing minimally invasive hepatic cyst treatment, though clinical evidence remains limited. This study explores the feasibility, safety, and early efficacy of 980/1470 nm dual-wavelength laser in laparoscopic hepatic cyst fenestration, summarizes its technical essentials, and reports a preliminary single-port laparoscopic application of this laser system as an illustrative case.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A retrospective analysis was conducted of 10 patients who underwent laparoscopic hepatic cyst fenestration and drainage using 980/1470 nm dual-wavelength laser between May 2024 and September 2026. Intraoperatively, the 980/1470 nm dual-wavelength laser was used for cyst fenestration, combined with 1470 nm laser for precise superficial epithelial ablation of the cyst wall. Preoperative demographics, laser parameters, operative time, intraoperative blood loss, postoperative hospital stay, and complications were analyzed. Short-term imaging follow-up was performed to assess cyst recurrence and cavity healing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ten patients were enrolled, all of whom underwent successful laparoscopic surgery, including one case performed with a flexible single-port laparoscope. Postoperative pathology confirmed biliary hepatic cysts in all patients. Intraoperative blood loss was minimal, surgical trauma and stress were low, and no severe complications such as bile leakage, intra-abdominal hemorrhage, or infection occurred. All patients recovered uneventfully. Short-term imaging at a mean follow-up of 3 months demonstrated cyst cavity reduction or closure in all patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this small pilot cohort, 980/1470 nm dual-wavelength laser laparoscopic fenestration and drainage appeared feasible and safe, with no severe perioperative complications and favorable short-term imaging outcomes; the single-port application described here represents a single illustrative case. Given the small sample size, absence of a comparator group, and short follow-up, these findings are preliminary and require confirmation in larger controlled studies with longer-term surveillance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Prediction of oxide coating thickness on moving polymer films using quantum cascade laser spectroscopy and machine learning
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nanometer-accurate inline monitoring of oxide coating thickness on polymer films is&#xD;essential for quality control in roll-to-roll production. However, measuring coatings in the&#xD;nanometer range on moving polymer films remains challenging because the measurement&#xD;samples spatially varying polymer thickness and reflective background conditions along the&#xD;measurement path, in addition to the low optical contrast between oxide and polymer in&#xD;the mid-infrared. We present a transflection measurement approach that combines&#xD;quantum cascade laser (QCL) spectroscopy with data-driven spectral analysis. We apply it&#xD;to moving oriented polypropylene (OPP) and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) films&#xD;coated with silicon oxide under laboratory conditions to assess its feasibility for future&#xD;inline monitoring. In transflection mode, reflected intensity is captured across a spectral&#xD;range covering the Si–O absorption band, enabling measurements on both transparent and&#xD;opaque films. Two spectral analysis approaches are proposed and compared. The first&#xD;combines spectral averaging with linear regression, achieving a mean root mean square&#xD;error (RMSE) of 7.6 nm for OPP and 15.9 nm for PET. The second combines linear&#xD;regression and Gaussian process regression (LR-GPR) on blockwise-aggregated spectra.&#xD;For thickness levels represented in the training data, this approach reduces the RMSE to&#xD;approximately 4nm for both OPP and PET, corresponding to improvements of&#xD;approximately 50% for OPP and 75% for PET. While the former approach offers&#xD;simplicity and interpretability, the latter captures nonlinear spectral relationships.&#xD;However, generalization of LR-GPR to unseen thickness levels remains the central&#xD;limitation, with RMSE values of approximately 10 nm to 11 nm. The results show&#xD;potential for oxide coating thickness estimation, while improved generalization and further&#xD;validation are needed to establish broader applicability.</jats:p>

title: Discrete-EDFA-Free Amplification: EDF-Assisted Random DFB Raman Laser
abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a simulation-based study of an erbium-doped-fibre-assisted random distributed-feedback (rDFB) Raman amplifier for long-haul wavelength-division multiplexed transmission. The proposed architecture combines distributed Raman amplification over a 50 km standard single-mode-fibre span with a 25 cm terminal erbium-doped fibre (EDF) section pumped only by the residual 1460 nm rDFB field. The terminal EDF is intended to compensate span-end connection losses without a dedicated 980 nm or 1480 nm pump source. The model is calibrated against an experimentally measured optical-time-domain-reflectometer (OTDR) power profile, and an additional 2 dB EDF-gain margin is introduced to represent inter-span losses. The study considers a single 2 dB net-gain operating point, selected by minimizing signal-power variation along the span. The optimized configuration is applied to a 50-channel C-band WDM system over an equivalent 150-span, 7500 km link with idealized per-span power reset. The simulated central-channel OSNR reaches approximately 18.9 dB after 7500 km, while the channel OSNRs remain between about 17.5 and 19 dB. However, central-channel optimization produces a strongly nonuniform gain profile, increasing from approximately 2 dB near the band centre to 6.5 dB at the long-wavelength edge. The Kerr nonlinear-product power also increases by about 30 dB between one span and 7500 km. These results demonstrate the potential of the proposed architecture for span-end loss compensation, while showing that gain flattening, multi-channel optimization, system-level nonlinear analysis, and experimental validation are required before practical deployment.</jats:p>

title: Laser-Induced Crystal Structure Stabilization and Europium (III) Doping of Hydroxyapatite Nanoparticles via Pulsed Liquid Fragmentation
abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to develop a method for the heterovalent doping of hydroxyapatite (HA) with europium (III) ions using laser fragmentation of a micropowder in a liquid medium. The samples examined after laser fragmentation of the hydroxyapatite micropowder in liquid exhibited ultrathin nanosheets (with an approximate thickness of 2–5 nm) while retaining the hydroxyapatite crystal structure; furthermore, when the process is carried out in a europium nitrate solution, it leads to the preferential incorporation of europium (III) ions into Ca(I) sites. The phase homogeneity and structural evolution of the fragmentation-derived samples were investigated by Raman and FTIR spectroscopy. Raman spectroscopy revealed that laser treatment of the HA micropowder for 30 min in the presence of 2 mol% europium nitrate (sample Eu2%-HA) modifies the crystal lattice symmetry. Conversely, the FTIR Weiner-Shemesh crystallinity index increased reflecting ordering within the basal planes. The incorporation of Eu3+ ions was confirmed by fluorescence spectroscopy supporting the predominant stabilization of europium at the Ca(I) site. Dynamic light scattering, atomic force microscopy, and transmission electron microscopy combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy mapping were used to investigate particle morphology and assess elemental homogeneity and dopant distribution.</jats:p>
