title: Plasma Immersion Ion Implantation of AISI 316L Stainless Steel Parts Manufactured by Laser Powder Bed Fusion
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Austenitic stainless steel (SS) AISI 316L is highly compatible with laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), an advanced additive manufacturing (AM) technique for producing high-quality near-net-shape parts with complex geometries, especially for aerospace and medical applications. To further enhance its surface properties, temperature-controlled nitrogen plasma immersion ion implantation (TC-NPIII) was applied to LPBF-manufactured AISI 316L to obtain an expanded austenite (
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    N) layer, thereby enhancing surface performance and expanding the applicability of this material in demanding environments. The present work investigates the influence of TC-NPIII treatment temperature and duration on the microstructural evolution and mechanical performance of LPBF-manufactured AISI 316L. Samples were produced by LPBF in a laser-adapted powder bed system and subsequently treated by TC-NPIII, varying treatment duration for 1 and 3 h at controlled temperatures (450-520 °C). Microstructural analysis after treatment revealed a modified layer with a thickness that ranged from approximately 18.30 to 28.40 µm, superimposed on the characteristic LPBF microstructure. Grazing Incidence x-ray Diffraction (GI-XRD) analysis confirmed the formation of the desired
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    N phase, while no diffraction peaks associated with chromium nitrides were detected within the investigated processing window. Cross-sectional nanoindentation measurements of the treated samples yielded hardness values of approximately 386-751 HV, representing a substantial increase compared with the untreated LPBF sample (238 HV). These results indicate that, among the treatment temperatures and durations investigated, 450 °C for 3 h represents the optimal processing condition, promoting
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    N formation while preventing chromium nitride precipitation. The present work demonstrates that TC-NPIII can effectively produce expanded austenite and achieve significant surface hardening within treatment durations as short as 1-3 h. Moreover, these findings confirm the effectiveness of the TC-NPIII treatment in modifying the surface of LPBF-produced AISI 316L stainless steel, thereby enhancing its mechanical performance while preserving the characteristic hierarchical microstructure generated during LPBF.
                  </jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cold atmospheric plasma is applied to dental implants for surface activation, osseointegration, infection control and host modulation. This review reads those four uses as one reactive‐species mechanism with a separate exposure axis per target (an organizing interpretation, not a measured law) and audits what an illustrative sample of thirty‐three protocols reports about dose. Plasma medicine has a source‐characterization specification (DIN SPEC 91315) and candidate dose descriptors, delivered energy and equivalent total oxidation potential, whose inputs no audited protocol reports in full. Of twenty‐five atmospheric‐pressure protocols, working gas is stated in twenty‐four, flow in nineteen, power or voltage setting in eleven; across all thirty‐three, treated area and delivered dose in none, a measured output in two. Human endpoints are mostly surrogates.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We start with a brief introduction to the many faces of the Sun, the dynamic star that is the main source of space weather. We explain the need for spacecraft observations, the structure of the solar atmosphere, and the Sun’s magnetic cycle. Next, we focus on the Sun’s influence on Earth, define ‘space weather,’ and briefly discuss its effects on our technology and related socio-economic impacts. Then, we present data-driven, physics-based simulation models with predictive capabilities that enable forecasting and mitigation. We focus on models developed by my team at KU Leuven and the results and predictions they produce: the heliospheric wind and CME evolution models EUHFORIA and ICARUS, the global solar corona model COCONUT, and the solar energetic particle acceleration and transport model Particle Radiation Asset Directed at IP Space Exploration. We end with a few take-home messages.</jats:p>

title: A simple model for evaporation-driven migration of liquid metal between plasma pulses in a fusion reactor with liquid metal plasma-facing components

affiliation.name: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Liquid metal plasma-facing components (PFCs) are being considered for a variety of fusion power plant designs, and careful control of the liquid metal inventory will be essential in these systems to mitigate challenges with liquid metal corrosion and hydrogen fuel retention. Since many power plant designs and existing test facilities rely on pulsed plasma sources, it is critical to understand how liquid metal evaporation leads to material migration within a reactor over the periods of time when no plasma is present. This work addresses this question by developing a simple particle balance model to efficiently calculate liquid metal vapor transport patterns over indefinitely long time periods, using a particle redistribution matrix to capture the vapor transport details. After developing the mathematical model, characteristics of a future Liquid Metal Core-Edge (LMCE) research facility with liquid lithium divertors are used as a reference to demonstrate how the particle balance model can be used. Examples of lithium migration during the cooldown period between plasma pulses show that the pattern of lithium deposition depends primarily on the system geometry. An important secondary effect in these scenarios is the relative cooldown rate of the lithium divertor with respect to other PFCs in the device. Examples are also provided to demonstrate how the particle balance model can be used to optimize the design of a cold finger to collect liquid metal condensation for extraction and reprocessing, with the results showing that a future LMCE facility may be capable of collecting all of the lithium evaporated between plasma pulses if the main chamber walls can be maintained above 350 C during operation.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The objectives of the current study were (a) to identify profiles of treatment-seeking youth with depression and/or suicidal thoughts and behaviors based on patterns of physical health (i.e., functioning-mobility, fatigue, pain interference, pain severity, medical comorbidities), (b) to explore demographic and treatment correlates of profiles (i.e., age, sex, race, ethnicity, family income, and treatment type), (c) to explore associations among profiles and mental health outcomes (i.e., anxiety, depression, suicidal risk, suicidal propensity) at baseline, and (d) to examine whether the profiles were associated with mental health changes over time (i.e., 6 months).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants were 1,174 youth ages 8–17 (M age = 14.5; 70.9% female; 69.6% White, 44.8% Hispanic/Latino). Youth completed measures of physical health, depression, anxiety, and suicide symptoms. Latent variable mixture modeling was conducted.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three profiles emerged: (1) “High Physical Health” (49.3%), (2) “Moderate Physical Health” (39.9%), and (3) “Low Physical Health” (10.7%). Youth in the “High Physical Health” profile had the lowest depression, anxiety, suicide propensity, and suicide risk, and youth in the “Low Physical Health” profile had the highest depression, anxiety, and suicide propensity. Mental health symptoms improved over time for all profiles, and the rate of change was not different.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Results highlight the importance of examining physical health in treatment-seeking youth, as physical health symptoms may impact depression, anxiety, and suicide propensity over time and indicate a treatment targeting both mental and physical health.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Separating thermal and laser intensity effects in plasmonic photocatalysis has proven challenging because the two are frequently intertwined. Higher laser intensities will increase any laser-induced heating, making it difficult to isolate the influence of laser intensity and complicating efforts to disentangle thermal versus nonthermal contributions to plasmonic photocatalysis. Here, we decouple laser intensity and laser heating effects by fabricating plasmonic nanostructures with nearly identical optical properties but divergent thermal properties, allowing us to modulate and even eliminate laser heating while applying the same range of laser intensities. We simultaneously perform upconverting nanoparticle (UCNP)-based microscale thermometry and monitor the photocatalyzed dimerization of 4-nitrothiophenol (4-NTP) to 4,4′-dimercaptoazobenzene (DMAB) with Raman spectroscopy. We show that larger temperature rises enhance the reaction and, even more importantly, the temperature rise alone dictates the degree of 4-NTP to DMAB conversion, independent of the applied laser intensity. These results are consistent across two different plasmonic nanostructures. External heating combined with a threshold laser intensity can also drive the reaction, with the degree of conversion again determined solely by the temperature rise. However, despite the critical influence of the temperature rise, external heating alone fails to catalyze the reaction. Leveraging ultrahigh thermal conductivity diamond substrates, which let us increase the laser intensity without inducing heating, we further demonstrate that higher laser intensities increase the reaction rate yet have no effect on the degree of conversion. Thus, although temperature plays an outsize role, the plasmonic photocatalysis process nonetheless cannot be explained by a purely thermal mechanism.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>
                    Polarization control is essential for modern optical systems. Recently, 2D materials featuring highly anisotropic absorption across broad wavelength regions have emerged as a promising solution for realizing optical polarizers with operation bandwidths far exceeding those achievable using bulk materials. Despite this, existing 2D‐material‐based optical polarizers face critical limitations in simultaneously delivering high polarizer figures of merit (FOMs), robust power endurance, and scalable fabrication, hindering their practical deployment beyond the laboratory. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by demonstrating optical polarizers through integrating 2D MXene films onto silicon photonic devices and subsequently converting them in situ into 2D titanium dioxide (TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ). The 2D TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    exhibits significantly improved anisotropic absorption and thermal/chemical stability compared with MXene, enabling the hybrid polarizers that achieve high polarizer FOMs of up to ∼19.3 (a record among 2D‐material‐coated devices) and excellent power tolerance (stable under > 2 W coupled average power), together with a broad operation bandwidth (> 140 nm) and a high fabrication yield (∼98%). We also demonstrate microring resonator polarizers achieving high polarization extinction ratios of up to ∼12 dB. With outstanding overall performance and strong potential for large‐scale manufacturing, these devices represent a solid step toward industrial implementation of 2D‐material‐based optical polarizers.

                  <jats:p>
                    Laser-based visible-light communication (VLC) can exploit wavelength and polarization multiplexing, but amplifier, channel, and coherent-receiver impairments interact. This paper develops an impairment-aware simulation of an eight-wavelength, dual-circular-polarization link carrying a 380.16-MHz occupied orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) resource grid within a nominal 400-MHz fifth-generation New Radio (5G NR)-aligned channel. The model includes laser-diode/semiconductor-optical-amplifier (LD–SOA) saturation and amplified spontaneous emission, wavelength-dependent gain ripple, Lambertian line-of-sight loss, residual wavelength-division-multiplexing (WDM) crosstalk, polarization mixing, coherent-receiver noise, phase/frequency offsets, and quadrature imbalance. The receiver combines covariance whitening, pilot-estimated 2 × 2 regularized multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) separation, pilot-assisted phase correction, and damped decision-directed refinement. With quadrature phase-shift keying, the nominal net payload rate after applying a 7 % FEC-overhead factor for rate reporting is 8.527 Gb/s. In the controlled reference realization, the proposed receiver remains below the 3.8 × 10

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Excess fat mass is causally linked to multiple diseases, but the use of existing therapies, such as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, is limited by varying effects and common side effects, including loss of fat-free mass.                     <jats:p>Here we present evidence on the associations of genetically predicted levels of 21 proteins with fat mass, including five which also colocalise with the trait (AGER, CRIM1, DNER, NEFL, and PRRT3). affiliation.name: Rezolute , Bend,

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Peritumoral brain edema (PTBE) is managed primarily with dexamethasone, which imposes dose-limiting toxicity and potentially steroid dependence. The role of plasma kallikrein signaling in PTBE remains poorly defined, and no mechanistic framework currently exists to predict whether plasma kallikrein inhibition (PKI) could achieve steroid-sparing edema control. A four-module ordinary differential equation framework was constructed from published rate constants, receptor pharmacology, and DCE-MRI permeability data. The framework integrated kallikrein cascade kinetics, dual-pathway kinin receptor signaling, tumor-class permeability decomposition (structural, VEGF, bradykinin, and cross-talk fractions), and Starling-based fluid accumulation with capacity-limited drainage. The framework was used to generate quantitative predictions for steroid-sparing thresholds, treatment-duration requirements, post-cessation durability, and tumor-class–specific edema-resolution kinetics. The model identified a steroid-sparing threshold: the minimum bradykinin-driven permeability fraction at which plasma kallikrein inhibition maintained edema below the dexamethasone baseline. The nominal threshold was 30%, with a full range of 14–52% across all 81 parameterizations. The bradykinin receptor B1R, which is transcriptionally induced by inflammation, does not undergo agonist-induced desensitization, and drives its own expression through NF-κB positive feedback, emerged as the dominant modeled chronic permeability driver. The framework generated four testable clinical predictions: dexamethasone taper without PKI produces rebound; PKI enables steroid discontinuation above the bradykinin threshold; no rebound occurs during PKI treatment; and edema control persists after PKI cessation due to treatment-induced B1R receptor depletion predicted from published receptor turnover kinetics. Residual Ktrans following bevacizumab exposure may identify patients most likely to benefit from PKI, while tumor class informs expected edema-resolution kinetics. A bridge-and-sustain protocol emerged from the exposure/response analysis: dexamethasone for rapid edema reduction and PKI for sustained maintenance. This model-defined pharmacology approach translates first-principles mechanistic biology into a personalized treatment framework for PTBE, enabling patient-specific prediction of steroid-sparing potential and individualized edema-management strategies for primary and metastatic brain tumors.</jats:p>

title: Kinetic inverse bremsstrahlung absorption in magnetized fusion plasmas beyond the constant Coulomb logarithm: Velocity-dependent collisions, super-Gaussian electrons, and plasma screening

affiliation.name: Department of Physics, Laboratory of Physics of Radiations and Their Interactions with Matter (LRPRIM), Faculty of Matter Sciences, University of Batna 1 , Batna 05000,

abstract: <jats:p>We develop a kinetic model of electron–ion inverse bremsstrahlung absorption in magnetized fusion plasmas that extends the conventional constant-Coulomb-logarithm treatment. The model incorporates the velocity dependence of the Coulomb logarithm and plasma screening directly into the electron–ion collision frequency, while a super-Gaussian electron distribution is used to account for non-Maxwellian distortions. The formulation explicitly retains magnetization and circular-polarization effects and yields asymptotic scaling laws for magneto-inertial fusion (MIF) plasmas and microwave-heated magnetically confined plasmas. The results show that the velocity-dependent Coulomb logarithm can either reduce or enhance absorption depending on the electron distribution, whereas plasma screening systematically suppresses it. Under the conditions studied, the complete collisional model changes the MIF absorption rate by about 19% relative to the thermal-logarithm approximation. In the microwave-heated regime, the corresponding reduction is about 6% over the whole density range considered. These results highlight the need to treat non-Maxwellianity, velocity-dependent collisions, and plasma screening self-consistently when modeling inverse bremsstrahlung absorption in magnetized fusion plasmas.</jats:p>

title: PLASMA RICO EN PLAQUETAS ACTIVADO COMO ADYUVANTE A LA DILATACIÓN ENDOSCÓPICA EN ESTENOSIS ESOFÁGICAS BENIGNAS

abstract:
<jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Introducción:</jats:bold>
                    Las estenosis esofágicas benignas pueden recurrir tras la dilatación endoscópica por inflamación y remodelación fibrótica, condicionando nuevas sesiones. El plasma rico en plaquetas (PRP) aporta mediadores de reparación tisular y podría modular la cicatrización esofágica.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Objetivos:</jats:bold>
                    Describir factibilidad técnica, eventos adversos y evolución clínica y endoscópica tras dilatación con Savary-Gilliard sobre guía Savary e infiltración submucosa de PRP autólogo activado con gluconato de calcio al 10%.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Métodos:</jats:bold>
                    Estudio observacional retrospectivo, descriptivo y unicéntrico de cinco adultos con estenosis benignas: tres pépticas, una cáustica y una postquirúrgica por ascenso gástrico secundario a estenosis cáustica. La dilatación se realizó con Savary-Gilliard sobre guía Savary. El PRP se obtuvo de 20 mL de sangre citratada mediante doble centrifugación (1500 rpm/8 min y 2500 rpm/5 min); se recuperaron 8 mL, activados con 0,20 mL de gluconato de calcio al 10% e infiltrados submucosamente en cuatro cuadrantes post dialtacion. Se evaluaron disfagia (Mellow-Pinkas), número de dilataciones, cicatrización endoscópica a 8 semanas despues de la última sesión, recurrencia y eventos adversos mediante análisis descriptivo.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Resultados:</jats:bold>
                    Tres mujeres y dos hombres; edad media 43 años (22–63). El diámetro inicial fue 8–10 mm en cuatro pacientes y 2 mm en uno. La mediana de disfagia disminuyó de 3 (2–4) a 0; todos alcanzaron Mellow-Pinkas 0. Tres pacientes requirieron dos sesiones, uno tres y el caso de 2 mm, ocho. A las 8 semanas hubo cicatrización mucosa adecuada en 5/5 y no se observaron perforación, sangrado significativo ni otros eventos adversos relacionados. El seguimiento mediano fue 70 semanas (35–144); dos pacientes presentaron recurrencia tardía de disfagia a las 70 y 72 semanas.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Conclusión:</jats:bold>
                    La dilatación con Savary-Gilliard sobre guía Savary seguida de PRP activado fue factible y no presentó eventos adversos relacionados. La mejoría clínica, la cicatrización endoscópica y las recurrencias tardías respaldan estudios prospectivos controlados para determinar eficacia.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Palabras clave:</jats:bold>
                    Estenosis Esofágica; Endoscopía Gastrointestinal; Plasma Rico en Plaquetas; Trastornos de Deglución.
                  </jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As a proximal fluid to gliomas, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) has become of significant interest for biomarker discovery, including cell-free DNA, proteomics, and other -omics. However, we and others have demonstrated that plasma and blood contamination, both from frank sample contamination and the blood-brain barrier that is inherently disrupted in many high-grade gliomas, can significantly impact candidate CSF biomarker identification. As such, we sought to deconvolute the proteomic impacts of plasma and blood on the CSF proteome to enable improved downstream identification of glioma CSF protein biomarkers. To identify plasma and/or whole blood-associated proteins in CSF, platelet-poor plasma or whole blood was spiked into CSF at 10%, 1%, 0.01%, 0.01%, and 0.001%. Aptamer-based proteomics was performed on these CSF samples and the non-spiked CSF via the SomaScan platform. Regression analyses were subsequently performed to identify proteins most strongly correlated with plasma or blood contamination across the dilution curves, generating estimated blood and plasma contamination scores for each sample. The blood and plasma contamination scores were highly correlated (Spearman r = 0.987), with few proteins found to be uniquely specific to blood-or-plasma abundance in CSF. Instead, contamination proteins were largely shared between plasma and blood in CSF. In evaluating contamination sensitivity via moderate slopes, the proteins with the greatest sensitivity for plasma/blood contamination included DBNDD1, SCARB1, PGLYRP1, CES1, and PTRHD1. Gene ontology biological process enrichment confirmed hypothesized enrichment for hemostasis, complement activation, coagulation, and platelet activation pathways. Contamination scores were then applied to cranial glioma versus non-oncologic CSF to identify candidate contamination-controlled, glioma-associated proteins. Numerous proteins were found to be significantly more abundant in glioma CSF than controls after controlling for contamination, including but not limited to GFAP, VEGFA, PRKCA, COPE, and MRTO4. In conclusion, plasma-or-blood-associated proteins can be deconvoluted from CSF to aid in glioma biomarker discovery.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>The Saha ionization equation, originally formulated within the framework of stellar astrophysics, is reinterpreted in this work as a high-temperature extension of classical chemical equilibrium theory. Ionization is treated as a reversible chemical reaction whose equilibrium state is governed by temperature, electron pressure, and the thermodynamic properties of the participating species. By employing the formalism of Gibbs free energy, equilibrium constants, and molecular partition functions, we demonstrate that the Saha relation is mathematically equivalent to the canonical expression [Formula: see text] used in physical chemistry. Building on this equivalence, we introduce a quantitative Van’t Hoff-style analysis of the Saha equilibrium, showing that the characteristic curvature of [Formula: see text] versus [Formula: see text] is a direct, measurable signature of the translational entropy carried by the liberated electron. Worked numerical examples for hydrogen and calcium connect this thermodynamic treatment directly to the Balmer-line maximum in A-type stars and the Ca II H&K lines of solar-type stars. The electron number density is identified as a chemical control parameter analogous to pressure in Le Chatelier’s principle. The implications of this framework are discussed in the context of astrochemistry: ionization balance governs spectral classification across the Harvard O–M sequence, structures the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram as a plasma-chemical phase space, and determines astrochemical reaction pathways in diffuse interstellar clouds and cold molecular cloud environments. This work establishes a quantitative, chemistry-first conceptual bridge between laboratory plasma chemistry and astrophysical stellar behavior.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) is a minimally invasive treatment for glioblastoma (GBM) cytoreduction via thermal coagulation of the tumor mass. It leaves a sublethal thermal penumbra where resistant tumor cells persist, yet the molecular basis of this adaptation is poorly understood. We hypothesized that post-LITT recurrence carries a distinct transcriptomic signature relative to the pre-LITT primary tumor and sought druggable targets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Orthotopic U251N GBM xenografts in RNU/RNU rats underwent MRI-guided LITT. Bulk RNA-seq from primary (pre-LITT, n = 3) and recurrent (post-LITT, n = 3) tumors was analyzed after xengsort cross-species read sorting (k = 25). Differential expression used DESeq2 (Wald test, ashr shrinkage, BH/independent filtering; FDR&lt;0.05, |log2FC|&gt;1) via nf-core/differentialabundance, with global structure by PCA/PERMANOVA on variance-stabilized counts, hub genes from a STRING protein–protein interaction network, subtypes by GSVA with limma, and drugs prioritized by an Integrated Score combining therapeutic enrichment (|NES|^1.5) with predicted blood–brain-barrier (BBB) permeability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Primary and recurrent transcriptomes were globally distinct by PCA (PC1 41.8%, PC2 26.2%); PERMANOVA quantified this separation, attributing 27.8% of transcriptome-wide variance to recurrence (R²=0.278). DESeq2 identified 35 genes (23 up, 12 down). GSEA showed dominant downregulation of the translational machinery in recurrence—eukaryotic translation elongation (NES = −3.17, FDR=1.6 × 10⁻26), ribosome, translation initiation, and the EIF2AK4/GCN2 amino-acid-starvation response—indicating translational shutdown with integrated stress. Subtypes shifted toward Garofano Mitochondrial, away from Neftel Astrocyte-like/NPC-like. Hubs were ECM/calcium genes (BGN, COL1A1, IGFBP3, CALB1). Drug prioritization nominated the iron-chelator/HIF agent ciclopirox (Integrated Score 3.40, BBB 1.0) and HIF-stabilizer dimethyloxalylglycine (3.04); the PI3K/mTOR inhibitor LY-294002 ranked 7th.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Translational shutdown, characterized by an integrated stress/starvation response and a mitochondrial-metabolic subtype shift, seems to be one post-LITT recurrence mechanism, consistent with stress-adapted, persistent cells. Based on this analyses, HIF/iron-axis agents (ciclopirox, DMOG) and the PI3K/mTOR inhibitor LY-294002 emerge as potential adjuvant therapeutic candidates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Brain metastases (BM) are the most common intracranial malignancy in adults and remain associated with poor morbididty and mortality despite advances in multimodal therapy. Plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) offers a minimally invasive approach to assess disease biology, but its relationship to clinical, radiographic, and survival outcomes in BM remains poorly characterized.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We retrospectively analyzed perioperative plasma cfDNA concentration in 108 consecutive patients who underwent surgical resection of BM from breast cancer, lung cancer, or melanoma between 2010 and 2019. cfDNA was extracted from peripheral plasma and quantified by fluorometric assay. Patients were dichotomized at cfDNA &gt;21 ng/mL, corresponding to the upper tertile.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Plasma cfDNA was elevated in patients with uncontrolled systemic disease (p = 0.013) and leptomeningeal disease (p = 0.002), but was not associated with intracranial tumor volume, lesion number, edema volume, or proximity to CSF or venous structures. High cfDNA was associated with worse OS across the full cohort (p = 0.044), but not PFS or cumulative incidence of intracranial progression. This OS association was most pronounced in melanoma BM (p &lt; 0.001), with no significant association in breast or lung BM. On univariate Cox regression, cfDNA concentration was associated with worse OS (HR 1.01/ng/mL, 95% CI 1.00–1.01, p = 0.048), along with uncontrolled systemic disease, high BM volume, lower KPS, partial resection, and prior hormonal/immunotherapy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Perioperative plasma cfDNA concentration tracks systemic disease burden rather than intracranial tumor load and carries prognostic significance for overall survival in patients with BM. The histology-dependent nature of this association, particularly in melanoma, warrants validation in larger, molecularly annotated cohorts. These findings highlight the need for more sensitive, CNS-directed liquid biopsy strategies to capture intracranial disease burden.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a simulation-based study of an erbium-doped-fibre-assisted random distributed-feedback (rDFB) Raman amplifier for long-haul wavelength-division multiplexed transmission. The proposed architecture combines distributed Raman amplification over a 50 km standard single-mode-fibre span with a 25 cm terminal erbium-doped fibre (EDF) section pumped only by the residual 1460 nm rDFB field. The terminal EDF is intended to compensate span-end connection losses without a dedicated 980 nm or 1480 nm pump source. The model is calibrated against an experimentally measured optical-time-domain-reflectometer (OTDR) power profile, and an additional 2 dB EDF-gain margin is introduced to represent inter-span losses. The study considers a single 2 dB net-gain operating point, selected by minimizing signal-power variation along the span. The optimized configuration is applied to a 50-channel C-band WDM system over an equivalent 150-span, 7500 km link with idealized per-span power reset. The simulated central-channel OSNR reaches approximately 18.9 dB after 7500 km, while the channel OSNRs remain between about 17.5 and 19 dB. However, central-channel optimization produces a strongly nonuniform gain profile, increasing from approximately 2 dB near the band centre to 6.5 dB at the long-wavelength edge. The Kerr nonlinear-product power also increases by about 30 dB between one span and 7500 km. These results demonstrate the potential of the proposed architecture for span-end loss compensation, while showing that gain flattening, multi-channel optimization, system-level nonlinear analysis, and experimental validation are required before practical deployment.</jats:p>

journal: Strojniški vestnik - Journal of Mechanical Engineering
abstract: <jats:p>Reliable process monitoring is critical for advancing laser powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), as it provides the process information required for corrective control actions to prevent defects such as lack-of-fusion and keyhole porosity. A promising approach for PBF-LB/M process monitoring is coaxial measurement of light emitted from the meltpool area. More than two hundred research studies on coaxial monitoring of the meltpool have been performed, but there is still no validated and reliable method for measuring a suitable variable that could be directly used as an input for high-resolution control of the PBF-LB/M process, enabling process parameters such as laser power and scan speed to be dynamically adjusted not only at the part level, but locally for individual micrometer-scale segments along the scan track. This work reviews existing research studies on coaxial meltpool monitoring and identifies potential future research and development directions toward a standard and reliable meltpool monitoring method. Meltpool depth is identified as a particularly promising control-relevant variable. With the ability to monitor and control meltpool depth, it is possible to avoid undesirable process conditions due to too high or too low energy input, which would result in defects like keyhole porosity or lack-of-fusion. However, only five studies have attempted to estimate the melt pool depth coaxially during the PBF-LB/M process. Despite these attempts, there is no sufficiently validated method for high-resolution coaxial monitoring of meltpool depth in PBF-LB/M. The potential solution seems to be in combining concepts and recent discoveries from two-color coaxial camera- and photodiode-based meltpool area monitoring approaches. Based on the existing literature and hands-on experiences with establishing and working with coaxial monitoring systems, this work also provides guidelines and lists the most common challenges for implementing coaxial monitoring of the meltpool in the PBF-LB/M process.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>Enhancing volume increased relative to baseline in 48% of patients (n = 10) at 2 weeks and 57% (n = 12) at 6 weeks, before declining to only 10% (n = 2) by 12 months. In comparison, FLAIR volume increases were only observed in 33% (n = 7) at 2 weeks, falling to 19% (n = 4) at 6 weeks and 3 months, 14% (n = 3) at 6 months, and 0% at 12 months. Pathology, ongoing systemic therapy, lesion size, and LITT energy delivered were not significantly associated with enhancing or FLAIR volume trajectories. Decreased FLAIR volume was significantly more common in RN than in PD (71% vs. 14%, p = 0.049) only at 12 months.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Perilesional edema changes post-LITT were not reflective of enhancing lesion dynamics in this study. Notably, increased edema post-LITT was observed in only one-third of patients at 2 weeks and only 20% at 6 weeks. abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) uses controlled hyperthermia to ablate tumor tissue. A recent phase II trial found low-dose doxorubicin after LITT improved survival, but systemic toxicity and poor CNS penetration limit clinical benefit. We investigated Lyso-Thermosensitive Liposomal Doxorubicin (LTLD) for targeted CNS chemotherapy during LITT, hypothesizing that heat-triggered release above 41.5 °C, guided by MRI thermography, would enable predictable spatiotemporal control of drug delivery with high local concentrations and minimal systemic toxicity. U87 gliomas were induced in immunosuppressed Yucatan minipigs and ablated via commercial LITT following LTLD infusion (50 mg/m²). Pixel-wise time-temperature data were translated in real time into spatial drug concentration maps using known LTLD pharmacodynamics, validated against quantitative fluorescence imaging and MALDI mass spectrometry. Animals were sacrificed immediately or at 14 days for drug release and neurotoxicity assessment. The algorithm enabled real-time spatial prediction of drug distribution and concentration, validated by quantitative ex-vivo tissue analysis. LITT + LTLD extended the effective treatment zone by 1.5-2x, with peri-ablative doxorubicin concentrations exceeding 20× the minimum cytotoxic threshold. No systemic or neurological toxicity was observed over 14 days, and surveillance MRI showed no additional cerebral edema versus LITT alone. Intraoperative imaging visualized drug release at wide-field and cellular scales. LITT-mediated heat-triggered LTLD release enables safe, targeted CNS drug delivery, overcoming limitations of conventional doxorubicin. Real-time predictive drug mapping provides intraoperative guidance to maximize therapeutic coverage. Combined with LTLD’s established systemic safety profile, these findings support rapid clinical translation. Ongoing studies will refine thermal dosing across ablative and sub-ablative temperature zones.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Subcortical glioblastomas present surgical challenges owing to their proximity to critical anatomy. Here, we assessed the utility of Laser interstitial thermal therapy(LITT) in the management of subcortical glioblastomas. Clinical outcomes were evaluated in 80 consecutive patients with subcortical glioblastoma (isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) wild-type, H3K27 non-mutant) treated surgically between 2017 and 2025. During this time period, LITT was increasingly incorporated into stereotactic needle biopsy (SNB) and surgical resection (SR) workflows, enabling comparisons between SNB versus SNB+LITT and between surgical resection (SR) only versus planned subtotal resection (STR)+LITT. Among 46 treatments involving SNB, 24 underwent SNB only and 22 SNB+LITT. Lesion size was similar between these groups (1.72±0.38 vs 1.92±0.36 cm, p = 0.07), with comparable procedural morbidity (4.2% vs 4.5%, p = 1.0). In newly diagnosed glioblastoma, SNB+LITT was associated with improved overall survival compared with SNB alone (median 375 vs 162 days, p = 0.0012). Thirty-four patients underwent resections (18 SR, 16 STR+LITT). Lesion size was comparable between these cohorts (3.77±0.68 vs 3.74±0.83 cm, p = 0.9) as was the extent of cytoreduction (77.8% vs 93.8%, p = 0.34). But, STR+LITT was associated with fewer permanent postoperative deficits (0% vs 27.8%, p = 0.047). Survival did not differ between STR+LITT and SR (median 368 vs 289 days, p = 0.43). Across all patients, postoperative motor deficits were associated with worse survival (112 vs 254 days, p &lt; 0.001). Our results support incorporating LITT as a staged procedure into planned STR or in conjunction with SNB in the management of subcortical glioblastoma. Post-operative motor deficit is associated with poor survival outcomes.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Early detection of heat stress in intensive pig production is critical for maintaining animal welfare and production efficiency; however, routine rectal thermometry is labor-intensive and impractical under farm conditions. This study aimed to evaluate the reliability and agreement of non-contact temperature measurement methods—digital laser thermometry and infrared thermography (IRT)—against rectal core temperature on a commercial farm. Measurements were performed at multiple anatomical sites (ear, flank, labial, and rectal surface regions), and data were analyzed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Bland–Altman methods. Traditional handheld infrared measurements showed poor reliability (ICC: 0.09–0.27) and substantially underestimated core temperature (−1.16 to −2.27 °C), with wide limits of agreement. In contrast, IRT demonstrated higher but imprecisely estimated reliability (ICC: 0.56–0.67; labial region: 95% CI 0.19–0.76; rectal region: 95% CI 0.41–0.82), lower bias (−0.37 to −0.59 °C), and narrower agreement intervals. However, significant proportional bias (p < 0.001) indicated temperature-dependent deviations between methods. Closer agreement with rectal temperature was observed for infrared thermography than for handheld infrared thermometry, particularly at the labial and perianal measurement sites.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study proposes a framework for automatically generating 3D structural as-built models of aging buildings by predicting the structural dimensions of members concealed behind finishes using laser scanning and machine learning, particularly when original construction drawings are unavailable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Laser scanning captures building geometry but includes both structural components and non-structural finishes (e.g. plaster), making it unsuitable for directly extracting structural dimensions. To address this, the proposed framework extracts geometric features from point clouds and employs machine learning techniques to predict structural dimensions of columns, beams, walls and slabs. Six machine learning models – Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Linear Regression and Support Vector Regression (SVR) – were trained using data collected on 1,560 column elements, 2,875 beam elements, 870 wall elements and 148 slab elements across 50 buildings and validated through two real-world case studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The best-performing model achieved MAPE of 10.51% for column width (95%CI: 8.47–12.71), 12.98% for column depth (95% CI: 10.86–15.41), 14.91% for beam width (95% CI: 13.63–16.15), 18.91% for beam depth (95% CI: 17.94–19.90), 10.42% for walls (95% CI: 8.89–12.00) and 10.70% for slabs (95% CI: 7.11–14.50). The predicted dimensions enabled reconstruction of 3D structural as-built models without relying on original drawings; the estimates are intended for planning-stage use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework provides a non-destructive, full-coverage estimate of structural member dimensions that would otherwise require original drawings or local removal of finishes. In practice, it is intended to reduce reliance on destructive investigation and, through the SHAP analysis, indicates where confirmatory openings could be prioritized, thereby supporting planning-stage decisions for the maintenance and retrofitting of buildings whose drawings are missing or outdated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study is among the first to formulate the discrepancy between laser-scanned surface geometry and concealed structural dimensions as a prediction problem and to propose a framework that returns the predicted dimensions to a 3D structural as-built model. Machine learning provides the enabling component, and explainability is used to direct in situ verification rather than as a methodological contribution in itself.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>SUMMARY</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ground-shaking site effects, which are anomalous earthquake ground motions at the Earth’s surface, are caused by the generation of specific wavefields in specific near-surface structures. The best known are effects in surface sedimentary layers, sedimentary basins and valleys, which are related to wave trapping in softer materials. To a lesser degree, topographic effects, associated with irregular surface geometry and often also with collocated softer or cracked material, have also received much attention and gave rise to specific provisions in some building codes (e.g., EC8). By contrast, site effects related to sharp lateral boundaries between media with very different stiffness have been much less investigated, despite consistent macroseismic observations of a significant increase in damage intensity on “stripes” located along strong lateral discontinuities. In this study we consider a semi-infinite layer as a canonical model for many real situations with sediments relatively sharply laterally bounded or with abrupt change of sediment thickness. We investigate numerically simulated particle velocity, rate of rotational motion and rate of axial strain for the vertically incident SH, SV and P waves. We use a novel type of characterization of transfer properties – time-frequency transfer functions for the particle velocity and rates of rotational motion and axial strain. We found that the rates of rotational motion and axial strain display sharp peaks at the lateral discontinuity mainly in the case of the incident SV and P waves. Particle-velocity components exhibit a maximum close to the discontinuity, but at variable distances depending on central frequency and incident wave type (“basin-edge” effect). At larger distances from the discontinuity, the decay of rotational motion and axial strain is controlled by the attenuation in sediments. The sharp peaks of the rates of rotational motion and axial strain across the lateral discontinuity, together with the well-known basin-edge effects for translational motion, are found to be the key site effects of the laterally bounded sedimentary layer.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most aggressive and treatment-resistant primary brain tumors, with limited therapeutic options and poor patient outcomes. Radiotherapy is a cornerstone of GBM management, and the recent clinical adoption of tile-based radiation therapy (TBRT), in which implantable cesium-131-embedded collagen tiles placed at resection sites, has enabled localized, sustained radiation delivery to the tumor bed. Limited accessibility, poor compatibility, and lack of precise dose control at small scales limit the ability to replicate clinically relevant radiation conditions in controlled lab settings. In addition, studying the effects of these tiles in vitro is important for validating and better understanding their therapeutic potential observed in vivo.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>To address this gap, we developed a novel in vitro platform integrating tile-based radiation therapy with organotypic brain slice cultures (OBSC) and standard plate-based cell cultures to study dose-dependent radiation effects in GBM cells. GBM cell lines were cultured within physiologically relevant microenvironments and exposed to localized continuous radiation that closely mimics clinically relevant brachytherapy conditions. This system enables precise modulation of radiation dose and spatial distribution while preserving critical cell-microenvironment interactions.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Our findings demonstrate a robust and quantifiable radiation response in GBM cells following TBRT exposure. Specifically, we observed a marked increase in phosphorylated H2AX (γ-H2AX), a sensitive marker of DNA double-strand breaks, in a time- and dose-dependent manner. This response was consistent across varying radiation doses in various cell lines, both in vitro and on organotypic brain slice cultures.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Importantly, this in vitro TBRT-OBSC model serves as a translational bridge between conventional radiation studies and clinical applications. By incorporating a clinically relevant radiation modality already used in GBM patients, this platform enhances the predictive value of preclinical studies for brachytherapy. Overall, our approach provides a powerful tool for evaluating radiation dose effects to advance precision radiotherapy research in GBM.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most therapy-resistant brain malignancies, with recurrence driven by adaptive responses to treatment and dynamic interactions within the brain microenvironment. Although radiotherapy is a cornerstone of the GBM treatment, how repeated radiation exposure reshapes therapeutic response within astrocyte-rich tumor niches, such as the invasive tumor front, remains poorly understood.                   <jats:p>Co-cultures were exposed to a clinically relevant fractionated radiation regimen consisting of 2 Gy daily × 5 days per cycle, recovery for 2 days post-radiation, for three cycles. This was followed by screening against a panel of 12 clinically relevant and investigational compounds targeting DNA damage, receptor tyrosine kinases, and nuclear export.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Pre-radiation, we noted that the presence of even 10% astrocytes within the co-culture significantly reduced drug sensitivity of GBM cells across multiple compounds, with significant upward shifts in dose-response curves, supporting astrocyte-induced therapeutic resistance. Following radiation, direct GBM-astrocyte co-cultures demonstrated drug-specific and cycle-dependent remodeling of therapeutic response. Standard-of-care Temozolomide remained ineffective, showing persistent resistance after radiation cycles. In contrast, targeted agents displayed heterogeneous adaptive responses. Afatinib and Crenolanib demonstrated transient sensitization following early radiation cycles, particularly in HW1 co-cultures, while Altiratinib sensitivity remained unchanged across conditions. Most notably, Selinexor demonstrated the most robust and sustained induced sensitivity following radiation despite baseline astrocyte-mediated resistance. This vulnerability emerged after a single radiation cycle in HW1 co-cultures.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Collectively, our findings suggest findings demonstrate that repeated radiation does not uniformly promote resistance, but dynamically reshapes drug response in a cycle- and drug-dependent manner within astrocyte-rich GBM niches, revealing actionable vulnerabilities that may inform rational therapeutic sequencing in recurrent disease.</jats:p>

title: Three-Year Polymerase Chain Reaction-Based Surveillance of Respiratory Tract Infections in Adults and Seasonal Patterns
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Objective: This study investigated the aetiological composition, seasonal variation and risk factors of adult respiratory tract infections in Ganzhou, Jiangxi Province, during 2023–2025. Methods: A total of 8,493 adults (≥18 years) with respiratory symptoms were enrolled from a tertiary hospital during 2023–2025. Oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal swabs were tested using multiplex real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) panels targeting six categories of seven respiratory pathogens: influenza A and B viruses, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), parainfluenza virus types I and III, adenovirus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Mixed infections (two or more pathogens) were reported separately. Data were analysed by univariate analysis and multivariate logistic regression. Results: The overall pathogen detection rate was 4.14% (352/8,493), comprising 325 single infections (92.33%) and 27 mixed infections (7.67%). Among single infections, M. pneumoniae (39.69%), influenza A virus (28.00%) and RSV (16.00%) predominated. Infections peaked in winter–spring (December–March). Age ≥65 years (OR = 2.35, 95% CI: 1.78–3.09), underlying diseases (OR = 2.41, 95% CI: 1.89–3.08) and emergency department admission (OR = 1.58, 95% CI: 1.24–2.01) were independent risk factors. Conclusion: Adult respiratory infections in Ganzhou show clear winter–spring seasonality, with M. pneumoniae, influenza A virus and RSV as leading pathogens. These findings support seasonally targeted surveillance – with enhanced monitoring for M. pneumoniae and influenza during winter–spring months – and prioritised vaccination, expanded diagnostic panels and early PCR-based diagnosis for adults aged ≥65 years and those with underlying diseases, thereby strengthening local respiratory infection prevention and control strategies.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Urban digitalization requires site-specific evidence to determine where intelligent sensing, edge processing, warning actuation and energy management functions are justified. This repeated cross-sectional field study quantified changes in smartphone-related behaviour and electrified micromobility at an unsignalized roundabout in Kielce, Poland, and translated them into technical requirements and an energy budget for a privacy-preserving, energy-aware crossing infrastructure. Two observers recorded 27,487 crossing-area users in 1728 arm-specific five-minute intervals during 18 standardized two-hour sessions in 2023–2025. Any phone use increased from 41.87% to 48.63% (difference 6.76 percentage points, 95% CI 5.31–8.20; Cohen’s h = 0.14), and a combined electric micromobility exposure indicator increased from 11.84% to 22.39% (h = 0.28), while bicycle prevalence remained near 8%. The phone-use trend was robust to the clustering of observations: session-clustered logistic regression, a random-intercept model and an exact stratified permutation test using the 18 sessions as independent units (p < 0.001) gave consistent results, and a composition analysis showed that the trend was not explained by the growing share of micromobility users. The effects are small in standardized terms but correspond to approximately 120 additional phone-engaged users per hour at peak volumes. The framework specifies homography-based trajectory prediction, time-to-collision conflict detection, a logistic risk score with data-driven threshold selection, k-anonymous aggregate data release and a staged validation plan with key performance indicators. A field-calibrated, state-based energy budget estimated 0.63–0.73 kWh/day for event-based operation of a four-approach edge node, 28–42% less than presence-activated and 60–65% less than continuously active operation. Transport-energy savings cannot be inferred because trip distances and displaced modes were not observed.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>For decades, research has shown what children need to grow up healthy and well, reiterating what families have always known: Children need consistent, warm, and responsive caregivers. Children also need access to quality, unbiased health care; socioeconomic security that can facilitate stable housing, nutritious food, and well-resourced, safe communities; and quality education, particularly early education. These critical areas of well-being are interrelated and intertwined in their impact on children’s development and learning. And the conditions to nurture each area are not—nor have ever been—evenly or fairly accessible across sociodemographic groups. This chapter focuses on these issues and the urgency to create educational and social contexts that can promote just futures for young children, especially those from historically marginalized communities</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sunspot decay is a fundamental and debated topic in solar physics. Numerical simulations suggest that enhanced convection beneath sunspots drives their decay, yet direct observational evidence is still lacking. Using Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO)/Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) data, we analyze the decay of eight sunspots associated with strong light bridge (LB) formation, covering 48 hr before, during, and 24 hr after the LB splits the umbra. The sunspot area exhibits three distinct decay modes: (1) immediate acceleration at the initial emergence of the LB (5/8), (2) delayed rapid decay after the LB completely splits the umbra (2/8), and (3) temporary deceleration after the umbra is completely split (1/8). In contrast, magnetic flux decay shows a uniform but weak acceleration in all eight cases, insufficient for the same classification. This asymmetry indicates that area and magnetic flux respond differently to LB formation. Moreover, area and flux decay initiates before LB formation, suggesting that LBs are a manifestation of ongoing decay rather than its trigger. The coexistence of distinct area decay modes and a uniform magnetic flux response indicates that the influence of LB formation on sunspot decay is not uniform across events. Our findings provide observational constraints for future simulations and raise questions about the reliability of LBs as tracers of subphotospheric activity.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive and lethal primary brain tumor in adults. Despite aggressive standard-of-care treatment including surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, GBM has a median survival of just nine months after diagnosis. A primary driver of mortality in GBM is resistance to radiation and chemotherapy. This resistance is mediated by a subpopulation of cells known as glioblastoma stem-like cells (GSCs). GSCs are capable of tumor propagation, survival under harsh microenvironmental conditions, and promotion of therapeutic resistance. However, the role of the neural microenvironment in supporting these effects remains incompletely understood. Astrocytes, the most abundant glial cell in the brain, are closely associated with GSCs. Astrocytes promote GSC migration by expressing chemoattracts, such as GBNF, and support stemness through signaling pathways including the SPP1-CD44 axis. Here, we investigate how varying proportions of co-cultured astrocytes influence the GSC state, therapeutic resistance, and ultimately disease recurrence using single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). Patient-derived GSCs (3691) and primary human astrocytes (mid-passage) were cultured in both mono- and co-culture conditions at three astrocyte:GSC ratios: 10:90, 50:50, and 90:10. Cultures were analyzed with and without exposure to fractionated irradiation (2 Gy / day for 5 days). Approximately 100,000 nuclei were isolated and fixed across the 10 experimental conditions and submitted for snRNA-seq using the Parse Evercode Whole Transcriptome kit. Preliminary analysis demonstrates that GSC transcriptional programs primarily vary as a function of astrocyte co-culture condition, indicating that astrocyte abundance influences GSC cell state. In contrast, astrocyte transcriptional profiles segregate primarily by irradiation status, consistent with a distinct radiation-responsive program in the astrocyte compartment. These findings support a model in which astrocytes modulate GSC transcriptional states, while independently mounting irradiation-associated responses within the tumor microenvironment. Further analyses will identify the molecular basis of the radiated astrocyte-GSC crosstalk underlying the promotion of the malignant state in GBM.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>The role of the Hall effect in fast magnetic reconnection (MR) in the presence of plasma instabilities remains poorly understood, particularly how guide fields influence the Hall-field evolution and the fast MR mechanism when tearing instability develops. Using 2.5D particle-in-cell MR simulations with Harris current sheets across varying guide-field strengths, we find that the primary MR transitions from an initial slow laminar MR phase to a nonlinear fast spontaneous MR (SMR) phase. Our results demonstrate that increasing the guide field reduces the rates of both the tearing growth and the primary MR. In the weak guide-field regime (Bg/B0≤1.0), the primary Hall magnetic field couples with those of local SMRs, producing a distorted Hall magnetic structure. In the strong guide-field regime (Bg/B0&gt;1.0), the coupled Hall magnetic field weakens progressively; however, the localized Hall signatures sustain fast SMRs until they are strongly attenuated at Bg/B0=5.0. Using the electron agyrotropy indicator Ag by Che et al., [Phys. Plasmas 25, 032101 (2018)], we identify electron diffusion regions and further discover that the mechanism breaking the electron frozen-in condition in the weak guide-field regime is primarily governed by the agyrotropic electron pressure term. However, with the guide field increased to Bg/B0=1.0 and 2.0, the convective electron inertia becomes significant as the magnetic null point separates from the flow stagnation point and electron inflow asymmetry leads to a finite electron flow velocity at the magnetic null point, revealing a distinct electron dynamics operating in tearing-driven guide-field MR.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Motivation</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Enzymes catalyse most of the metabolic reactions in living organisms. The functional characterization of enzymes is critical to understand the metabolic processes involved in different fields such as biotechnology, nutrition, ecology, and drug development. The Enzyme Commission (EC) numbers provide a hierarchical framework for classifying enzymatic reactions, linking gene and protein sequences to biochemical transformations. However, the incomplete annotation of biochemical reaction databases limits the accurate representation of metabolism of living organisms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To address this gap, several computational methods have been developed to predict EC numbers from reaction chemical structures, broadly classified into reaction similarity-based and machine/deep learning approaches. We systematically review these tools, comparing their performance predicting EC numbers from different databases, and assessing their robustness across enzyme classes. We also apply these methods to predict EC numbers from drug metabolism reactions, highlighting their potential to improve functional annotation of uncharacterized metabolic pathways.</jats:p>

title: Acute diarrhea following the first subcutaneous dose of tafolecimab: a case report of a probable adverse drug reaction

affiliation.name: Department of Cardiology, Beijing Anzhen Nanchong Hospital, Capital Medical University and Nanchong Central Hospital

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Tafolecimab is a fully human monoclonal antibody targeting proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9). Diarrhea is a recognized adverse reaction, but detailed post-marketing case descriptions with clear timing, differential assessment, and outcome remain limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Case Summary</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 51-year-old man hospitalized for non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction received his first one-time 600-mg subcutaneous dose of tafolecimab (SINTBILO) at 15:14 on 13 July 2026. Approximately 7 h 46 min later, he developed abdominal pain and diarrhea occurring 5–8 times daily, with nausea and mild periumbilical pain but no fever, tenesmus, visible hematochezia or melena, dehydration, hypotension, rebound tenderness, or guarding. Stool testing showed loose yellow stool, positive occult blood and red blood cells, 0–1 white blood cells/high-power field, and a negative rotavirus test; electrolytes and liver and kidney function were normal. Stool culture and testing for Clostridioides difficile, norovirus, and adenovirus were not performed. Tafolecimab was not re-administered. After fluid replacement, montmorillonite, and loperamide hydrochloride, diarrhea decreased within 1 day and resolved after approximately 2 days, with no recurrence after discharge. Long-term stable acarbose therapy was continued without recurrence. The Naranjo score was 5, indicating a probable adverse drug reaction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This case supports probable tafolecimab-associated acute diarrhea. New-onset diarrhea after PCSK9 inhibitor initiation should prompt precise temporal documentation, medication reconciliation, targeted microbiological evaluation, and pharmacovigilance reporting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: TMIC-51 Radiation unmasks a GBM-intrinsic vulnerability to XPO1 inhibition modulated by dynamic astrocyte crosstalk

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common malignant primary brain tumor with near-universal recurrence despite aggressive treatment. Recurrence is driven by therapy-resistant states shaped by the tumor microenvironment, where astrocytes are abundant glial components. In a prior coculture drug screen, HW1 GBM cells were sensitive to selinexor (an XPO1 inhibitor), but astrocyte incorporation reduced this sensitivity, while coculture radiation restored and enhanced selinexor sensitivity, suggesting a radiation-induced collateral vulnerability to XPO1 inhibition. Here, we asked whether this phenotype could be modeled genetically using lentiviral XPO1 knockdown. HW1 GBM cells and primary human astrocytes were transduced with one of three XPO1-targeting lentiviral shRNAs or a scramble control and evaluated under non-radiated and radiated conditions. Incucyte imaging measured longitudinal confluency and fluorescence intensity. To test whether astrocyte-derived soluble factors alter GBM growth, HW1 cells were exposed to conditioned media from non-radiated and radiated, transduced astrocytes and assessed by Incucyte confluency and CellTiter-Glo. Astrocyte-GBM transwell cocultures tested whether soluble factors in dynamic exchange recapitulated the coculture phenotype. Astrocytes tolerated XPO1 knockdown without affecting proliferation under either condition, indicating that astrocyte XPO1 inhibition is not overtly toxic. In contrast, HW1 GBM cells showed reduced proliferation following XPO1 knockdown, mirroring the selinexor phenotype, with a stronger effect after radiation. Transwell coculture recapitulated the astrocyte-mediated modulation of selinexor sensitivity, whereas conditioned media from XPO1-knockdown astrocytes did not consistently suppress HW1 growth, viability, or growth rate. Radiation reveals a GBM-intrinsic vulnerability to XPO1 inhibition that is recapitulated by genetic knockdown in HW1 cells alone. Astrocytes modulate this response through soluble factors requiring dynamic exchange, as the effect is preserved in transwell coculture but not transferred by static conditioned media, suggesting GBM-responsive astrocyte secretion rather than constitutive factors. Future studies will confirm XPO1 knockdown, distinguish slowed growth from cell death, and characterize the astrocyte-secreted factors driving this dynamic crosstalk.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Radiation necrosis, a delayed adverse effect of cranial irradiation, might appear clinically and radiographically as tumour recurrence. Because of its effect on vasogenic edema, bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody, is routinely used to treat symptomatic, steroid-resistant RN. However, discordance between neurologic function and imaging complicates diagnosis and treatment.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>We discuss the case of a 78-year-old male with a history of meningioma, who was treated with craniotomy followed by adjuvant proton beam radiation therapy. Approximately two years after radiotherapy, he had progressive weakness on the left side, gait instability, and cognitive loss. The MRI revealed progressive radiation necrosis, as well as interval expansion of the lateral and third ventricles. Bevacizumab was started to treat symptomatic radiation necrosis (RN), and an oncological examination revealed a low risk of tumor development due to anti-VEGF medication. However, despite the medication, the patient continued to undergo neurologic and functional decline, shifting from being ambulatory to bedbound and requiring lift help. This example highlights the limits of relying solely on radiographic responses to evaluate treatment efficacy in situations with radiation necrosis. Bevacizumab may reduce edema without addressing underlying structural damage to the white matter or aberrant cerebrospinal fluid flow. Patients who continue to deteriorate despite anti-VEGF medication should be evaluated for secondary hydrocephalus and other radiation-related delayed effects. Neuro-oncology, radiation oncology, and neurosurgery must work together to effectively manage and diagnose complex post-radiation circumstances.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Radiation and chemotherapy are standard treatments for most solid tumors and hematologic cancers and are associated with significant adverse effects in cancer patients and survivors. Patients treated for brain cancers, such as Glioblastoma (GBM), have been observed to experience severe cognitive decline as a result of radiation and chemotherapy. In order to examine the effects of radiation and chemotherapy at single cell resolution and predict potential treatments to mediate these effects, we examined longitudinal single-nuclei RNA sequencing data of paired tumors from 20 patients before and after treatment with TMZ and radiation. We found that following treatment, gene expression related to brain aging and Alzheimer’s-like phenotypes are enriched. Within specific cell populations, we found that oligodendrocytes show an increase in hypoxia and angiogenesis signatures, neurons show increased synaptic plasticity and synapse generation, and astrocytes show a reactive phenotype that may impair myelination. Using single-cell drug connectivity analysis (scFOCAL) we sought to prioritize compounds that may revert non-malignant cell transcriptional states towards their pre-treatment state in order to restore functionality. This technique identified a set of compounds as potential mediators of chemotherapy and radiation damage in the brain. These analyses suggest the potential utility of pharmacotranscriptomic approaches toward identifying actionable targets and drug candidates for the functional treatment of radiation and chemotherapy-induced neurotoxicity.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Papillary craniopharyngiomas are a rare suprasellar tumor, usually affecting adults, often arising from the pituitary stalk. Papillary craniopharyngioma is strongly associated with BRAF V600E mutation, enabling the use of targeted BRAF/MEK inhibition.                     <jats:p>In this retrospective, single institutional cohort study of six patients with papillary craniopharyngioma harboring BRAF V600E mutation treated with BRAF/MEK inhibitors (vemurafenib and cobimetinib) between 2023-2026, we evaluated clinical outcomes, including radiographic response, duration of response, and time to progression.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>MGMT promoter–unmethylated (MGMTu) glioblastoma remains one of the most challenging forms of the disease to treat, owing to its intrinsic resistance to the current standard‑of‑care therapy. Despite maximal surgical resection and concurrent chemoradiation, patients with unmethylated tumors experience early progression and markedly inferior survival, underscoring a critical unmet need for therapeutic strategies that can overcome this biologically entrenched resistance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RNA profiling of matched newly diagnosed/recurrent MGMTu glioblastoma samples, live cell imaging, characterization of extracellular vesicles (EVs), and molecular and cell biology techniques.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RNA profiling of matched pre‑ and post‑radiation clinical MGMTu glioblastoma specimens showed that, while most miRNAs were unchanged after treatment, a small subset, most notably miR‑603, was selectively reduced in the post‑radiation samples. Analysis of miR‑603 downstream targets revealed that miR‑603 suppresses the expression of insulin‑like growth factor 1 (IGF1) and the IGF1 receptor (IGF1R). Live‑cell imaging demonstrated that ionizing radiation (IR) induced miR-603 export via microvesicle release, and not through exosomes. This export derepressed IGF1 and IGF1R expression, promoting a cancer stem‑cell state and radiation resistance. Proteomic profiling of microvesicle‑associated proteins that bind miR‑603 identified annexin A2 (ANXA2), a protein recruited to IR‑damaged membranes to facilitate extrusion of injured membranes as microvesicles. Computation modeling and mutational analysis revealed ANXA2 tyrosine 23 (Y23) phosphorylation, required for its IR-induced localization to damaged membranes, is also essential for miR-603 binding. Phosphorylation of ANXA2 Y23 depends on IR-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) that activate SRC kinase through C185A and C245A sulfenylation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our findings showed that membrane‑repair–mediated microvesicle shedding and miR‑603 export operate as a coupled process that sustains the cancer stem‑cell state and reveals a therapeutically targetable vulnerability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Automated construction of chemical reaction networks is limited by the combinatorial growth of possible molecules, intermediates, and formal transformations. We present alchemy, an open-source Python workflow for systematic enumeration and interactive exploration of small-molecule radical reaction networks. Within an explicitly bounded graph space, alchemy generates connected, neutral C/N/H molecular graphs with single, double, or triple bonds and specified radical counts; RDKit sanitization and canonicalization then remove graph-invalid and duplicate records. Formal reaction candidates are constructed without learned reaction templates by combining bond-dissociation records into rearrangement and transfer stoichiometries. Parallel generation, persistent disk-backed storage, and Kuzu graph representation make the resulting formal network searchable. An independent brute-force control recovers exactly the same 416 neutral molecular graphs as alchemy in a three-heavy-atom C/N/H space. In a trimethylamine case study limited to at most five heavy atoms and one unpaired electron per reaction side, the workflow generated 41,735 unique molecular graphs and a seed-0 bounded sample of 60,035 first-generation reaction records. The reaction construction is not complete because high-frequency shared fragments are handled by a documented deterministic sampling cap. An optional PaiNN molecular-energy model is distributed with the software, but its closed-shell QM9 benchmark does not validate the open-shell species considered here, and its output is not used to rank, filter, or interpret the case-study records. Alchemy therefore, provides a reproducible route to bounded reaction-space construction and downstream graph inspection.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Radiation necrosis (RN) is a common complication of brain radiation. Many options are available to treat radiation necrosis including corticosteroids, boswellia, and bevacizumab. Bevacizumab has demonstrated significant efficacy in the treatment of RN.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical Case</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We present a case of a 68-year-old female with a germline BRCA1 mutation and history of resected stage II non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in 2003. In April 2020, she presented with repeated falls and found to have 4 cm mass in the left parietal lobe. Following gross total resection, pathology was consistent with metastatic NSCLC. She received adjuvant fractionated stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) to 30 Gy in 5 fractions, completed in May 2020. In July 2021, a new brain metastasis developed in the left temporal lobe, and was treated with Gamma Knife (GK) SRS (20 Gy prescribed to the 47% isodose line). At that time of the GK, increased enhancement was noted at the treated left parietal site. Serial MRI imaging with perfusion were performed and findings were consistent with RN. The patient was treated with 15 cycles of bevacizumab at 10 mg/kg from June 2022 through January 2023. MRI in March 2023 demonstrated near resolution of the left parietal enhancement. By May 2023, there was a return of notable enhancement. Further worsening enhancement and size was observed in January 2024 of both the left parietal and temporal areas. Despite these imaging findings, the patient remained clinically asymptomatic and elected to continue MRI surveillance without confirmatory lumbar puncture. An FDG PET/CT performed in November 2025 demonstrated no metabolic activity within either lesion, findings consistent with radiation necrosis rather than recurrent disease. The patient continues with MRI surveillance with no evidence of recurrence or symptoms, and no radiographic or clinical concern for carcinomatosis</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This case demonstrates a delayed rebound radiation necrosis mimicking leptomeningeal progression, with persistent imaging abnormalities over years of follow-up.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: IMG-75 SMART Syndrome: Delayed Radiation Neurotoxicity with Key Clinical and Radiologic Features for Early Recognition
