abstract: <jats:p>Fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensors are widely used for temperature monitoring because of their compact size, wavelength-encoded response, corrosion resistance, multiplexing capability, and immunity to electromagnetic interference. However, the accuracy of physics-based FBG models depends strongly on the thermal and optical parameters adopted in the simulation. This study developed a MATLAB-based physics-driven framework for calibrating the temperature response of a uniform silica FBG using particle swarm optimization (PSO). The model was formulated from the Bragg condition and incorporated temperature-dependent variations in effective refractive index and grating period through the thermo-optic and thermal-expansion coefficients. A published 17-point temperature–wavelength dataset spanning approximately 9.49–90.34 °C was digitized for model calibration and comparison. The extracted experimental sensitivity was 9.9450 pm/°C, compared with 10.13 pm/°C reported in the source study. The baseline model predicted a sensitivity of 14.1799 pm/°C, with RMSE, MAE, MAPE, and R² values of 0.20353 nm, 0.17446 nm, 43.90%, and 0.3151, respectively. Following PSO calibration, the predicted sensitivity decreased to 9.8888 pm/°C, differing by only 0.57% from the extracted experimental value. The calibrated model achieved an RMSE of 0.00521 nm, MAE of 0.00405 nm, MAPE of 1.38%, and R² of 0.99955. These results demonstrate that bounded PSO calibration can substantially improve agreement between a transparent physics-based FBG model and experimental data. Because the same dataset was used for parameter estimation and performance assessment, the results represent in-sample calibration performance rather than independent predictive validation.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Microfluidic stabilizers effectively suppress flow fluctuations and are, therefore, essential for peristaltic pump-driven microfluidic systems and high-precision instrumentation. Air-chamber-based passive microfluidic stabilizers are structurally simple, but their performance depends on multiple geometric parameters, making customized design challenging. To address these issues, this study proposes a particle-swarm-optimization-based optimization strategy to engineer the key structural parameters of a microfluidic stabilizer according to specific demands. A theoretical dynamic model is established to elucidate the stabilization mechanism and identify the key parameters governing device performance. Global optimization of the geometric parameters is then performed using particle swarm optimization, yielding an improved design with enhanced stabilization capability and practical manufacturability. The optimized device was fabricated and evaluated through instantaneous flow measurements at different flow rates and in intracranial pressure drainage simulations and droplet generation experiments. The results show that over the tested wide flow-rate range, the device achieves a flow pulsation suppression rate of more than 95%, reduces the flow fluctuation rate to less than 0.2%, and effectively attenuates pulsations above 0.1 Hz. These results confirm that the proposed optimization strategy effectively improves both stabilization performance and manufacturability, providing a complete design framework that integrates theoretical modeling, particle swarm optimization-based global optimization, and experimental validation for the rapid development of customized microfluidic stabilizers.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:p>
                    X-ray single particle imaging (SPI) offers the potential to visualize the structures of biomolecules at near-atomic resolution. However, current structural determination at X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) is limited to moderate resolution, primarily due to background scattering. Here, we propose a modified SPI technique based on holographic enhancement from a strongly scattering 2D crystal lattice placed near the object. The lattice Bragg peaks act as a structured reference, converting the weak object signal into measurable intensity modulations above the noise in the background and enabling structure retrieval. Numerical simulations, with a custom reconstruction algorithm, show high-fidelity reconstructions even when the background is up to 10
                    <jats:sup>5</jats:sup>
                    times stronger than the signal. These simulations establish periodic crystalline references as a route toward background-tolerant fixed-target SPI and motivate their development for synchrotron sources.
                  </jats:p>

title: Mesenchymal Stromal Cell Therapy for Acute Graft-Versus-Host Disease: Timing, Disease Context, and Biomarkers as Determinants of Clinical Response
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose of Review</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is a therapy for hematological malignancies and inherited disorders. However, graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) have emerged as a cellular therapy because of their immunomodulatory and tissue-repair properties, although clinical responses have been inconsistent. This review examines evidence supporting MSC use for GVHD, focusing on treatment timing, disease stage and severity, patient characteristics, MSC product properties, and biomarkers predicting response.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Recent Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>MSCs modulate innate and adaptive immunity, including T cells, B cells, natural killer cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages, through paracrine mediators, extracellular vesicles, and cell-cell interactions. Clinical studies have reported activity in GVHD prophylaxis and treatment, particularly in selected patients with steroid-refractory acute GVHD (SR-aGVHD), whereas randomized studies have not consistently demonstrated benefit across unselected populations. The clinical development of remestemcel-L provided important translational evidence, culminating in FDA approval of remestemcel-L-rknd (Ryoncil) in December 2024 for pediatric patients aged 2 months and older with SR-aGVHD, the first FDA-approved MSC-based therapy for GVHD. Biomarkers including ST2, REG3α, elafin, CXCL10, IL-7, FGFR1, and immune-cell phenotypes may aid risk stratification and treatment monitoring.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Summary</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Evidence supports a context-dependent model of MSC efficacy rather than a uniform therapeutic effect. Clinical activity may depend on disease stage, inflammatory burden, patient characteristics, MSC source and quality, dosing, and timing. Future studies should clarify which patients benefit, when treatment should be administered, and which cellular or molecular characteristics predict response.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: ANGI-09 Model-defined pharmacology identifies steroid-sparing potential of plasma kallikrein inhibition in peritumoral brain edema and informs personalized treatment strategy

affiliation.name: Rezolute , Bend,

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Peritumoral brain edema (PTBE) is managed primarily with dexamethasone, which imposes dose-limiting toxicity and potentially steroid dependence. The role of plasma kallikrein signaling in PTBE remains poorly defined, and no mechanistic framework currently exists to predict whether plasma kallikrein inhibition (PKI) could achieve steroid-sparing edema control. A four-module ordinary differential equation framework was constructed from published rate constants, receptor pharmacology, and DCE-MRI permeability data. The framework integrated kallikrein cascade kinetics, dual-pathway kinin receptor signaling, tumor-class permeability decomposition (structural, VEGF, bradykinin, and cross-talk fractions), and Starling-based fluid accumulation with capacity-limited drainage. The framework was used to generate quantitative predictions for steroid-sparing thresholds, treatment-duration requirements, post-cessation durability, and tumor-class–specific edema-resolution kinetics. The model identified a steroid-sparing threshold: the minimum bradykinin-driven permeability fraction at which plasma kallikrein inhibition maintained edema below the dexamethasone baseline. The nominal threshold was 30%, with a full range of 14–52% across all 81 parameterizations. The bradykinin receptor B1R, which is transcriptionally induced by inflammation, does not undergo agonist-induced desensitization, and drives its own expression through NF-κB positive feedback, emerged as the dominant modeled chronic permeability driver. The framework generated four testable clinical predictions: dexamethasone taper without PKI produces rebound; PKI enables steroid discontinuation above the bradykinin threshold; no rebound occurs during PKI treatment; and edema control persists after PKI cessation due to treatment-induced B1R receptor depletion predicted from published receptor turnover kinetics. Residual Ktrans following bevacizumab exposure may identify patients most likely to benefit from PKI, while tumor class informs expected edema-resolution kinetics. A bridge-and-sustain protocol emerged from the exposure/response analysis: dexamethasone for rapid edema reduction and PKI for sustained maintenance. This model-defined pharmacology approach translates first-principles mechanistic biology into a personalized treatment framework for PTBE, enabling patient-specific prediction of steroid-sparing potential and individualized edema-management strategies for primary and metastatic brain tumors.</jats:p>

title: Cuproptosis in the tumor microenvironment: metabolic–immune regulatory mechanisms and therapeutic potential

abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Copper is an essential trace element involved in mitochondrial respiration, redox homeostasis, and numerous enzymatic reactions. Recent studies across multiple cancers have reported changes in tissue copper levels, circulating copper-related indicators, and networks governing copper uptake, transport, and efflux. The discovery of cuproptosis, a copper-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by mitochondrial metabolism, further linked copper homeostasis to cell death regulation. Its key molecular features include copper binding to lipoylated tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle proteins, aggregation of lipoylated proteins, loss of iron–sulfur cluster proteins, and proteotoxic stress. Within the tumor microenvironment, heterogeneity in copper uptake and export, TCA cycle activity, ferredoxin 1 (FDX1) function, protein lipoylation, and redox buffering collectively shapes cuproptosis susceptibility, which cannot be reliably predicted by tissue copper content or a single metabolic phenotype alone. Preclinical studies of cuproptosis-inducing interventions have also reported damage-associated molecular pattern release, dendritic cell maturation, CD8
                    <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                    T-cell infiltration, and myeloid-cell remodeling; however, these effects often coexist with oxidative stress, other forms of cell death, or multimodal therapies, and their mechanistic specificity for cuproptosis remains variable. This review examines cuproptosis from a tumor microenvironment perspective by integrating clinical and molecular evidence of altered copper homeostasis, defining the boundaries among copper dysregulation, general copper-related cytotoxicity, and cuproptosis, and discussing how copper availability, the FDX1–protein lipoylation axis, mitochondrial metabolic states, and microenvironmental adaptation influence susceptibility. We further evaluate immune effects according to the strength of available evidence and summarize therapeutic strategies involving copper ionophores, copper-homeostasis modulation, metabolic sensitization, nanodelivery, and combination immunotherapy. This framework clarifies the relationships among copper homeostasis, tumor metabolism, cuproptosis susceptibility, and immune responses, while highlighting priorities for mechanistic investigation and therapeutic translation.
                  </jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>We develop a kinetic model of electron–ion inverse bremsstrahlung absorption in magnetized fusion plasmas that extends the conventional constant-Coulomb-logarithm treatment. The model incorporates the velocity dependence of the Coulomb logarithm and plasma screening directly into the electron–ion collision frequency, while a super-Gaussian electron distribution is used to account for non-Maxwellian distortions. The formulation explicitly retains magnetization and circular-polarization effects and yields asymptotic scaling laws for magneto-inertial fusion (MIF) plasmas and microwave-heated magnetically confined plasmas. The results show that the velocity-dependent Coulomb logarithm can either reduce or enhance absorption depending on the electron distribution, whereas plasma screening systematically suppresses it. Under the conditions studied, the complete collisional model changes the MIF absorption rate by about 19% relative to the thermal-logarithm approximation. In the microwave-heated regime, the corresponding reduction is about 6% over the whole density range considered. These results highlight the need to treat non-Maxwellianity, velocity-dependent collisions, and plasma screening self-consistently when modeling inverse bremsstrahlung absorption in magnetized fusion plasmas.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Glioblastoma (GBM) exhibits a complex regulatory landscape that drives its cellular heterogeneity, plasticity, and therapeutic resistance—features not fully explained by genetic alterations alone. Chromatin profiling is therefore essential to uncover the epigenetic mechanisms that encode tumor cell identity, enable state transitions, and reveal potential therapeutic vulnerabilities. Here, we implement Droplet Paired-Tag (DpT) to perform simultaneous single-cell CUT&Tag and transcriptomic profiling in GBM samples with the objective to establish a multimodal framework to define epigenetic heterogeneity and its relationship to malignant cell states in GBM. IDH-wildtype tumors from primary resections were profiled using DpT alongside complementary single-cell and spatial modalities including scRNA-seq, 10X Multiome (RNA+ATAC), and whole-transcriptome Stereo-seq. We profiled over 20,000 cells and integrated transcriptional programs with five key histone modifications marking active (H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K4me3) and repressive (H3K27me3, H3K9me3) chromatin. Using RNA-anchored and unbiased approaches, we explored combinatorial chromatin states underlying canonical GBM cell identities and assessed coordinated regulatory programs across modalities. Active chromatin landscapes were broadly conserved across malignant cell states, and repressive chromatin—particularly Polycomb-associated domains—showed evidence of dynamic remodeling, suggesting a role for repression in shaping cell identity and plasticity. Integration with spatial transcriptomics further enabled mapping of these regulatory states within the tumor microenvironment. Together, these results establish a spatially resolved, multimodal framework of chromatin regulation in GBM and demonstrate that malignant cell states are encoded by layered chromatin architecture rather than transcription alone.</jats:p>

title: Palmitoylation of Smad2 assists TGFβ-Smad signaling to promote breast cancer metastasis
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Although the role of palmitic acid (PA) as a membrane component in promoting cancer invasion and migration has been explored, it remains unclear whether and how PA enhances breast cancer metastasis via palmitoylation modification. Here, we observed that PA promotes epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), invasion, and migration in breast cancer cells, which could be antagonized by the palmitoyl-transferase inhibitor 2-bromopalmitate (2-BP) through regulating TGFβ-Smad pathway. Specifically, we screened and identified that Smad2 undergoes ZDHHC7-mediated palmitoylation, which stabilizes Smad2 protein, enhances Smad2/Smad3 interaction, and promotes their binding to DNA elements following TGFβ stimulation, thereby promoting EMT. Consequently, ZDHHC7 enhanced breast cancer cell migration, and its depletion effectively suppressed breast cancer lung metastasis. Based on these findings, we generated cell-penetrating peptides to block Smad2 palmitoylation, resulting in disrupting its interaction with Smad3, and in turn attenuate breast cancer EMT, invasion, and migration in cells and in orthotopic mouse models. In summary, our study reveals a novel mechanism by which PA promotes breast cancer metastasis through ZDHHC7-mediated palmitoylation of Smad2, and proposes a therapeutic strategy to inhibit breast cancer lung metastasis by using a specific peptide targeting this modification.</jats:p>

title: PLASMA RICO EN PLAQUETAS ACTIVADO COMO ADYUVANTE A LA DILATACIÓN ENDOSCÓPICA EN ESTENOSIS ESOFÁGICAS BENIGNAS

abstract:
<jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Introducción:</jats:bold>
                    Las estenosis esofágicas benignas pueden recurrir tras la dilatación endoscópica por inflamación y remodelación fibrótica, condicionando nuevas sesiones. El plasma rico en plaquetas (PRP) aporta mediadores de reparación tisular y podría modular la cicatrización esofágica.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Objetivos:</jats:bold>
                    Describir factibilidad técnica, eventos adversos y evolución clínica y endoscópica tras dilatación con Savary-Gilliard sobre guía Savary e infiltración submucosa de PRP autólogo activado con gluconato de calcio al 10%.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Métodos:</jats:bold>
                    Estudio observacional retrospectivo, descriptivo y unicéntrico de cinco adultos con estenosis benignas: tres pépticas, una cáustica y una postquirúrgica por ascenso gástrico secundario a estenosis cáustica. La dilatación se realizó con Savary-Gilliard sobre guía Savary. El PRP se obtuvo de 20 mL de sangre citratada mediante doble centrifugación (1500 rpm/8 min y 2500 rpm/5 min); se recuperaron 8 mL, activados con 0,20 mL de gluconato de calcio al 10% e infiltrados submucosamente en cuatro cuadrantes post dialtacion. Se evaluaron disfagia (Mellow-Pinkas), número de dilataciones, cicatrización endoscópica a 8 semanas despues de la última sesión, recurrencia y eventos adversos mediante análisis descriptivo.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Resultados:</jats:bold>
                    Tres mujeres y dos hombres; edad media 43 años (22–63). El diámetro inicial fue 8–10 mm en cuatro pacientes y 2 mm en uno. La mediana de disfagia disminuyó de 3 (2–4) a 0; todos alcanzaron Mellow-Pinkas 0. Tres pacientes requirieron dos sesiones, uno tres y el caso de 2 mm, ocho. A las 8 semanas hubo cicatrización mucosa adecuada en 5/5 y no se observaron perforación, sangrado significativo ni otros eventos adversos relacionados. El seguimiento mediano fue 70 semanas (35–144); dos pacientes presentaron recurrencia tardía de disfagia a las 70 y 72 semanas.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Conclusión:</jats:bold>
                    La dilatación con Savary-Gilliard sobre guía Savary seguida de PRP activado fue factible y no presentó eventos adversos relacionados. La mejoría clínica, la cicatrización endoscópica y las recurrencias tardías respaldan estudios prospectivos controlados para determinar eficacia.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Palabras clave:</jats:bold>
                    Estenosis Esofágica; Endoscopía Gastrointestinal; Plasma Rico en Plaquetas; Trastornos de Deglución.
                  </jats:p>

abstract:

                    Coral lead (Pb) isotope records provide multi-decadal perspectives on marine Pb histories, but how individual records represent regional isotope histories remains an important interpretive question. We present a 1951–1998 Pb isotope record from a
                    <jats:italic>Porites</jats:italic>

                    <jats:sup>208</jats:sup>

                    <jats:sup>208</jats:sup>
                    Pb/

                    Pb composition than Dongsha, whereas the middle-to-late change within Lutao itself was not statistically resolved. This contrast shows that inter-site isotopic differences need not imply an equivalent temporal shift at an individual site. Published Pb isotope reference fields are compatible with multiple possible source combinations but do not uniquely identify historical sources or marine transport mechanisms. Together, these results reveal spatial heterogeneity in coral Pb isotope histories, with smaller inter-site differences during 1964–1984, and highlight the need to evaluate the spatial representativeness of individual coral Pb isotope records before extrapolating site-specific signatures to regional historical interpretations.

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Diffuse midline gliomas (DMG) primarily rely on glycolysis but exhibit a critical dependence on glutamine (Gln) to fuel the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, maintain epigenetic landscapes, and support proliferation. Consequently, amino acid transporters (AATs), particularly the primary Gln transporter ASCT2, are promising theranostic targets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To characterize the interplay of glucose (Glc), Gln, and AAT metabolism in DMG using in silico, in vitro, and in vivo models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RNA-sequencing data from 505 high-grade tumor patients (CBTN) underwent pathway enrichment and survival modeling. Three patient-derived DMG cell lines were cultured under varying Glc/Gln gradients to evaluate survival and SLC1A5 expression. 13C-isotope tracing was performed on the line with lowest baseline SLC1A5 expression. An orthotopic murine tumor model growth was monitored via bioluminescence, 7T MRI, dynamic [18F]F-Gln, and static [18F]FDG PET/CT. Explanted brains underwent immunohistochemistry (IHC) for metabolic transporters.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Analysis of 1,190 metabolic genes revealed significant amino acid pathway enrichment in DMG. Elevated SLC1A5 transcription correlated with poorer event-free and overall survival (p = 0.02, p = 0.003). In vitro, SLC1A5 expression dynamically increased under Gln deprivation and extreme Glc concentrations. While cells were highly Glc-dependent, only 30% survived Gln deprivation. Isotope tracing confirmed Glc primarily drives glycolysis, whereas Gln supplements the TCA cycle (Glc:Gln contribution—lactate 65.83%:4.47%; succinate 7.2%:44.4%; malate 11.6%:59.8%). In vivo, F-Gln tumor uptake was modest compared to FDG (SUVmax 0.5±0.2 vs 2.86±1.2) but demonstrated a higher tumor-to-background ratio (2.37±0.46 vs 1.07±0.01, p = 0.02). IHC confirmed reduced Glut1 and slightly elevated SLC1A5 expression relative to healthy brain tissue.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>DMGs exhibit a targetable partial metabolic reliance on Gln for tumor growth. SLC1A5 expression is dynamically regulated by nutrient availability, serving as a strong prognostic indicator. Targeting SLC1A5 and utilizing F-Gln PET as a biomarker warrant further investigation for metabolic and epigenetic interventions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hydrogen governs virtually every stage of heterogeneous catalytic reactions, yet its chemical identity, location, mobility, and mechanistic role are often difficult to establish by experiments. Recent advances in neutron spectroscopy have enabled direct observation of hydrogen species across increasingly complex catalytic systems, generating a rapidly growing body of mechanism insights. However, general principles of hydrogen behaviour have not been fully extracted. In this mini‐review, we present a hydrogen‐centred framework that reorganises recent neutron‐spectroscopic studies around four fundamental questions: what hydrogen species exist, where hydrogen resides, how it moves, and how it participates in catalytic reactions. This mini‐review integrates hydrogen species, spatial distribution, dynamics, and reactivity into understanding across diverse systems, and emphasises how neutron spectroscopy provides direct mechanism insights into the chemistry of hydrogen and enables discrimination between competing catalytic pathways. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future opportunities for combining neutron spectroscopy with complementary experimental and theoretical approaches to establish a more comprehensive understanding of hydrogen‐controlled catalysis.</jats:p>

Stable carbon and nitrogen isotope analyses of animal bone collagen (fourth-second centuries BCE and twelfth-fifteenth centuries CE) and human bone collagen (twelfth-fifteenth centuries CE) were combined with archaeobotanical evidence (fourth century BCE to eighteenth century CE) and published palaeoenvironmental data to examine subsistence strategies in these desert-oasis settings. This research challenges several hypotheses previously proposed by scholars, including Aral regressions in Antiquity due to intensive agriculture and irrigation (the second half of the first millennium BCE) and the shift to pastoralism after the Mongol Conquest (the thirteenth to fifteenth century CE). abstract:
<jats:sec id="sec001">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Rodents (order Rodentia) are the most diverse and geographically widespread order of mammals, occupying virtually all terrestrial ecosystems and playing key ecological roles in food webs and ecosystem functioning. Stable isotope analysis has become a tool for investigating trophic ecology, resource use, habitat use, and movement across spatial and temporal scales. Although isotope applications in rodent ecology have expanded in recent decades, the literature remains diverse, and no comprehensive synthesis currently maps this evidence. This scoping review aims to systematically map and synthesize how stable isotope analysis has been applied in ecological studies of the order Rodentia across diverse ecosystems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="sec002">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This protocol follows the methodology of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI), Adelaide, South Australia for scoping reviews and will be reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches will be conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, SciELO, and Google Scholar (first 200 results sorted by relevance), covering studies from database inception to January 2026. Eligible sources will include peer-reviewed articles, master’s theses, and doctoral dissertations published in any language, searches will be conducted in ProQuest, BTDT (Biblioteca digital brasileira de teses e dissertações) and CAPES Theses and Dissertations. Nine reviewers will screen randomized titles and abstracts in pairs, with a pilot-test of 100 random articles to ensure reviewers consistency. Full-text assessment and data charting will be conducted by the reviewer pairs using a standardized form, with a pilot-test verification of a subset of included studies to ensure consistency. No critical appraisal will be performed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="sec003">
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This review will provide a structured overview of stable isotope applications in rodent ecology, identifying methodological patterns, ecosystem and geographic coverage, and knowledge gaps to inform future research and evidence syntheses.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>In spinal correction surgery, metallic rods are commonly bent intraoperatively by surgeons to conform to the patient-specific spinal curvature and are then fixed with pedicle screws. However, intraoperative rod contouring can introduce surface scratches and notches, which may reduce fatigue strength and act as initiation sites for fracture. In this study, spinal correction rods with a prescribed spinal contour were fabricated from a Co–28Cr–6Mo–0.11N alloy (hereafter referred to as the CCMN alloy) by electron beam powder bed fusion (PBF-EB) to reduce dependence on intraoperative bending. Their compressive response, cyclic compression behavior, and fracture characteristics were experimentally evaluated, and their deformation behavior was further examined by finite element analysis (FEA). The CCMN rods were subjected to one, two, or three cycles of combined aging and reverse transformation heat treatment, denoted RT, 2RT, and 3RT, respectively. Under a compressive load of 1000 N, the displacement decreased with an increasing number of reverse transformation cycles, and the 3RT specimen showed the highest apparent resistance to deformation. The loads required to produce a displacement of 5 mm were 812, 843, 865, and 896 N for the as-built, RT, 2RT, and 3RT rods, respectively; thus, the 3RT rod exhibited an increase of 84 N relative to the as-built rod. Although all specimens were fabricated using the same CAD geometry and adjusted to the same nominal dimensional profile, small specimen-specific geometric deviations could not be independently quantified. Therefore, the observed differences in load–displacement response cannot be attributed exclusively to heat-treatment-induced microstructural changes. Furthermore, increasing the maximum diameter of the middle region of the variable-diameter rod from 7 to 8 mm reduced the displacement under 1000 N from 3.3 to 2.7 mm. In a single-specimen cyclic compression screening test at 0–300 N, 1 Hz, and 1 × 106 cycles, no apparent macroscopic residual deformation or fracture was observed. This result represents runout under the specified loading condition and does not establish a fatigue limit. These results support the feasibility of using PBF-EB to fabricate CCMN rods with prescribed curved and variable-diameter geometries and demonstrate a stable mechanical response under the specific static and cyclic loading conditions examined in this study.</jats:p>

title: Kinetic inverse bremsstrahlung absorption in magnetized fusion plasmas beyond the constant Coulomb logarithm: Velocity-dependent collisions, super-Gaussian electrons, and plasma screening

affiliation.name: Department of Physics, Laboratory of Physics of Radiations and Their Interactions with Matter (LRPRIM), Faculty of Matter Sciences, University of Batna 1 , Batna 05000,
Department of Physics, Laboratory of Physics of Radiations and Their Interactions with Matter (LRPRIM), Faculty of Matter Sciences, University of Batna 1 , Batna 05000,

abstract: <jats:p>We develop a kinetic model of electron–ion inverse bremsstrahlung absorption in magnetized fusion plasmas that extends the conventional constant-Coulomb-logarithm treatment. The model incorporates the velocity dependence of the Coulomb logarithm and plasma screening directly into the electron–ion collision frequency, while a super-Gaussian electron distribution is used to account for non-Maxwellian distortions. The formulation explicitly retains magnetization and circular-polarization effects and yields asymptotic scaling laws for magneto-inertial fusion (MIF) plasmas and microwave-heated magnetically confined plasmas. The results show that the velocity-dependent Coulomb logarithm can either reduce or enhance absorption depending on the electron distribution, whereas plasma screening systematically suppresses it. Under the conditions studied, the complete collisional model changes the MIF absorption rate by about 19% relative to the thermal-logarithm approximation. In the microwave-heated regime, the corresponding reduction is about 6% over the whole density range considered. These results highlight the need to treat non-Maxwellianity, velocity-dependent collisions, and plasma screening self-consistently when modeling inverse bremsstrahlung absorption in magnetized fusion plasmas.</jats:p>

title: A Reproducible Multi-Target Computational Framework for Prioritizing Plant-Derived Natural Products in Alzheimer’s Disease

affiliation.name: Pharmaceutical Sciences Department, College of Pharmacy, Umm Al-Qura University, Makkah 21955, Saudi Arabia

abstract: <jats:p>Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is biologically heterogeneous, and plant-derived natural products provide chemically diverse starting points for multi-target discovery. Reproducible prioritization is needed to distinguish literature-supported evidence from candidate-specific predictions not yet generated. Our objective was to develop a reproducible, evidence-informed framework for prioritizing plant-derived natural products in AD and define a transparent candidate library and prespecified screening set for subsequent computational and experimental evaluation. Completed work included selection of an AD target panel (AChE/BChE, BACE1, GSK-3β and MAO-B), synthesis of a published target-specific machine-learning (ML) benchmark, curation of a 20-compound candidate library with traceable chemical identities and literature support, and selection of a 13-compound prespecified screening set. Published performance metrics were treated solely as external benchmark evidence. Study-specific model training, prospective ML screening, molecular docking, BBB/drug-likeness and ADMET evaluation, multi-objective ranking, and experimental validation were prespecified as future work and were not performed. The framework links mechanistically justified targets, published ML benchmarks, a chemically diverse 20-compound library, and a 13-compound set for future screening. The library includes evidence-rich reference compounds and comparatively underexplored scaffolds; no candidate-specific computational ranking or selection outcome is reported. This study presents an evidence-informed, multi-target computational framework for prioritizing plant-derived natural products in Alzheimer’s disease. Its methodological contribution lies in integrating a mechanistically defined target panel, published machine-learning benchmarks, a traceable 20-compound candidate library, and a prespecified 13-compound screening set within a transparent prospective evaluation strategy. By distinguishing completed framework-development activities from future computational and experimental analyses, the study establishes a structured foundation for subsequent model validation, multi-objective prioritization, and experimental investigation.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Uptake of oxidized and other forms of modified low-density lipoprotein (LDL) drives formation of foam cells, a hallmark of atherosclerotic plaques. Experimental studies demonstrating the proinflammatory and cytotoxic properties of oxidized LDL have led to the concept of LDL oxidation as one key factor in both development and destabilization of atherosclerotic plaques. Such data positioned oxidized LDL as a promising target for prevention or mitigation of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Yet the failure of multiple antioxidants to reduce cardiovascular risk in large randomized clinical trials has hampered this prospect. Such null studies have stimulated interest in an alternative approach: the therapeutic potential of antibodies against oxidized LDL. High levels of IgM against oxidized LDL phospholipids are associated with lower cardiovascular risk and these antibodies function primarily through neutralization and stimulation of clearance of modified LDL. IgG antibodies against aldehyde-modified peptide sequences in apolipoprotein B-100, the signature protein component of LDL, are also associated with lower risk of cardiovascular disease but experimental studies have shown that these antibodies function by locally forming immune complexes with oxidized LDL that limit the inflammatory activity of certain plaque macrophages. A phase 2 pilot study showed that one such antibody, orticumab, reduces an imaging index of local coronary arterial inflammation in patients with psoriasis. Thus, emerging evidence supports the possibility of using oxidized LDL antibodies to limit atherothrombotic disease.</jats:p>

title: TMET-14 Novel Therapeutic Target for Glioma: PLIN2 Regulates Glioma Metabolism and Ferroptosis

affiliation.name: Sichuan university , chengdu,
West china hospital , chengdu,
West china hospital , chengdu,

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Glioma is a primary malignant tumor of the central nervous system, among which glioblastoma has the highest degree of malignancy. Gliomas enhance their survival capacity through metabolic reprogramming. Previous studies have shown that enhanced lipid metabolism promotes the malignant progression of gliomas, indicating that lipid metabolism plays a crucial role in this context. Lipid droplets are organelles responsible for lipid storage. In recent years, researchers have discovered that lipid droplets not only serve as storage compartments for lipids but also participate in cellular energy metabolism, homeostasis regulation, and interactions with the tumor microenvironment. Previous studies have found that the lipid droplet-coating protein PLIN1 affects the malignant biological behavior of gliomas. We investigated another protein of the PLIN family, PLIN2, which is primarily involved in maintaining the stability of cellular lipid droplets. Through analysis of the public database TCGA, we found that high expression of PLIN2 in glioma cohorts is associated with poor prognosis in glioma patients. Subsequently, we constructed PLIN2-overexpressing and PLIN2-knockout cell lines in glioma cell lines U87 and T98G. Our study found that under treatment with the ferroptosis inducer RSL3, U87 cells overexpressing PLIN2 exhibited lower lipid peroxide levels compared to their control counterparts. We then investigated the effect of PLIN2 on ferroptosis in T98G knockout cell lines and found that PLIN2 knockout increased the sensitivity of T98G cells to ferroptosis, making the cells more prone to undergo ferroptosis. We performed EdU proliferation assays and Transwell migration assays on T98G PLIN2 knockout cell lines and found that the proliferation and migration abilities of PLIN2 knockout cells were weaker than those of the control group. Therefore, in glioma cells, PLIN2 is involved in regulating glioma cell metabolism and the ferroptosis process.</jats:p>

title: Memory-window engineering: target specifications for duration, retention through division, and amplitude in immune epigenome editing

affiliation.name: American Heritage School

abstract: <jats:p>Immune activation, tolerance, exhaustion, trained immunity and regulatory stability are held in place by chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, histone modification, and enhancer-promoter wiring. CRISPR-based epigenome editors rewrite these layers without cutting DNA, but most reports address editing efficiency and leave time unanswered. Target duration is a design input to be specified before an editor is chosen; the duration achieved remains an experimental outcome. Memory-window engineering defines a candidate immune edit by three parameters: duration after editor clearance, retention through cell division, and amplitude at single-cell resolution, with target-compartment division rate as an explicit modifier. For passively diluted marks, division rate constrains post-clearance duration; transcriptional and phenotypic persistence may follow different trajectories. Published results from methylation editing at IL1RN, FOXP3 enhancer demethylation, PD-1 enhancer tuning, exhaustion circuits and CRISPRoff programming of primary human T cells are interpreted using their readouts and observation windows; some persistence endpoints remain censored by study duration. Three testable predictions concern CpG density, transcript-versus-mark recovery and division-dependent loss, with competing mechanisms and measurement artefacts considered. Specificity, the nuclease-knockout comparison, and the ethics of durable edits are treated as parts of the same specification. Two design consequences follow. TET-dependent erasure requires oxygen and 2-oxoglutarate; reduced erasure in hypoxic or metabolically inhibitory tumour regions is therefore a hypothesis for edited immune cells. Sustained programming of circulating monocyte output requires an upstream progenitor strategy, whereas long-lived resident myeloid cells are a separate case. A worked CAR T example and five-item reporting minimum distinguish development-stage characterisation from lot-release testing.</jats:p>

title: SoccerNet-Guided Domain-Ordered Transfer Learning for Tiny Football Detection with GVRE-Augmented Target Data

affiliation.name: Faculty of Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong

abstract: <jats:p>Detecting a football in broadcast video remains difficult because the object is often only a few pixels wide and is easily obscured by motion blur, compression, or nearby players. This study tests a SoccerNet-guided domain-ordered transfer schedule while holding the target training data constant. The target set contains 298 original images and 257 accepted ball-containing images produced by bounding-box-guided generative visual representation enhancement (GVRE). TargetBaseline trains directly on these 555 images. DomainTransfer first trains on 8,550 SoccerNet-derived frames and then uses the same target set. Three matched You Only Look Once version 8, nano (YOLOv8n) seeds, 1280-pixel inputs, and a validation-first gate define the comparison. On validation, DomainTransfer raises mean Ball Average Precision at Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold 0.50 (AP50) by 0.0548 and fixed-threshold Ball Recall by 0.0741. The single gated test evaluation raises Ball AP50 from 0.5367 to 0.5913 and overall mAP50-95 from 0.6292 to 0.6448. These results support the ordered transfer schedule, although the 25-image test set, target-validation checkpoint selection, and use of one detector scale limit the strength of the conclusion.</jats:p>

title: Sensing electron vortices with nanomechanics
Propofol-remifentanil target-controlled infusion for emergency craniotomy following multiple trauma in a resource-limited setting
abstract:
<jats:sec id="st1">
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Target-controlled infusion (TCI) allows intravenous anesthetics to be titrated to model-predicted plasma or effect-site concentrations. In emergency neuroanesthesia, however, its clinical value depends not only on the selected target concentration but also on how these targets are adjusted in response to changing surgical stimulation while maintaining cerebral and systemic physiologic stability. We report the use of propofol TCI with the Schnider model and remifentanil TCI with the Minto model during emergency craniotomy in a patient with severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) and major thoracic trauma in Eastern Indonesia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="st2">
                    <jats:title>Case Description:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 32-year-old male weighing approximately 80 kg presented with severe TBI after a 5-m fall, accompanied by right hemopneumothorax, multiple rib fractures, and a clavicular fracture. A chest tube was inserted before anesthetic induction. Propofol was administered using the Schnider model with an effect-site target concentration (Ce) of 3–5 µg/mL during induction and 2.5–4 µg/mL during maintenance. Remifentanil was administered using the Minto model at target concentrations of 4–5 ng/mL during induction and 2–3 ng/mL during maintenance, although the anesthesia record did not consistently specify whether plasma or effect-site targeting was used for remifentanil during maintenance. After induction, the targets were reduced and subsequently adjusted according to the stage and intensity of surgical stimulation, hemodynamic response, ventilation, and surgical conditions. During the 4-h procedure, systolic blood pressure remained between 102 and 125 mmHg, oxygen saturation was maintained at 99–100%, and end-tidal carbon dioxide remained between 30 and 35 mmHg. The brain remained relaxed without clinically apparent swelling. This case illustrates how separate hypnotic and opioid targets can be used to guide stepwise titration of propofol and remifentanil during emergency craniotomy when advanced depth-of-anesthesia and intracranial monitoring are not available.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="st3">
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Propofol TCI using the Schnider model and remifentanil TCI using the Minto model provided a practical framework for independently titrating the hypnotic and opioid components of anesthesia during emergency craniotomy. In a resource-limited setting, model-predicted concentrations should not be regarded as fixed doses but rather as adjustable targets interpreted in conjunction with surgical stimulation, hemodynamic tolerance, ventilation, brain relaxation, and the limitations of available monitoring.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Drug Target Interaction Prediction and Anticancer Drug Screening Based on Spatio Temporal Sequence Prediction and Machine Learning

affiliation.name: Institute of Science and Technology, Beijing Normal-Hong Kong Baptist University (BNBU)

abstract: <jats:p>Cancer treatment has long faced problems such as long drug development cycle, high cost of experimental screening, drug resistance of monotherapy and complex mechanism of combination therapy. Based on the existing introduction, this paper reviews the drug target interaction prediction, drug combination synergy evaluation, spatio-temporal sequence modeling and data-driven anti-cancer drug screening. Firstly, this paper introduces DTI, anti-cancer drug screening process, common databases and collaborative scoring indicators; Secondly, the applications of traditional machine learning, deep learning and ensemble learning methods in DTI and drug combination prediction were compared; Thirdly, the value of spatio-temporal sequence prediction in modeling drug concentration, action time and cell response dynamics was analyzed; Finally, the problems of data heterogeneity, sample imbalance, lack of interpretability of the model and difficulties in clinical transformation faced by the current research are summarized, and it is proposed that in the future, the integration of multi omics, interpretable artificial intelligence and experimental verification closed loop should be strengthened. Research shows that machine learning and spatio-temporal sequence prediction can effectively improve the efficiency of anti-cancer drug screening, and provide important method support for combination drug optimization and precision treatment.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors (ATRTs) are malignant, multi-lineage neoplasms of early childhood in the central nervous system. ATRTs are subdivided into TYR, SHH, and MYC groups based on their transcriptional and epigenetic characteristics, and recent histopathological studies revealed that the MYC subtypes harbor mesenchymal features. Patient-derived ATRT cancer cell lines express high levels of vimentin, a marker for EMT. Therefore, we hypothesize that targeting mesenchymal cell state in ATRT is feasible by utilizing FiVe1 and its derivative FMP-502, which lead to hyperphosphorylation of vimentin at the S39, S56, and S83, resulting in multinucleation and mitotic collapse.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We treated three patient-derived ATRT-SHH cell lines (CHLA-02-ATRT, CHLA-04-ATRT, CHLA-05-ATRT), three ATRT-MYC cell lines (CHLA-06-ATRT, CHLA-266, BT-12), and 293T with FiVe1 or FMP-502 and used CellTiter-Glo (CTG) to determine the half-maximal inhibitor concentration (IC50). We confirmed vimentin phosphorylation at S39, S56, and S83 via Western blot. To determine transcription-level changes, we performed RNA-sequencing of CHLA-05-ATRT and CHLA-266 following 24 hours of treatment with FMP-502 at IC75 dose or DMSO.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>IC50 of FiVe1 for ATRT-MYC (1.130-8.621 µM) was significantly lower than that of ATRT-SHH (2.694-55.033 µM). FMP-502 yielded similar results (108.0-317.2 nM for ATRT-MYC and 252.0 nM-1.598 µM for ATRT-SHH). Non-malignant 293T cells demonstrated extremely high IC50 values (18.68 µM for FMP-502). ATRT cells treated with FMP-502 showed significantly increased vimentin phosphorylation at S39, S56, and S83 via Western blot. Differential RNA-sequencing analysis showed that ATRT cells treated with FMP-502 display significant depletion of gene sets relating to DNA repair and replication initiation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our preliminary findings suggest that ATRT-MYC cells are more susceptible to FiVe1 and FMP-502 than ATRT-SHH cells. Furthermore, vimentin hyperphosphorylation in ATRT may disrupt its mesenchymal state by decreasing DNA repair capacity. Our study demonstrates that targeting the mesenchymal state may be a novel approach for ATRT treatment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome integrates metabolic risk, kidney dysfunction, and cardiovascular disease. Whether statin-ezetimibe combination therapy is associated with lower subsequent myocardial infarction risk than statin monotherapy among patients across modified cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk groups remains uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using the Korean National Health Insurance Service database, we emulated separate two-arm landmark target trials within modified early and late cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk groups. Adults aged 30-74 years with dyslipidemia who received prescriptions covering a total of 180 days with statin monotherapy or a fixed-dose statin-ezetimibe combination were eligible. Treatment was assigned at the 180-day landmark. Stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting and cause-specific Cox regression were used to calculate hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence interval (CI), with death treated as a competing event for cumulative incidence estimation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 309,371 treated participants, 239,954 had modified early risk and 69,417 had modified late risk. Compared with statin monotherapy, statin-ezetimibe therapy was associated with lower myocardial infarction risk after weighting in both early-risk participants (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.81-0.95) and late-risk participants (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.79-0.98). 10-year weighted cumulative incidence was 1.97% versus 2.23% in the early-risk group and 3.52% versus 3.94% in the late-risk group. In same-intensity comparisons, the association was most evident with moderate-intensity therapy, particularly in the early CKM group (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.79-0.95).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among adults with dyslipidemia who received prescriptions covering a total of 180 days, statin-ezetimibe combination therapy was associated with a lower subsequent risk of myocardial infarction than statin monotherapy across modified CKM risk groups. The association was most evident in moderate-intensity comparisons.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In industrial production, the real‐time detection of falling small targets in complex scenarios is critical for ensuring both production safety and operational efficiency. Traditional RGB cameras are limited by inherent defects, such as insufficient dynamic range and motion blur, which hinder their ability to meet the demands of high‐speed dynamic scenarios. Event cameras offer significant advantages, owing to their characteristics, such as high temporal resolution (microsecond‐level), low latency and high dynamic range (>120 dB). However, challenges persist, including data sparsity, noise interference, the scarcity of specialised datasets and the demands of real‐time processing. In response to complex industrial scenarios, this paper constructs a specialised dataset, EvFallDet, which contains multiple types of target objects and compound interferences, and proposes a lightweight detection framework, EvFall‐Net. The framework enhances the feature representation capability of small targets through an event encoding strategy, which incorporates spatiotemporal feature decoupling. Experiments demonstrate that this method leads to significant improvements in detection accuracy and robustness when applied to small targets in complex industrial environments.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>High classification scores are meaningful only if the prediction target is physically consistent. We audited image-only, tabular-only and fusion experiments on 9000 ZooScan objects drawn from the 1,153,507-object PELGAS collection. The archived three-class labels were tertiles of the stored equivalent spherical diameter (ESD), not biomass classes. All 893,542 records exported with version v7.26 followed the documented ESD formula, whereas all 259,965 v7.24 records equalled twice the integer part of projected area divided by π. All 2017 v7.24 objects in the subset fell in the highest archived class. Recomputing ESD consistently from area and pixel calibration changed 3430 of the 9000 labels. The subset spans 13 cruises and 697 cruise–station groups and includes 2639 objects annotated as non-living. On the corrected target, tree-based controls using all descriptors reached a macro-F1 of about 0.998 under both object-stratified and station-grouped evaluation. In preliminary single-seed neural runs without area- or length-based descriptors, tabular networks reached a macro-F1 of 0.89, a Swin-T image model 0.946 and gated fusion 0.944; the image-based runs covered three folds and retained scale cues, so they do not isolate the contribution of each modality. Target provenance should be verified before multimodal performance rankings are used in ecological monitoring.</jats:p>

title: STEM-04 Identification and characterization of the quiescent IDH-wildtype ancestral founder CSC, the cell to target to overcome both causes of therapeutic resistance

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>After frustrating decades of therapeutic deadlock, it’s finally emerging that some traditional concepts regarding IDH-wildtype glioblastoma need to be updated and supplemented to overcome the two causes of therapeutic resistance. It is now clear that IDH-wildtype glioblastoma primordial CSC originated as premalignant progenitor in the ribbon layer of the SVZ. Once acquired the proper genetic events, it will give rise to a population of founder CSCs that spread and micro-infiltrate quiescently throughout the entire brain parenchyma. Without any doubt nowadays, this pre-growth dormant micro-infiltration is the only one able to give rise later to distant relapses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The collection of separate multiregional samples in the tumor bulk enabled us to reconstruct the phylogenetic tree of the primary tumor mass. However, the therapeutic solution to IDH-wildtype glioblastoma lies in the micro-infiltrated brain where the ancestral founder CSCs reside quiescently. We are using the four ethical methods (as part of normal glioblastoma surgery) to sample the micro-infiltrated brain parenchyma to identify the dormant ancestral founder CSCs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In the bulk, multiregional sampling can enable us to infer and reconstruct the phylogenetic tree of the tumor. The codified ethical methods to sample the micro-infiltrated brain parenchyma are enabling us to identify and characterize the ancestral founder CSCs (typified by stem cell and radial glia markers), which lie dormant in the perivascular parenchymal niches across the whole brain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Two causes of resistance are currently invalidating all therapeutic strategies. The first cause of therapeutic resistance is due to intratumor heterogeneity, while the second cause is the silent presence in the entire supratentorial brain of dormant ancestral founder CSCs from the pre-growth micro-infiltration. After finishing the process of identification and characterization of the quiescent ancestral founder CSC, we’ll obtain the target that can overcome both causes of resistance and provide quickly novel, effective therapeutic solutions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumour with extremely poor patient prognosis. Despite aggressive therapy, the disease invariably progresses or recurs as chemoresistance develops. Thus, more effective therapies are desperately needed. Sphingosine kinases (SKs) are intracellular signalling enzymes which have been implicated in cancer initiation, progression and chemotherapeutic resistance. We have examined the potential of sphingosine kinase 2 (SK2) as a therapeutic target in GBM. To this end, our analysis of GBM patient tumours show that SK2 is hyper-activated in almost all GBM tumours, due to the loss of a key negative regulator of SK2, DYNC1I1, releasing SK2 to have an oncogenic role in these tumours. Application of clinically relevant SK2 inhibitors to mouse and human GBM cell lines and GBM patient-derived glioma neural stem cells in vitro induced a clear reduction in cell proliferation, with cells isolated from recurrent GBM appearing at least as sensitive to those from primary tumours. We then generated SK2 knockout (SK2-KO) mouse glioma CT2A and SB28 cells using CRISPR/Cas9 and showed that genetic ablation of SK2 dramatically reduced the proliferation, colony forming ability and cell cycle progression of these cells in vitro. When orthotopically engrafted into C57Bl/6 mice, these SK2-KO cells displayed significantly reduced tumour growth and increased mouse survival time. Examination of the mechanisms driving this reduced tumour growth found a dramatic increase in the infiltration of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells into the tumours lacking SK2, suggesting involvement of the immune system in reducing tumour progression. Indeed, when we orthotopically engrafted the SK2-KO glioma cells into immune-compromised NSG mice, no survival advantage was observed, providing strong evidence that loss of SK2 enhances anti-tumour immunity in GBM. Collectively, these findings strongly indicate that SK2 represents an actionable new therapeutic target for GBM that enhances anti-tumour immunity.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Re-irradiation is increasingly utilized for recurrent glioma, yet no standard second-line regimen exists. Brachytherapy offers a single-intervention approach combining surgical resection and focal radiation delivery, but its outcomes relative to external beam re-irradiation (EBRT) are poorly characterized.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Forty patients receiving re-irradiation for recurrent glioma at a single institution (2000–2025) were retrospectively analyzed. Techniques included IMRT/VMAT (30-45 Gy in 10-25 fractions) (35%), Cs-131 tile-based brachytherapy (60 Gy to 5mm depth) (32.5%), SBRT/SRS (18-30 Gy in 1-5 fractions) (22.5%), and 3D-CRT (30 Gy in 10-15 fractions) (5%). Survival outcomes, including overall survival from diagnosis (OS), overall survival from re-irradiation (OS-ReRT), and post-re-irradiation progression-free survival (PFS-ReRT), were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression adjusting for initial tumor grade and Karnofsky Performance Score (KPS) at recurrence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>On univariable analysis, patients receiving brachytherapy had a median OS-ReRT of 6.2 months versus 13.4 months for other modalities (log-rank p = 0.296). On multivariable analysis adjusting for potential confounders, no significant difference in OS-ReRT was observed between brachytherapy and EBRT (HR 2.02, 95% CI 0.815–4.999, p = 0.129). KPS at recurrence was the sole significant independent factor impacting survival (OS-ReRT: HR 0.60 per 10-point increase, 95% CI 0.424–0.844, p = 0.003). No grade 4 or 5 toxicity was observed across any modality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Within this smaller retrospective cohort, after adjusting for functional status and tumor grade, Cs-131 brachytherapy achieved comparable OS-ReRT to EBRT. Given its ability to integrate radiation delivery with surgical resection in a single intervention, brachytherapy may represent a reasonable and comparable alternative to other re-irradiation modalities for select patients with recurrent glioma planned for surgical resection, particularly in this group of patients for whom reducing treatment burden is a meaningful clinical consideration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To develop deep learning super-resolution (SR) models for enhancing cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seventy CBCT volumes (75 µm voxel size) served as references. Paired low-resolution (LR) volumes (300 µm) were simulated using physics-based degradation. Four architectures were each trained with three loss configurations (L1; L1+edge; L1+edge+perceptual): Swin Transformer for Image Restoration (SwinIR), Hybrid Attention Transformer (HAT), Hybrid Multi-Axis Aggregation Network (HMA-Net), and Dense-Residual-Connected Transformer (DRCT). Performance was assessed with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index measure (SSIM), learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS), and deep image structure and texture similarity (DISTS). Three dentists ranked the 12 configurations in 28 sets using blinded forced-choice pairwise comparisons. Correlations of metrics and expert ranks were assessed using Spearman correlation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>All configurations outperformed LR input and bicubic interpolation on every metric (p &lt; 0.05). HMA-Net trained with L1+edge+perceptual loss performed best on LPIPS (0.216) and DISTS (0.186). HAT with L1 loss achieved the highest PSNR (28.79 dB) and SSIM (0.820). Experts ranked DRCT and HAT with L1 loss, and DRCT with L1+edge loss, as the best configurations (p &lt; 0.001 versus others). Expert rank correlated moderately only with PSNR (rho = -0.65) and SSIM (rho = -0.60; both p &lt; 0.05).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Transformer-based SR improved the perceived quality of clinical CBCT images. HAT and DRCT trained with L1 pixel loss alone, and DRCT trained with L1 and edge loss, demonstrated superior performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Advances in knowledge</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Transformer-based super-resolution improved expert-perceived detail of simulated low-resolution in vivo CBCT scans without additional radiation dose, supporting further validation on directly acquired low-resolution scans.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Exploring the Role of DDIT3 in Tumorigenesis and Its Potential as a Target for Novel Cancer Therapies

abstract: <jats:p>Cancer continues to be the leading cause of death globally, with mounting evidence associating cellular stress with tumor initiation, progression, and therapeutic resistance. DNA damage-inducible transcript 3 (DDIT3), a key stress-responsive transcription factor, plays a central role in cellular stress responses by regulating apoptosis, cell survival, and the tumor microenvironment. Although DDIT3 has been extensively studied in neurodegenerative and metabolic diseases, its dual role in cancer has only recently begun to emerge. This review systematically explores the intricate functions of DDIT3 in cancer biology, emphasizing its involvement in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, apoptosis regulation, and modulation of the tumor microenvironment. We investigate how DDIT3 interacts with key signaling pathways and its impact on cellular stress responses, such as autophagy and macrophage recruitment within the tumor microenvironment. Furthermore, we evaluate the therapeutic potential of targeting DDIT3 through clinical and preclinical drug studies, concentrating on compounds that enhance its pro-apoptotic functions or inhibit its cancer-promoting activities. This review seeks to provide a comprehensive understanding of DDIT3′s role in tumors, offering insights into future therapeutic strategies targeting this stress-related protein in oncology.</jats:p>

title: Sequence-Driven Classification of Aptamers by Target Type: Algorithm Development and Validation
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>DNA aptamers are short, single-stranded oligonucleotides that bind molecular targets with high affinity and specificity. Traditionally, aptamers are identified through SELEX (systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment), an iterative process that is time-consuming and requires specialized equipment. To simplify and accelerate aptamer discovery, particularly across multiple molecular targets, computational approaches have gained momentum.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this study, we present a sequence-only framework for classifying DNA aptamers by target type using curated datasets of experimentally validated sequences. Target type here refers to the broad class of ligands that an aptamer binds to.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Aptamer-target records were curated from the UTexas Aptamer Database, retaining only those sequences with complete annotations and a clearly defined target category. From these filtered records, the 2 target categories with the highest number of unique aptamer sequences—cell and steroid, comprising a total of 236 sequences—were selected for this study. Each sequence was then represented using character-level term frequency–inverse document frequency of n-gram motifs (n=3‐6) combined with guanine-cytosine content and sequence length. The dataset was then split into 70% training, 20% testing, and 10% validation sets. An ensemble of 9 bagged extreme gradient boosting classifiers was selected for its established performance on high-dimensional tabular data and native handling of class imbalance. The model was trained to distinguish between aptamers targeting cellular and steroidal molecules, with class weighting, oversampling, probability calibration, and per-class threshold optimization applied to address class imbalance. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, macro-
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      scores, and recall on the test dataset and an independently generated external validation set comprising 13 new laboratory-generated steroid (aldosterone)–binding aptamers. The novelty of these laboratory aptamers relative to the training set was also confirmed using the pairwise Levenshtein distance.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The ensemble classifier achieved 97.92% accuracy and a macro-
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score of 0.95 on a test set of 236 curated DNA aptamer sequences, demonstrating strong performance in distinguishing cell-binding from steroid-binding aptamers. The calibrated and threshold-optimized model was further validated on a set of 13 new laboratory-created aptamers for steroid aldosterone using experimental SELEX, achieving 100% recall and confirming its ability to generalize to new experimental data.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These results demonstrate that informative, target-specific patterns can be directly extracted from DNA sequences, establishing a scalable, data-driven complement to SELEX in this preliminary proof-of-concept study for rapid prescreening of candidate aptamers. More broadly, this sequence-only approach could support faster, lower-cost triage of candidate aptamers, reducing reliance on iterative wet-laboratory SELEX as aptamer databases and target categories continue to expand.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Recently, numerous studies have been carried out on terahertz flat-top beam shaping with the help of meta-devices. However, the majority of these devices are single-functional and multi-layered, require complicated fabrication processes, and are suitable only for the axial transformation of the incident beam. Herein, we propose two bifunctional reflective metasurfaces consisting of anisotropic unit cells etched onto a grounded RO3035 substrate. Aside from transforming a Gaussian beam into a high-quality non-axial flat-top beam at 0.1 THz, the first device realizes linear-to-circular polarization conversion, while the second splits the Gaussian beam into two orthogonally polarized tilted flat-top beams. The geometric dimensions of the constitutive building blocks are adjusted based on an integration of the Gerchberg–Saxton algorithm and the Rayleigh–Sommerfeld (RS) diffraction formula, proposing a novel method, to our knowledge, for phase profile design. The performance of the proposed metasurfaces is evaluated through both the finite element method and a memory-efficient local response (LR)–RS method that combines the LR of the embedded inclusions with the RS diffraction formula. With non-uniformity values of 4.5%–10.2%, roll-off values between 1 dB and 1.1 dB, and beam conversion efficiencies exceeding 84.5% across both scenarios, the proposed metasurfaces produce high-quality flat-top beams. This positions the proposed metasurfaces as a promising candidates for compact terahertz imaging and sensing systems, and establishes a new basis for combining polarization conversion and beam splitting with flat-top beam shaping.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Diffuse midline glioma (DMG) H3K27-altered remains uniformly fatal despite intensive multimodal therapy. Epigenetic dysregulation is a hallmark of these tumors, yet the contribution of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) to disease maintenance and therapeutic targeting is poorly understood. Our previous whole-genome sequencing (WGS) analysis of 60 DMG samples revealed recurrent structural variants (SVs) involving the lncRNA CCDC26, including focal amplification and exon-containing fusion events, suggesting a potential role in DMG biology. We investigated the functional significance of CCDC26 alterations and their downstream epigenetic consequences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>WGS and RNA-seq/lncRNA-seq from DMG tumors and patient-derived cell lines were analyzed to characterize CCDC26 expression, SV breakpoints, and fusion transcripts. Functional studies used doxycycline-inducible shRNA knockdown and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout constructs targeting distinct CCDC26 exons, including non-coding exons involved in SVs and fusion breakpoints. Proliferation, colony formation, apoptosis, and differentiation were assessed, and EZH2/H3K27me3 levels were evaluated by immunoblotting. Orthotopic xenografts with inducible CCDC26 depletion were used to assess in vivo tumor growth.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RNA-seq identified marked CCDC26 overexpression in SV-positive tumors and patient-derived DMG lines, as well as CCDC26–GSDMC fusion transcripts joining CCDC26 exon 1 to GSDMC coding exons. Consistent with these genomic alterations, targeting either the fusion-associated non-coding exons or the distal exon of CCDC26 significantly reduced DMG cell viability and colony formation and induced morphological and molecular features of differentiation. CCDC26 loss also decreased EZH2 and global H3K27me3 levels. In orthotopic xenografts, inducible CCDC26 knockdown impaired tumor growth and prolonged survival.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CCDC26 is a functionally essential lncRNA whose SV‑driven activation reveals a key dependency in DMG. Its loss impairs tumor growth and promotes differentiation, establishing CCDC26 as a targetable lncRNA and promising therapeutic target in diffuse midline glioma.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                      Effect-directed analysis in high-performance thin-layer chromatography (HPTLC–EDA) was applied as a rapid screening platform for the localization of enzyme inhibitory constituents with potential relevance to neurodegenerative disorders. An HPTLC–EDA workflow enabling simultaneous localization of acetylcholinesterase, butyrylcholinesterase and tyrosinase inhibitors was established and demonstrated using extracts of three cosmopolitan weed species. Distinct and spatially resolved inhibition profiles were observed, revealing multiple bioactive zones particularly in methanolic extracts of
                      <jats:italic>Stellaria media</jats:italic>
                      (L.) Vill. and
                      <jats:italic>Chenopodium album</jats:italic>
                      L., indicating a high diversity of cholinesterase inhibitors. In contrast, tyrosinase inhibition was more pronounced in dichloromethane extracts, suggesting the presence of less polar inhibitory constituents. Spectrophotometric assays confirmed higher phenolic content and antioxidant activity in methanolic–aqueous extracts, supporting a complementary role of redox-active compounds. The integration of multi-target enzyme profiling with effect-directed analysis highlights these widely distributed plant species as underexplored sources of bioactive constituents with potential neuroprotective properties. The applied approach enables rapid prioritization of complex extracts and supports the identification of candidate fractions for further phytochemical and pharmacological characterization.
