abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment in hematologic malignancies but has shown limited success in pediatric brain tumors due to inadequate persistence, T-cell exhaustion, and antigen escape leading to relapse. To address these barriers, we are developing a dual-target CAR T-Cell strategy directed against B7-H3 and GPC2, two tumor associated antigens with complementary and heterogeneous expression across pediatric brain tumors, with the goal of reducing antigen-negative tumor outgrowth and improving durability. We generated and evaluated a panel of nine dual-specific CAR constructs that differ in intracellular activation and costimulatory signaling domains. Human T cells from healthy donors were transduced with each construct, enabling a systematic comparison of CAR signaling architecture. Using standardized in vitro assays and orthotopic in vivo tumor models, we assessed cytotoxicity, proliferation, persistence, and exhaustion to identify an optimal CAR design. While single-target CAR T cells achieved transient tumor control, they ultimately failed due to tumor relapse. In contrast, select dual-target CAR configurations demonstrated enhanced persistence, reduced functional exhaustion, and sustained antitumor activity. The primary goal of this work is to define a dual-CAR architecture that balances potent tumor killing with long-term T-cell functionality. These studies directly inform construct selection for clinical translation. Based on these data, we are advancing a lead candidate toward IND-enabling studies, with the goal of opening a first-in-human clinical trial, DEFEAT, at CNH by the end of 2026 for children with pediatric brain tumors.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Gradient-boosted tree ensembles are widely fitted to economic and financial series that trend, yet a regression tree predicts an average of its training targets and cannot follow a target that rises above its training range. This study measures how much of the forecast error of such ensembles that restriction accounts for, and what the available correction costs. It is a diagnostic study rather than a forecasting one: the log level of the S&P 500 is used as a stress test asset because it drifts steadily beyond any training window. The log index is forecast from five United States macroeconomic indicators lagged one month, over January 2003 to January 2026, at seven rolling origins under two training window rules. We define excursion depth, the distance of a test target beyond the training target range, computed in a backtest from the targets alone. Four boosting implementations are compared with a ridge regression, linear leaf boosting, a linear trend, a random walk with drift, and anchored residual boosting (ARB), which fits the ensemble to the residual of a ridge anchor. The error gap between unanchored and anchored boosting widens with excursion depth, from 0.0065 to 0.1498 in root mean squared error between the shallowest and deepest thirds of beyond-range months, and it tracks depth and not forecast horizon when both are controlled. Diebold–Mariano tests reject equal accuracy for one of the four families and not for their average. Ridge alone is ahead of three of the four anchored ensembles under the expanding origin, while linear leaf boosting leaves the range without the same gain, so a linear term fitted to the whole window is what matters. Inside the training range, unanchored boosting remains more accurate for three of the four families. The random walk with drift is the most accurate forecast of the level, and on monthly log returns no model improves on the historical mean. The results identify the conditions under which boosted trees are an unsuitable estimator for a level target, and excursion depth locates those conditions in a backtest before any model is fitted.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Pediatric ependymomas (EPNs) lack effective targeted therapies, and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells have not yet produced objective clinical responses against this tumor type. Resistance to CAR T cell therapy in central nervous system tumors is thought to arise from immune suppression within the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) and insufficient CAR T cell trafficking. The EPN TIME is characterized by robust myeloid cell infiltration, but the mechanisms driving this recruitment remain poorly understood. We previously identified constitutive secretion of the monocyte chemoattractant C-C motif chemokine ligand 2 (CCL2) by EPN cells, which is further increased upon exposure to both CAR and non-tumor-targeting T cells. The goal of this project is to investigate the role of tumor-derived CCL2 in EPN progression, myeloid infiltration, and resistance to CAR T cell therapy, and to explore its potential as a therapeutic target to improve CAR T cell trafficking. Analysis of pediatric EPN RNA sequencing datasets revealed that CCL2 is among the most highly expressed chemokines in EPNs and that elevated expression correlates with significantly poorer overall survival. CCL2 deletion in a ZFTA-RELA fusion-driven orthotopic xenograft model significantly delayed tumor progression and modestly improved the efficacy of human B7-H3.CAR T-cells in vivo. To determine whether CCL2 could be therapeutically leveraged rather than inhibited, we engineered B7-H3.CAR T cells to overexpress C-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (CCR2). This modification significantly enhanced in vivo trafficking to orthotopic EPNs following systemic delivery and produced a rapid, early anti-tumor response; however, this effect was not sustained over time. Together, our findings support the development of combinatorial strategies to enhance tumor homing and sustain CAR T cell function within the EPN TIME.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Proton beam radiotherapy is a frequently used modality in the treatment of meningiomas, but models to predict treatment response have yet to be developed. In this study, we explore whether Molecular Group may better predict outcomes after proton beam in intracranial meningiomas compared to traditional WHO grading</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Eligible patients included those with an intracranial meningioma with available methylation profiling that underwent surgical resection followed by proton beam radiotherapy. Molecular Group was determined for each meningioma based on previously described techniques, resulting in four groups: MG1(Immunogenic), MG2(NF2-wildtype), MG3(Hypermetabolic), MG4(Proliferative). Progression-free survival was calculated from time of completion of proton beam radiotherapy to in-field recurrence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>55 patients were included with median age at surgery of 57 years and 60% of which were female(n = 33). There were 11 in-field recurrences with median PFS after proton beam of 2.63 years(IQR:1.25-4.41). Median proton beam dose was 57 Gy(IQR:50.4-60.0Gy) and median follow-up was 2.8 yr(IQR:1.6-4.8). 24 meningiomas were MG2 (median PFS: 2.74yr, IQR:1.26-4.62), 11 were MG3 (median PFS: 2.80 yr, IQR:1.44-5.04), and 20 were MG4 (median PFS: 2.58 yr, IQR:1.58-3.64). 22 were WHO Grade 1 (median PFS: 2.74 yrs, IQR: 1.00-4.23), 31 were WHO Grade 2 (median PFS: 2.59 yr,IQR: 1.70-4.67) and 2 were WHO Grade 3 (median PFS: 1.9 yr, IQR: 1.06-2.74). After adjusting for age, sex, and extent of resection, MG4 was predictive of progression-free-survival (HR:7.16, 95%CI: 1.12-45.77, p = 0.04) but neither MG3 (p = 0.47), WHO Grade 2 (p = 0.16), or WHO Grade 3 status (p = 0.10) were predictive of PFS.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides data supporting the use of Molecular Group to predict outcomes after proton beam radiotherapy in surgically resected intracranial meningioma. MG4 status may identify patients with poor local control after conventional dose proton radiotherapy for which treatment escalation is warranted.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM) is an aggressive brain tumour showing low survival and characterised by poor therapeutic opportunities. We have recently described the expression of Acid Sensing Ion Channel 3 (ASIC3), a proton gated ion channel, in GBM cancer stem cell (CSC) derived from human biopsies, while low ASIC3 levels in the healthy human brain tissue. We have demonstrated that the chronic activation of ASIC3 by 2-guanidine-4-methylquinazoline (GMQ) selectively induces GBM CSC death while being virtually safe for neurons. To investigate the therapeutic potential of ASIC3 modulation, we virtually designed and synthesized a library of GMQ like compounds. We developed an automated imaging platform to screen compounds affecting CSC-derived neurospheres growth, and we selected a promising lead. ASIC3 specificity was validated using the selective toxin APETx2, as well as the lentiviral shRNA mediated downregulation of ASIC3. The pharmacokinetic of our putative lead was assessed following intravenous administration in mice. ASIC3 modulation by GMQ demonstrated to be more effective than Temozolomide (TMZ), the standard drug used in clinic against GBM, in controlling GBM CSCs growth in vitro. Based on this evidence, a virtual screening of GMQ analogues was performed, enabling the design of novel ASIC3 agonists with enhanced potency and improved predicted pharmacokinetic properties. Subsequent synthesis and a preliminary structure activity relationship (SAR) on GMQ-inspired analogues led to the identification of a new, patentable ASIC3 activator more potent than TMZ and GMQ itself. The efficacy of our lead across GBM CSCs subtypes strongly correlated with ASIC3 expression levels and account for its potential use as a therapeutic opportunity in controlling GBM CSCs growth. Our findings identify chronic ASIC3 activation as a meaningful strategy for the control of GBM CSCs growth. We identified a novel highly selective ASIC3 modulator as an innovative approach for GBM treatment.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The blood–brain barrier (BBB) blocks therapeutic agents, limiting treatment of CNS tumors. Current BBB breaching methods are limited by brief permeabilization, high neurotoxicity, and procedural complexity, highlighting a need for a platform that allows continuous, safe drug passage across the BBB while simplifying procedure. We have previously found that transferred hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) massively infiltrate into brain tumor and tumor‑derived chemokine signals direct their migration. We hypothesize that intravenously transferred chemokine-receptor-engineered HSCs will deliver therapeutic payloads efficiently and selectively to brain tumor sites when administrated post focused irradiation. In this study, we established methodology for efficient transient and constitutive HSC engineering (80% electroporation positive rate, 40–50 % lentiviral infection rate, no significant viability loss). Mouse and human HSCs were successfully engineered to secrete an immune checkpoint inhibitor, human PD1‑decoy (hPD1-decoy). The decoy bound to both human and murine PD‑1 ligands on GBM cells, and conditioned medium containing hPD1‑decoy significantly enhanced T‑cell IFNγ production and GBM cytotoxicity in co-culture of OT1 T cell and KR158B-luc-OVA. In conclusion, we have established a versatile HSC‑based platform capable of delivering a functional immune checkpoint inhibitor, hPD1‑decoy, with demonstrated T‑cell function booster bioactivity. Building on these findings, future studies will evaluate in vivo delivery of hPD1‑decoy‑expressing, chemokine‑receptor‑engineered HSCs in combination with focal tumor irradiation. This strategy offers a simple intravenous approach that bypasses cumbersome biologic manufacturing, achieves tumor‑specific drug delivery, and has broad translational potential for CNS oncology and beyond.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We start with a brief introduction to the many faces of the Sun, the dynamic star that is the main source of space weather. We explain the need for spacecraft observations, the structure of the solar atmosphere, and the Sun’s magnetic cycle. Next, we focus on the Sun’s influence on Earth, define ‘space weather,’ and briefly discuss its effects on our technology and related socio-economic impacts. Then, we present data-driven, physics-based simulation models with predictive capabilities that enable forecasting and mitigation. We focus on models developed by my team at KU Leuven and the results and predictions they produce: the heliospheric wind and CME evolution models EUHFORIA and ICARUS, the global solar corona model COCONUT, and the solar energetic particle acceleration and transport model Particle Radiation Asset Directed at IP Space Exploration. We end with a few take-home messages.</jats:p>

title: A Progressive Instructional Paradigm for Physics-informed Neural Networks
abstract: <jats:p>Physics-informed neural networks as an interdisciplinary field combining deep learning and physical modeling, which needs high demands on student ability to transfer knowledge across disciplines. To address the cognitive gap students face when transitioning from traditional mathematical modeling to deep learning methods, this paper develops a three-stage progressive instructional paradigm. Taking the one-dimensional heat conduction equation as an example, teacher guides students through three successive cognitive stage, i.e., mechanistic modeling, data-driven modeling, and physics-informed modeling, corresponding respectively to the finite difference method, pure data-driven MLP fitting, and the PINNs approach. Rather than introducing PINNs directly as a new algorithm, the proposed design organizes their learning as a problem-driven cognitive progression. This can help students understand the paradigm shift from traditional numerical computation to data-driven learning and ultimately to physics-informed integration.</jats:p>

title: A physics-informed machine learning framework for high-resolution land subsidence prediction in the Greater Houston Area
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Land subsidence induced by groundwater extraction poses significant threats to urban infrastructure and flood resilience in rapidly urbanizing coastal regions worldwide. This study presents a novel physics-informed machine learning framework that integrates Persistent Scatterer Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (PS-InSAR) observations, consolidation theory principles, and convolutional neural networks (CNN) for comprehensive land subsidence prediction in the Greater Houston Area. Processing 155 Sentinel-1 SAR images spanning January 2020 to March 2023 generated a high-resolution deformation dataset of 10,652 persistent scatterer points validated through comprehensive integration with 54 continuously operating GPS reference stations, achieving RMSE of 2.1 mm/year and correlation coefficient of 0.96. The hybrid framework integrates twelve mapped conditioning factors representing geological, hydrogeological, topographic, and anthropogenic domains, supplemented by clay-thickness and growth-fault inputs, within a physics-guided CNN architecture, achieving an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) of 0.9862, precision of 0.94, and recall of 0.92, which substantially exceed those of conventional machine learning approaches. Spatial analysis reveals that 18.66% of the study area (approximately 1,848 km
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    ) exhibits high to very high land subsidence susceptibility, with maximum observed rates reaching 24.3 mm/year in western Harris County near the Katy Prairie region. Unlike purely data-driven models that infer temporal dependence from empirical associations, the proposed framework embeds consolidation-derived temporal memory, allowing delayed aquitard response to influence subsidence susceptibility. Results indicate continued land subsidence despite significant regulatory interventions aimed at reducing groundwater extraction, with emerging subsidence hotspots identified in suburban areas experiencing rapid development. This framework provides critical insights for sustainable groundwater management, infrastructure planning, and flood risk mitigation in the Houston metropolitan region and offers a transferable methodology for similar coastal subsidence-prone areas worldwide.
                  </jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We present the first application of spectral nudging in a probabilistic ensemble forecasting framework, combining the physics‐based European Centre for Medium‐Range Weather Forecasts' Integrated Forecasting System ensemble (IFS‐ENS) with forecasts from the probabilistic machine‐learned Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System Ensemble. Large scales of virtual temperature and vorticity are relaxed toward the machine‐learned forecasts, while mesoscale structures remain governed by the physics‐based model. This hybrid ensemble shows substantial improvements in large‐scale forecast skill, with gains in predictive skill extended by up to 2 days in the Tropics and by approximately half a day in the extratropics relative to IFS‐ENS. Despite nudging being applied only to upper‐air fields, improvements are also found in several near‐surface parameters. Tropical cyclone track forecasts improve significantly, consistent with improved representation of the large‐scale steering flow, without degrading storm intensity or ensemble spread. These results demonstrate that spectral nudging can be successfully extended to ensemble prediction and provide an attractive pathway for combining machine‐learned and physics‐based weather prediction systems.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Objective</jats:italic>
                    . Scintillation detectors with excellent timing resolution enable more precise localization of radiation sources in positron emission tomography, leading to substantial improvements in diagnostic capability for diseases such as cancer and dementia. At the timing precision required for such applications at the picosecond scale, detector performance is governed by the dynamics of scintillation photons generated within the detector and their subsequent detection processes. However, detector signals have conventionally been treated only as collective responses of many photons due to structural constraints inherent to photodetectors. In this study, we overcome this fundamental limitation using deep learning framework.
                    <jats:italic>Approach</jats:italic>
                    . The proposed method estimates photon-by-photon arrival times directly from detector waveforms without requiring any modification to the detector structure; the method operates on an event-by-event basis without ground-truth labels by integrating an unsupervised learning framework with a physically informed detector-response model.
                    <jats:italic>Main results</jats:italic>
                    . Through comprehensive validation combining Monte Carlo simulation and experimental measurements across various detector configurations, we experimentally demonstrate improved timing resolution, visualized depth-of-interaction-dependent photon transport, and classified Cherenkov and scintillation photons based on the estimated photon-level timing information using a unified deep learning-based framework.
                    <jats:italic>Significance</jats:italic>
                    . These results provide experimental access to photon dynamics, bridging the gap between theoretical modeling and experimental observation, and they open a new data-driven pathway for discovery in detector physics and optimization.

abstract: <jats:p>Identifying employees who may need additional professional-learning support could help organisations allocate training resources, but model comparisons in this area often omit trivial baselines and class-specific metrics. We compare seven classifiers (decision tree, random forest, logistic regression, k-nearest neighbours, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) with a rule-based and a majority-class baseline under one protocol: stratified hold-out, the same tuning procedure, paired bootstrap confidence intervals, a descriptive repeated cross-validation check, and SHAP and LIME explanations. Experiment 1 predicts a KPI label of undocumented origin for 17,415 employees (35.9% positive); it is an illustrative comparison using the label as distributed, not validated evidence about KPI attainment. Experiment 2 predicts promotion for 54,808 employees (8.5% positive), a related task from the same public source and not an external validation. In Experiment 1, learning models reached macro-F1 of 0.628 to 0.663, against 0.590 for the rule-based baseline; a depth-5 decision tree was 0.005 below the reference random forest (95% bootstrap CI −0.016 to +0.005) but was not shown non-inferior at a 0.01 margin. In Experiment 2, boosting models were best (macro-F1 0.734 to 0.739), the decision tree was clearly worse (−0.030), and only about 35% of promoted employees were identified. Associations with training indicators are not causal, and no effect on decisions was tested.</jats:p>

<jats:p>Soft drinks, often high in added sugars, have raised significant public health concerns due to

outcomes associated with excessive sugar consumption. Overall, our findings contribute

highlight the efficacy of Ensemble Learning approaches in assessing and addressing public
health concerns. This study provides actionable recommendations for individuals and health
organizations to promote healthier dietary habits and mitigate the risk of sugar-related health
complications, emphasizing the importance of evidence-based interventions in safeguarding
public health.</jats:p>

title: Machine Learning-based Churn Customer Prediction

affiliation.name: Computer Science and Technology, Nanjing Normal University

abstract: <jats:p>This paper goes through and puts together earlier work on predicting customer churn, giving a structured look at the methods and approaches that appear in the literature. A large portion of studies still lean on traditional machine learning, though some treat churn as a special binary problem using a modified One-Class SVM, compare it with standard methods, and check how well it performs. Several studies step away from conventional machine learning by applying deep learning, running comparisons across different machine learning techniques, and using AdaBoost to lift classification performance, with Monte Carlo simulations doing the evaluation. Some teams have also turned to ensemble learning, pitting 11 machine learning algorithms against seven sampling methods. Using ensembles built on logistic regression (LR), XGBoost, and random forests (RF), together with various sampling strategies, the best pipeline was chosen based on AUC scores. These studies have not been free of trouble; they run into problems like weak interpretability or poor generalization in some models, and sometimes not enough attention is paid to customer privacy, raising privacy concerns. But these problems are not unsolvable: federated learning can block privacy leaks, and combining expert systems with transfer learning can fix limited interpretability and poor generalization.</jats:p>

title: Erratum: “Predicting the spatio-temporal distribution of the droplets based on the machine learning algorithm” [Phys. Fluids 37 , 023337 (2025)]
Forecasting High Electricity Demand Using Explainable Machine Learning
journal: Balkan Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering

affiliation.name: BATMAN ÜNİVERSİTESİ

abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">The objective of this study was to predict the onset of high demand, the highest half-hourly average power, and the total duration of high demand over the next two hours using historical electricity consumption data from residential households. Half-hourly measurements from 2013 for 200 standard-tariff residential households selected from the Low Carbon London dataset were used. High demand was defined as exceeding the 90th percentile of each household’s average power values during the January–February period. The models were developed using data from 160 households; transfer performance was evaluated on the 40 households not included in model training. The process was divided into a training period (March–June), model selection in July, calibration of prediction intervals in August, and a testing period (September–December). The selected models were retrained using March–July data. Separate models were built for the three targets; Random Forest, histogram-based gradient boosting (HistGB), XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost were compared against a weekly seasonal reference. Model selection was initially based on average precision (AP) for the target and mean absolute error (MAE) for power and duration. For the residential units used in the training, the HistGB model selected during the testing period produced an AP of 0.4183; the CatBoost models produced an MAE of 0.2704 kW for power and 9.2361 minutes for duration. The contributions of historical consumption and calendar features to the model predictions were examined using the SHAP method. In the early warning evaluation, 78.81% of relevant events in known residential units were detected in advance; 60.93% of early warnings were identified as false alarms. The improvement in duration prediction relative to a reference that yields a duration of zero in every window remained limited. The findings indicate that the approach could contribute to monitoring residential demand; however, the burden of false alarms and the limited success in duration prediction must be taken into account from a practical standpoint.</jats:p>

title: Deep-Feature Fusion and Hybrid Machine Learning for Canine Dermatological Image Classification

affiliation.name: Department of Veterinary Biostatistics, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Selçuk University, Konya 42130, Turkey

abstract: <jats:p>Automated classification of canine dermatological images is challenging because visually overlapping lesions, uncertain repository labels, and repeated or transformed source photographs can influence performance estimates. This study evaluated fixed ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet201, ResNet50, and EfficientNetB0 features, alone and in fusion, with support vector machine (SVM), multilayer perceptron (MLP), and logistic regression classifiers for six repository-provided categories. Transformation-robust source auditing yielded 3088 images: 2862 development images from 864 source groups and a source-group-separated held-out internal test set of 226 images from 226 groups. Model selection used five-fold source-group-aware outer cross-validation with source-group-aware inner grid search. DenseNet201–EfficientNetB0 + SVM achieved the highest mean outer-fold balanced accuracy (0.9462 ± 0.0174), while triple fusion was comparable (0.9449 ± 0.0142) with a larger feature representation. On the held-out internal test set, accuracy was 0.8319 (95% CI 0.7832–0.8805), balanced accuracy was 0.7806 (0.7219–0.8384), and macro F1 was 0.7871 (0.7234–0.8432). Independent, clinically annotated external validation remains necessary to assess generalizability. These findings highlight the value of source-aware evaluation and parsimonious feature fusion when assessing multiclass canine dermatological image classification using repository-based datasets.</jats:p>

title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of College Students’ Employment Status

affiliation.name: School of Information Science and Technology, Shanghai Sanda University

abstract: <jats:p>As the number of college graduates continues to increase, improving the accuracy of employment prediction has become an important research topic. This study uses public college students’ employment datasets and machine learning (ML) to investigate students’ employment outcomes. Key factors, including academic performance, technical skills, internship experience, project experience, and institutional background, were selected as predictive features. After data preprocessing, four ML models were developed for classification. Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 values were used for evaluation. In addition, the employment rate analysis, feature importance analysis, and correlation analysis were carried out to examine the factors related to the employment results. Among the four models, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) achieved the highest accuracy (69.67%), only 1.2 percentage points above the blind-guessing baseline (68.47%), while Decision Tree (DT) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) (both 68.48%) performed no differently from this baseline; Random Forest (RF) achieved the best overall balance across evaluation metrics. Correlation analysis further revealed moderate positive associations between employment outcomes and wage level with internship experience, technical competence, and academic performance. These findings suggest that feature-level analysis, rather than classification accuracy alone, offers practical value for universities in guiding students’ career development and planning.</jats:p>

title: Correction to: Machine learning quantifies within-subject facial change in acromegaly
Lassa Fever Predictive Model Using Machine Learning Techniques

abstract:
<jats:p>Lassa Fever, a severe hemorrhagic fever caused by the Lassa virus, is notably prevalent in
West Africa and can be fatal if not managed properly. Effective outbreak control and mitigation
rely heavily on early detection. This study introduces a predictive model for forecasting Lassa
Fever using machine learning techniques. The research employs an extensive dataset that
includes epidemiological and environmental data collected over multiple years to construct a
reliable predictive model. Several machine learning algorithms, such as Random Forest,
Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Gradient Boosting, are utilized to analyze historical data
and predict potential Lassa Fever outbreaks. To improve model accuracy and minimize false
positives, feature engineering and data preprocessing methods are applied. The dataset was
divided into 80% for training and 20% for testing, with various algorithms—including SVM,
K-Nearest Neighbor, Naïve Bayes, and Logistic Regression—tested to build the predictive
models. The performance of these models was assessed using metrics like accuracy, precision,
recall, and F1 score. The SVM model demonstrated the highest performance, achieving
accuracy, precision, and F1 scores of 90%, 91%, and 96%, respectively. Consequently, SVM
was selected as the preferred algorithm for this research. The study recommends the use of this
model in Nigeria's medical industry to enhance diagnostic speed and reduce medical errors in
healthcare settings. Keywords: Lassa Fever, Predictive Model, Machine Learning, Support
Vector Machines (SVM), and Healthcare Diagnostics</jats:p>

title: IMG-01 Emerging Applications of Machine Learning in Glioblastoma: Opportunities for Clinical Integration

university of california Davis , Sacrament,

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most lethal primary brain tumor, characterized by significant molecular and clinical heterogeneity that limits effective diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate the utility of machine learning (ML) approaches applied to longitudinal plasma-based metabolomic datasets for classification of treatment states and assessment of clinical applicability in GBM.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Longitudinal plasma samples from 36 patients with GBM undergoing standard-of-care treatment were analyzed using untargeted metabolomics, lipidomics, and biogenic amine profiling. Supervised ML models were applied to classify treatment phases and disease states.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ML models accurately classified treatment phases and disease states with high performance (AUC up to 0.91).                     <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ML-driven analysis of longitudinal plasma metabolomic data represents a promising approach for real-time disease monitoring in GBM. title: Machine Learning Approaches for Predicting Consumer Purchase Intention in E-Commerce

affiliation.name: School of Computer Science and Engineering, The University of New South Wales

abstract: <jats:p>As more and more activities are required in the new era market, the personalised marketing activities have been extended step-by-step. The study used four machine learning algorithms to analyze the prediction performance of Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) on the prediction for the purchase intention of online shoppers in the University of California, Irvine (UCI) Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention dataset. The dataset was preprocessed by handling missing values, encoding categorical features, and standardising numerical features. From this experiment, the gradient boosting model gave better accuracy than the others, and XGBoost gave better accuracy in all the other models, with an accuracy of 90.31% and a Receiver Operating Characteristic – Area Under the Curve (ROC-AUC) score of 0.9334. The feature importance analysis (FIA) also shows that PageValues, ExitRates, and ProductRelated_Duration are relatively more indicative of purchase behaviour. Thus, the above research has achieved its objective of enhancing the accuracy of the prediction of purchase intention in intelligent e-commerce.</jats:p>

title: Modelling Loan Default Data of German Customers: Predictive Machine Learning Studies

affiliation.name: Federal University of Technology Akure

abstract: <jats:p>This study considered logistic regression and random forest models in modelling the loan default data of German Customers. The data were randomly partitioned into an 80% training set and a 20% test set. The train set was used to fit the data, while the test set served as the out-of-sample data used to evaluate the performance of the model. On the train set, the random forest performs better than the logistic regression model across all the evaluation metrics. On the test dataset, the random forest has superior specificity, precision, accuracy, and F1-score, but the logistic regression model produced a better sensitivity. This means that the model was better at identifying a bad loan; this is, in fact, the desire and priority of every financial institution – a model that is capable of detecting the risk of loan default. In terms of efficiency, the logistic regression model produced lower variance than the random forest, which had high variance.</jats:p>

title: Optimization of duty-cycled plasma actuation parameters over a square cylinder using surrogate-assisted evolutionary reinforcement learning

affiliation.name: Department of Aerodynamics, School of Aeronautics, Northwestern Polytechnical University 1 , Xi'an 710072,

National Key Laboratory of Aircraft Configuration Design 2 , Xi'an 710072,

abstract: <jats:p>Plasma-based flow control has emerged as a promising approach for suppressing wake instabilities and reducing aerodynamic drag in bluff-body flows; however, its effectiveness depends on complex nonlinear interactions between actuation parameters and vortex dynamics. In this study, a surrogate-assisted evolutionary reinforcement learning (SA-ERL) framework is used to optimize duty-cycled plasma actuation over a square cylinder at Reynolds number Re=200. The control space consists of duty-cycle frequency f, duty-cycle ratio τ, and phase difference ϕ between symmetric trailing-edge actuators, forming a coupled, three-dimensional, multi-objective optimization problem. A hybrid Gaussian process-Transformer (GP-Transformer) surrogate is trained on computational fluid dynamics samples and refined through uncertainty-guided active learning, coupled with an evolutionary reinforcement learning (ERL) optimizer that combines a genetic algorithm (GA) for global search and proximal policy optimization for local refinement. The surrogate achieves high predictive accuracy, while the ERL optimizer outperforms standalone GA and deep reinforcement learning by converging to a higher and more stable terminal reward. Compared with the baseline, the optimized actuation (f=20 Hz, τ=0.9, ϕ=0) achieves about 52% reduction in mean drag and 97% suppression of lift oscillations, while reducing normalized actuation power nearly 10% relative to continuous forcing. Flow-field analysis shows the optimized frequency dominates over natural vortex shedding, reducing resonance risk, weakening coherent wake structures, and weakening the recirculation region. These results demonstrate that SA-ERL offers a computationally efficient, interpretable framework for multi-parameter plasma control, extendable to higher Reynolds numbers and three-dimensional flows.</jats:p>

title: Machine Learning Technique for Determination of Normal and Abnormal ECG Heartbeat

proper attention and care besides the ribs. The alarming rate of heart defects and increasing
death toll calls for the urgent need to improve the ECG platform with enhance machine

title: Causal Machine Learning for Treatment Effect Heterogeneity: Interpretation, Benchmarking, Validation

affiliation.name: Department of Neuroradiology, University Hospital Heidelberg , Heidelberg ,
LMU Munich , Munich ,
Munich Center for Machine Learning , Munich ,
LMU Munich , Munich ,
Munich Center for Machine Learning , Munich ,
Division of Pharmacoepidemiology, Brigham and Women's Hospital , Boston ,
Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health , Boston ,
LMU Munich , Munich ,
Munich Center for Machine Learning , Munich ,

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Causal machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising approach for predicting individualized treatment effects and advancing precision medicine, moving beyond the limitations of conventional one-variable-at-a-time subgroup analyses of randomized trials. A recent benchmarking study by Chen and colleagues evaluated several causal ML learners across two large trials and concluded that current methods do not yet demonstrate reliable performance for clinical application. While such applied methodological investigations are valuable, this conclusion warrants a more nuanced examination. Multiple independent research groups have successfully applied causal ML across respiratory medicine and critical care, identifying clinically meaningful treatment effect heterogeneity that prior subgroup analyses had not resolved, although these applications have methodological limitations and do not yet establish that the detected heterogeneity is robust across internal and external validation. We outline four sequential and iterative dimensions central to credible causal ML analyses: choice of learner, model training with cross-fitting, internal validation using calibration-for-benefit and rank-weighted metrics, and external validation aligned with the original causal question. With careful methodological execution, causal ML holds considerable promise for personalized treatment decisions and warrants continued development; dismissing the field prematurely risks overlooking a powerful tool for personalized treatment decisions.</jats:p>

title: PATH-63 Comparison of Feature-Based Machine Learning and Deep Learning for Grading Glioma Using Fractional Anisotropy

affiliation.name: The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center , Houston,
University of Sussex , Brighton,
University of Southern California , Los Angeles,
University of Pennsylvania , Philadelphia,
The University of Texas at Austin , Austin,
The University of British Columbia , Vancouver,
University of Washington , Seattle,

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fractional anisotropy (FA) has been explored as an imaging biomarker of diffuse glioma grade, but the relative performance of interpretable machine learning and image-based deep learning approaches remain uncertain. As part of a 2025 NeuroHackademy group project, we compared machine learning and deep learning models for FA-based classification of low-grade (WHO grade 2–3) versus high-grade (WHO grade 4) diffuse gliomas using the publicly available UCSF-PDGM dataset, a preoperative MRI resource containing 501 adults with grade II–IV diffuse gliomas.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were split into training (80%) and test (20%) cohorts, with class imbalance handled by weighting in both pipelines. The machine learning model was a random forest using tabular imaging features derived from FA, including whole-brain, hemispheric asymmetry, and peritumoral distance-based measures, with and without clinical and molecular variables. The clinical model included age, sex, IDH status, and MGMT methylation status. The deep learning pipeline used FA images directly and employed a 10-layer residual neural network trained for 30 epochs with a learning rate of 0.0001.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The imaging-only machine learning model achieved test AUC 0.873 and 84% accuracy, with sensitivity 0.951, specificity 0.750, positive predictive value 0.939, and negative predictive value 0.789. The corresponding confusion matrix included 77 true positives and 15 true negatives. Adding clinical and molecular variables improved discrimination, with AUC increasing to approximately 0.94. Feature analysis showed that molecular variables accounted for 53.9% of total importance; the age-IDH interaction (13.6%) and IDH wildtype status (11.9%) were among the strongest predictors. In contrast, the deep learning model achieved 74.0% test accuracy, 84.5% sensitivity, and 30.0% specificity, with findings suggesting overfitting on training data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this cohort, FA-based classification was more robust with interpretable tabular machine learning than with image-based deep learning. Performance improved further when clinical and molecular features were incorporated, supporting multimodal and explainable approaches for preoperative glioma grading.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Medical Insurance Cost Prediction: Heterogeneous Machine Learning Models and SHAP-Based Interpretability

abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Medical insurance cost prediction supports premium design, risk assessment, reserve planning, and healthcare resource allocation. This study used a public dataset containing 2,772 records and seven variables. Because 1,435 rows were fully duplicated and the dataset lacked identifiers or timestamps that could verify their independence, the main analysis retained 1,337 unique observations. Potential high-BMI and high-charge observations identified by the interquartile range rule were preserved because they may represent genuine insurance risk. The target was transformed using log1p, and predictions were returned to the original cost scale for evaluation. Six heterogeneous models were compared: Huber Regression, Kernel Ridge Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Machine, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and a Back Propagation (BP) Neural Network. XGBoost achieved the highest mean cross-validated Coefficient of Determination (R
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    ) on the log scale, whereas Random Forest obtained the lowest test Mean Squared Error (MSE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the highest original-scale R
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    of 0.905. Error analysis showed larger underprediction in the highest-cost quartile. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identified smoking status and age as the dominant predictors. The results demonstrate the importance of combining heterogeneous model comparison, scale-aware evaluation, and transparent interpretation.
                  </jats:p>

title: AI-Based Spacecraft Health Monitoring System: A Machine Learning Approach for Telemetry-Based Health Classification

affiliation.name: Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Gaya College of Engineering, Bihar Engineering University, Gaya, Bihar, India.

abstract: <jats:p>Spacecraft continuously generate telemetry data from onboard sensors and subsystems to support monitoring of health, performance, and operational status. Manual observation of large volumes of telemetry can be difficult and may delay recognition of abnormal conditions. This paper presents an AI-Based Spacecraft Health Monitoring System developed during a research internship at Acceleron Aerospace. The proposed prototype combines ESP8266-based sensor acquisition, synthetic telemetry generation, Python-based data processing, a Random Forest machine learning classifier, and an interactive Streamlit dashboard. The dataset contains temperature, humidity, light, three-axis acceleration, and three-axis gyroscope measurements, with spacecraft health classified into HEALTHY, WARNING, and CRITICAL states. A balanced synthetic dataset of 3,000 samples was generated and divided into training and testing subsets. The trained model was integrated into the monitoring application to provide rapid health classification and graphical telemetry visualization. The work demonstrates a modular foundation for AI-assisted spacecraft monitoring and can be extended toward real telemetry, anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, and intelligent alerting.</jats:p>

title: Anti-AI Infringement Methods for Image Data: A Machine Learning Lifecycle Perspective

affiliation.name: School of Computer and Electronic Information, Nanjing Normal University

abstract: <jats:p>The rapid development of the diffusion model has promoted the wide application of AI-generated images, and also brought serious copyright issues. For this reason, the anti-AI infringement methods in the image field came into being. However, the existing research involves multiple technical paths such as data poisoning, adversarial perturbation, machine unlearning, content detection, but lacks a unified classification framework. Starting from the lifecycle of machine learning, this paper constructs a five-level classification system covering data-level, input-level, model-level, output-level and system-level, systematically combs the mainstream methods and their technical characteristics, and summarizes the commonly used evaluation datasets and performance indicators. On this basis, the challenges of current methods in terms of robustness, transferability and engineering deployment are analyzed. This review aims to provide a structured reference for image copyright protection research. By mapping each anti-infringement strategy to a specific phase of the AI lifecycle, the proposed framework clarifies the logical relationships among different approaches and facilitates cross-method comparison and practical selection.</jats:p>

title: Machine Learning-Assisted Experimental Electronic Nose Measurements for Biopesticide Treatment Discrimination in Tomatoes

affiliation.name: Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, İstanbul Kültür University, 34158 İstanbul, Türkiye
Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering, Yıldız Technical University, 34220 İstanbul, Türkiye
Computer Programming, Vocational School of Higher Education, İstanbul Atlas University, 34403 İstanbul, Türkiye
Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering, Yıldız Technical University, 34220 İstanbul, Türkiye

abstract: <jats:p>This study evaluated whether a compact electronic nose could distinguish intact tomatoes treated with wood vinegar or neem oil from those without experimental biopesticide application. The dataset comprised 38 tomatoes and 228 technical runs, including six additional controls measured in triplicate initially and after 16 h: three untreated and three water-sprayed. Six commercial SnO2 sensors recorded voltages during a 180 s cycle. Six classifiers were compared using identical tomato-wise nested cross-validation with three outer folds, two inner folds, and five repetitions. With 54 full-cycle features, linear discriminant analysis (LDA) achieved 97.02% accuracy and 95.72% balanced accuracy; an artificial neural network (ANN) achieved 96.93% and 95.14%, respectively. Paired conditional intervals did not establish superiority of either model. Models trained on the original 32 fruits produced false biopesticide alarms in the new controls, including 17/36 ANN predictions. Incorporating eligible control fruit into training improved matched held-out performance, mainly under the new negative conditions. The separate two-treatment task included 32 fruits. These findings support exploratory recognition of patterns associated with application and show the value of procedural controls. Small control groups, unlogged chamber conditions, and missing chemical reference measurements limit chemical attribution and external screening claims.</jats:p>

title: Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Models for Flow-Level Multi-Class Darknet Traffic Classification
journal: Asian Journal of Research in Computer Science

affiliation.name: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Visakha Institute of Engineering & Technology (Autonomous), Visakhapatnam, affiliated with Jawaharlal Nehru Technological University, Gurajada, Vizianagaram, Andhra Pradesh, India.
Department of Information Technology, Indira Gandhi Delhi Technical University for Women, Delhi, India.
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, GMR Institute of Technology, Deemed to be University, Rajam, Andhra Pradesh, India.

abstract: <jats:p>Encrypted traffic classification is a key problem in network security because encryption and anonymity technologies limit access to packet contents used for monitoring and intrusion detection. This study compares six machine-learning and deep-learning models for classifying Layer 2 darknet traffic, distinguishing among Freenet, I2P, Tor, VPN, and ZeroNet traffic using the SafeSurf dataset. After removing duplicate records and observations with missing or infinite values, the final dataset comprised 75,201 flows described by 79 flow-level features, including port and protocol fields. Random Forest, XGBoost, Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and CNN-LSTM models were evaluated using identical stratified training, validation, and test partitions. Source and destination IP addresses and timestamps were excluded to avoid potential collection-specific information leakage. XGBoost achieved the highest test accuracy (94.78%), macro-F1 (0.9440), and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC; 0.9308), followed by Random Forest (93.50% accuracy, 0.9299 macro-F1, and 0.9136 MCC). MLP achieved 87.74% accuracy, followed by CNN-LSTM (84.84%), CNN (79.16%), and LSTM (77.13%). I2P and Tor were frequently confused, whereas tree-based models classified minority-class VPN traffic effectively. Removing the port fields lowered tree-model accuracy by 1.3 to 1.61 points without changing their ranking. McNemar’s tests on paired test-set predictions showed significant differences (all p < 0.001) for XGBoost versus Random Forest, XGBoost versus MLP, XGBoost versus CNN-LSTM, and MLP versus CNN-LSTM. These findings demonstrate the potential of flow-level features for five-class darknet technology classification, identify persistent classification challenges, and provide a baseline for evaluating generalisation to independent network environments.</jats:p>

title: A Machine Learning-Based Framework for Highway Traffic Behavior Modeling Using Vehicle Trajectory Data

affiliation.name: Faculty of Arts and Sciences, Beijing Normal University

abstract: <jats:p>Highway ramps are bottlenecks where merging and diverging maneuvers reduce speeds and disrupt headways. Accurate statistical modeling of traffic flow parameters is needed for microsimulation calibration and autonomous driving validation. Using the Mirror-Traffic dataset, this paper analyzes 760 vehicle trajectories comprising 143,160 frames, examines marginal distributions of speed, acceleration, time headway, and lane-changing frequency, and employs Copula functions to model speed-headway dependence. Weibull fits speed best across vehicle types, though truck speeds show some tail deviations; Laplace fits acceleration best. Lane-changing counts follow a negative binomial model with overdispersion, outperforming Poisson. The Gumbel copula captures upper-tail dependence between short headways and low speeds better than Clayton and Frank. Lane-specific speeds show the innermost lane has the highest and most concentrated speeds, while the outermost lane exhibits a bimodal distribution. Time headway varies across lanes, with median values of 2.149 s, 2.479 s, and 5.023 s for Lanes 1 through 3. These results provide parametric inputs for traffic flow modeling in Chinese ramp scenarios.</jats:p>

title: An Explainable Machine Learning Framework for Insider Threat Detection Using Behavioral Feature Engineering
journal: Dasinya Journal for Engineering and Informatics
abstract: <jats:p>Insider threat detection remains one of the most challenging problems in cybersecurity because malicious activities are often difficult to distinguish from legitimate user behavior. Many existing machine learning approaches rely on limited behavioral representations, high-dimensional feature spaces, and black-box models with limited interpretability, which constrains their practical utility in security operations. This paper proposes an explainable machine learning framework for insider threat detection based on behavioral feature engineering. The framework constructs daily user-level behavioral profiles from heterogeneous sources in the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) Insider Threat Dataset (Release 4.2), including logon, email, web browsing, file access, Universal Serial Bus (USB) device usage, and psychometric records. A Genetic Algorithm (GA) reduces the engineered feature space from 53 to 35 features while retaining comparable predictive performance. A LightGBM classifier is then optimized through Bayesian hyperparameter tuning with Optuna, followed by decision threshold optimization to balance precision and recall. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provide global and local explanations, enabling security analysts to examine the factors behind individual decisions. On the independent test set, the framework achieved 99.79% accuracy, 83.78% precision, 60.78% recall, 70.45% F1-score, 97.92% ROC-AUC, 71.14% PR-AUC, 80.37% balanced accuracy, and 71.27% MCC. The gap between high accuracy and lower recall and F1-score reflects the severe class imbalance of the dataset. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of integrating behavioral feature engineering, feature selection, model optimization, and explainable AI within a unified framework.</jats:p>

title: Predictive Modeling for Early Detection of Cardiovascular Diseases Using Machine Learning
journal: International Journal of Computer Science and Mathematical Theory

affiliation.name: Computer Science Department Modibbo Adama University, Yola, Adamawa State, Nigeria

abstract:
<jats:p>Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading cause of death globally. Early diagnosis and
intervention are crucial for improving patient outcomes. This study explores the development and
evaluation of machine learning models for predicting CVD. The research employed a retrospective
cohort design, analyzing electronic health records (EHRs) to identify patients with and without
CVD. Machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest and Gradient Boosting, were
compared for their effectiveness in predicting CVD based on patient data. The analysis involved
pre-processing the data to ensure quality and then training and evaluating the models.
Performance metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score were used to assess the models'
ability to identify patterns and predict CVD risk. The results revealed that both Random Forest
and Gradient Boosting models achieved promising results in predicting CVD. The models were
able to classify patients into high-risk and low-risk categories based on their characteristics. This
study suggests that machine learning has the potential to be a valuable tool for supporting CVD
diagnosis and risk assessment. Further research is needed to validate these findings in larger and
more diverse populations.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Accurate and interpretable classification of angiographically defined coronary artery disease (CAD) remains a relevant benchmark for clinical machine-learning research. This study compares eight supervised-learning models using the Cleveland Heart Disease dataset. After complete-case exclusion, 297 records with 13 clinical and diagnostic predictors were analyzed. Nominal predictors were one-hot encoded, binary predictors were retained in their original coding, and continuous predictors were standardized for scale-sensitive models. Preprocessing parameters were estimated using training data only and re-estimated within each cross-validation fold. Logistic Regression, a Decision Tree, k-Nearest Neighbors, a Multilayer Perceptron, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, a Support Vector Machine, and an equal-weight Soft-Voting Ensemble were assessed using a stratified 80/20 train–test split and stratified 10-fold cross-validation. Test performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score, confusion matrices, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Under stratified 10-fold cross-validation, Logistic Regression achieved the highest mean accuracy (83.83%), followed by the Multilayer Perceptron (83.16%), while Logistic Regression also achieved the highest mean ROC AUC (0.9093). On the complementary 60-record held-out test partition, the Support Vector Machine and Multilayer Perceptron achieved the highest observed accuracy (86.67%), whereas the Support Vector Machine achieved the highest ROC AUC (0.9565). Tree-based feature-importance analyses and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis of the Gradient-Boosting model showed relatively large model-attribution values for the number of major vessels visualized by fluoroscopy, the asymptomatic chest-pain category, age, ST-segment depression, cholesterol, and specific thallium stress-test categories. More complex models showed no consistent performance advantage. Excluding the fluoroscopy-derived predictor ca reduced mean cross-validation accuracy and ROC AUC for all eight classifiers. In the more restrictive seven-predictor analysis, which additionally excluded thallium and exercise-test variables, the highest mean cross-validation accuracy was 78.15% (Logistic Regression), while the highest ROC AUC was 0.8315 (Random Forest). Given the small, historical, single-center sample, the inclusion of target-proximal diagnostic predictors, the absence of calibration assessment, and the lack of external validation, the findings should be interpreted as an internal comparative benchmark rather than evidence of clinical applicability or readiness for clinical deployment.</jats:p>

title: Smoking-Status Determination from Human Nails Based on Attenuated Total Reflection Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy and Machine Learning

abstract: <jats:p>Human nails are a durable, non-invasively collected keratin matrix that records exposure over months. We assessed whether attenuated total reflection Fourier transform infrared (ATR FT-IR) spectroscopy of intact fingernail clippings, combined with machine learning, can discriminate self-reported smokers from non-smokers. Spectra (n = 3681) from 87 donors (42 smokers, 45 non-smokers) were second-derivative transformed, truncated to the informative regions and L2-normalized. PLS-DA and a radial-basis-function support-vector-machine discriminant analysis (SVM-DA) were developed with fully nested, donor-grouped tuning and evaluated over ten repeated 20-donor hold-outs at the spectrum and donor levels. Aggregating spectra per donor improved discrimination (+0.07–0.09 AUROC). SVM-DA on all nails reached a donor-level AUROC of 0.86 (95% CI 0.75–0.98; balanced accuracy 0.77, specificity 0.91, sensitivity 0.62); PLS-DA, logistic regression and random forest reached 0.79–0.84, with no statistically significant differences. Smokers were older and predominantly male: sex and age alone gave an AUROC of 0.79; adding the spectral score raised it to 0.89, an uncertain gain (95% CI −0.04 to 0.23), and SVM-DA retained an AUROC of 0.79 in male donors only. ATR FT-IR of nails carries a smoking-associated signal, but confirmation in a demographically matched, biochemically verified, independent cohort is required before forensic use.</jats:p>

title: Assessing Machine Learning Model Stability and the Value of Hyperparameter Transfer: Effects of Sample Size and Dataset Heterogeneity

affiliation.name: Muğla Sıtkı Koçman Üniversitesi

abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">This study investigates two critical factors affecting the performance of traditional machine learning (ML) models: training dataset size and the impact of integrating external, potentially noisy data (dataset heterogeneity). Additionally, we evaluate the effectiveness of hyperparameter transfer. Experiments utilized three distinct COVID-19 blood test datasets: the Wuhan dataset (356 cases), used as the source for hyperparameter extraction; the San Raffaele Hospital (OSR) dataset (1,624 cases), serving as the primary target for training, testing, and creating balanced subsets of varying sizes; and the Istituto Ortopedico Galeazzi (IOG) dataset (58 cases), which was integrated to simulate heterogeneity due to its collection via different devices and clinical settings. The discussion extends to a simple TL approach in which optimal hyperparameters were transferred from the Wuhan source to OSR target models. Both Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) and Generalized Linear Model (GLM) algorithms were tested in traditional and TL settings. Performance was evaluated using accuracy, area under the curve, sensitivity, and specificity. Results show that data quantity and quality substantially influence model performance, with saturation typically observed around 450–500 observations. The addition of external, noisy data (IOG) significantly impacted specificity, particularly in GBM models trained on smaller OSR samples. Specifically, the GBM-based hyperparameter transfer learning (HTL) model demonstrated a “crossover” effect; while it initially lagged behind traditional ML in accuracy at low data volumes (0.74 vs. 0.78 at n = 50), it surpassed ML in larger datasets, reaching a peak accuracy of 0.87 (vs. 0.84 for ML) at n = 1,100. However, due to heterogeneity, this approach also exhibited sensitivity fluctuations in high-data regimes. GLM models demonstrated greater robustness with consistent accuracy levels (~0.84) and minimal variance, possibly due to their simpler structure and better alignment with underlying data characteristics. This study highlights the importance of considering both training data volume and integrity in ML and TL applications. While increasing the quantity of data can enhance performance, the unfiltered inclusion of noisy external data may degrade it. Hyperparameter transfer is a promising strategy for maintaining model reliability across varying data conditions.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:p>Machine Learning has developed rapidly and increasingly becoming significant in agricultural
domain as there is need of efficient logical practice for detecting new and valuable information
in agricultural domain. Agriculture serves as the primary economic driver and major
employment provider for the majority of the population in Nigeria. However, the sector is
vulnerable to challenges stemming from inadequate agronomic practices. This study built an
Agricultural land assessment model that predict optimum yield using logistic regression model
and Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifiers using Python and VScode. Comparing Logistic
Regression and Support Vector Machine (SVM) for classifying crops based on their nutrient
content and yield, both algorithms exhibit high overall accuracy of around 87%. However,
SVM stands out due to its consistently high precision, recall, and F1-scores across various
crops. This indicates that SVM provides a more balanced and robust performance, vital for
accurate agricultural predictions. The study also introduces a novel application of machine
learning techniques to the field of agriculture and bridges the gap between traditional
agricultural practices and modern data analytics, fostering innovation and improving
agricultural efficiency and sustainability. The study can further enhance its impact on
agricultural productivity and sustainability by Incorporate Internet of Things (IoT) devices to
collect real-time data on soil moisture, temperature, and other environmental factors, promote
improving the accuracy of crop suitability predictions. Also to extend the model to include a
wider variety of crops and explore its applicability to different climatic and geographical
regions, ensuring broader relevance and utility</jats:p>

title: Drug Target Interaction Prediction and Anticancer Drug Screening Based on Spatio Temporal Sequence Prediction and Machine Learning

affiliation.name: Institute of Science and Technology, Beijing Normal-Hong Kong Baptist University (BNBU)

abstract: <jats:p>Cancer treatment has long faced problems such as long drug development cycle, high cost of experimental screening, drug resistance of monotherapy and complex mechanism of combination therapy. Based on the existing introduction, this paper reviews the drug target interaction prediction, drug combination synergy evaluation, spatio-temporal sequence modeling and data-driven anti-cancer drug screening. Firstly, this paper introduces DTI, anti-cancer drug screening process, common databases and collaborative scoring indicators; Secondly, the applications of traditional machine learning, deep learning and ensemble learning methods in DTI and drug combination prediction were compared; Thirdly, the value of spatio-temporal sequence prediction in modeling drug concentration, action time and cell response dynamics was analyzed; Finally, the problems of data heterogeneity, sample imbalance, lack of interpretability of the model and difficulties in clinical transformation faced by the current research are summarized, and it is proposed that in the future, the integration of multi omics, interpretable artificial intelligence and experimental verification closed loop should be strengthened. Research shows that machine learning and spatio-temporal sequence prediction can effectively improve the efficiency of anti-cancer drug screening, and provide important method support for combination drug optimization and precision treatment.</jats:p>

title: Explainable Machine Learning for Dataset-Defined Digital Eye Strain Risk Categories: Comparative Evaluation and Sensitivity Analysis

abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: This study compared eight machine-learning classifiers for three dataset-defined digital eye strain (DES) categories and examined the robustness and interpretation of their predictions. Methods: A publicly available dataset containing 800 observations and 11 nonconstant predictors was analyzed using training-only preprocessing, repeated stratified cross-validation, randomized hyperparameter optimization, and an 80:20 stratified train–test split. Additional analyses included nested cross-validation of support vector machine (SVM) and logistic regression (LR), feature ablation, probability calibration, and SHAP-based interpretation. Results: SVM achieved the highest mean repeated-CV macro-F1 (0.9861). On the held-out test set, SVM achieved 0.9625 accuracy and 0.9636 macro-F1, while LR achieved 0.9688 and 0.9714, respectively. Nested-CV macro-F1 values were similar for SVM (0.9777) and LR (0.9768). Excluding symptom-related predictors reduced test macro-F1 to 0.5141 (SVM) and 0.4902 (LR); additionally, excluding daily screen time reduced these values to 0.3714 and 0.3724. Multiclass Brier scores were 0.0506 for SVM and 0.0456 for LR. Screen time and ocular symptoms also contributed prominently to SHAP explanations. Conclusions: Classification performance depended strongly on symptom and screen-exposure variables. The reported metrics quantify agreement with dataset-defined labels, not clinical diagnostic accuracy or the ability to predict future DES risk. The label-generation criteria are undocumented, supporting clinical gold-standard evidence is unavailable, and potential overlap between predictors and label-generation criteria cannot be excluded. Without validation against independently established clinical outcomes and in external populations, these findings remain dataset-specific classification results and do not establish real-world clinical risk-prediction capability.</jats:p>

title: Prediction of Sea Surface Temperature in the South China Sea Using Machine Learning with Consideration of ENSO Variability

affiliation.name: School of Marine Science, Sun Yat-sen University

abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Accurate sea surface temperature (SST) prediction is important for understanding regional marine environments. In this study, monthly SST observations over the South China Sea together with the Niño3.4 anomaly index covering 1993–2024 were used to establish a unified forecasting framework. Six forecasting models were selected for comparison, including Seasonal AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average with eXogenous regressors (SARIMAX), Linear Regression, Support Vector Regression (SVR), Random Forest, XGBoost, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). All models were trained and tested using an identical chronological data split. Predictor variables included the calendar month, SST values lagged by 1, 3, and 6 months, and the concurrent Niño3.4 index. Model performance was assessed using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), R
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    , Pearson correlation coefficient, and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). The results show that LSTM achieved the highest overall prediction accuracy, whereas Linear Regression produced the largest errors. Feature importance analysis further demonstrates that lagged SST and seasonal information contribute substantially more to SST prediction than the contemporaneous Niño3.4 index. These findings indicate that local SST persistence provides stronger predictive information than large-scale El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) forcing for monthly SST prediction in the South China Sea.
                  </jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Proton beam radiotherapy is a frequently used modality in the treatment of meningiomas, but models to predict treatment response have yet to be developed. In this study, we explore whether Molecular Group may better predict outcomes after proton beam in intracranial meningiomas compared to traditional WHO grading</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Eligible patients included those with an intracranial meningioma with available methylation profiling that underwent surgical resection followed by proton beam radiotherapy. Molecular Group was determined for each meningioma based on previously described techniques, resulting in four groups: MG1(Immunogenic), MG2(NF2-wildtype), MG3(Hypermetabolic), MG4(Proliferative). Progression-free survival was calculated from time of completion of proton beam radiotherapy to in-field recurrence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>55 patients were included with median age at surgery of 57 years and 60% of which were female(n = 33). There were 11 in-field recurrences with median PFS after proton beam of 2.63 years(IQR:1.25-4.41). Median proton beam dose was 57 Gy(IQR:50.4-60.0Gy) and median follow-up was 2.8 yr(IQR:1.6-4.8). 24 meningiomas were MG2 (median PFS: 2.74yr, IQR:1.26-4.62), 11 were MG3 (median PFS: 2.80 yr, IQR:1.44-5.04), and 20 were MG4 (median PFS: 2.58 yr, IQR:1.58-3.64). 22 were WHO Grade 1 (median PFS: 2.74 yrs, IQR: 1.00-4.23), 31 were WHO Grade 2 (median PFS: 2.59 yr,IQR: 1.70-4.67) and 2 were WHO Grade 3 (median PFS: 1.9 yr, IQR: 1.06-2.74). After adjusting for age, sex, and extent of resection, MG4 was predictive of progression-free-survival (HR:7.16, 95%CI: 1.12-45.77, p = 0.04) but neither MG3 (p = 0.47), WHO Grade 2 (p = 0.16), or WHO Grade 3 status (p = 0.10) were predictive of PFS.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides data supporting the use of Molecular Group to predict outcomes after proton beam radiotherapy in surgically resected intracranial meningioma. MG4 status may identify patients with poor local control after conventional dose proton radiotherapy for which treatment escalation is warranted.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: RADT-44 Re-irradiation for recurrent glioma: Comparison of brachytherapy and external beam radiotherapy at a single institution

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Re-irradiation is increasingly utilized for recurrent glioma, yet no standard second-line regimen exists. Brachytherapy offers a single-intervention approach combining surgical resection and focal radiation delivery, but its outcomes relative to external beam re-irradiation (EBRT) are poorly characterized.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Forty patients receiving re-irradiation for recurrent glioma at a single institution (2000–2025) were retrospectively analyzed. Techniques included IMRT/VMAT (30-45 Gy in 10-25 fractions) (35%), Cs-131 tile-based brachytherapy (60 Gy to 5mm depth) (32.5%), SBRT/SRS (18-30 Gy in 1-5 fractions) (22.5%), and 3D-CRT (30 Gy in 10-15 fractions) (5%). Survival outcomes, including overall survival from diagnosis (OS), overall survival from re-irradiation (OS-ReRT), and post-re-irradiation progression-free survival (PFS-ReRT), were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression adjusting for initial tumor grade and Karnofsky Performance Score (KPS) at recurrence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>On univariable analysis, patients receiving brachytherapy had a median OS-ReRT of 6.2 months versus 13.4 months for other modalities (log-rank p = 0.296). On multivariable analysis adjusting for potential confounders, no significant difference in OS-ReRT was observed between brachytherapy and EBRT (HR 2.02, 95% CI 0.815–4.999, p = 0.129). KPS at recurrence was the sole significant independent factor impacting survival (OS-ReRT: HR 0.60 per 10-point increase, 95% CI 0.424–0.844, p = 0.003). No grade 4 or 5 toxicity was observed across any modality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Within this smaller retrospective cohort, after adjusting for functional status and tumor grade, Cs-131 brachytherapy achieved comparable OS-ReRT to EBRT. Given its ability to integrate radiation delivery with surgical resection in a single intervention, brachytherapy may represent a reasonable and comparable alternative to other re-irradiation modalities for select patients with recurrent glioma planned for surgical resection, particularly in this group of patients for whom reducing treatment burden is a meaningful clinical consideration.</jats:p>
