                  <jats:p>NRG-BN001 (NCT02179086) randomized newly diagnosed glioblastoma patients 2:1 to DI-PRT vs. SD-XRT XRT with temozolomide. From 10/2014 to 5/2022, 160 patients completed neurocognitive function (NCF) testing. Pretreatment clinical and demographic characteristics were balanced. Overall survival favored DI-PRT (HR = 0.81, 70% CI: 0.67-0.98, one-sided p = 0.11). Patients were to complete NCF testing (HVLT-R, TMT, COWA) at baseline, cycle 3 (within 7 days of cycle 4), and cycle 12 (day 22-28 of cycle 12, or 60 weeks from completion of chemoradiation). At baseline, 83-85% of eligible patients completed NCF testing. Compliance for evaluable patients at cycles 3 and 12 was 48-51% and 26-28%, respectively, across the NCF test battery. The most common reasons for missing data were institutional error (baseline: 4.4%) and withdrawn consent prior to timepoint (cycles 3 and 12: 15% and 23%). A prespecified secondary endpoint analysis was conducted to evaluate differences in NCF between DI-PRT and SD-XRT based on the Clinical Trial Battery Composite (CTB COMP), which is the mean of the standardized scores from the NCF test battery. There was a statistically and clinically significant between arm difference in z-score change from baseline on the CTB COMP at cycle 3 (DI-PRT vs SD-RT mean/SD, 0.01 +/- 1.34 vs -0.78 +/- 1.11, p = 0.046, Cohen’s d = 0.614). Across the tests comprising the CTB COMP, patients treated with DI-PRT compared to SD-RT maintained better NCF on tests of episodic verbal learning and memory at cycle 3 (HVLT-R TR mean/SD z-score change, -0.29 +/- 1.14 vs -1.06 +/- 1.51, p = 0.04; HVLT-R DR -0.13 +/- 1.54 vs -1.26 +/- 1.43, p = 0.013). Dose-intense proton radiotherapy compared to standard dose photon radiotherapy with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide resulted in greater NCF preservation at 3 months driven by better episodic verbal learning and memory function.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Radiation therapy (RT) provides excellent control of vestibular schwannomas; however, literature shows mixed results regarding toxicity between stereotactic radiosurgery/radiotherapy (SRS/T) and fractionated external beam radiation therapy (EBRT). We sought to investigate our institutional outcomes between the two modalities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients with vestibular schwannomas who received EBRT (1.8Gy/fraction [fx]) or SRS/T from 2010-2025 were included. Tumor progression was evaluated per RECIST criteria. Clinical outcomes were documented at baseline and last follow-up; toxicities were defined as new onset events post-RT. Cochlear dosimetry was evaluated for violation of institutional constraints (Dmax for SRS/T: &lt;12Gy, &lt;17.1Gy, &lt;25Gy for 1, 3, 5 fractions, respectively; Dmean for EBRT: &lt;45Gy). Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards analyses were performed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>61 patients were included (44% EBRT, 56% SRS/T) with median follow up of 76.3 months (range:1.1-187.7 months). Median EBRT dose was 50.4Gy (range:39.6-54). SRS/T regimens were 12-13Gy/1fx (n = 7, 21%), 18Gy/3fx (n = 6, 18%), and 25Gy/5fx (n = 21, 62%). Baseline tumors were larger in the EBRT group (mean 2.1cm [SD 0.7] vs 1.6cm [SD 0.8], p = 0.006). Tumor control was achieved in all patients. Tumor regression did not differ between groups (p = 0.56). Cochlear constraint violation was not associated with hearing loss (HR = 1.28, 95%CI:0.41-4.05, p = 0.67). Higher cochlear Dmean did not impact hearing loss (HR = 1.00, p = 0.86). No patients developed new tinnitus. Vertigo was uncommon (n = 5) and did not differ between groups (HR = 1.02, p = 0.99). Among 35 patients with baseline serviceable hearing, 13 experienced hearing loss post-RT (62% had received EBRT) with hearing preservation rates at 1-, 3-, and 5-years of 93%, 74%, and 67% post-EBRT and 100%, 93%, and 93% post-SRS/T, respectively, with no significant difference between groups (HR = 0.49, p = 0.23).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this contemporary cohort treated for vestibular schwannoma, cochlear constraint violations and RT modality were not predictive of hearing loss, supporting the need for refined, patient-specific toxicity risk stratification in neuro-oncology radiotherapy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The optimal radiation dose for pediatric craniopharyngioma is not established. While doses ≥54 Gy are commonly employed, evidence supporting a dose-response relationship is limited. We evaluated the association between radiation dose and progression-free survival (PFS) in a large multi-institutional pediatric craniopharyngioma cohort.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We queried the Pediatric Proton Photon Consortium Registry (PPCR) and identified 252 patients with craniopharyngioma treated with definitive radiation therapy (protons or photons). 242 (96%) received proton therapy, 5 (2.0%) received photon treatment, and 5 received mixed treatments. PFS was defined as time from radiation completion to radiographic or clinical progression or death, estimated by Kaplan-Meier and compared using the log-rank test. Subgroup analyses were performed by extent of initial resection. GTR patients were observed after resection and referred for radiation at disease progression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Median follow-up was 48 months. The most common doses were 52.2 Gy (49%) and 50.4 Gy (30%) in the &lt;54 Gy arm, and 54 Gy (92%) in the ≥54 Gy arm. The ≥54 Gy group had a higher initial STR rate (66% vs. 52%). Despite this imbalance, 5-year PFS was 85.3% (95% CI: 71.4%–92.8%) vs. 86.5% (95% CI: 79.9%–91.5%) for &lt;54 Gy and ≥54 Gy, respectively (log-rank p = 0.995), with overlapping survival curves throughout follow-up. No significant PFS difference was observed on subgroup analysis by STR (p = 0.397) or among GTR patients irradiated at progression (p = 0.578).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dose escalation to ≥ 54 Gy did not improve PFS compared to lower doses, even accounting for the higher initial STR rate in the escalated-dose group. These results do not support a dose-response relationship in pediatric craniopharyngioma and provide rationale for prospective evaluation of dose de-escalation, with potential to reduce neuroendocrine, neurocognitive, and cerebrovascular late effects in this population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Radiotherapy is frequently used for management of grade 2 and 3 isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutated gliomas, as it offers longer overall survival of 5-10 years. However, treatment-related toxicities such as radiation necrosis (RN) can cause significant functional impairment. Proton radiotherapy offers the advantage of more conformal dose distribution. This study aims to evaluate whether proton radiotherapy alters the risk of radiation necrosis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A single-center retrospective cohort study was performed to identify individuals with IDH-mutant gliomas receiving proton or photon radiotherapy at diagnosis between 2010 and 2020. Patient records were reviewed to identify cases of clinically significant RN. This was defined as the initiation of treatment for new neurological symptoms attributed primarily to RN per clinical documentation or surgical resection with pathology revealing predominantly necrosis, occurring within three years of radiotherapy. Multivariable regression analyses were performed to evaluate potential associations between clinical factors and the development of RN.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At diagnosis, 214 patients with IDH-mutant grade 2 (n = 88, 41.0%) and grade 3 (n = 126, 59.0%) gliomas received radiotherapy. Of these, 126 patients (58.9%) received proton radiotherapy with remainder receiving photon therapy. In this cohort, 123 patients (57.0%) had astrocytomas, and 91 (43.0%) had oligodendrogliomas. The overall rate of clinically significant RN was 8.1% (n = 17) occurring in eight patients who received photon radiotherapy and nine who received proton radiotherapy. Multivariable regression analyses revealed no statistically significant association between the development of RN and histologic grade (OR = 0.57, 95%CI=0.0071 to 3.70, p = 0.34), presence of 1p/19q codeletion (OR 2.14, 95%CI=0.61 to 7.39, p = 0.23), or radiotherapy modality (OR = 0.81, 95%CI 0.29 to 2.35, p = 0.70).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The prevalence of RN was low among this cohort of patients with IDH-mutant gliomas. Crucially, radiation modality was not associated with risk of RN. Further investigation is required to identify long-term clinical benefit of proton therapy in this patient population.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Surgical resection of glioblastoma is never radical, and residual tumor cells remain untreated for several weeks within a post-surgical microenvironment that may impact treatment outcome. This untreated interval represents a critical opportunity to challenge the current treatment paradigm to achieve better outcomes. Tumor Treating Fields (TTFields), a non-invasive therapy with proven efficacy in the adjuvant setting, may offer an opportunity to target tumor cells earlier in the disease course. The PORTRAIT study investigates whether TTFields therapy can be administered preoperatively, followed by postoperative TTFields prior to radiotherapy. PORTRAIT is a safety and feasibility study that provides a unique opportunity to examine treatment-induced changes in the newly diagnosed setting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PORTRAIT is a prospective phase I cohort study (NCT06136611) enrolling 14 patients. Patients receive TTFields therapy in addition to standard-of-care. Serial MRI, blood, tear fluid, and tumor tissue are collected at five predefined timepoints. The primary endpoint is safety and feasibility; secondary endpoints include imaging biomarkers and molecular/translational changes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As of February 2026, 9 patients have been recruited. TTFields delivery in the preoperative and postoperative windows was feasible without delaying surgery, with high device usage being observed. Preoperative treatment duration ranged from 7 to 30 days (median = 15 days), with median device usage of 86%. Postoperative treatment duration ranged from 11 to 26 days (median = 19 days), with median usage of 83%. The usage calculation included days when patients underwent MRI and CT scans and were unable to wear the device. Comprehensive longitudinal data acquisition, including advanced MRI, liquid biopsies, and tissue sampling, was successfully achieved across all study time-points.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Early findings support the feasibility of delivering TTFields therapy prior to surgery and radiotherapy, enabling initiation of oncological treatment from diagnosis. This approach provides unique access to treatment-exposed tumor biology in newly diagnosed glioblastoma. Ongoing analyses will determine the full safety profile and deliver unique scientific insights into TTFields treatment.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Gliomas are common adult brain tumours with diverse histologic and molecular subtypes, yet their management remains controversial. While radiotherapy (RT) remains standard treatment, adjuvant therapy with alkylating agents has shown promise. This GRADE-assessed, PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted using MEDLINE, EMBASE, CENTRAL, and SNO/ASCO proceedings (1986–2025). RCTs and observational studies reporting overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and grade ≥3 adverse events were included. Two independent researchers extracted data and pooled hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals for OS and PFS using the inverse-variance method. Subgroup analyses included tumour grade, chemotherapy type, and molecular markers (IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT). Heterogeneity was assessed using I² and Cochran’s Q test, while sensitivity, trial sequential, and GRADE certainty analyses were also performed. Of 4,663 records identified, 25 RCTs and 8 cohort studies were included, with 3,740 patients reporting 1-year PFS data. Overall survival significantly improved with chemoradiotherapy compared to RT alone (RR 1.108, 95% CI) despite marked heterogeneity (I²=71.3%) and low GRADE certainty. No significant PFS benefit was observed (RR 1.151, 95% CI; I²=73.2%), and chemotherapy significantly increased grade ≥3 hematologic toxicities. TMZ-based regimens demonstrated significant OS benefit, whereas PCV did not, with greater effect in grade 4 gliomas. Sensitivity analysis confirmed robustness of OS findings, while trial sequential analysis suggested a trend toward improved survival despite insufficient information size. RoB2 assessment showed overall low risk among RCTs, while cohort studies were of good quality on NOS assessment. Chemotherapy with alkylating agents alongside RT improves overall survival but not PFS and is associated with increased toxicity. Despite encouraging trends, larger future trials are needed.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas (AC) are WHO Grade 1 tumors that are derived from remnants of Rathke’s pouch. These tumors are typically managed with surgical resection with residual or recurrent tumors often treated with radiation therapy. The use of BRAF/MEK therapy for BRAF V600E mutated craniopharyngiomas is documented for papillary craniopharyngiomas. There is limited evidence for the use of medical therapy (such as targeted therapy) for recurrent AC. In this clinical scenario the use of cobimetinib (a MEK inhibitor) was given to a patient who had progression within one year of proton therapy and was able to achieve disease stability with eventual partial response. This clinical scenario, along with review of current literature and trials, shows the potential to use targeted therapy with MEK monotherapy for recurrent AC. Further large scale studies will be needed to determine overall effectiveness.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Sinonasal malignancies are rare, biologically heterogeneous tumours arising in a confined anatomical space bounded by the orbit, skull base and brain. This combination of rarity, histological heterogeneity and anatomical constraint influences treatment selection and limits the evidence available to guide it. Radiotherapy is central to management in both the postoperative and definitive settings, and intensity-modulated radiotherapy is now the photon standard, with proton and carbon-ion therapy available in a small number of centres. This review appraises the evidence underlying current practice. Pooled outcome data derived from mixed-histology institutional series are difficult to interpret; definitive radiotherapy cohorts are subject to confounding by treatment allocation; the clinical evidence supporting particle therapy is weaker than the dosimetric evidence; and the evidence base for elective nodal irradiation is inadequate. The review identifies where the evidence supports firm recommendations and where it does not. Because most patients with these tumours are treated in settings without particle therapy, routine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or daily volumetric image guidance, it also describes resource-adapted alternatives and their limitations.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Post-treatment imaging assessment after whole-brain radiotherapy (WBRT) for brain metastases remains challenging because intracranial progression occurs through heterogeneous patterns including local progression, new metastatic disease, leptomeningeal spread, hemorrhagic evolution and mixed treatment response. We evaluated longitudinal MRI patterns of intracranial control and CNS failure after WBRT and their association with treatment escalation and clinical outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective study included 279 patients with brain metastases who underwent WBRT followed by serial MRI surveillance between 2016 and 2020 yielding 1146 follow-up examinations. MRI examinations were categorized into longitudinal intracranial evolution patterns: controlled intracranial disease, mixed response, target-lesion progression, new-lesion dominant progression, leptomeningeal/dural progression and hemorrhagic-destabilized progression. MRI features assessed included enhancing lesion burden, hemorrhagic evolution, edema progression, leptomeningeal enhancement and temporal imaging behavior. Reference outcome was established using multidisciplinary consensus, treatment escalation, neurologic deterioration and longitudinal imaging follow-up.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Controlled intracranial disease represented the dominant early post-treatment MRI pattern (46%), whereas mixed response (14%), target-lesion progression (16%), and new-lesion dominant progression (15%) emerged as major longitudinal CNS failure trajectories. Leptomeningeal/dural progression demonstrated the worst survival outcome and highest rate of neurologic decline. Mixed-response and hemorrhagic-destabilized patterns frequently preceded treatment escalation despite stable aggregate lesion burden. Longitudinal MRI evolution patterns showed stronger association with multidisciplinary treatment decisions than conventional size-based assessment alone. Persistent intracranial control was associated with significantly longer overall survival compared with diffuse or leptomeningeal CNS failure (p &lt; 0.001). Inter-reader agreement for evolution-pattern assignment was substantial (κ = 0.76).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Longitudinal MRI evolution patterns after WBRT capture clinically meaningful trajectories of intracranial control and CNS failure beyond conventional size-based assessment and may improve treatment stratification in patients with brain metastases.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Brain tumors make up 15–20% of all childhood tumors, and more than half of these occur in the posterior fossa. Surgery plays a vital role in the management of these tumors, but it is limited when eloquent areas of the brain are involved. As such, radiotherapy is required in the adjuvant setting or as a definitive treatment modality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This was a retrospective study conducted at KNH through data abstraction from patient records managed between 2018 and 2024. The variables included clinicopathologic features and treatment modalities administered. The inclusion criteria comprised brain tumor diagnosis, treated with either radiation, chemotherapy, or surgery. The census sampling technique was utilized. Descriptive statistics were analyzed using R, employing means and standard deviations. Ethical approval was granted by the KNH/UON Ethical Committee. Results are presented using tables and graphs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>45 files were reviewed, with a female predominance of 53.3%. The mean age was 9.8 years, and the average symptom duration was 5.1 months. The average tumor size was 4.4 cm in diameter. Medulloblastoma accounted for 48.9%, brainstem gliomas for 40%, and 11.1% were ependymomas. 77.8% brainstem gliomas received definitive radiotherapy at a dose of 54 Gy/30 fractions, while 22.2% received 39 Gy/13 fractions. All patients with medulloblastoma underwent craniotomy followed by radiation; 72.7% were stratified as high risk, receiving CSI at 36 Gy/20 fractions followed by a boost to 54 Gy to the tumor bed . Low-risk cases constituted 27.3%, with patients receiving CSI of 23.4 Gy/13 fractions with a tumor bed boost to 54 Gy. title: DISP-02 Echo Chambers, Specialty-Specific Silos, and the Reporting of Negative Neuro-Oncological Radiotherapy Outcomes: A 5-Year Comprehensive Review

affiliation.name: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley School of Medicine , Edinburg,
David Geffen School of Medicine at University of California , Los Angeles, Los Angeles,

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Radiotherapy is a cornerstone of neuro-oncology. However, treatment paradigms informed by peer-reviewed literature may be susceptible to underlying biases, such as specialty-specific silos. While prior studies have evaluated broad publication trends, the specific impact of author or journal specialty type on the reporting of positive or negative patient outcomes remains underexplored. Thus, a comprehensive review of 510 papers published between 2021 and 2025 regarding neuro-oncology and radiation therapy was conducted. Data were extracted to isolate key variables of interest: Journal Specialty (RO, Neuro, or Other), Journal Impact Factor (IF), First Author Specialty (RO vs Non-RO), Article Category, Radiotherapy Recommendation/Patient Outcome Presented (Positive vs Negative), Financial Backing, and Conflicts of Interest (COI). Statistical analyses (Pearson’s Chi-square test, Fisher’s Exact test, and Kruskal-Wallis test) and multivariate logistic regression were performed using Python. Of the 510 papers (RO = 126, 25%, Neuro=134, 49%, and Other=250, 26%), papers published in RO journals reported a 100% positive radiotherapy portrayal, significantly higher than the non-RO journals (p &lt; 0.05). Non-RO authors rarely published in RO journals, whereas RO authors published across all journal types (p &lt; 0.0001). Lead RO authorship was significantly associated with positive portrayals (98.7% positive for RO vs 94.6% for Non-RO; p &lt; 0.05). While financial backing independently correlated with positive outcome reporting (OR 2.93, 95% CI 1.05-8.12, p = 0.047), the author’s specialty remains a significant driver regardless of funding status (OR 3.48, 95% CI 1.12-10.8, p = 0.039). No negative radiotherapy cases or outcomes were published in Radiation Oncology journals (n = 0); all negative findings correlated to radiotherapy were found in neurology or general medical literature (n = 16). RO journals and authors are more likely to publish exclusively positive radiotherapy portrayals, creating a specialty-driven echo chamber. Multivariate analysis confirms this bias is a characteristic of specialty-siloed research rather than a byproduct of financial funding. The systematic relegation of negative outcomes to non-specialty literature suggests a potential barrier to the dissemination of critical data within the specialty.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Radiotherapy is a cornerstone of glioblastoma (GBM) treatment, yet dose selection relies on population-level standards rather than tumor-intrinsic radiosensitivity. The radiosensitivity index (RSI) characterizes tumor-specific radiation sensitivity, the derived genomic-adjusted radiation dose (GARD) quantifies the biological effect of a delivered dose, and the biologically optimized prescription dose (RxRSI) estimates the patient-specific dose required to achieve a target biological effect. Here, we evaluated whether GARD predicts radiotherapy response and assessed RxRSI as a framework for dose personalization in GBM.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We evaluated 158 GBM tumor samples treated with radiotherapy (45–70 Gy) from TCGA, with RSI derived from RNA-sequencing. Associations between GARD and overall survival (OS) were assessed using Cox proportional hazards and Kaplan-Meier analyses. Subgroup analyses were stratified by MGMT promoter methylation status and age to assess whether radiosensitivity heterogeneity tracked with established prognostic biomarkers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GBM patients demonstrated substantial variability in the expected biological effect of radiotherapy independent of physical dose administered (GARD range: 3 – 42). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated improved OS in GARD-high versus GARD-low patients (1-year OS: 85% versus 65%, p = 0.03). In multivariable Cox analysis, continuous GARD was independently associated with OS (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.89–0.98; p = 0.01). GARD heterogeneity was observed across MGMT methylation and age subgroups. RxRSI modeling suggested 53.8% of patients would benefit from dose escalation and 9.5% from de-escalation relative to standard dosing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GBM patients demonstrated substantial variability in the expected biological effect of radiotherapy independent of physical dose delivered. GARD heterogeneity suggests that tumor radiosensitivity may provide prognostic information beyond currently used clinical and molecular markers. RxRSI modeling suggests individualized dose strategies may optimize biological effect, supporting prospective investigation of genomically informed radiotherapy personalization in GBM.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Neoadjuvant radiotherapy (NART) in high-grade gliomas (HGG) holds potential to improve outcomes by capitalizing on pre-surgical tumor oxygenation for greater radiosensitivity, enabling precise target delineation before operative distortion of anatomy, and allowing treatment to begin during protracted surgical waiting periods. Pre-surgical radiation may additionally debulk tumor, facilitating resection and yielding more favorable pathological findings. To our knowledge, this represents the first clinical study of NART in HGG — a single-institute phase 1 trial.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aim</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate the safety and feasibility of NART in newly diagnosed HGG.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methodology</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ten patients were enrolled for this pilot MD thesis study. Patient selection was based on Multiparametric CEMRI Brain review by a multidisciplinary tumor board comprising a Radiation Oncologist, Neuro-radiologist, and Neurosurgeon. NART was delivered to the primary lesion at 45 Gy in 15 fractions over 3 weeks, with concurrent Temozolomide (TMZ) at 75mg/m2. Following a 4-6 week interval, patients underwent Maximum Safe Resection. Adjuvant Temozolomide at 150-200 mg/m2 for 6-12 months was initiated 4 weeks post-surgery. The primary endpoint is Safety and Feasibility of NART in HGG. Secondary endpoints include surgical ease, Quality of Life (QoL), overall treatment time, radiation dosimetry, and progression-free and overall survival. Patients are followed up clinically, radiologically, and for QoL using EORTC QLQ-C30 and BN-20. Neurosurgeons are interviewed post-operatively via a self-designed questionnaire.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This is an ongoing study#. All 10 patients completed NART without significant complications. Two patients developed RTOG grade 2 CNS toxicity requiring outpatient Dexamethasone cover post-radiation. No patient deteriorated during treatment. One patient died before surgery due to ARDS secondary to aspiration. Nine patients have undergone surgery and commenced adjuvant TMZ. Interim data suggest that NART is well tolerated. Though it remains early to draw firm conclusions, the initial outcomes are encouraging. # By June 2026, all 10 patients are expected to have undergone Definitive Surgery.</jats:p>

title: TMOD-01 Elucidating acute response of the blood-brain-tumor barrier in diffuse midline glioma following fractionated radiotherapy

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Diffuse midline glioma (DMG) remains a uniformly fatal rare pediatric brain tumor, in part attributed to the restrictive nature of the blood–brain–tumor barrier (BBTB), which limits therapeutic delivery. While radiation therapy remains a cornerstone of clinical management, whereby conventional radiotherapy is delivered in low fractionated doses daily, its effects on patient brain and tumor-associated vasculature over the course of treatment remains poorly understood. A major obstacle for studying the DMG tumor-vascular niche, both pre- and post-irradiation, is the ability to probe live, functional, human microvasculature. We previously established an in vitro microphysiological model of the DMG-BBTB, comprised of patient-derived DMG tumor cells, primary human brain microvascular endothelial cells, astrocytes, and vascular pericytes, embedded in a fibrin matrix within a microfluidic chip. Our DMG-BBTB model advances preclinical modeling of vascular-tumor interactions for DMG, offering a human-representative platform ideal for investigating the tumor microenvironment and developing novel therapeutics, as it enables both quantitative solute perfusion studies and in-depth investigation of key tumor-vascular interactions. Using our validated model of the DMG-BBTB, we examined the effects of low-dose photon irradiation on microvascular function over an acute time course in devices with and without tumor cells. We comparatively investigated both the transcriptomic and proteomic landscape across multiple timepoints within the first 24 hours following radiation within BBB vs DMG-BBTB devices, revealing unique changes in protein expression and transcript enrichment in irradiated DMG-BBTB. In summary, we utilized our DMG-BBTB model to examine the effects of clinically relevant radiation doses on human microvasculature, enabling investigation of vascular response over a period reflective of a standard fractionated dose, identifying a potential therapeutic window to explore for dosing combination therapies.</jats:p>

title: Platelet-rich fibrin in dental extraction sockets of patients with planned or previous head and neck radiotherapy: a systematic review
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients with head and neck cancer (HNC) planned for radiotherapy (RT) frequently require pre-treatment dental extractions. Osteoradionecrosis (ORN) is a serious late complication of RT. Maximising the extent of socket healing before RT commences is critical to the prevention of ORN. Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) concentrates autologous growth factors and may accelerate socket healing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To analyse the literature and identify whether PRF supports earlier healing or reduced incidence of ORN.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Study design, setting, sample</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This systematic review evaluates clinical evidence for PRF in dental extraction sockets in patients with planned or prior head and neck RT. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and the HaNDLE-on-QoL database were searched from database inception to December 2025.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Predictor/Exposure/Independent variable</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Studies of any design evaluating PRF in extraction sockets of patients with HNC receiving or planned for RT were eligible.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Main outcome variable(s)</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The primary outcome variables were time to healing and incidence of ORN.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Covariates</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Covariates were assessed based on reporting in individual studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Analysis</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Studies were assessed for methodological robustness, including the PRISMA 2020 framework. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB) 2.0 tool.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Two primary studies, both randomised controlled trials (RCTs), met the inclusion criteria for the qualitative synthesis; one systematic review with meta-analysis was retained separately as contextual evidence. Neither RCT demonstrated a statistically significant benefit over conventional socket management. The single systematic review identified only one eligible PRF study (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 11), precluding meta-analysis. No studies were conducted in the pre-RT setting.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Current evidence is insufficient to recommend the routine use of PRF for ORN prevention in this population. Critically, both RCTs were substantially underpowered and at high risk of type II error. Both studied only post-irradiated patients and administered antibiotics to every participant in both arms, which is likely to have suppressed the baseline ORN event rate. No pre-RT evidence exists, despite this representing the most clinically and biologically relevant scenario. Adequately powered, multicentre RCTs in the pre-RT setting are required.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Single-voxel proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy(1HMRS)is an analytical method used for the identification and quantification of metabolites. This study aimed to characterize adult-type diffuse gliomas using choline (Cho), N-acetyl-aspartate (NAA) and creatine (Cr)on 1HMRS, as well as to distinguish between adult-type diffuse glioma subtypes and other etiologies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We retrospectively reviewed medical records of pathlogically confirmed adult-type diffuse glioma patients treated in our institution between 2007 and 2026. Patients who underwent 1HMRS before treatment was included in this study. This study focused on tumors whose main component showed no or partial contrast enhancement by gadolinium. The tumors exhibiting ring or homogeneous enhancement were excluded. The Cho/Cr ratios were obtained and classified as follows: normal range (&lt;1.2), borderline (1.2-1.4), or tumor pattern (&gt;1.4).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seventy-four patients were included in this study: 32 with astrocytoma, 33 with oligodendroglioma, and 9 with molecular glioblastoma (mGB). The proportions of normal, borderline and tumor patterns were 34%/12%/17% in astrocytoma, 42%/9%/48% in oligodendroglioma, and 44%/11%/44% in mGBM. Cho/NAA ratios below 1.0 were observed in 28% of patients with astrocytoma and 22% with oligodendroglioma. Cho/Cr ratios were significantly lower in non-enhancing tumors than in partially enhancing tumors (p = 0.0014, Mann–Whitney U test), whereas no difference was observed in Cho/NAA ratios among these groups. Evaluating Cho, Cr, NAA by 1HMRS could not give additional information to differentiate diffuse glioma subtypes. Around 1/4 to 1/3 diffuse gliomas did not show tumor pattern.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The information of Cho, Cr, NAA obtained by 1HMRS might not be useful for differentiating glioma subtypes. Adult-type diffuse glioma should not be excluded from differential diagnosis candidate based on the absence of a typical tumor pattern on 1H-MRS.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: EXTH-11 A next-generation B7-H3-targeted antibody-drug conjugate synergizes with radiotherapy to enhance DNA damage, antitumor immunity, and therapeutic efficacy in diffuse midline glioma

affiliation.name: University of Michigan , Ann Arbor,

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Diffuse midline glioma (DMG) with histone H3 lysine 27-to-methionine (H3K27M) mutation is a universally fatal pediatric malignancy. Radiotherapy is standard-of-care but provides limited and transient clinical benefit, underscoring the need for novel radiation (RT) combination therapeutic strategies. B7-H3/CD276 is uniformly and highly expressed in DMG with minimal expression in normal tissues, making it an attractive target for antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) therapy. We here investigated the antitumor activity of a next-generation B7-H3-targeted pyrrolobenzodiazepine (PBD) dimer ADC, called m276-SL-PBD, both as a monotherapy and in combination with radiotherapy in DMG. We found that m276-SL-PBD showed potent cytotoxic effects across human DMG neurospheres in a target-dependent pattern, with IC50 values consistently in the picomolar range. Compared with ifinatamab deruxtecan, a B7-H3-targeted ADC that delivers a topoisomerase I inhibitor payload, m276-SL-PBD demonstrated substantially greater in vitro potency and survival benefit in orthotopic DMG mouse models. Mechanistically, m276-SL-PBD induced DNA interstrand cross linking, DNA replication stress, S-phase cell cycle arrest, persistent γH2AX levels, and DMG cell apoptosis. Further, m276-SL-PBD activated multiple antitumor innate immune responses including type I interferon production and signaling, NK cell activating (NKG2D) ligand (MICA/B and ULBP3) upregulation, and immunogenic cell death characterized by calreticulin and HSP70 expression. m276-SL-PBD ADC exhibited potent radiosensitizing activity in DMG by augmenting radiation-induced DNA damage and apoptotic cell death. Moreover, the combination of m276-SL-PBD and radiotherapy synergistically enhanced antitumor immune responses in DMG cells. Consistent with these findings, concurrent treatment with m276-SL-PBD and radiotherapy was well tolerated and significantly prolonged survival in preclinical DMG mouse models compared with either monotherapy alone. Taken together, these findings establish m276-SL-PBD as a highly potent and immunomodulatory B7-H3-targeted therapeutic strategy for DMG and provide strong preclinical rationale for its clinical translation, particularly in combination with radiotherapy, to enhance tumor control and antitumor immunity in this devastating pediatric brain tumor.</jats:p>

title: RADT-37 Genomic radiosensitivity profiling predicts radiotherapy response and supports dose personalization in pediatric brain tumors

affiliation.name: Cleveland Clinic , Cleveland,
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center , New York,
Cleveland Clinic , Cleveland,
Cleveland Clinic , Cleveland,
Moffitt Cancer Center , Tampa,

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Radiotherapy remains central to treatment for pediatric CNS tumors, yet dose selection is still largely based on histology and clinical risk rather than tumor-intrinsic radiosensitivity. We previously demonstrated that the radiosensitivity index (RSI) can characterize tumor-specific radiation sensitivity and the derived genomic-adjusted radiation dose (GARD) can measure the biologic effect of a delivered radiation dose. The biologically optimized prescription dose (RxRSI) has been proposed to estimate the patient-specific dose required to achieve a target biologic effect. Here, we evaluated whether GARD predicts radiotherapy response and assessed RxRSI as a framework for radiotherapy personalization in pediatric brain tumors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We evaluated 207 pediatric CNS tumor samples from the Children’s Brain Tumor Network (CBTN) treated with radiotherapy. Associations between GARD and clinical outcomes were assessed using Cox proportional hazards, with overall survival (OS) and event-free survival (EFS) as primary endpoints. RxRSI was derived from GARD to compute patient-specific radiation dose to achieve a target GARD.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients demonstrated broad variability in the expected biological effect of radiotherapy regardless of physical dose or tumor type (Range: 0 – 74). Pooled cox analyses demonstrated GARD was associated with EFS (HR = 0.91 [0.85-0.97], p = 0.004) and OS (HR = 0.91 [0.85-0.99], p = 0.019). This association reflects a robust 9% benefit per unit increase in GARD, supporting its efficacy for patient-specific radiation benefit. We additionally noted that the RxRSI predicted for benefit with dose de-escalation in ependymoma (70%, n = 45), high-grade glioma (16%, n = 11), and medulloblastoma (22%, n = 16).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Pediatric CNS tumors demonstrate heterogeneity in radiosensitivity and biologic radiation effect despite receiving of similar radiation doses. RxRSI modeling suggests that the optimal therapeutic dose may be achieved from personalized dose-de-escalation/escalation strategies. These findings support further investigation of genomically informed radiotherapy personalization strategies in pediatric neuro-oncology.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

NCMP-16 Secondary Parkinsonism and Related Movement Disorders After Cranial Radiotherapy: A Systematic Review of 40 Patients Spanning Four Decades of Latency

affiliation.name: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine , Baltimore,
Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine , Baltimore,
Johns Hopkins Welch Medical Library , Baltimore,
Johns Hopkins Medicine Department of Neurosurgery , Baltimore,

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As survival among patients with intracranial malignancies improves, delayed neurological toxicities are increasingly encountered in clinical practice. Movement disorders following cranial radiotherapy represent a poorly characterized complication of growing relevance. Existing literature consists predominantly of isolated case reports with inconsistent phenotypic characterization, limiting understanding of clinical presentation, latency, neuroimaging patterns, and treatment response. We therefore systematically reviewed the literature to characterize these features, including levodopa responsiveness and proposed mechanisms of radiation-induced movement disorders.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A librarian-assisted PRISMA-based systematic review of PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase was performed through March 2026. Studies reporting original patient-level data on movement disorders following cranial irradiation were included. Data was extracted on demographics, tumor type, radiation modality and dose, latency, movement disorder phenotype, neuroimaging findings, treatment, and clinical outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty publications reporting 40 patients were included. Radiation modalities included whole brain radiotherapy, focal radiotherapy, stereotactic radiosurgery, and craniospinal irradiation. Age at irradiation ranged from 16 months to 72 years; Latency from radiation to symptom onset ranged from 2 weeks to 39 years (median = 7 months; IQR = 2 months to 4 years). For cases reporting levodopa use (n = 35), response was complete in 8 patients, partial in 14, and absent in 13. RT dosing ranged from 24 to 62 Gy (median = 50.4 Gy; IQR = 36.0 to 54.8 Gy). For cases reporting phenotype and imaging (n = 21), leukoencephalopathy was the most common imaging finding (n = 9), predominantly associated with freezing-of-gait and akinetic-rigid phenotypes, while basal ganglia abnormalities (n = 6) were more frequently associated with tremor-dominant presentations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As all reported cases received radiotherapy in an adjuvant or neoadjuvant context, direct causality cannot be definitively ascertained. Further research is warranted to clarify underlying mechanisms and identify at-risk populations. These findings should inform long-term movement disorder surveillance following cranial irradiation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Management of recurrent glioblastoma is challenging, with median survival ranging between 6 and 12 months. Treatment decisions can be complex, and standard options include repeat surgery, second-line chemotherapy, reirradiation (reRT), or combinations. Hypo fractionated reRT is increasingly used in selected patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We retrospectively reviewed patients treated at The Royal Marsden Hospital between March 2019 and December 2023. Patients with recurrent IDH-wildtype glioblastoma who received reRT to 35 Gy in 10 fractions (with or without concurrent Bevacizumab) were included. Data were collected from hospital electronic patient record and analysed using SPSS version 31.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Forty-three patients IDH-wild type-high grade glioma underwent reRT were analysed. Median age of the cohort was 53 years (IQR 46.5 - 60). The male-to-female ratio was 2:1. Forty-three patients had grade 4 disease, and 1 patient had grade 2 disease. MGMT methylation was present in 48% (n = 21). ECOG Performance status at relapse was 0-1 in 79.5%, 2 in 13.6%, and 3 in 6.8%. All patients completed planned reRT. Median GTV and PTV were 32cm³ and 83cm³ respectively. Thirteen patients underwent redo surgery prior to reRT. Median interval between radiotherapy courses was 12 months (range 9 -18). Sixteen patients received Bevacizumab concurrently. 73% of patients (n = 32) required concomitant dexamethasone, and 64% patients (n = 28) remained steroid-dependent. Median follow-up was 23 months. 1 patient had alive at the time of analysis. From diagnosis, median PFS and OS were 9 months (95% CI, 7.5 to 9.4) and 23 months (95% CI, 20.1 to 25.8). Median PFS and OS post-reRT were 4 months (95% CI, 2.9 to 5 months) and 8 months (95% CI, 6.6 to 9.3), respectively. The radiation necrosis rate was 4.5% (n = 2).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this retrospective series, hypo fractionated reRT was feasible in selected patients with recurrent IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, with acceptable toxicity & survival</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) implants minimize beam perturbation and imaging artifact relative to titanium, potentially enabling safer, more conformal postoperative SBRT to the spine. We evaluated feasibility, toxicity, and local control after postoperative SBRT delivered following neurosurgical procedures using CFRP instrumentation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods and Materials</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RR of patients who underwent decompression and/or stabilization with CFRP hardware followed by SBRT. We evaluated local recurrence and toxicity. Freedom from local failure (FFLF) from SBRT completion was estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods; patients without local recurrence were censored at lastfollow-up or death.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty-four patients (12 female, 12 male; median age 64, range 41-79) were treated at primarily thoracic targets. Nine patients had a prior course of radiotherapy at the site of interest. All courses used VMAT-SBRT: 3 fractions in 12/24 (50%) and 5 fractions in 12/24 (50%); median dose 27.5 Gy (range 21-35 Gy). Median time from surgery to RT start was 39.5 days (range 16-74). The cranio-caudal target length had a median of 70.5 mm (range 31-256 mm). Median follow-up from RT completion was 8.7 months (range 0.9-20.2). Primary histologies included renal cell (n = 8), melanoma (n = 3), breast (n = 3), non-small cell lung (n = 3), prostate (n = 2), sarcoma (n = 2), cervical (n = 1), colorectal (n = 1), and unknown primary (n = 1). Eighteen of 24 sites (75%) were free of in-field recurrence at last assessment. Estimated FFLF (Figure 1) was 77.4% (95% CI, 49.8-91.1) at 6-months and 67.8% (95% CI, 36.8-85.9) at 12-months. No grade ≥3 radiation-related acute or late toxicity at the treated levels were observed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Postoperative VMAT-SBRT following neurosurgical procedures employing carbon-fiber instrumentation was feasible and delivered safely with no grade ≥3 toxicity in this cohort. Early local control was favorable (12-month FFLF 67.8%). These findings support the practicality of combining CFRP hardware with postoperative SBRT for metastatic spine disease and motivate prospective evaluation with longer follow-up.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: RADT-31 Rapid Neurologic Improvement After Short-Course Whole-Brain Radiotherapy for Recurrent Bing-Neel Syndrome

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Central nervous system (CNS) involvement in Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma/Waldenström macroglobulinemia (LPL/WM) is known as Bing-Neel syndrome (BNS). It is a rare complication (1-1.5% of LPL/WM patients) that decreases overall survival compared to LPL/WM alone. Currently, BNS management typically includes systemic therapy and intrathecal chemotherapy. The role of radiotherapy remains less well-defined, particularly for recurrent leptomeningeal disease and in patients with extensive prior therapy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Case Presentation</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We report a patient with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance diagnosed in 2007 that progressed to LPL in 2012. The patient underwent multiple lines of systemic therapy over the subsequent decade and later developed extranodal soft-tissue disease. In 2022, the patient presented with neurologic symptoms and was diagnosed with leptomeningeal disease based on magnetic resonance imaging and cerebrospinal fluid cytology, consistent with BNS. The patient received CNS-directed therapy including intrathecal chemotherapy and systemic treatment with clinical improvement. Several years later, the patient developed recurrent neurologic decline with imaging and cerebrospinal fluid findings consistent with leptomeningeal relapse. Given symptomatic recurrent disease and the need for rapid cytoreduction, short-course whole-brain radiotherapy (9 Gy in 3 fractions) was delivered. The goal of radiotherapy was to achieve rapid neurologic stabilization while minimizing treatment burden and enabling continuation of intrathecal and systemic therapy. Following radiotherapy, the patient experienced improvement in neurologic symptoms and was able to resume intrathecal chemotherapy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This case highlights the potential role of short-course whole-brain radiotherapy as a rapid cytoreductive strategy for symptomatic leptomeningeal disease in LPL. In a patient who had been experiencing neurologic decline and had already been treated with extensive therapy, radiation provided meaningful neurologic improvement and enabled the continuation of systemic therapy and intrathecal chemotherapy. These findings demonstrate that radiation therapy can serve as a bridge for further therapy in selected patients with recurrent CNS involvement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Malignant melanotic nerve sheath tumors (MMNST) are rare but aggressive tumors making standard treatment paradigms challenging to define. Typically, they are treated with en bloc resection +/- adjuvant radiation. No reports exist explicitly describing prescription dose, technique, constraints, and outcomes of radiation. Cases of MMNST treated with adjuvant radiation at our single institution from 2010-2025 were retrospectively reviewed. Detailed clinical, radiographic, surgical, pathologic, and dosimetric information were reviewed. Case 1 had a 2.4 cm MMNST at the L4 nerve root initially treated with decompression of the thecal sac and subtotal resection (STR). Local progression (LP) was seen on MRI 3.5 months later. Subsequent treatment with stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) to L4-L5 with 24 Gy in 3 fractions was delivered. LP occurred again 1 year later, and the patient entered hospice care. Case 2 represents a patient who underwent initial L4-S1 bilateral laminectomies for non-mass neural foraminal stenosis found to have a new mass-like structure at S1-S2 5 months later. The mass was resected and treated with 63 Gy in 35 fractions. Over two years later, this patient had no evidence of progression. Case 3 was a patient found to have a mass at T12-L1 who underwent STR. Postoperative MRI revealed leptomeningeal enhancement. This patient was treated with craniospinal irradiation to a dose of 41.4 Gy in 23 fractions to the neuroaxis and a 59.4 Gy in 33 fraction boost to gross disease with mixed proton and photon techniques. This patient is without disease progression at the 6-month mark. Respective BED10s were 36 Gy, 62 Gy, and 58.4 Gy. Spinal cord/thecal sac maximum doses were 22.8 Gy, 59.5 Gy, and 59.3 Gy. This is the first report of detailed radiation technique, prescription, and dosimetry for MMNST treatment. We highlight the range of MMNST presentations that necessitate personalized radiation techniques for each situation with higher doses possibly improving control in some patients.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>craniopharyngiomas, histologically benign, locally aggressive tumors of the anterior skull base, are managed through endoscopic endonasal resection. Historically, their management via open craniotomy yielded equal tumor control whether it resulted in a gross total resection (GTR) or in a subtotal resection (STR) followed by radiotherapy (XRT). Whether this is the case for endoscopic resection remains unclear. In this study, a systematic review of the literature and meta-analysis were performed, comparing tumor control and complication outcomes (diabetes insipidus, hypopituitarism, and visual deterioration) between endoscopic GTR and STR plus XRT.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, Pubmed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane were searched for articles assessing outcomes of endoscopic resection of craniopharyngiomas in which, specifically, GTR was compared to STR plus XRT.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>a total of 2877 studies were identified. Following duplicate removal, abstract screening, and full text review, a total of 12 studies were included in this analysis (491 patients). Recurrence was less likely in patients who underwent GTR than in those who had a STR followed by XRT (OR 0.21 [0.07, 0.56], p &lt; 0.001). There was no difference with the odds of diabetes insipidus (OR 1.57 [0.27, 9.06], p = 0.62), hypopituitarism (OR 0.86 [0.19, 3.86], p = 0.84), or visual deterioration (OR 0.42 [0.12, 1.49], p = 0.18). Comparison between GTR and STR regardless of postoperative XRT showed how GTR had higher rates of diabetes insipidus (OR 2.45 [1.33, 4.51], p = 0.004); hypopituitarism was not different (OR 1.32 [0.99, 1.76], p = 0.07); visual deterioration was more likely following STR (OR 0.61 [0.42, 0.89], p = 0.012).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>in this largest-to-date review, endoscopic GTR shows superior tumor control than endoscopic STR followed by XRT, with a similar complication profile. When surgically feasible and endocrinologically safe, endoscopic GTR should be the treatment of choice for craniopharyngiomas.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: INNV-02 Papaya leaf extract use and chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia during concurrent temozolomide/radiotherapy for high-grade glioma: a retrospective cohort study

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia (CIT) during concurrent temozolomide/radiotherapy (TMZ/RT) for high-grade glioma (HGG) can necessitate dose reductions, treatment delays, or discontinuation of treatment. Thrombocytopenia was noted in 15-20% underscoring the increasing burden of CIT during TMZ/RT treatment. Papaya leaf extract (PLE) has been reported to support the platelet counts, but clinical data of its use in TMZ/RT treatment are limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a single-institution retrospective cohort study of adults with HGG receiving concomitant TMZ/RT. PLE was recommended after noting its benefit. The cohorts were defined by electronic health record (EHR)–documented oral PLE use. Patients treated for HGG between 2016-2025 were screened; only patients with platelet counts on weeks 4-6 after TMZ/RT treatment were included. Platelet counts were categorized by degree of thrombocytopenia: absent (&gt;150 K/µL), mild (100 to &lt; 150), moderate (50 to &lt; 100), or severe (&lt;50). Weekly assessments were pooled across weeks 4-6 and compared between cohorts using two-sided Fisher’s exact tests.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sixty-two patients were evaluable (39 PLE-compliant; 23 non-PLE). Across pooled week 4-6 assessments, severe thrombocytopenia occurred in 0 PLE vs 8 non-PLE assessments (Fisher p = 0.000283). Moderate thrombocytopenia was numerically less frequent in the PLE compliant group (2 vs 5 assessments; Fisher p = 0.0952). Mild thrombocytopenia did not differ in the control vs PLE compliant groups (10 vs 4 assessments; Fisher p = 1.00). TMZ was held for a decrease in the platelet counts &lt;100 K/µL during RT, and TMZ holds occurred in 2 of 33 (6.1%) PLE vs 5 of 20 (25.0%) non-PLE patients. There were no reported adverse events associated with PLE.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this real-world retrospective cohort of HGG patients receiving concurrent TMZ/RT, PLE use was associated with no severe thrombocytopenia across pooled weeks 4-6 assessments and fewer required TMZ holds. Moderate thrombocytopenia trended lower and mild thrombocytopenia was unchanged, suggesting specificity of PLE for higher-grade CIT.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: RADT-51 Phase 2b Imaging Study of 18F-RAD101 PET for Detection of Recurrent Brain Metastases Following Radiotherapy

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Distinguishing tumor progression (TP) from radiation necrosis (RN) after stereotactic radiosurgery or radiotherapy for brain metastases remains challenging because conventional imaging has limited specificity. 18F-RAD101 is a novel Positron Emission Tomography (PET) radioligand targeting short-chain fatty acid metabolism in brain metastases, with low uptake in normal brain tissue. This open-label, single-dose, single-arm, multicenter Phase 2b study (NCT06777433) evaluates 18F-RAD101 PET in participants with suspected recurrence of previously irradiated brain metastases. Thirty-two ­participants received a single intravenous dose of 18F-RAD101 (≤370 MBq) followed by whole-brain PET/CT and a separate high-resolution MRI. The primary endpoint was concordance between 18F-RAD101 PET/CT and ­contrast-enhanced MRI on blinded central review. TP versus RN was determined by longitudinal imaging and/or histopathology within 6 months after 18F-RAD101 PET/CT. Secondary endpoints included diagnostic accuracy for TP versus RN, safety, tolerability, optimal dose, and pharmacokinetics. At the July 6 2026 interim data cutoff, 31 participants were evaluable for concordance. Patient-level agreement between PET/CT and MRI for all-lesion detection was 93.5% (Gwet’s AC1, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.82–1.00). Agreement for previously treated lesions was 83.9% (26/31; Gwet’s AC1, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.56–0.99). Quantitative agreement in tumor burden was strong (Lin’s CCC, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.70–0.92). Among 16 participants evaluable for diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity for recurrent metastatic disease was 85.7% (12/14; 95% CI, 57.2–98.2). Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 5/32 participants (15.6%), predominantly Grade 1; one Grade 2 headache occurred, and only two headache events were considered treatment-related. No treatment-emergent serious adverse events or clinically significant cardiac, hepatic, laboratory, or ECG abnormalities were observed. Interim data demonstrate high concordance between 18F-RAD101 PET/CT and MRI, encouraging sensitivity for recurrent brain metastases, and favorable tolerability. Final analyses, including specificity and longitudinal diagnostic performance on follow-up, are expected by the end of 2026.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To determine whether the addition of chemotherapy is associated with longer survival in patients with pelvic recurrence of cervical cancer following radiotherapy who undergo Iodine-125 (¹²⁵I) brachytherapy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This single-centre retrospective comparative cohort study analysed survival outcomes and their determinants in patients with pelvic recurrence of cervical cancer treated with ¹²⁵I seed implantation at Yichang Second People’s Hospital between January 2019 and June 2024. Patients were stratified into a brachytherapy-alone group (Group A,
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 22) and a brachytherapy combined with chemotherapy group (Group B,
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 16). In total, 25 deaths were recorded (Group A: 15; Group B: 10). Overall survival was assessed using Kaplan–Meier analysis with log-rank testing, and factors independently associated with overall survival were identified using multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression. Post-hoc sensitivity analyses examined the influence of baseline extrapelvic metastases and age imbalance on the primary results.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Median overall survival was 36 months in Group B and 16 months in Group A (log-rank
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.021). In the primary multivariable Cox regression model, pelvic tumour size (HR = 1.721, 95% CI: 1.272–2.328,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001) and combination chemotherapy (HR = 0.293, 95% CI: 0.115–0.745,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.010) were independently associated with overall survival. Local tumour response was excluded from the primary model as a post-baseline variable that may partly reflect the chemotherapy effect. In a sensitivity analysis excluding 2 patients with baseline extrapelvic metastases (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 36), the association between combination chemotherapy and longer overall survival remained materially unchanged (HR = 0.300, 95% CI: 0.117–0.768,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.012). After additional adjustment for age, this association was attenuated (HR = 0.366, 95% CI: 0.132–1.018,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.054).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>¹²⁵I brachytherapy combined with chemotherapy was associated with longer overall survival in patients with pelvic recurrence of cervical cancer following radiotherapy. However, given the retrospective design, limited sample size, and potential for selection bias, this association should not be interpreted as evidence of treatment efficacy. The findings are most relevant to settings in which bevacizumab and immune checkpoint inhibitors are unavailable or unsuitable and warrant validation in prospective, multi-centre studies.</jats:p>

title: RADT-27 Can Proton Therapy Improve Disease Control While Limiting Neurotoxicity in Olfactory Neuroblastoma? A Meta-Analysis of Rare Skull Base and Intracranial Tumors

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Olfactory neuroblastoma (ONB) is a rare sinonasal malignancy frequently involving the skull base and intracranial compartment, where treatment aims to balance durable tumor control against the risk of neurotoxicity to adjacent critical structures. Proton therapy offers dosimetric advantages for organ-at-risk sparing. However, pooled clinical outcome data remains limited. We performed a meta-analysis evaluating disease control and toxicity outcomes following proton therapy for ONB.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PubMed and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception through May 15, 2026. Studies reporting clinical outcomes following proton therapy for ONB were included. Duplicate and overlapping cohorts were resolved manually. Outcomes included local control (LC), local recurrence (LR), overall recurrence (OR), recurrence patterns, grade ≥3 adverse events, and radiation necrosis/radiation-related brain injury. Random-effects models were used to generate pooled estimates, prediction intervals, and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 10 studies comprising 332 patients were included. High-confidence analyses demonstrated pooled LC of 81.7% (95% CI, 70.6%–89.2%; I²=54.4%), with pooled LR of 18.0% (95% CI, 10.6%–28.8%; I²=46.1%). Pooled OR was 23.1% (95% CI, 15.1%–33.7%; I²=0%), while distant recurrence and regional recurrence were estimated at 16.3% (95% CI, 9.5%–26.6%) and 10.9% (95% CI, 2.6%–35.6%), respectively. The pooled incidence of radiation necrosis or radiation-related brain injury was 3.0% (95% CI, 1.1%–7.8%), corresponding to 4 reported events across 132 evaluable patients. Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 16.3% (95% CI, 9.5%–26.6%), whereas pooled grade ≥3 optic neuropathy incidence was 1.6% (95% CI, 0.2%–10.3%). Leave-one-out analyses demonstrated overall directional stability without a single study driving pooled estimates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Proton therapy for ONB was associated with favorable local disease control and relatively low rates of severe radiation-related toxicity across heterogeneous retrospective cohorts, supporting its role as a promising skull base–sparing treatment strategy for rare adult CNS-adjacent sinonasal tumors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive primary brain tumor characterized by therapeutic resistance and poor survival outcomes. Existing preclinical models of GBM rarely recapitulate the clinical sequence of treatment observed in patients: surgical resection, adjuvant chemoradiotherapy, and tumor recurrence. Hence, the biological and metabolic evolution that occurs in tumors following standard-of-care treatment is missing from the pre-clinical setting. We developed a clinically relevant murine model of recurrent GBM incorporating surgical tumor resection, chemotherapy, and optimized fractionated radiotherapy to generate recurrent tumors for longitudinal characterization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Murine GBM cell lines (KR158B and GL261) were intracranially injected into mice and allowed to establish prior to surgical resection. Using a precision tissue aspiration system, tumors were resected and tumor tissue was collected for ex vivo culture. Following resection, mice received temozolomide with either two or three fractions of 5 Gy radiotherapy to determine conditions most conducive to recurrence. Tumor burden and recurrence kinetics were monitored by bioluminescence imaging (BLI). Primary and recurrent tumor cells were analyzed for proliferation, migration, metabolic function, and transcriptomic alterations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>BLI demonstrated successful near-total tumor removal after resection and chemoradiotherapy, followed by reproducible tumor recurrence. Mice receiving two fractions of 5 Gy demonstrated a more consistent pattern of tumor recurrence compared to those receiving three fractions. Recurrent KR158B and GL261 tumors showed significantly increased proliferative capacity relative to primary tumors, while migration assays demonstrated greater invasiveness in primary tumor cells. Metabolic characterization revealed recurrent tumors were less dependent on glucose and oxygen utilization, suggesting metabolic adaptation following treatment. RNA sequencing identified metabolic pathway genes as the predominant transcriptomic distinction between primary and recurrent tumors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This novel resection-chemoradiation model generates reproducible recurrent GBM that phenotypically and metabolically evolves following therapy, closely mirroring human disease progression. The adoption of reproducible surgical resection and chemoradiation provides a highly translational platform for studying recurrent GBM biology and evaluating therapeutics targeting treatment-resistant tumors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aim</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To perform a dosimetric comparison between hypo fractionated Stereotactic Radiotherapy (SRT) and Conventionally Fractionated Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy (VMAT) in target coverage, dose conformity, dose homogeneity, and dose bath to normal brain tissue.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dosimetric data from seven patients diagnosed with GBM who were prospectively treated with SRT were included in this study. For each patient, SRT plans delivering 42 Gy in 6 fractions and VMAT plans delivering 60 Gy in 30 fractions were generated. Dosimetric evaluation was performed for both treatment techniques. Planning Target Volume (PTV) parameters analyzed included V80, V95, V100, V105, V110, Homogeneity Index (HI), and Conformity Index (CI). Dose–volume parameters for normal brain tissue excluding the PTV (Brain–PTV) included V5Gy, V10Gy, V25Gy, V28.8Gy, and V30Gy. A paired statistical analysis was conducted to compare dosimetric parameters between the two planning approaches, with a p-value of &lt; 0.05 considered statistically significant.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>SRT plans demonstrated significantly higher values of PTV V95, V105, V110, and Homogeneity Index (HI) compared with conventionally fractionated VMAT plans (p = 0.0434, 0.0097, 0.0163, and 0.0009, respectively), indicating increased dose heterogeneity and greater hotspot formation within the target volume in SRT plans. No statistically significant differences were observed between the two techniques with respect to PTV V80, V100, and Conformity Index (CI), suggesting comparable target coverage and conformity. Evaluation of normal brain tissue excluding the PTV (Brain–PTV) showed statistically significant differences in dose–volume, including V5Gy, V10Gy, V25Gy, V28.8Gy, and V30Gy with p value &lt; 0.001 for all parameters, demonstrating a distinct dose distribution pattern between SRT and conventionally fractionated VMAT techniques.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>SRT demonstrated greater dose heterogeneity and increased high-dose regions within the target volume compared with VMAT plans. Significant differences in dose bath to normal brain were also observed between the two treatment techniques. SBRT provides effective dose intensification with better dosimetric characteristics in normal brain parenchyma that may be advantageous in selected clinical scenarios</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
